    CyberPatriot field guide

    Press / and type what you need: a task, a setting, a command or an error message. Results open at the exact step.

    First 15 minutes Forensics playbook Image planner Score went down Practice with images Converter and subnet tools

    How to use this guide

    jump:start-howto

    Fast path

    1. Press / or Ctrl+K and type what you need, for example guest account or ufw.
    2. Press Down to pick a result and Enter to jump to that exact subheading.
    3. Follow the numbered steps in the Fast path box at the top of the section.
    4. Click a highlighted placeholder such as <username>, type the real value, then press Copy on the command.
    5. Press Alt+Left to go back to where you were.

    #Search the guide

    Press / or Ctrl+K from anywhere on the page and start typing. Results are ranked by relevance and each one shows the matching subheading, so Enter lands on the exact spot inside a long section. Small typos and half-typed words still match.

    Key Does
    / or Ctrl+K Jump to the search box
    Up / Down Move through results
    Enter Open the highlighted result at its subheading
    Esc Close the results and clear the search
    Alt+Left Go back to where you were before the last jump

    The filter chips under the search box limit results to one area (All, Windows 11, Server, Linux, Cisco quiz, Packet Tracer, General). Use them when a word like "firewall" matches every image.

    #Home screen and quick links

    The top of the page is a home screen with one tile per area. Each tile shows how much of that area's checklists the team has ticked. The quick links go straight to the sections teams open most during a round.

    #Image planner

    Open the Image planner, pick the operating system and round level, and tick the README's critical services, required software and scenario details. It lists every Do, Don't and Check for that exact image in working order, with links to the steps. Higher round levels add deeper checks.

    #Line-by-line lookup

    Paste lines from a scoring report, answer key or README into the lookup tool and each line links to the step that explains it. Use it to review a practice image against its answer key.

    #Round clock

    The round clock on the home screen counts down the 4-hour competition period. The same time shows in the clock button in the top bar.

    1. Click Start clock now when the first image powers on, or click Set start time and enter the time it powered on.
    2. Follow the phase line under the clock. It walks through the 6 phases of the round plan and plays a sound when the next phase starts.
    3. Listen for the alerts at 60, 30, 10 and 5 minutes left.
    4. Click Stop clock to clear it.

    In team live mode the clock is shared, so starting, setting or stopping it changes it for the whole team.

    #Fast path boxes, tabs and "why" blocks

    Block How to use it
    Fast path box Numbered exact steps at the top of a task section. Do them in order; the details and variations are below the box.
    Tabs Alternative ways to do the same job: GUI, PowerShell or cmd on Windows, Mint GUI or Terminal on Linux. Pick one tab. The first tab is the one most people should use.
    Collapsible "why" block Background and edge cases. Closed by default, so skip it mid-round and read it later.

    #Fill in placeholders once

    Placeholders such as <username> and <service-name> are highlighted inside commands. Click one, type the value once, and every command on the page that uses the same placeholder fills in. The Copy button then copies the filled-in command.

    The Values button in the top bar lists everything you have filled in and clears it. Clear values when you move to another image, because a Windows username left filled in will also appear in the Linux commands.

    If you type a command by hand, replace the whole placeholder, angle brackets included.

    #Copy buttons and checklists

    Every code block has a Copy button. Paste with a right-click or Ctrl+V in PowerShell, Ctrl+Shift+V in a Linux terminal, and right-click or Ctrl+V in the Packet Tracer CLI.

    Click a checklist item to tick it. Progress shows on each section header, in the sidebar for each area, and on the home screen tiles. The Reset checklists button in the sidebar clears the ticks in your browser after a confirmation. In team live mode the ticks are shared and the button becomes Reset team, which clears everyone's ticks, so agree as a team before anyone presses it.

    A tick says a step is done. It does not record what you changed or which score it moved, so keep a change log as well (how).

    #Sounds and theme

    The page plays quiet sounds when you tick an item, copy a command, finish a checklist and receive a team message. Turn them off or on with the speaker button in the top bar or the M key.

    The theme button in the top bar switches between light and dark.

    #Jump codes for Ctrl+F

    Every section header shows a jump code. If search ever stops working, press Ctrl+F and type jump, a colon and the section id with no spaces (for example the code for Windows users ends in w11-users). It matches once on the page, in that section's header. The Jump code index at the end lists every code.

    #Team live mode

    One laptop can host this guide on your local network so the whole team shares checklist ticks, the round clock, a team chat and notes on each section. The Team button in the top bar opens the chat. Setup and the rules question are in Team live mode.

    #Reading the callouts

    Box color and title Means
    Danger Can cost points, break a required service, lock you out or break scoring. Read it before you act.
    Warning A common mistake.
    Tip A faster way to do the job.
    Verify The command that proves the fix worked.
    Note Background or a side fact.

    #Opening this file during a round

    Keep the file on the physical computer (or a USB drive) and open it by double-clicking. It runs fully offline with no installs and nothing loaded from the web. Open it in a browser on the physical computer, outside the competition virtual machine, so it never touches the image you are scored on.

    Team live mode (shared checklists and chat)

    jump:start-live

    Live mode runs a small server on one laptop (the host). Teammates open the guide from that laptop over the local network and share ticks, the round clock, chat and notes within a second or two. Nothing goes to the internet.

    Fast path

    1. On the host laptop, open the live folder and double-click Start live (Python).bat. If it says Python 3.8 or newer was not found, double-click Start live (PowerShell).bat instead and click Yes on the administrator prompt.
    2. Python only: if Windows shows a firewall prompt, tick Private networks and click Allow access.
    3. Read the address (like http://192.168.1.23:8080) and the 4-digit room PIN from the server window. Leave the window open and do not click inside it.
    4. On each teammate's computer, join the same network and type that address, starting with http:// and including :8080, into a browser on the physical computer, outside the competition VM.
    5. In the Join dialog, enter a display name and the room PIN.
    6. If a teammate cannot connect, work through Fix network problems.

    Check the rules first

    Ask your coach before you use live mode in a scored round. The reasons are in Rules and safety.

    #What live mode gives the team

    Feature What you see
    Shared checklists A tick appears on every teammate's screen within a second or two, with the initials of whoever ticked it.
    Team panel The Team button in the top bar (it shows how many are online) opens a panel with Chat, Activity and Online tabs.
    Team chat The Chat tab has channels for General, Windows 11, Server, Linux, Cisco and Change log.
    Activity feed The Activity tab lists recent ticks and messages from the whole team.
    Who is online The Online tab lists each teammate's name and the section they are reading.
    Section notes Each section header gets a Notes button that opens a thread for that section.
    Shared round clock The round clock on the home screen is the same for everyone. Starting, setting or stopping it changes it for the team.
    Reset team The Reset checklists button becomes Reset team. After a confirmation it clears everyone's ticks.
    Saved state Everything is saved on the host laptop in cp-live-state.json and reloaded when the server restarts.

    Use the Change log channel as the team's change log: time, image, what you changed, score before and after.

    #What is in the live folder

    File What it is
    CyberPatriot-Field-Guide.html The guide itself. It also works opened directly, offline, without live features.
    cp-live-server.py The live server for computers with Python 3.8 or newer.
    cp-live-server.ps1 The same server written in PowerShell, for Windows without Python.
    Start live (Python).bat Double-click to start the Python server.
    Start live (PowerShell).bat Double-click to start the PowerShell server (asks for administrator approval).
    README-live.txt Setup notes in plain text.

    Keep the files together in one folder. The servers look for CyberPatriot-Field-Guide.html next to them.

    #Start the server with Python (option A)

    The Python launcher needs Python 3.8 or newer. To check, open cmd and run either command:

    py --version

    python --version

    You should see a version line:

    Python 3.12.4

    Any version from 3.8 up works. If you see "Python was not found", the Microsoft Store opens, or the version is older than 3.8, use option B.

    Double-click Start live (Python).bat. To start it from cmd instead, open the folder in File Explorer, type cmd in the address bar, press Enter, and run:

    py cp-live-server.py

    Open a terminal in the live folder and run:

    python3 cp-live-server.py

    The server uses port 8080 and makes up a random 4-digit room PIN each time it starts. To choose the port and the PIN yourself, add the optional flags (on Mac or Linux start the line with python3 instead of py):

    py cp-live-server.py --port 8090 --pin 2468
    Python flag Sets
    --port TCP port (default 8080)
    --pin Room PIN (default: random 4 digits)
    --file Guide HTML file (default: CyberPatriot-Field-Guide.html next to the script)
    --state State file (default: cp-live-state.json next to the script)
    --host Address to listen on (default 0.0.0.0, all addresses; 127.0.0.1 means only this laptop)

    The same flags work after the launcher name when you run Start live (Python).bat from cmd.

    The first time the Python server runs, Windows shows a firewall prompt. Tick Private networks and click Allow access (details).

    #Start the server without Python (option B)

    1. Double-click Start live (PowerShell).bat.
    2. Click Yes on the User Account Control prompt. The server starts in a new window.

    Without administrator rights the PowerShell server only serves the host laptop itself (http://localhost:8080), and teammates cannot connect. The window says so when it is not running as administrator. While elevated, it adds an inbound firewall rule named "CP Live Guide" (TCP, that port) for Private and Domain networks. The rule does not cover Public networks, so a Wi-Fi connection set to Public will block teammates (fix).

    PowerShell parameter Sets
    -Port TCP port (default 8080)
    -Pin Room PIN (default: random 4 digits)
    -File Guide HTML file
    -State State file (default cp-live-state.json)
    -NoFirewall Do not add the firewall rule
    -LocalOnly Serve only this laptop, for testing

    To pass parameters, open cmd and go to the live folder:

    cd /d "<path>"

    Then run the launcher with the parameters:

    "Start live (PowerShell).bat" -Port 8090 -Pin 2468

    If cmd is not running as administrator, the launcher asks for approval and restarts itself elevated with the same parameters.

    Check the rule exists (PowerShell):

    Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "CP Live Guide"

    Remove the rule when you are done. Run this in PowerShell as administrator:

    Remove-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "CP Live Guide"

    #Read the address and PIN

    The server window prints one or more addresses for teammates, like http://192.168.1.23:8080, the 4-digit room PIN, and where the shared state is saved. On the host laptop itself, use http://localhost:8080.

    If it prints more than one address, use the one from the Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter and try the others if it fails. Ignore addresses from virtual adapters (vEthernet, VirtualBox, VMware VMnet1 and VMnet8). To see which address belongs to which adapter, run this in cmd and look at "IPv4 Address" under the Wi-Fi or Ethernet heading:

    ipconfig

    Keep the server running

    Closing the server window stops live mode for everyone. Keep the host laptop plugged in and stop it from sleeping. Press Ctrl+C in the window to stop the server; the state is saved automatically.

    Stop the host laptop from sleeping while plugged in (Settings > System > Power & battery > Screen, sleep and hibernate timeouts > set the plugged-in sleep time to Never), or run this in cmd:

    powercfg /change standby-timeout-ac 0

    #Join as a teammate

    1. Connect your computer to the same network as the host laptop.
    2. Open a browser on your physical computer, outside the competition VM.
    3. Type the address from the server window exactly, for example http://192.168.1.23:8080: http (not https), with the :8080 part.
    4. In the Join dialog, enter a display name and the room PIN. Your initials are taken from the name and mark your ticks.

    Use the host laptop's network address. localhost and 127.0.0.1 always mean "this computer", so on a teammate's machine they point at the wrong computer.

    If live mode is down, double-click CyberPatriot-Field-Guide.html to open the guide offline. Everything works except the shared features.

    #Fix network problems

    Work through these in order. Most failures are the firewall prompt, a Public network profile, or a school network that blocks device-to-device traffic.

    #Allow Python through the Windows firewall

    On the first run, Windows shows "Windows Defender Firewall has blocked some features of this app" for Python. Tick Private networks and click Allow access.

    If someone clicked Cancel, Windows saves a block rule for Python. Fix it:

    1. Press Win+R, type firewall.cpl, press Enter.
    2. Click "Allow an app or feature through Windows Defender Firewall", then "Change settings".
    3. Find every Python entry and tick Private.
    4. Click OK and restart the server.

    #Change the network from Public to Private

    Windows treats a Public network as untrusted and blocks incoming connections on it. Do this on the host laptop.

    Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi (or Ethernet) > click the network you are on > Network profile type > Private network.

    List the connections and their profile:

    Get-NetConnectionProfile

    Set one to Private (PowerShell as administrator), using the InterfaceAlias from the list, usually Wi-Fi or Ethernet:

    Set-NetConnectionProfile -InterfaceAlias "<adapter-name>" -NetworkCategory Private

    The other option is to allow the server on Public networks in the firewall prompt or rule. That accepts connections from everyone on that network, so the PIN becomes the only barrier. Prefer Private on a network you trust.

    #School network blocks device-to-device traffic

    Many school and guest Wi-Fi networks use client isolation: every device reaches the internet, but devices cannot reach each other. Live mode cannot work through that.

    Put the team on its own network instead: a phone hotspot or a small travel router. The competition images still need internet to send scores, so the network you pick must have working internet. On a phone hotspot that traffic uses mobile data.

    #Test the connection from a teammate's computer

    Test the port from a teammate's Windows computer (PowerShell), with the host's address in place of <host-ip>. Replace 8080 if the server printed a different port:

    Test-NetConnection <host-ip> -Port 8080

    You should see:

    TcpTestSucceeded : True

    A quick ping also works when the host allows it:

    ping <host-ip>

    Windows blocks incoming ping by default, so a failed ping to a Windows host proves nothing. A failed Test-NetConnection means the firewall, network profile or client isolation is still blocking. If it succeeds, open the address in the browser.

    Also turn off any VPN on the host laptop.

    #The server stopped answering

    Someone probably clicked inside the server window and put it in Select mode, which pauses it. Click the window and press Esc. To stop it happening again, right-click the window's title bar > Properties and untick QuickEdit Mode.

    #Port is already in use

    The server is probably already running in another window. If it is not, start it on another port (for example --port 8090 or -Port 8090) and give teammates the new address.

    #The address changed

    If the host laptop slept or changed networks, its address may have changed. Restart the server and read the new address from the window.

    #Start over or clean up

    To clear everyone's ticks, use Reset team in the sidebar. To clear everything, including chat and notes, stop the server and delete cp-live-state.json from the live folder. If the state file is damaged, the server renames it to cp-live-state.json.bad and starts fresh.

    When you are done with live mode, remove the PowerShell server's firewall rule as shown in option B.

    #Rules and safety

    Live mode stays on your local network and does not use the internet. It only carries your own team's ticks, chat and notes, so it works as a team communication tool.

    The Rules Book also forbids outside assistance and online resources made specifically for CyberPatriot during a round (rules summary). Ask your coach whether live mode is allowed before you use it in a scored round.

    • Never expose the server to the internet (no port forwarding, no tunnels).
    • Never share the PIN with anyone outside the team.

    #If live mode will not work on your network

    Use a shared Google Sheet as the team checklist and a group chat for messages and the change log. The same rules question applies, so check with your coach first.

    Rules that affect how you work

    jump:start-rules

    A summary of the CyberPatriot 19 Rules Book. Before Round 1, open the real Rules Book (uscyberpatriot.org or your coach's dashboard) and confirm anything that matters; the Rules Book wins wherever this summary differs.

    Before you power on the first image

    1. Start only when the whole team is ready. The 4-hour clock starts when the first image powers on.
    2. Run each image on one computer only.
    3. Leave the CyberPatriot folder, the CCS Client and the scoring report shortcut alone.
    4. During the round: no outside help, no AI tools, no online resources made for CyberPatriot.
    5. Read the README before you change anything (first 15 minutes).

    #Time and images

    • Each round runs from Thursday to Sunday. Your team picks one continuous 4-hour period inside that window.
    • The clock starts when the first image is powered on. Opening an image early "just to check" starts your round.
    • Run only one copy of each image at a time. Opening the same image on a second computer, or a second copy on the same computer, triggers a multiple instance penalty.
    • Do not modify, delete or stop anything in the CyberPatriot folder, the scoring service (CCS Client) or the scoring report shortcut.
    • Do not snapshot, clone or copy images unless the round instructions say you may.

    #People and help

    • The roster has 2 to 6 students. At most 5 compete at one time, with one substitution allowed per round.
    • No outside assistance once the round starts. Coaches and mentors may handle logistics and timekeeping but may not give advice.
    • Posting questions on forums or talking with other teams during the round counts as outside assistance.

    #Resources, scripts and AI

    Item What the rules say
    Printed or handwritten notes and checklists Allowed.
    General online documentation (Microsoft Learn, man pages, CIS Benchmarks) Allowed during online rounds.
    Online resources made specifically for CyberPatriot (shared checklists, posted scripts) Prohibited during a round. Publicly posting CyberPatriot resources is also prohibited.
    Scripts your team wrote Allowed in online rounds at your own risk. Banned at the National Finals.
    AI tools during a round (chatbots, AI-generated scripts) Prohibited.
    Paid AI products in connection with the competition Prohibited at any time. Free AI tools are allowed for training outside rounds.
    How this guide and live mode fit the rules

    This guide is an offline file on your own computer, used like printed notes. Keep it that way: do not post it publicly or host it online.

    The scripts in this guide were not written by your team. Read the Rules Book's paragraphs on scripts and AI and decide as a team how you will use them in scored rounds.

    Team live mode stays on your local network and only carries your own team's messages. Ask your coach before using it in a scored round.

    #Scoring rules worth knowing

    • Not every vulnerability is scored. A fix that earns nothing may still be correct.
    • Changes that conflict with the README scenario cost points: deleting an authorized user, stopping a required service, removing required software. Undoing the change returns the points.
    • The score updates every few minutes and only while the image can reach the scoring server (scoring problems).

    Round plan and 4-hour timeline

    jump:start-round

    Round start in order

    1. Give each image one person who makes the changes, and give the Cisco quiz and Packet Tracer to one person.
    2. Power on the images one at a time, enter the Unique Identifier and check the scoring report says connected.
    3. Read each README fully and answer the Forensics Questions before fixing anything (playbook).
    4. Do the basics on every image: users, admins, passwords, password and lockout policy, firewall, updates, antivirus.
    5. Write every change in the change log with the time and the score before and after.

    #What is in each round

    Open and All Service high school division, per the official CP-19 challenges page ("Competition Challenges and Scoring Values") and the CP-19 competition timeline. That page says all images, challenges and values are subject to change, so confirm each round in the round instructions.

    Round Dates (ET) Images (points) Cisco NetAcad Challenge (points) Other Total
    Training Round 1 (unscored, basic, answer keys in the ReadMe) Sep 3 to Oct 5, 2026 Windows 10, Server 2019, Ubuntu 22 none unscored
    Practice Round (unscored, required connection test) Oct 7-20, 2026 Windows 11, Mint 21, Server 2022 Quiz modules 1-2; Packet Tracer "Modules Intro" unscored
    Round 1 Oct 22-25, 2026 Windows 11 (100), Mint 21 (100) Quiz modules 3-7 (10); Packet Tracer modules 1-7 (20) 230
    Training Round 2 (unscored, intermediate, answer keys) Oct 30, 2026 to Jan 19, 2027 Windows 10, Server 2019, Ubuntu 22, Mint 21 none unscored
    Round 2 Nov 12-15, 2026 Windows 11 (100), Server 2022 (100), Mint 21 (100) Quiz modules 8-11 and 21-22 (10); Packet Tracer modules 1-11 and 21-22 (20) 330
    State Round (same content in all three tiers) Dec 10-13, 2026 Server 2022 (100), Mint 21 (100), Ubuntu 24 (100) Quiz modules 12-17 (30); Packet Tracer modules 1-17 (70) 400
    Semifinals, Platinum Jan 21-23, 2027 Mint 21 (100), Server 2022 (100), Server 2019 (100) Quiz modules 18-20 and 23 (72); Packet Tracer modules 1-23 (168) Web-Based Challenge (80) 620
    Semifinals, Gold Jan 21-23, 2027 Mint 21, Server 2022, Server 2019 (100 each) Quiz (30); Packet Tracer (70) Web-Based Challenge (80) 480
    Semifinals, Silver Jan 21-23, 2027 Mint 21, Server 2022 (100 each) Quiz (30); Packet Tracer (70) none 300
    National Finals (in person, Maryland) Mar 12-16, 2027 Not published yet for CP-19 Cisco NetAcad Challenge Network Security Master Challenge (details)

    The module numbers are the CyberPatriot NetAcad Content Course's own numbering, found on the Coach Dashboard. Modules 1-17 line up with Cisco ITN v7 modules 1-17 (networking modules); the titles of modules 18-23 are not public, so open the Content Course and write them down.

    Debian 12 and FreeBSD rumors

    One secondary CP-19 guide says later rounds add Debian 12 and that Semifinals add FreeBSD. The official CP-19 challenges page lists neither in any round. Learn Debian basics anyway (Debian differences); Debian 11 was a Round 2 and Semifinals image in CP-16.

    #Tiers and advancement

    • Round 1 plus Round 2 scores place high school teams into Platinum (top 30%), Gold (middle 40%) and Silver (bottom 30%) for the State Round.
    • State starts every high school team from zero.
    • In CP-18 the top 25% of each tier, plus wildcards, advanced to Semifinals.
    • Only Platinum teams can qualify for the National Finals.
    • Each round is one consecutive 4-hour block inside the window: Thursday 9:00-22:00, Friday 9:00-23:59, Saturday 8:00-23:59, Sunday 10:00-20:00 Eastern. Semifinals run Thursday to Saturday only.

    #Where the points are in each round

    Round Images Cisco quiz + Packet Tracer Web-Based Challenge
    Round 1 200 of 230 30 none
    Round 2 300 of 330 30 none
    State 300 of 400 100 none
    Semifinals Platinum 300 of 620 240 80
    Semifinals Gold 300 of 480 100 80
    Semifinals Silver 200 of 300 100 none

    In Rounds 1 and 2 the images carry almost every point, so most hands belong on the images and the Cisco pieces get finished early. From State on, the Cisco portion is a quarter of the round or more, and at Platinum Semifinals Packet Tracer alone (168) is worth more than any one image. Put your strongest networking person on Packet Tracer for the whole round there, and one person on the Web-Based Challenge at Platinum and Gold.

    Packet Tracer files must carry the team number in the file name and inside the activity, or they score zero (CP-16 instructions). Round 1 used the desktop Packet Tracer app in CP-18 and Round 2 switched to the online version; read each round's instructions for which one to use.

    #4-hour timeline

    Time Do
    0:00-0:10 Open the images one at a time, enter the Unique Identifier, confirm the scoring report shows the image connected. Everyone reads their image's README fully.
    0:10-0:40 Forensics Questions first on every image, because fixes can destroy evidence. Write down the authorized users and administrators from the README.
    0:40-1:30 High-value basics on every image: users, admins, passwords, password and lockout policy, firewall, updates started, antivirus. These are scored on almost every image.
    1:30-3:00 Services, unwanted software, prohibited files, malware and persistence, security options, application hardening (SSH, FTP, browsers).
    3:00-3:40 Deep pass: registry, sysctl and PAM details. Take a second look at anything that did not score and re-read the README for missed requirements.
    3:40-4:00 Stop making risky changes. Confirm the score is stable, finish any Cisco piece that is left, and record the final score.

    Run the Cisco quiz and Packet Tracer alongside the images. Start them early so a slow website cannot eat the last hour.

    #Work as a team without stepping on each other

    • One person changes each image at a time. When two people change the same image, nobody knows which change scored or which one cost points.
    • Keep a shared change log (paper, a text file on the physical computer, or the Change log channel in live mode): time, image, what you changed, score before and after. When the score drops, the log tells you what to undo.
    • Say score changes out loud. A drop right after a change is the cheapest moment to undo it.
    • Ask before deleting anything the README might care about: users, services, software, files in home folders.
    • Swap images when stuck. If an image has not moved in 30 minutes, trade with someone for a fresh look.
    • Use the one team password everywhere and tell everyone when you set it (team password).

    First 15 minutes on any image

    jump:start-first15

    Before changing anything

    Read the whole README and answer (or at least read) every Forensics Question. Many answers live in files, logs, users or processes that your fixes would remove.

    Fastest high-value order

    Users and admins, passwords, password policy, lockout policy, firewall, automatic updates, antivirus, then services and software. These categories appear on nearly every image.

    PreviousRound plan and 4-hour timelineNextScoring report, penalties and connection problems
    GO

    Scoring report, penalties and connection problems

    jump:start-scoring

    Score dropped

    1. Open the scoring report and read the Penalties list.
    2. Find the change in your change log made just before the drop.
    3. Undo that change.
    4. Wait 2-3 minutes and refresh the report to see the points return.

    #Reading the scoring report

    The scoring report is a desktop shortcut that opens in a browser. It shows:

    • total points and the number of vulnerabilities found out of the total
    • each scored item in plain words
    • penalties
    • connection status and the time of the last update

    It updates on its own every few minutes. Refresh the page to see the latest.

    #Score went down

    1. Read the penalties list on the report. It names what was penalized, for example a removed user or a stopped service.
    2. Check the change log for the change made just before the drop and undo it.
    3. Refresh after 2-3 minutes. Undoing the change returns the points.

    Common causes:

    • removing an authorized user
    • taking a user out of Administrators (or sudo) when the README lists them as an admin
    • stopping or removing a required service (SSH, Apache, Samba, FTP, IIS, RDP)
    • uninstalling required software
    • deleting files in a folder the README says is needed
    • breaking a config file so the service crashes

    #Score is not updating

    1. Wait 2-3 minutes and refresh. Updates are not instant.
    2. Check the image has network access (commands below). If you disabled the network adapter, changed DNS or edited the hosts file, undo it.
    3. Check the firewall still allows outbound traffic (commands below). The score cannot upload if outbound is blocked.
    4. Do not restart, reinstall or stop the scoring service. If the report says the image is not connected for more than 10 minutes, tell the coach, who contacts the CyberPatriot Operations Center.

    #Test network access from the image

    ping 8.8.8.8

    Some networks block ping. Test a web connection too (PowerShell):

    Test-NetConnection www.google.com -Port 443

    TcpTestSucceeded : True means the image can reach the internet.

    ping -c 3 8.8.8.8

    Some networks block ping. Test a web connection too:

    wget -q --spider https://www.google.com && echo online

    #Check outbound traffic is allowed

    Show the outbound default for each profile (PowerShell):

    Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultOutboundAction

    Allow or NotConfigured is fine. If any shows Block, run this as administrator:

    Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -DefaultOutboundAction Allow

    sudo ufw status verbose

    The Default line should include allow (outgoing). If it says deny (outgoing) or reject (outgoing):

    sudo ufw default allow outgoing
    PreviousFirst 15 minutes on any imageNextForensics questions playbook (any OS)
    GO

    Forensics questions playbook (any OS)

    jump:start-forensics

    Answer forensics first

    Fixes delete evidence. Answer the Forensics Questions before removing users, files, software or services.

    Fast path

    1. Open the Forensics Question file on the desktop with Notepad (Linux: xed or nano), logged in as the normal desktop user and without sudo.
    2. Read exactly what format the question wants: full path or file name, upper or lower case, one answer or several.
    3. Find the answer with the commands below.
    4. Type it after ANSWER: on the same line and save the file.
    5. Wait a few minutes and refresh the scoring report.

    #How to write the answer

    • Do not change the file name or the question text.
    • Type the answer after ANSWER: on the same line, exactly as asked (case, spacing, full path or file name).
    • If the question wants several answers, put one on each ANSWER: line.
    • A wrong answer does not cost points, so you can change it and try again.
    • Answer every question before changing anything on the image. The training keys repeat this because a fix (deleting a user, a file or a backdoor) can destroy the evidence.

    #Question types seen in past answer keys

    Every type below appeared in a real CyberPatriot answer key or round answer list unless marked as practice-image only. Jump to the commands from the last column.

    The question asks for Example from a key Commands
    A source or destination IP in a capture file Attacker IP in attack.pcap (Windows 11 training) IPs in a pcap
    Credentials sent in clear text in a capture Two FTP passwords in ftp_capture.pcap (Mint 21 training) Credentials in a pcap
    A file carried inside a capture Hivestorm only Export objects
    Decrypt a one-time pad, XOR or other cipher One-time pad with a hex key (Windows 11 training) Ciphers
    Decode Base64, then follow the hint Base64 pointing to a deleted file in the Trash; Base64 passphrase for steghide (Ubuntu and Mint training) Decode, Trash, steghide
    Hash of a file (MD5, SHA256) MD5 of a notes file; SHA256 of a named file Hash a file
    Absolute path of the prohibited MP3 folder /home/benjamin/Music/ (Mint, Round 1) Path of a file or folder
    Path of a share, folder or executable Path of a named share; full path of GooseDesktop.exe Path of a file or folder
    Which port a backdoor listens on, or where its program lives The "bd" port (Server 2022 training); a python listener on 1337 Listening port
    UID of a user UID of one user (Ubuntu practice) User ID
    Members of a group, or users meeting a condition Members of Event Log Readers (Windows 10 training) Groups
    Computer name Full device name (Windows 10 training) Computer name
    A banner or config value FTP banner "220 Welcome to AFA" (Mint, Round 2) Banner
    Name of a deleted user Hivestorm only Deleted user
    Data inside an application database Hivestorm only (PostgreSQL users, MediaWiki ban) Databases
    A message hidden in a service description Practice-image only Service description
    A scheduled task or persistence item Practice-image only Scheduled jobs
    A registry key or value Practice-image only Registry
    A renamed or polyglot file, app cache Practice-image only File type

    #Decode hidden text

    #Tell which encoding it is

    Looks like Probably
    Letters A-Z a-z, digits, + and /, often ends with = Base64
    Only 0-9 and a-f, even length Hex
    Groups of 8 zeros and ones Binary
    Real-looking words with the wrong letters ROT13 or another Caesar shift

    The decoder tool in this guide handles these too and tries all 25 Caesar shifts.

    #Decode Base64

    [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('<base64-text>'))

    If the result has a gap after every letter, it was UTF-16 text. Swap UTF8 for Unicode and run it again.

    echo '<base64-text>' | base64 -d

    #Decode hex

    -join (('<hex-text>' -replace '[^0-9a-fA-F]','') -split '(..)' | Where-Object {$_} | ForEach-Object {[char][Convert]::ToInt32($_,16)})

    echo '<hex-text>' | xxd -r -p

    If xxd is missing, use Python:

    python3 -c "print(bytes.fromhex('<hex-text>').decode())"

    Both handle hex with or without spaces between the bytes.

    #Decode binary

    -join (('<binary-text>' -replace '[^01]','') -split '(.{8})' | Where-Object {$_} | ForEach-Object {[char][Convert]::ToInt32($_,2)})

    echo '<binary-text>' | perl -lpe '$_=pack("B*",join("",split))'

    Both handle 8-bit groups with or without spaces.

    #Decode ROT13 or another Caesar shift

    ROT13:

    -join ('<encoded-text>'.ToCharArray() | ForEach-Object { $c = [int]$_; if ($c -ge 65 -and $c -le 90) { [char](65 + ($c - 52) % 26) } elseif ($c -ge 97 -and $c -le 122) { [char](97 + ($c - 84) % 26) } else { $_ } })

    All 25 shifts, one per line, numbered by shift:

    1..25 | ForEach-Object { $n = $_; "$n " + -join ('<encoded-text>'.ToCharArray() | ForEach-Object { $c = [int]$_; if ($c -ge 65 -and $c -le 90) { [char](65 + ($c - 65 + $n) % 26) } elseif ($c -ge 97 -and $c -le 122) { [char](97 + ($c - 97 + $n) % 26) } else { $_ } }) }

    ROT13:

    echo '<encoded-text>' | tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'

    All 25 shifts, one per line, numbered by shift:

    python3 -c "import sys,string as s;t=sys.argv[1];[print(n,t.translate(str.maketrans(s.ascii_letters,s.ascii_lowercase[n:]+s.ascii_lowercase[:n]+s.ascii_uppercase[n:]+s.ascii_uppercase[:n]))) for n in range(1,26)]" '<encoded-text>'

    Read down the list and pick the line that is real words.

    #Hashes

    #Hash a file

    Change SHA256 to MD5 or SHA1 as the question asks:

    Get-FileHash '<file>' -Algorithm SHA256

    certutil -hashfile "<file>" MD5

    md5sum '<file>'

    sha1sum '<file>'

    sha256sum '<file>'

    Get-FileHash prints hashes in upper case; certutil and the Linux tools print lower case. Both are the same hash; type it in the case the question asks for.

    #Hash a piece of text

    [BitConverter]::ToString([Security.Cryptography.MD5]::Create().ComputeHash([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes('<plain-text>'))).Replace('-','').ToLower()

    For SHA-256, change MD5 to SHA256.

    The -n stops echo from adding a newline, which would change the hash:

    echo -n '<plain-text>' | md5sum

    #Find the file that has a given hash

    Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Recurse -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5 | Where-Object Hash -eq '<hash>' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Path

    sudo find /home -type f -exec md5sum {} + | grep -i '<hash>'

    Change MD5/md5sum to match the hash type (MD5 is 32 characters, SHA-1 is 40, SHA-256 is 64). Widen the search to C:\ or / if nothing turns up.

    #Find files and text

    #Find a file by name

    Get-ChildItem C:\ -Recurse -Force -Filter '*<file-name>*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName

    sudo find / -iname '*<file-name>*' 2>/dev/null

    #Find text inside files

    Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Recurse -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-String -Pattern '<search-text>' -SimpleMatch -List | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Path

    sudo grep -rIl '<search-text>' /home /etc /var/www 2>/dev/null

    #Find hidden files and alternate data streams

    Hidden files under the user folders:

    Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Recurse -Force -Hidden -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName

    Alternate data streams on one file, then the contents of a stream:

    Get-Item '<file>' -Stream *

    Get-Content '<file>' -Stream '<stream-name>'

    Every file under the user folders that has an extra stream:

    Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Recurse -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Get-Item -Stream * -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Stream -ne ':$DATA' | Select-Object FileName, Stream, Length

    Zone.Identifier streams are normal on downloaded files. Anything else is worth a look.

    Hidden files start with a dot. List them in a folder:

    ls -la '<path>'

    Find hidden files and folders in the usual places:

    sudo find /home /root /tmp /var/tmp -name '.*' 2>/dev/null

    #File details

    #Owner of a file

    (Get-Acl '<file>').Owner

    stat -c '%U' '<file>'

    #Created and modified time

    Get-Item '<file>' | Select-Object CreationTime, LastWriteTime, LastAccessTime

    stat '<file>'

    Modify is the last content change and Birth is the creation time (shown on ext4 with Mint 21).

    #Image metadata and hidden text in images

    Right-click the image > Properties > Details for camera, author, comments and dates.

    Pull readable text out of any file (prints every run of 6 or more printable characters):

    [regex]::Matches([Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(28591).GetString([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes((Resolve-Path '<file>').Path)), '[\x20-\x7E]{6,}') | ForEach-Object Value

    exiftool is often not installed on Mint. Install it (needs internet), then read every metadata field:

    sudo apt install libimage-exiftool-perl

    exiftool '<file>'

    Pull readable text out of any file:

    strings '<file>' | less

    If strings is missing (it comes with the binutils package), use grep:

    grep -a -o '[[:print:]]\{6,\}' '<file>'

    #Users and groups

    #Groups a user belongs to

    Look at "Local Group Memberships" (add /domain on a domain controller):

    net user <username>

    Members of one group:

    net localgroup <groupname>

    id <username>

    Members of one group:

    getent group <groupname>

    #User ID (SID or UID)

    Get-LocalUser <username> | Select-Object Name, SID

    id -u <username>

    #Recent logins

    The "Last logon" line of net user <username> shows one user's last login. For the full history, read Security events with ID 4624 (PowerShell as administrator):

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4624} -MaxEvents 50 | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{n='User';e={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{n='LogonType';e={$_.Properties[8].Value}}

    Logon type 2 is at the keyboard, 3 is over the network, 10 is Remote Desktop. In the GUI: Event Viewer > Windows Logs > Security, filter on 4624.

    last

    lastlog

    sudo grep -a 'session opened' /var/log/auth.log | tail -n 20

    #Processes, ports and scheduled jobs

    #Program listening on a port

    TCP:

    Get-Process -Id (Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort <port> -State Listen).OwningProcess

    UDP:

    Get-Process -Id (Get-NetUDPEndpoint -LocalPort <port>).OwningProcess

    The last column is the PID:

    netstat -ano | findstr :<port>

    tasklist /fi "PID eq <pid>"

    sudo ss -tulpn | grep ':<port> '

    #Path and command line of a running process

    Use the full process name including .exe (PowerShell as administrator to see other users' processes):

    Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='<process-name>'" | Select-Object ProcessId, ExecutablePath, CommandLine

    Find the PID, then the program file and its command line:

    pgrep -a <process-name>

    sudo readlink -f /proc/<pid>/exe

    sudo cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '

    #What a scheduled task or cron job runs

    schtasks /query /tn "<task-name>" /v /fo LIST

    Just the program and its arguments (PowerShell):

    (Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName '<task-name>').Actions | Select-Object Execute, Arguments

    sudo crontab -l -u <username>

    cat /etc/crontab

    ls -la /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.weekly /etc/cron.monthly

    systemctl list-timers --all

    #Installed software

    #Installed program or package version

    Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*, HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* | Where-Object DisplayName -like '*<app-name>*' | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion

    The GUI shows the same list: Settings > Apps > Installed apps.

    dpkg -l | grep -i <package>

    apt policy <package>

    #Network captures (pcap files)

    A .pcap or .pcapng on the desktop means a capture question. Wireshark reads it in the GUI; tshark is its command-line side. On Windows, Wireshark is often installed on the image (check the README before removing it, because some images list it as required). On Mint, Ubuntu or Debian, install the command-line tool if it is missing (answer No if it asks about non-root capture; reading a file does not need it):

    sudo apt install tshark

    On Windows, tshark.exe sits in the Wireshark folder. Run it from PowerShell with the full path:

    & 'C:\Program Files\Wireshark\tshark.exe' -r '<file>' -q -z 'conv,ip'

    #Find IP addresses in a pcap

    1. Open the file in Wireshark.
    2. Statistics > Conversations > IPv4 tab lists every pair of hosts with packet and byte counts.
    3. Statistics > Endpoints > IPv4 lists every address once.
    4. To see what one host did, type a display filter such as ip.addr == <ip-address> and press Enter.

    Every pair of hosts that talked:

    tshark -r '<file>' -q -z conv,ip

    Every address seen:

    tshark -r '<file>' -q -z endpoints,ip

    The attacker is usually the address that sends many connection attempts (a port scan shows one source hitting many ports) or the one that logs in to a service. Read the question for "source" or "destination".

    #Recover clear-text credentials from a pcap

    FTP, Telnet and plain HTTP send passwords unencrypted.

    1. Filter on ftp (or telnet, http) and press Enter.
    2. Right-click a packet of the login > Follow > TCP Stream.
    3. Read the USER and PASS lines. Change the stream number at the bottom right to see the next session.

    FTP usernames and passwords with the client address:

    tshark -r '<file>' -Y 'ftp.request.command == "USER" || ftp.request.command == "PASS"' -T fields -e ip.src -e ftp.request.command -e ftp.request.arg

    Print one whole TCP conversation as text (stream numbers start at 0):

    tshark -r '<file>' -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,0

    #Extract files from a pcap

    File > Export Objects > HTTP (or SMB, TFTP and others, depending on the version) > pick the file > Save. For an FTP transfer, Follow the TCP stream of the data connection, set "Show data as" to Raw, then Save as.

    Save every HTTP object into a folder:

    tshark -r '<file>' --export-objects "http,<path>"

    #Ciphers and one-time pads

    Unknown encodings first go through Tell which encoding it is. The general-purpose online tools CyberChef (its Magic operation guesses the encoding) and dCode's cipher identifier help when the format is unclear.

    #Decrypt a one-time pad or XOR message

    A one-time pad given as two hex strings (ciphertext and key) is a byte-by-byte XOR. A repeating XOR key works the same way with the key reused.

    Hex ciphertext and hex key:

    python3 -c "import sys;c=bytes.fromhex(sys.argv[1]);k=bytes.fromhex(sys.argv[2]);print(bytes(b^k[i%len(k)] for i,b in enumerate(c)).decode(errors='replace'))" '<hex-text>' '<hex-key>'

    Hex ciphertext and hex key (PowerShell). For a text key, replace the second line with $k = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes('<key-text>'):

    $c = ('<hex-text>' -replace '[^0-9a-fA-F]','') -split '(..)' | Where-Object {$_} | ForEach-Object {[Convert]::ToByte($_,16)}
$k = ('<hex-key>' -replace '[^0-9a-fA-F]','') -split '(..)' | Where-Object {$_} | ForEach-Object {[Convert]::ToByte($_,16)}
-join (0..($c.Count-1) | ForEach-Object { [char]($c[$_] -bxor $k[$_ % $k.Count]) })

    If you know part of the plaintext (a flag format or a word that must appear), XOR the ciphertext with that text: the output is the key.

    #Decrypt a letter one-time pad or Vigenere message

    When the ciphertext and key are both letters, each letter is shifted back by the key letter.

    python3 -c "import sys;c=[x for x in sys.argv[1].upper() if x.isalpha()];k=sys.argv[2].upper();print(''.join(chr((ord(x)-ord(k[i%len(k)]))%26+65) for i,x in enumerate(c)))" '<encoded-text>' '<key-text>'

    $t = ('<encoded-text>'.ToUpper() -replace '[^A-Z]',''); $k = ('<key-text>'.ToUpper() -replace '[^A-Z]',''); -join (0..($t.Length-1) | ForEach-Object { [char](((([int]$t[$_]) - ([int]$k[$_ % $k.Length])) + 26) % 26 + 65) })

    Both drop spaces and punctuation and print capitals; put the spaces back by reading it.

    #Other hash algorithms

    Windows PowerShell 5.1 (the built-in one) supports RIPEMD160, SHA384 and SHA512 too:

    Get-FileHash '<file>' -Algorithm RIPEMD160

    openssl dgst -ripemd160 '<file>'

    If OpenSSL answers "unsupported", load the legacy provider:

    openssl dgst -provider legacy -provider default -ripemd160 '<file>'

    #Steganography, QR codes and the Trash

    #Extract a message hidden with steghide

    steghide hides data in JPEG, BMP, WAV and AU files behind a passphrase. In past keys the passphrase was itself hidden as Base64 in another file. Install it on Linux (needs internet):

    sudo apt install steghide

    Check whether a file holds hidden data:

    steghide info '<file>'

    Extract it; steghide asks for the passphrase and writes the hidden file into the current folder:

    steghide extract -sf '<file>'

    There is no built-in steghide on Windows images. Try strings style extraction from Image metadata and hidden text and the file type check first.

    #Turn Base64 into a file or QR code

    Write the decoded bytes to a file and see what it is:

    base64 -d '<file>' > decoded.bin

    file decoded.bin

    Read a QR code image:

    sudo apt install zbar-tools

    zbarimg '<file>'

    [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("$PWD\decoded.bin", [Convert]::FromBase64String((Get-Content '<file>' -Raw)))

    Rename it to the right extension after the file type check. Windows has no built-in QR reader, so open the image in a general online QR decoder.

    #Restore a deleted file from the Trash or Recycle Bin

    Open Files > Trash > right-click > Restore. From a terminal, the files and their original paths are here:

    ls -la ~/.local/share/Trash/files ~/.local/share/Trash/info

    Every user's Trash:

    sudo ls -la /home/*/.local/share/Trash/files /root/.local/share/Trash/files

    Each .trashinfo file in info holds the original Path= and DeletionDate=.

    Open the Recycle Bin on the desktop, right-click the file > Restore. List what is in your own Recycle Bin (PowerShell):

    (New-Object -ComObject Shell.Application).NameSpace(10).Items() | Select-Object Name, Path

    Every user's Recycle Bin (PowerShell as administrator). $I files hold the original path; $R files hold the content:

    Get-ChildItem 'C:\$Recycle.Bin' -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime

    #Paths, ports and system facts

    #Full path of a file, folder or share

    Copy the format the question shows. One Mint key wanted /home/benjamin/Music/ with the trailing slash.

    In File Explorer, select the file and press Ctrl+Shift+C or right-click > Copy as path (older builds: Shift+right-click). For a running program: Task Manager > Details > right-click > Open file location.

    Folders that hold MP3 files:

    Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Recurse -Force -File -Include *.mp3 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty DirectoryName -Unique

    Shares and the folders behind them:

    Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path, Description

    Folders that hold MP3 files:

    sudo find / -iname '*.mp3' -not -path '/proc/*' -printf '%h\n' 2>/dev/null | sort -u

    Samba shares and their paths:

    testparm -s 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^\[|path'

    Absolute path of a file you can see:

    readlink -f '<file>'

    #List every listening program with its file

    In cmd as administrator. -b shows the program name under each line:

    netstat -abno

    Then find the program's file with Path and command line of a running process.

    sudo ss -tulpn

    sudo lsof -i -P -n | grep LISTEN

    #Computer name

    Settings > System > About shows Device name. On a domain the full name is the name plus the domain:

    Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain

    hostnamectl

    #Banner or config value

    The vsftpd banner:

    grep -i banner /etc/vsftpd.conf

    Any text across the config files:

    sudo grep -rin '<search-text>' /etc 2>/dev/null

    The logon banner text:

    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v LegalNoticeText

    The IIS FTP banner:

    Select-String -Path C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\config\applicationHost.config -Pattern 'bannerMessage'

    #Name of a deleted user

    Profiles left behind, with their SIDs. Compare them with Get-LocalUser:

    Get-CimInstance Win32_UserProfile | Select-Object LocalPath, SID

    Accounts deleted while auditing was on (event 4726, PowerShell as administrator):

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4726} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{n='Deleted';e={$_.Properties[0].Value}}

    userdel writes to the auth log:

    sudo zgrep -a 'delete user' /var/log/auth.log*

    A home folder owned by a bare number belonged to a deleted user:

    ls -l /home

    #Query an application database

    PostgreSQL roles, databases and the postgres user's command history:

    sudo -u postgres psql -c '\du'

    sudo -u postgres psql -c '\l'

    sudo cat /var/lib/postgresql/.psql_history

    MySQL or MariaDB accounts, databases and WordPress users:

    sudo mysql -e 'SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user;'

    sudo mysql -e 'SHOW DATABASES;'

    sudo mysql -e 'SELECT user_login, user_email FROM <database>.wp_users;'

    For a web app (WordPress, MediaWiki), the admin pages in the browser often answer faster.

    #Message in a service description

    sc qdescription <service-name>

    Search every service description for a word:

    Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object Description -like '*<search-text>*' | Select-Object Name, Description

    systemctl cat <service-name>

    grep -ri 'Description=' /etc/systemd/system

    #Find a registry key or value

    In regedit, press Ctrl+F to search; right-click a key > Copy Key Name gives the full path. From cmd:

    reg query "<registry-key>" /s

    Search a hive for text in key names, value names and data (slow):

    reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE /f "<search-text>" /s

    #Real file type and polyglot files

    Format-Hex -Path '<file>' | Select-Object -First 2

    file '<file>'

    xxd '<file>' | head -n 2
    First bytes (hex) Text Real type
    50 4B 03 04 PK ZIP (also docx, xlsx, jar)
    89 50 4E 47 .PNG PNG
    FF D8 FF JPEG
    47 49 46 38 GIF8 GIF
    25 50 44 46 %PDF PDF
    4D 5A MZ Windows program
    7F 45 4C 46 .ELF Linux program

    A file that opens as a picture but also contains PK further in is a polyglot with a ZIP appended. On Linux unzip '<file>' extracts it after a warning about extra bytes; on Windows open it with 7-Zip if the image has it.

    Vulnerability categories mapped to this guide

    jump:start-categories

    CyberPatriot answer keys and round answer sheets group every scored item into these 13 categories. The names and definitions below are the official ones printed on the CP-18 Round 1 answer sheet. Each image's key shows which category an item belongs to, and the category count sheets released after State tell you how many items each category held.

    #Official categories and where to look

    Category What it covers (official definition) Windows 11 and 10 Server 2019 and 2022 Linux (Mint, Ubuntu, Debian)
    Account Policies Password and lockout policy w11-passpol srv-gpo lin-passpol, lin-lockout
    Application Security Settings Settings for critical services and required applications, and application permissions w11-remote, w11-browsers, w11-apps srv-iis, srv-ftp, srv-rdp, srv-smb, srv-dns-dhcp lin-ssh, lin-required-services, lin-services-web, lin-services-db, lin-services-files, lin-services-mail, lin-firefox
    Application Updates Third-party app versions, including automatic update settings w11-updates srv-updates-defender lin-updates
    Defensive Countermeasures Firewall, antivirus and encryption w11-firewall, w11-defender w11-firewall, srv-updates-defender lin-firewall, lin-apparmor-audit
    Forensic Questions Questions in desktop files start-forensics, w11-forensics srv-forensics lin-forensics, lin-readme
    Local Policies Audit policy, user rights assignment and security options w11-secopts, w11-audit, w11-registry srv-gpo, srv-ad-hardening lin-kernel, lin-sudo, lin-login
    Operating System Updates OS patches and automatic update settings w11-updates srv-updates-defender lin-updates
    Policy Violation: Malware Backdoors, remote administration tools (RATs), keyloggers and password sniffers w11-malware w11-malware, srv-ad-attacks lin-malware, lin-rootkits
    Policy Violation: Prohibited Files Media files, password lists and other files the README forbids w11-files w11-files, srv-smb lin-files
    Policy Violation: Unwanted Software Games, servers, scareware, adware, potentially unwanted programs and hacking tools w11-software, w11-unwanted srv-roles, srv-roles-more lin-software
    Service Auditing Services that should be stopped and disabled, or kept running w11-services, w11-features srv-services, srv-roles lin-services
    Uncategorized OS Settings Remote access, file sharing, screen locking, group policy and OS permissions w11-uac-misc, w11-shares, w11-remote srv-smb, srv-rdp lin-files, lin-login
    User Auditing Authorized users, groups and user-specific settings w11-users srv-ad-users lin-users, lin-sudo

    Every item each category has held in past keys, with the scoring-report wording, is in the answer-key indexes: Windows, Server, Linux.

    A few real report lines per category, so you can tell which category an unscored item belongs to.

    Application Security Settings "RDP network level authentication enabled", "SSH root login has been disabled", "FTP users may log in with SSL", "SMB1 removed or disabled"
    Application Updates "Firefox has been updated", "Notepad++ has been updated", "OpenSSH has been updated"

    Image planner: what to do and avoid for this image

    jump:start-planner

    The README always describes a scenario, and the scenario changes what is right. A web server image must keep Apache running; a workstation image with the same Apache installed should lose it. The planner turns the scenario into a plan.

    Fast path

    1. Read the README once, fully.
    2. In the planner, pick the operating system and the round level (pick the level of the image you are practicing; higher levels add deeper checks).
    3. Tick every critical service, required program and scenario detail the README mentions.
    4. Work through the plan top to bottom. Items marked Don't are penalty traps for this scenario. Tick items as you finish them.
    5. Re-open the plan when you find something new in the README or on the image, and adjust the ticks.
    How the levels work

    Each rule has the first round level where it matters. Practice and Round 1 show the basics that are scored on almost every image. Round 2 adds more policy and service depth, State adds application settings and subtler policy, Semifinals adds hidden persistence, backdoors and obscure settings, and National Finals adds keeping services up under a live red team, monitoring and injects. Choosing a level shows that level and everything below it.

    Every rule in one place

    The full rule set is also listed as text, so search finds it: Windows 11 and 10, Windows Server, Linux and BSD, by README scenario and service.

    Practice with images and this guide

    jump:start-practice

    Fast path

    1. Pick one image for this session and set a timer (4 hours for a full mock, 2 hours for a short one).
    2. Read the README and copy the users, admins, required services and required software onto paper (README patterns).
    3. Answer the Forensics Questions before changing anything (playbook).
    4. Work down the area checklist (Windows, Server, Linux) and log every change with the score before and after.
    5. When the timer ends, open the answer key and paste its lines, or your scoring-report lines, into the line lookup in Tools.
    6. Read the guide section for every item you missed, then fix it on the image.
    7. Replay the same image type within a week, from a fresh copy.

    #Where practice images come from

    Source Images Answer key
    Training Round 1 (ended Oct 5, 2026) Windows 10, Server 2019, Ubuntu 22 Yes, in the ReadMe
    Practice Round (ended Oct 20, 2026) Windows 11, Mint 21, Server 2022 No key in past seasons
    Training Round 2 (Oct 30, 2026 to Jan 19, 2027) Windows 10, Server 2019, Ubuntu 22, Mint 21 Yes
    Earlier seasons' training images your coach kept Varies Usually
    Team-made practice images Varies Their own key; use as a supplement

    The coach downloads official images from the Coach Dashboard. Training Round 2 is the main source between now and Semifinals: intermediate difficulty, with keys, and it includes Server 2019 and Ubuntu 22, the closest stand-ins for the Server 2019, Server 2022 and Ubuntu 24 images in State and Semifinals.

    Keep a clean copy

    Keep the downloaded archive and extract a fresh copy for every attempt. If the training round instructions allow snapshots, take one in VMware before you start. Never snapshot or copy an image in a scored round unless the round instructions say you may (rules).

    #Run a practice session

    1. One person, one image, one timer. A second person may watch and take the log, but only one person changes the image.
    2. Start the clock when the image powers on, the same as a real round (round clock).
    3. Spend the first 10 minutes on the README and the forensics files, as in First 15 minutes.
    4. Follow the reading path for that image. Tick items in the area checklist as you go.
    5. Look at the scoring report after every few changes. Note which change moved the score and by how much.
    6. Stop at the timer even if items are left. The point is to learn your real pace.

    For a full team mock, run all the images of the round you are preparing for at once, plus a Packet Tracer activity, with the same people who will sit the round (study plan).

    #Keep a practice log

    Write one line per change. The log turns into your missed-items list after the review.

    Time Change Guide section Score before Score after
    0:14 Removed user <username> w11-users 0 4
    0:22 Set minimum password length 10 w11-passpol 4 8
    0:31 Stopped and disabled FTP service w11-services 8 8

    A change that did not move the score is still worth logging: either it is unscored on this image, or the engine checks something slightly different (Scoring patterns).

    #Compare with the answer key

    1. Open the key (or the README of a Training Round image that contains it).
    2. Open Tools in this guide and paste the key's item lines, or the lines from your scoring report, into the line lookup. It matches each line to the guide section that finds and fixes it.
    3. Mark every key item as one of four results:
    Result What it means What to do next
    Found and scored You know it Nothing, unless it took too long
    Found late You know it but your order is wrong Move it earlier in your reading path
    Tried but not scored The fix was wrong or incomplete Read the section's "how to find it" and verify steps, and redo it
    Never looked A gap Read the section, fix it on the image, add it to your missed list

    The answer-key indexes list every item seen in past keys with the report wording: Windows, Server, Linux.

    #Review what you missed

    • Keep one missed list per person, per OS. Read it before every practice session and every round.
    • For each missed item, open its guide section and do the fix on the practice image until the score moves. Reading alone does not stick.
    • If an item was missed because of a README detail, add it to the team's README traps list (README patterns).
    • After two sessions where an item was found and scored, cross it off.

    #Raise the difficulty over time

    Stage Practice on Aim for
    Basics Training Round 1 images and keys Every item on your OS found without the key
    Round 2 level Training Round 2 images All basics in the first hour, forensics answered in the first 30 minutes
    State level Training Round 2 images replayed without looking, plus two images at once No penalties, steady pace across a full 4 hours
    Semifinals level Three images in one session, team-made images with hidden persistence Hidden-item hunting from Scoring patterns
    Nationals level Images while a teammate plays red team and sends injects Services stay up, injects answered (National Finals)

    Rotate images between teammates once a month so every person can run the first hour of any image.

    GO

    Scoring patterns and hunting hidden items

    jump:start-scoring-patterns

    Score has stopped moving

    1. Read the top of the scoring report: "N out of M scored security issues fixed". M minus N items are left.
    2. Sort the items you have into the 13 categories and compare with the typical spread.
    3. Pick the categories that are empty or short and work through their rows in the answer-key index (Windows, Server, Linux).
    4. Re-read the README for users to create, groups to fill and services to harden.
    5. If still stuck after 30 minutes, swap images with a teammate.

    #What the engine checks

    Each scored item is one test with a pass condition, run every few minutes. Published scoring configs from older seasons show these test types:

    Test type Example
    File exists or does not exist C:\Windows\nc.exe absent; wp-login.php present
    File contents match a pattern PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config; allow-guest=false in a LightDM file
    Registry value LimitBlankPasswordUse=1, UserAuthentication=1 for RDP
    Service state Not running and start type above Automatic
    User property Exists, is admin, has a password, locked out, enabled
    Security policy value Minimum password age, history, lockout window
    File version or hash ntdll.dll version after updates; a changed binary hash after an app update
    Running process Backdoor process not running

    Because each item is a narrow test, a fix done a different way can miss. When a change does not score, check you changed the exact setting the report wording names, then check the engine's view from the rules below.

    #Rules the engine follows

    Seen in published configs What it means for you
    A file-removal item also checks that the parent folder still exists Delete the MP3 files, not the user's Music or home folder. Deleting the folder scores nothing and may trigger the "home directory deleted" penalty.
    Web-file removals check that WordPress is intact (wp-login.php still exists) Delete only info.php, phpinfo.php or the web shell (r57.php); never the web root.
    Windows service items need state not running and start type Manual or Disabled Stop the service and set it to Disabled. Stopping alone fails after the next reboot.
    Linux service items accept a removed binary, a removed init script or a disabled unit systemctl disable --now or apt purge, unless the README lists the service.
    Unauthorized-user items often accept a disabled account as well as a deleted one Delete the account; if unsure whether the README needs it, disabling is the safe first step.
    Password items test that the password changed from the weak value Any strong password passes; use the team password.
    App-update items test a version above a threshold or a changed binary hash Install the current version from the official installer, at the default path.
    OS-update items test core file versions Install updates and reboot; the item scores after the reboot.
    Policy items use thresholds: history above 2, minimum age at least 1 day, lockout window above 4 minutes with a threshold set Use the guide's values (history 24, minimum age 1, threshold 5-10, window 30); they clear every threshold seen.
    Guest on older Ubuntu was tested as allow-guest=false in LightDM files Set it in the file the guide names, then check the Guest login is gone.

    #How many items to expect per image

    Every image is worth 100 points, spread across all its items.

    Image level Items seen in past keys Forensics questions
    Practice and Training Round 1 12-16 (one Ubuntu practice key had 12 items for 77 points) 1-2
    Training Round 2 16-19 2-3
    Round 1 and Round 2 16-23 (CP-18 Round 1: 20 on Windows 11, 16 on Mint; Round 2: 18 on Windows 11, 23 on Mint) 2-3
    State Round 26-32 (CP-17 Platinum: 31 on Windows 10 and Server 2019; CP-18 Gold: 32 on Mint, 26 on Ubuntu 24) 2-3

    Item values vary; one real report shows a forensics question worth 6 points. A 30-item image averages about 3 points per item, so every category matters. Category counts are in start-categories.

    #Hunt hidden items when stuck

    Work from the count, not from memory.

    1. Count what is left and which categories are short. A State image with no Malware item yet probably has two or three waiting.
    2. Read your found items as hints. "Firefox has been updated" means the other installed apps are worth checking too; one removed hacking tool means look for the rest of the toolkit.
    3. Go back over the items that are easy to miss:
    Category Items teams often miss
    User Auditing Hidden users (UID under 1000 with a shell on Linux, hidden accounts on Windows), a lookalike guest_ account, "must change password at next login", users or groups the README tells you to create, the Remote Desktop Users group
    Account Policies Lockout duration and observation window, password history, null passwords (nullok)
    Local Policies A single Security Option such as blank-password console limit or CTRL+ALT+DEL; sysctl values; files in /etc/sudoers.d
    Application Updates Every installed third-party app, including the ones that are not browsers
    Application Security Settings The required service's own config: SSH, FTP, Samba, Apache, PHP, IIS, RDP NLA, SMB1
    Uncategorized OS Settings Extra shares such as USERS$, file permissions on /etc/shadow, the FTP root, grub.cfg
    Malware Cron lines, scheduled tasks, services and Run keys that start a listener; Defender exclusions that hide it
    Prohibited Files Media in other users' folders, password lists in shares, phpinfo files in the web root
    1. Check the forensics answers again: exact format, full path, case.
    2. Run the recon scripts for a fresh listing (Windows, Server, Linux), where the rules allow your team to use them.

    #Penalties to avoid

    Penalties seen in real keys. Each one is reversed by undoing the change.

    Penalty Points
    Account lockout threshold set below 5 -2 to -4
    Required software removed or moved from its default install path -5 each
    Critical service stopped, disabled or removed -5
    Remote Desktop disabled when the README requires RDP -5 to -10
    Required share or file sharing disabled -5
    Business file deleted from a required share -5
    Authorized user deleted (including root on Linux) -5 to -10
    Authorized user's home folder deleted -5 to -10
    Authorized administrator demoted -5

    Per-OS lists: Windows, Server, Linux. Recovery steps: Score went down.

    GO

    Reading the README and avoiding its traps

    jump:start-readme-patterns

    Read the README in 5 minutes

    1. Open the README shortcut on the desktop and read it top to bottom once without touching anything.
    2. Copy the Authorized Administrators list (with passwords) and the Authorized Users list onto paper.
    3. Circle every critical service and every piece of required software.
    4. Write down instructions to create users, add users to groups or change settings.
    5. Write down policy lines: prohibited media, hacking tools, games, which firewall to use.
    6. Write down every "do not" line, then answer the forensics questions before any fix.

    #Parts of a README

    Part What it gives you
    Scenario paragraph The company, your job, what the machine is for. The machine's purpose tells you which services are business-critical.
    Authorized Administrators Names and passwords of admin accounts. The account marked "you" is the one you are logged in as.
    Authorized Users Standard accounts that must stay. Everyone not listed in either list is unauthorized.
    Critical services or "the following services must remain running" Services to keep and harden.
    Required or authorized software Programs to keep, at their default install location.
    Competition guidelines or company policy Rules such as "non-work media files are prohibited" and "hacking tools, games and P2P software are not allowed".
    Specific tasks "Create user X", "Add X to group Y", "Turn on automatic update checks". These are scored items.

    #User lists

    • Build two lists from the README and compare them with the machine (Windows, Server, Linux). Remove accounts not listed, demote listed users who are admins but appear only under Authorized Users, and promote listed admins who are missing admin rights.
    • Create any user the README names who does not exist yet. Keys score "Created user account" and "Created new administrator account".
    • Add users to the groups the README names. Keys score "Added X to group Y" and "Updated Remote Desktop Users group".
    • Leave system accounts alone: Administrator, DefaultAccount and the service accounts on Windows; root and the daemon accounts with no login shell on Linux.
    • Check the spelling of every name. A lookalike such as guest_ or a name one letter off from a real user is unauthorized.

    #Critical services

    Services README files named as critical in past keys: OpenSSH Server, Remote Desktop, SMB file sharing with a named share, Apache with MySQL, PHP and WordPress, IIS with PHP, IIS FTP, FileZilla Server, vsftpd, PostgreSQL, Samba, MediaWiki, DNS, DHCP and the Event Log.

    • A critical service stays installed, running and enabled. Harden it in its config file instead of removing it (Linux services, Server roles).
    • Turning on the firewall must not cut it off: allow its port (sudo ufw allow OpenSSH, or keep the Remote Desktop firewall rule on Windows).
    • Test the service after every config edit. A typo that crashes the service costs the same penalty as stopping it.
    • A service that is not listed and not needed for the machine's purpose is fair game (Windows, Server, Linux).

    #Required software

    Software README files have required: Firefox, Thunderbird, Perl, Chrome, Notepad++, 7-Zip, Wireshark, Adobe Reader and LibreOffice.

    • Update required software from its official installer and keep it at the default path. Keys penalize "not installed at default location".
    • Wireshark has been required on some images and prohibited on others. Only the README decides.
    • Removing a required package on Linux can pull out its dependencies; read the list apt prints before you answer Yes.

    #Do-not lines and policy lines

    • "UFW is the only approved firewall" (seen in a key): use ufw, do not install another firewall.
    • "Non-work media files are prohibited": delete MP3s and videos in user folders, but keep files the business uses.
    • A named share (such as AFA or C:\Share) and the business files in it must stay. Remove only the plaintext password files and other prohibited content.
    • "Do not change the password of user X" or "do not remove X": follow it even if it looks insecure.

    #Traps that cause penalties

    Trap What happens Avoid it
    Deleting a user who is named outside the two lists, in a task line or the scenario paragraph Authorized user deleted, -5 to -10 Read the whole README; search it for the name before deleting
    Removing an admin listed under Authorized Administrators because they look suspicious Administrator demoted, -5 Admin status follows the README, not your judgement
    Deleting a user's whole folder to remove media Home folder deleted penalty and no credit Delete the files only
    Stopping SSH or RDP while "hardening" it Critical service penalty Edit the config and restart, never disable
    Enabling the firewall without allowing the required service Service unreachable, may count as down Allow the port first
    Uninstalling Wireshark or another tool the README requires Required software removed, -5 Check the required list before every uninstall
    Lockout threshold set to 3 Lockout threshold below 5 penalty Use 5-10
    Removing root or the account you are logged in as Authorized user removed, or lockout Never remove either

    #README summary template

    Fill this in on paper for every image in the first 5 minutes:

    Image:
Logged in as:
Authorized admins:
Authorized users:
Users to create / groups to change:
Critical services:
Required software:
Prohibited (media, tools, games):
