    Version: Help > About Adobe Acrobat Reader. Update: Help > Check for updates. Installing the 64-bit Reader over a 32-bit one changes the program path (Acrobat.exe under C:\Program Files\Adobe\Acrobat DC), and an older config tested AcroRd32.exe, so update in place with Check for updates.

    Settings worth setting (Edit > Preferences, or Menu > Preferences in the new interface):

    Page Setting Value
    Security (Enhanced) Enable Protected Mode at startup Checked
    Security (Enhanced) Enable Enhanced Security Checked
    JavaScript Enable Acrobat JavaScript Unchecked, unless the README needs forms that use it
    Trust Manager Allow opening of non-PDF file attachments with external applications Unchecked

    #Visual Studio Code updates and settings

    Version and update: Help > About, then Help > Check for Updates. Hivestorm scored Visual Studio Code has been updated. The user installer lives in the user's AppData, so update it while signed in as that user, or use winget for that user.

    Check %APPDATA%\Code\User\settings.json for "update.mode": "none" and "security.workspace.trust.enabled": false and delete both lines. Remove unknown extensions in the Extensions view.

    #Krita, Tiled and other apps without a scored setting

    Hivestorm scored Krita has been updated, and a practice round scored the Tiled map editor the same way. For any app like this: read Help > About, download the current installer from the app's official site, install it over the old version, and check the version again.

    #Wireshark or TeamViewer when required

    If the README requires either one, keep it and update it: Wireshark has Help > Check for Updates, TeamViewer has Help > Check for new version. Keep Npcap installed with Wireshark. For TeamViewer, remove saved unattended-access passwords and unknown partners in its settings. When the README does not require them, remove them (how).

    Verify

    The version check shows the new version, InstallLocation is unchanged, and the app starts from its Start menu shortcut.

    PreviousREADME scenarios seen on Windows imagesNextRemoving unwanted software, keyloggers and backdoors
    W11

    Removing unwanted software, keyloggers and backdoors

    jump:w11-unwanted

    README and forensics first

    Check the README's required software and answer every forensics question about a program before you remove it. Removing required software costs 5 points each in past keys.

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator.
    2. Run the trace script with a word from the program's name.
    3. Stop its processes, then uninstall it from appwiz.cpl or with winget uninstall --name "<program-name>".
    4. Run the trace script again and delete what is left: services, tasks, Run values, folders, firewall rules.
    5. Confirm its port is closed (how).

    #Find every trace of a program

    Set $k to one plain word from the name (for example teamviewer, torrent or tftp), then paste into elevated PowerShell. It lists uninstall entries (including hidden ones), folders, services, scheduled tasks, Run values, processes and firewall rules that match:

    $k = '<program-name>'
"--- Uninstall entries (SystemComponent 1 = hidden from Programs and Features) ---"
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'Registry::HKEY_USERS\*\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -match $k -or $_.PSChildName -match $k } | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, InstallLocation, UninstallString, SystemComponent | Format-List
"--- Folders ---"
Get-ChildItem 'C:\Program Files', 'C:\Program Files (x86)', 'C:\ProgramData', 'C:\Users\*\AppData\Local', 'C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Programs', 'C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming', 'C:\' -Directory -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Name -match $k | Select-Object FullName
"--- Services ---"
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.Name -match $k -or $_.DisplayName -match $k -or $_.PathName -match $k } | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, PathName | Format-List
"--- Scheduled tasks ---"
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -match $k -or (($_.Actions | ForEach-Object { $_.Execute }) -join ' ') -match $k } | Select-Object TaskPath, TaskName, State
"--- Run values ---"
'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run', 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run', 'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' | ForEach-Object {
    $key = $_
    $p = Get-ItemProperty $key -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    if ($p) { $p.PSObject.Properties | Where-Object { $_.Name -notlike 'PS*' -and "$($_.Name) $($_.Value)" -match $k } | ForEach-Object { "$key : $($_.Name) = $($_.Value)" } }
}
"--- Processes ---"
Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -match $k -or $_.Path -match $k } | Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path
"--- Firewall rules ---"
Get-NetFirewallRule | Where-Object DisplayName -match $k | Select-Object DisplayName, Direction, Action, Enabled

    Run values for users who are not signed in need their hive loaded (how).

    #Remove a program completely

    Work in this order so nothing restarts the program while you remove it:

    1. Record anything a forensics question asks about (path, hash, port).
    2. Stop the processes: Stop-Process -Name <process-name> -Force.
    3. Uninstall: appwiz.cpl, Settings > Apps > Installed apps, winget uninstall --name "<program-name>", or the UninstallString from the trace output.
    4. Delete leftover services (sc.exe delete <service-name>), scheduled tasks (how) and Run values (how).
    5. Delete the leftover program folder. Delete the program's own folder only, never C:\Program Files or a user's profile.
    6. Remove firewall rules it added: Remove-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "<rule-name>".
    7. Run the trace script again; every list should be empty.

    #Programs that hide from Programs and Features

    Trick How to find it
    Uninstall entry with SystemComponent = 1 The trace script shows it; Programs and Features does not
    Installed for one user only, in AppData\Roaming or AppData\Local\Programs Settings > Apps while signed in as that user, the HKEY_USERS uninstall keys, or the folder search
    Portable exe with no installer Portable program search
    Renamed to look like Windows (svchost.exe outside System32) Get-Process | Select-Object Name, Path and look for System32 names in other folders

    #Remote access tools

    Remove these unless the README authorizes them. TeamViewer was scored in a Windows 10 training key and AnyDesk in a Hivestorm key.

    Program Where it usually is Service Port
    TeamViewer C:\Program Files\TeamViewer (or (x86)) TeamViewer 5938
    AnyDesk C:\Program Files (x86)\AnyDesk, or a portable AnyDesk.exe in Downloads AnyDesk 7070
    VNC servers (TightVNC, UltraVNC, RealVNC) Program Files tvnserver, uvnc_service, vncserver 5900, 5800

    Uninstall from Programs and Features, then run the trace script for teamviewer, anydesk or vnc. A portable AnyDesk has no uninstall entry: end the process and delete the exe and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk if present.

    #Servers nobody asked for

    Program Scored as How to spot it
    Open TFTP Server Removed Open TFTP server Programs list "Open TFTP Server", a TFTP service, UDP port 69
    Home Web Server Removed Home Web Server A web server process listening on 80 or 8080; an old config also checked the process was gone
    Plex Media Server Removed Plex Media Server (Hivestorm) Program Files Plex, TCP 32400
    FileZilla Server, Apache, XAMPP, MySQL Seen as unwanted when no server is required Their services and ports 21, 80, 443, 3306

    Check UDP listeners, which Get-NetTCPConnection does not show:

    Get-NetUDPEndpoint -LocalPort 69 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

    #P2P and download tools

    BitTorrent and uTorrent install per user into C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\BitTorrent or ...\uTorrent, with a Run value in that user's HKCU. They do not appear in Programs and Features unless you are signed in as that user. BitComet and SpeedBit Video Downloader install under Program Files (an old config checked their exe was gone).

    1. Run the trace script for torrent, then bitcomet, then speedbit.
    2. Uninstall from Settings > Apps, or run the uninstaller exe inside the program folder.
    3. Delete the AppData folder and the Run value.
    4. Delete downloaded media the client left behind in that user's Downloads after forensics.

    #Network tools

    Program Notes
    Wireshark Check the README first; some images require it. Its uninstaller asks whether to remove Npcap too.
    Nmap and Zenmap Installs under C:\Program Files (x86)\Nmap and also installs Npcap.
    Npcap Separate entry in Programs and Features. Remove it only when nothing required (Wireshark) uses it.
    NetStumbler Old wireless scanner, scored in a practice round.

    #Cleaners, driver updaters and adware

    Program Scored as Leftovers to check
    CCleaner Removed CCleaner Scheduled tasks whose names start with CCleaner, its services, the Run value
    Adaware Web Companion Removed Adaware Web Companion A Web Companion service and a Lavasoft folder under Program Files
    SlimDrivers Removed SlimDrivers software Program Files folder, scheduled task
    Driver Booster Removed Driver Booster (Hivestorm) IObit folder under Program Files, IObit services
    RoboForm Removed RoboForm software Browser extensions in Chrome, Edge and Firefox
    CleanMyPC Removed CleanMyPC (Hivestorm) Program Files folder
    WebDiscover browser Removed WebDiscover browser (Hivestorm) Per-user install in AppData, desktop shortcuts, a Run value

    After uninstalling, check each browser's extensions page and its search engine and home page settings; adware often changes them.

    #Games and unapproved apps

    • Desktop games (TicTacToe and Tetris were scored) and Store games: Settings > Apps > Installed apps > Uninstall, or Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers *<app-name>* | Remove-AppxPackage -AllUsers.
    • Cursor (an AI code editor) was scored only because the README did not authorize it. It installs per user into C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Programs\cursor. Uninstall it from Settings > Apps as that user, or run the uninstaller inside that folder, then delete the folder.

    Apply the same test to any app: if the README's business does not need it, it is a candidate.

    #Malware seen in past keys

    Find the listener first (how), record the answer to any forensics question about it, then remove it and every way it restarts.

    #Tini backdoor

    Tini is a tiny Windows backdoor that gives a command shell to anyone who connects; the classic build listens on TCP 7777. Scored in a CP18 Windows 11 round and in Hivestorm.

    Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 7777 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object { Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess | Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path }

    A renamed copy can listen on another port, so check every listener with an unknown program. Stop it, delete the exe, then check services, tasks and Run values for its path.

    #Netcat backdoor

    nc.exe or nc64.exe started with -l -p <port> -e cmd.exe. An old config looked for C:\Windows\nc.exe; a training key found it in Task Manager. Show the command line, which gives the port and the path:

    Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.Name -match '^nc(64)?\.exe$|ncat' } | Select-Object ProcessId, ExecutablePath, CommandLine

    End the process, delete the file, then remove whatever starts it (a service, task or Run value pointing at the same path).

    #Keyloggers

    Refog Keylogger (scored in a real state-round report) and Actual Keylogger (Hivestorm) run hidden, without a tray icon, and may hide their uninstall entry.

    1. Run the trace script for refog, then keylog, then actual.
    2. Uninstall from the entry it finds, or run its uninstaller from its folder.
    3. Delete leftover folders under Program Files, ProgramData and AppData, and any service or Run value.
    4. Search for log folders it left: Get-ChildItem C:\ -Recurse -Directory -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Name -match 'refog|keylog'.

    #Cryptominers

    Hivestorm scored Remove Etherium cryptominer Geth. Geth is an Ethereum node; it listens on TCP and UDP 30303 and often on 8545. Other miners (xmrig and similar) show as a process with very high CPU in Task Manager.

    Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 Id, ProcessName, CPU, Path

    Stop the process, delete its folder and the blockchain data folder it created, and remove its persistence.

    #Unknown backdoor on a port

    Keys also scored generic Backdoor removed items and a Server 2022 "bd" program. Map every listening port to a program (how). Anything in C:\Users, Temp, ProgramData or a made-up folder in C:\, or a Windows name outside System32, is the backdoor. Task Manager > Details > right-click > Open file location shows the folder.

    Verify

    The trace script returns nothing for the program, the port no longer listens, and the scoring report shows the item.

    PreviousApplication updates and settings (Firefox, Notepad++, 7-Zip, PuTTY, FileZilla, Reader)NextWindows forensics playbook
    W11

    Windows forensics playbook

    jump:w11-forensics

    Answer before you fix

    Read every question first. Most ask about a user, file, program, port or setting you are about to remove. Answer it, then fix.

    Fast path

    1. Open each Forensics Question N.txt in Notepad and note its type (table).
    2. Answer the fast ones first: hashes, group members, computer name, paths, ports.
    3. Use the matching section below for the rest.
    4. Copy the example's format exactly after ANSWER: and save (how).
    5. Check the scoring report a minute later; if the item is missing, re-read the question's wording.

    #Question types seen in past keys

    Question seen Where to look
    Source IP of an attacker in a pcap on the Desktop Packet captures
    Decrypt a one-time pad or XOR message Ciphers and encodings
    Base64 that leads to a file, a password or a QR code Ciphers and encodings
    MD5 or SHA256 of a file Hash a file
    Members of a group (Event Log Readers) or users who meet a condition Users, SIDs and groups
    Full computer name System facts
    Path of a share, a folder or a running executable Paths of shares and programs
    Port a backdoor listens on Find the process that owns a listening port
    Name of a deleted user Users, SIDs and groups
    Hidden message in a service description Services and scheduled tasks
    Scheduled task that does something bad Services and scheduled tasks
    Registry key path or value Registry
    Renamed archive, appended data, app cache file File type and hidden content

    #Packet captures

    Wireshark is the tool. If it is not installed and the README does not forbid it, install it, answer, then uninstall it and log both steps; an installed Wireshark can count as unwanted software.

    Question Wireshark
    Who attacked Statistics > Conversations > IPv4, sort by Packets; or filter on the attack traffic and read the Source column
    Plain-text passwords Filter ftp.request.command == "PASS" or http.request.method == "POST", then right-click > Follow > TCP Stream
    A file sent over HTTP or SMB File > Export Objects > HTTP or SMB
    What a host looked up Filter dns

    The same FTP password search with tshark from cmd:

    "C:\Program Files\Wireshark\tshark.exe" -r "<file>" -Y "ftp.request.command == \"PASS\"" -T fields -e ip.src -e ftp.request.arg

    #Ciphers and encodings

    Base64, hex, binary and ROT13 are in the any-OS playbook. CyberChef (gchq.github.io/CyberChef) handles all of them, plus XOR and QR codes, if the image has internet.

    XOR a hex ciphertext with a hex key (a one-time pad is XOR with a key as long as the message). Paste both hex strings, spaces allowed:

    $c = '<cipher-hex>' -replace '\s', ''
$k = '<key-hex>' -replace '\s', ''
$cb = for ($i = 0; $i -lt $c.Length; $i += 2) { [Convert]::ToByte($c.Substring($i, 2), 16) }
$kb = for ($i = 0; $i -lt $k.Length; $i += 2) { [Convert]::ToByte($k.Substring($i, 2), 16) }
-join (0..($cb.Count - 1) | ForEach-Object { [char]($cb[$_] -bxor $kb[$_ % $kb.Count]) })

    A short key repeats across the message. If you know part of the plaintext (a flag format, a word like password), XOR it with the ciphertext to recover the key.

    Base64 that decodes to binary starting with 89 50 4E 47 is a PNG, often a QR code. In CyberChef use From Base64, then Render Image, or Parse QR Code.

    #Users, SIDs and groups

    Every account with its SID:

    Get-LocalUser | Select-Object Name, Enabled, SID, LastLogon, PasswordLastSet, Description

    The last number of a SID is the RID: 500 Administrator, 501 Guest, 1000 and up for created accounts in creation order.

    Members of a group, including built-in groups such as Event Log Readers:

    Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "<groupname>" | Select-Object Name, ObjectClass

    Name of a deleted user: profiles stay in the registry after the account is deleted. List each profile SID with its folder, then compare with Get-LocalUser:

    Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList' | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ SID = $_.PSChildName; Profile = (Get-ItemProperty $_.PSPath).ProfileImagePath } }

    A SID with no matching account belongs to the deleted user; its ProfileImagePath folder name is usually the username. Folders in C:\Users with no account point the same way.

    Who created, deleted or promoted an account, from the Security log (needs auditing on before the event happened):

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4720,4726,4732,4733} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
    $x = [xml]$_.ToXml()
    $d = @{}
    $x.Event.EventData.Data | ForEach-Object { $d[$_.Name] = $_.'#text' }
    [pscustomobject]@{ Time = $_.TimeCreated; Id = $_.Id; Target = $d['TargetUserName']; By = $d['SubjectUserName']; Member = $d['MemberSid'] }
} | Format-Table -AutoSize

    4720 is created, 4726 deleted, 4732 added to a group (Target is the group), 4733 removed from a group. More IDs are in w11-troubleshoot.

    #Logons

    Successful logons with their type and source address:

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4624} -MaxEvents 200 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
    $x = [xml]$_.ToXml()
    $d = @{}
    $x.Event.EventData.Data | ForEach-Object { $d[$_.Name] = $_.'#text' }
    [pscustomobject]@{ Time = $_.TimeCreated; User = $d['TargetUserName']; Type = $d['LogonType']; From = $d['IpAddress'] }
} | Where-Object { $_.User -notmatch '\$$|^(SYSTEM|LOCAL SERVICE|NETWORK SERVICE|DWM-\d+|UMFD-\d+)$' } | Format-Table -AutoSize

    Type 2 is at the keyboard, 3 over the network (shares), 7 returning to a locked screen, 10 Remote Desktop. Change the Id to 4625 for failed logons. net user <username> shows Last logon for one account.

    #What a user did

    Evidence Where How to read it
    PowerShell commands typed C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt Notepad
    Recently opened files C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent Shortcut list below
    Commands typed in Win+R HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU reg query (your own account; load another user's hive)
    Paths typed in File Explorer HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\TypedPaths reg query
    Programs run from Explorer HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist ROT13 names, decoder below
    Programs run on the machine C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf File name is the exe; modified time is about the last run
    Downloaded file origin The file's Zone.Identifier stream Get-Content "<path>" -Stream Zone.Identifier shows HostUrl
    Notepad++ open files C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Notepad++\session.xml Notepad

    Recent files with their real targets, newest first:

    $sh = New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell
Get-ChildItem "C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\*.lnk" -Force | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Opened = $_.LastWriteTime; Target = $sh.CreateShortcut($_.FullName).TargetPath } } | Sort-Object Opened -Descending

    UserAssist program names decoded from ROT13 (for the signed-in user):

    Get-ChildItem 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist' | ForEach-Object { (Get-Item "$($_.PSPath)\Count").Property } | ForEach-Object {
    -join ($_.ToCharArray() | ForEach-Object { $n = [int]$_; if ($n -ge 65 -and $n -le 90) { [char](65 + ($n - 52) % 26) } elseif ($n -ge 97 -and $n -le 122) { [char](97 + ($n - 84) % 26) } else { $_ } })
}

    Prefetch, newest first (elevated):

    Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\Prefetch -Filter *.pf | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 40 Name, CreationTime, LastWriteTime

    #Browser history

    Browser History file
    Chrome C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\History
    Edge C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\History
    Firefox C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\<profile>\places.sqlite

    These are SQLite databases and the browser locks them while it runs. Close the browser, copy the file, then pull every URL out of the copy:

    Copy-Item "<path>" "$env:TEMP\hist.db" -Force
$text = [System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString([System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes("$env:TEMP\hist.db"))
[regex]::Matches($text, 'https?://[\x21-\x7e]+') | ForEach-Object Value | Select-Object -Unique

    The end of a URL can run into the page title stored next to it, so read the results with care. For your own account, Ctrl+H in the browser is faster. Downloads are listed in the same file.

    #Deleted files

    Files deleted in Explorer sit in C:\$Recycle.Bin\<SID>: each $R... file is the content and the matching $I... file holds the original path and deletion time. Read every $I file (elevated):

    Get-ChildItem 'C:\$Recycle.Bin' -Recurse -Force -Filter '$I*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
    $b = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($_.FullName)
    [pscustomobject]@{ Deleted = [DateTime]::FromFileTime([BitConverter]::ToInt64($b, 16)); Original = [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString($b, 28, $b.Length - 28).TrimEnd([char]0); Data = $_.FullName.Replace('\$I', '\$R') }
} | Format-List

    Copy the $R file somewhere else to open it. Shadow copies can also hold older versions: vssadmin list shadows (elevated) lists them, and Properties > Previous Versions on a folder shows them.

    #Services and scheduled tasks

    Search every service description for a phrase (a practice image hid a message in the Windows Update description):

    Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object Description -match '<search-text>' | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, Description

    One service's description, path and account:

    sc qdescription <service-name>
sc qc <service-name>

    A task's program, triggers, author and last run:

    $t = Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "<task-name>"
$t.Actions | Select-Object Execute, Arguments
$t.Triggers | Select-Object StartBoundary, @{n='Every';e={$_.Repetition.Interval}}, Enabled
$t | Select-Object Author, Date, Description
$t | Get-ScheduledTaskInfo | Select-Object LastRunTime, NextRunTime, LastTaskResult

    The raw XML of every task is in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks, which you can search with Select-String. A trigger interval PT1H means every hour.

    #Registry

    • Search for a value or text: reg query HKLM /f "<text>" /s (options).
    • Last write time of a key: regedit > select the key > File > Export > Save as type Text Files. The text export prints "Last Write Time" for every key.
    • Another user's settings: load their hive with reg load HKU\Temp "C:\Users\<username>\NTUSER.DAT", read it, then reg unload HKU\Temp.
    • USB devices that were plugged in: Get-ChildItem HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR.
    • A team-made image asked for the Windows 11 setup bypass keys (HKLM\SYSTEM\Setup\LabConfig, values such as BypassTPMCheck). Copy key paths from regedit's address bar (right-click > Copy key name).

    #Paths of shares and programs

    Path of a share:

    Get-SmbShare -Name "<share-name>" | Select-Object Name, Path

    Full path and command line of a running program:

    Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='<process-name>.exe'" | Select-Object ProcessId, ParentProcessId, ExecutablePath, CommandLine

    In File Explorer, Shift+right-click a file > Copy as path gives the exact text with quotes; remove the quotes unless the example has them.

    #System facts

    Question Command
    Computer name hostname or $env:COMPUTERNAME
    Full computer name with domain or workgroup Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, Workgroup; or sysdm.cpl > Full computer name
    Windows version and build winver, or Get-ComputerInfo -Property OsName, OsVersion, OsBuildNumber
    Install date of a program InstallDate in the uninstall key list
    IP and MAC address ipconfig /all
    DNS names the machine resolved recently Get-DnsClientCache
    Established connections Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established

    #File type and hidden content

    The first bytes of a file tell its real type, whatever the extension says:

    Format-Hex -Path "<path>" | Select-Object -First 2
    First bytes Type
    50 4B 03 04 (PK) ZIP, also .docx, .xlsx, .jar
    89 50 4E 47 PNG
    FF D8 FF JPEG
    25 50 44 46 (%PDF) PDF
    4D 5A (MZ) Windows exe or dll
    47 49 46 38 (GIF8) GIF
    52 61 72 21 (Rar!) RAR
    37 7A BC AF 7z

    A renamed archive: copy it, give the copy a .zip extension and run Expand-Archive -Path "<path>" -DestinationPath "$env:TEMP\out". A file that is a valid image and also contains a ZIP (a polyglot) opens in 7-Zip if it is installed.

    Readable text hidden inside any binary file:

    $b = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes("<path>")
[regex]::Matches([System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($b), '[\x20-\x7e]{6,}') | ForEach-Object Value

    App caches (a practice image asked for a Discord cache file) are under each user's AppData\Roaming\<app-name> or AppData\Local\<app-name>, often in a Cache folder. Sort by name or time as the question asks.

    Check it worked

    A correct answer appears on the scoring report as Forensics Question N correct within a few minutes.

    PreviousRemoving unwanted software, keyloggers and backdoorsNextWindows 10 differences (training rounds)
    W11

    Windows 10 differences (training rounds)

    jump:w11-win10

    Fast path

    1. Run winver to confirm the version.
    2. Use the same commands as Windows 11; nearly every PowerShell, cmd, secpol.msc and gpedit.msc step is identical.
    3. Use the path table when a Settings page is not where the Windows 11 steps say.
    4. Check the Windows 10 defaults that leave extra items open.
    5. If Internet Explorer still runs, harden it (how).

    CP19 uses Windows 10 only in Training Rounds 1 and 2, which come with answer keys in the README. Work them with the past answer key list open.

    #Tell which version you are on

    Get-ComputerInfo -Property OsName, OsVersion, OsBuildNumber

    Windows 10 build numbers are below 22000 (22H2, the last release, is 19045). Windows 11 starts at 22000.

    #Settings paths that differ

    Task Windows 10 Windows 11
    Windows Update Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update Settings > Windows Update
    Windows Security Settings > Update & Security > Windows Security Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security
    Installed programs Settings > Apps > Apps & features Settings > Apps > Installed apps
    Other users Settings > Accounts > Family & other users Settings > Accounts > Other users
    AutoPlay Settings > Devices > AutoPlay Settings > Bluetooth & devices > AutoPlay
    Remote Desktop NLA Settings > System > Remote Desktop > Advanced settings Settings > System > Remote Desktop > expand the toggle
    Optional features (capabilities) Settings > Apps > Apps & features > Optional features Settings > System > Optional features
    Advanced sharing settings Control Panel > Network and Sharing Center > Change advanced sharing settings Settings > Network & internet > Advanced network settings > Advanced sharing settings
    Show file extensions File Explorer > View tab > File name extensions File Explorer > View > Show > File name extensions
    Configure Automatic Updates policy gpedit > Windows Components > Windows Update gpedit > Windows Components > Windows Update > Manage end user experience
    SmartScreen policy for apps and files gpedit > Windows Components > Windows Defender SmartScreen > Explorer Same path

    #Defaults that differ

    Item Windows 10 What to do
    Account lockout Usually no lockout (threshold 0); only new installs that had the October 2022 updates before setup get 10 Always set it (how)
    Windows PowerShell 2.0 Still installed as an optional feature Remove it (how)
    SMB 1.0 Can still be installed on images upgraded from old builds Remove it (how)
    Internet Explorer 11 The app may still open on unpatched images Harden it below, or turn off the Internet Explorer 11 feature in optionalfeatures if nothing needs it
    LSA protection No toggle in Windows Security; RunAsPPL = 2 is not supported Use RunAsPPL = 1 (how)
    winget Missing on some images Use each app's own updater (w11-apps)
    Support Support ended October 14, 2025 (only paid extended security updates after that) Install every update Windows Update offers; "The majority of Windows updates are installed" still scores

    #Internet Explorer settings on Windows 10

    Hivestorm Windows images scored Internet Explorer 8+ SmartScreen Filter [enabled] and Internet Properties: Enable Enhanced Protected Mode [Enabled].

    Win+R > inetcpl.cpl > Advanced > Security: check "Enable Enhanced Protected Mode" and "Enable Windows Defender SmartScreen" > OK.

    Run in elevated cmd. The first line is the IE SmartScreen policy, the second Enhanced Protected Mode:

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\PhishingFilter" /v EnabledV9 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\Main" /v Isolation /t REG_SZ /d PMEM /f

    Also in Internet Options: Security tab > Internet zone > Default level, and Privacy tab > Turn on Pop-up Blocker.

    PreviousWindows forensics playbookNextExtra hardening for hard images (nationals level)
    W11

    Extra hardening for hard images (nationals level)

    jump:w11-advanced

    Not every item here has been scored

    Only exploit protection (heap integrity, DEP) appeared in past keys, and only in Hivestorm and a practice image. Do the answer key list first, then these when time allows. None of them should break a README service, but log each change.

    Fast path

    1. Check exploit protection and fix anything Off (how).
    2. Turn off LLMNR and NetBIOS over TCP/IP (how).
    3. Turn on PowerShell logging and command-line auditing (how).
    4. Remove stored credentials with cmdkey (how).
    5. Add the ASR rules if Defender is the active antivirus (how).
    6. Confirm the items already covered elsewhere are done (table).

    #Check exploit protection system settings

    Show the system-wide mitigations:

    Get-ProcessMitigation -System

    Read the DEP, ASLR (BottomUp, HighEntropy), SEHOP, Heap (TerminateOnError) and CFG blocks. ON or NOTSET (Windows default, which is on) is fine; OFF was planted. Turn them back on:

    Set-ProcessMitigation -System -Enable DEP, SEHOP, BottomUp, HighEntropy, TerminateOnError, CFG

    In the GUI: Windows Security > App & browser control > Exploit protection settings > System settings. Set Control flow guard, Data Execution Prevention, Randomize memory allocations, High-entropy ASLR, Validate exception chains (SEHOP) and Validate heap integrity to "Use default (On)". Leave Force randomization for images at its default (Off); turning it on can break old programs. Restart when convenient.

    A practice image fixed DEP enabled system-wide with bcdedit. Check, then set it, in elevated cmd:

    bcdedit /enum {current}

    bcdedit /set {current} nx AlwaysOn

    The nx line reads OptIn by default. AlwaysOn can stop very old 32-bit programs; set it back with bcdedit /set {current} nx OptIn if a required app breaks.

    #Turn on attack surface reduction rules

    ASR rules are part of Defender and need it as the active antivirus with real-time protection on. These six are low-risk on a workstation:

    Rule GUID
    Block credential stealing from LSASS 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2
    Block persistence through WMI event subscription e6db77e5-3df2-4cf1-b95a-636979351e5b
    Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content d3e037e1-3eb8-44c8-a917-57927947596d
    Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts 5beb7efe-fd9a-4556-801d-275e5ffc04cc
    Block executable content from email client and webmail be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550
    Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers 56a863a9-875e-4185-98a7-b882c64b5ce5

    Add them in elevated PowerShell:

    $ids = @('9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2', 'e6db77e5-3df2-4cf1-b95a-636979351e5b', 'd3e037e1-3eb8-44c8-a917-57927947596d', '5beb7efe-fd9a-4556-801d-275e5ffc04cc', 'be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550', '56a863a9-875e-4185-98a7-b882c64b5ce5')
Add-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids $ids -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions (@('Enabled') * $ids.Count)

    Check:

    Get-MpPreference | Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids, AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

    Actions read 1 for Block, 2 for Audit, 0 for Off. Skip "Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands"; it breaks management tools.

    #Turn off LLMNR and NetBIOS over TCP/IP

    Both let an attacker on the network answer name lookups and capture password hashes. Turn off LLMNR (gpedit > Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off multicast name resolution = Enabled):

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient" /v EnableMulticast /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

    Turn off NetBIOS over TCP/IP on every adapter (the GUI is ncpa.cpl > adapter > Properties > IPv4 > Advanced > WINS > Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP):

    Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NetBT\Parameters\Interfaces' | ForEach-Object { Set-ItemProperty -Path $_.PSPath -Name NetbiosOptions -Value 2 }

    SMB file sharing keeps working over port 445 without NetBIOS. Skip this step only if the README mentions an old device that needs NetBIOS names.

    #Turn on PowerShell module logging and transcription

    Script block logging is in w11-gpedit. Module logging records every command of every module (gpedit > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on Module Logging, module names *):

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging" /v EnableModuleLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging\ModuleNames" /v * /t REG_SZ /d * /f

    Transcription writes a text copy of every session to a folder:

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription" /v EnableTranscripting /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription" /v EnableInvocationHeader /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription" /v OutputDirectory /t REG_SZ /d C:\PSTranscripts /f

    #Log process command lines

    Process creation events (4688) can include the full command line, which shows what a backdoor ran. Turn on the audit subcategory, then the policy (gpedit > System > Audit Process Creation > Include command line in process creation events):

    auditpol /set /subcategory:"Process Creation" /success:enable /failure:enable
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit" /v ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

    #Restrict printer driver installation

    Beyond the scored Security Option, the Point and Print policy limits driver installs from print servers to administrators (the PrintNightmare fix):

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint" /v RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

    If printing is not needed at all, disable the Print Spooler (services).

    #Remove stored credentials

    Credential Manager can hold saved passwords for shares and remote desktops. List them, record any a forensics question asks about, then delete the ones the README does not need:

    cmdkey /list

    cmdkey /delete:<target>

    <target> is the text after "Target:" in the list. cmdkey sees only the account you are signed in as.

    #Network stack values

    These come from the CIS and STIG baselines. All are DWORDs; run in elevated cmd and reboot when convenient:

    Purpose Key under HKLM Value Data
    Ignore IPv4 source routing SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters DisableIPSourceRouting 2
    Ignore IPv6 source routing SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters DisableIPSourceRouting 2
    Ignore ICMP redirects SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters EnableICMPRedirect 0
    Ignore NetBIOS name release requests SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NetBT\Parameters NoNameReleaseOnDemand 1
    Safe DLL search order SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager SafeDllSearchMode 1
    SEHOP SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\kernel DisableExceptionChainValidation 0 
    reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters" /v DisableIPSourceRouting /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters" /v DisableIPSourceRouting /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters" /v EnableICMPRedirect /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NetBT\Parameters" /v NoNameReleaseOnDemand /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager" /v SafeDllSearchMode /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\kernel" /v DisableExceptionChainValidation /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

    #Optional sign-in settings

    Setting secpol name Registry (under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System)
    Stop new Microsoft accounts Accounts: Block Microsoft accounts = Users can't add or log on with Microsoft accounts NoConnectedUser = 3
    Logon banner title Interactive logon: Message title for users attempting to log on LegalNoticeCaption (REG_SZ)
    Logon banner text Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on LegalNoticeText (REG_SZ)

    Set the banner only if the README gives text for it. Never block Microsoft accounts if a README user signs in with one.

    #Already covered in other sections

    Item Where
    SMB signing (client and server) Security options
    Secure channel signing Security options
    CD-ROM restriction, recovery console, shutdown without logon Security options
    LM hashes, NTLMv2 only, anonymous access Security options
    WDigest w11-uac-misc
    LSA protection w11-uac-misc
    RDP security layer, NLA, secure RPC, Plug and Play redirection Remote Desktop policies
    WinRM unencrypted traffic WinRM policy
    USERS$ hidden share Shares
    SMB1, PowerShell 2.0 Optional features
    AutoPlay and autorun w11-uac-misc
    Always install elevated, script block logging w11-gpedit
    Image File Execution Options, Winlogon, WMI persistence w11-malware

    Verify

    Get-ProcessMitigation -System shows no OFF, reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient" shows EnableMulticast 0x0, and every README service still works.

    PreviousWindows 10 differences (training rounds)NextWindows penalties and how to undo them
    W11

    Windows penalties and how to undo them

    jump:w11-penalties

    Fast path

    1. Read the penalty line on the scoring report; it names what broke.
    2. Find it in the penalty table.
    3. Undo it with the matching fix and wait one to two minutes.
    4. Refresh the report and confirm the penalty line is gone.
    5. Write the cause in the change log so nobody repeats it.

    #Penalties seen in past Windows keys

    Penalty Points Undo
    Account lockout threshold below 5 (1 to 4) -2 to -4 net accounts /lockoutthreshold:5
    Required software removed or not installed at default location (Firefox, Thunderbird, Chrome, Notepad++, 7-Zip, Wireshark, Adobe Reader) -5 each Reinstall it in its original folder
    Critical service from the README stopped or disabled (RDP and SMB file sharing in Windows keys) -5 Set-Service <service-name> -StartupType Automatic; Start-Service <service-name>
    Remote Desktop disabled when the README requires it -5 to -10 Turn it back on
    Authorized share disabled (AFA, C:\Share) -5 Re-create the share
    Business file deleted from a share -5 Restore it from the Recycle Bin
    Authorized user deleted -5 to -10 Re-create the account
    Authorized user's home folder deleted -5 to -10 Restore from the Recycle Bin or re-create the folder
    Authorized administrator demoted -5 Add-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators -Member <username>
    VirtualBox used instead of VMware 0 (warning) Use the supported VMware player next time; problems on VirtualBox cannot be appealed

    #Required software removed or moved

    1. Find the original folder from your change log or the app's default path (table).
    2. Reinstall the same architecture into that folder: winget install --id <package-id> -e, or the vendor installer with the folder set by hand.
    3. Check that the program file exists at the old path: Test-Path "<path>".

    Prevent it: update in place (w11-apps) and read the README's software list before uninstalling anything.

    #A required service was stopped

    Set it back to its old start type from the change log and start it. For Remote Desktop:

    Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections -Value 0
Enable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop"
Set-Service TermService -StartupType Manual
Start-Service TermService

    Also re-enable any firewall rule you removed for that service, and check the matching policy value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services is not denying connections.

    #A share or business file was removed

    Re-create the share on the same folder with the README's users:

    New-SmbShare -Name "<share-name>" -Path "<folder>" -ChangeAccess "<username>"

    Restore deleted files from the Recycle Bin (right-click > Restore). Files removed with Remove-Item or del skip the bin; check shadow copies with Properties > Previous Versions on the folder.

    #An authorized user was deleted or demoted

    Re-create the account with the same name and the README password, and put it back in its groups:

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
New-LocalUser -Name <username> -Password $pw
Add-LocalGroupMember -Group Users -Member <username>

    The new account gets a new SID, so its old profile folder is not reattached. Leave the old folder in C:\Users alone; the engine checks that it exists. If the folder was deleted, restore it from the Recycle Bin; re-creating an empty folder with the same path may clear an existence check but proves nothing about its contents.

    #Stop penalties before they happen

    How the engine decides

    Each scored item is a test: a registry value, a service state, a user property (exists, admin, has a password, locked out, enabled), a policy, a file version or hash, or a running process. Service items pass when the service is not running and its start type is Disabled, or when it is removed. Unauthorized-user items often pass when the account is disabled as well as deleted. File-removal items also check the parent folder still exists, and penalties are tests too, so undoing the change clears them on the next refresh.

    PreviousExtra hardening for hard images (nationals level)NextServer master checklist
    SRV

    Server master checklist

    jump:srv-checklist

    Work top to bottom. Items marked (DC) apply only on a domain controller. Items marked (role) apply only when that role is installed and the README needs it. Anything that works the same as on Windows 11 links to the Windows 11 section instead of repeating it here.

    Read the README first, every time

    The README decides which users are authorized, who is an admin, and which roles and services are required (for example "this server must continue to provide DNS and IIS"). Removing a required role or stopping a required service costs points and usually breaks other scoring checks too.

    #First 10 minutes on the server

    #Decide: standalone server or domain controller

    #Domain users and groups

    #Domain policy (GPO)

    #Active Directory hardening

    #Roles and features

    #Role hardening

    #Remote access

    #Services

    #Updates, Defender and firewall

    #Same as Windows 11

    #Final pass

    PreviousWindows penalties and how to undo themNextHow Server differs from Windows 11
    SRV

    How Server differs from Windows 11

    jump:srv-differences

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator (Start, type powershell, Run as administrator).

    2. Read the domain role number:

      (Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).DomainRole

    3. If it prints 4 or 5, the server is a domain controller: work from AD users and Group Policy on a domain.

    4. If it prints 2 (standalone) or 3 (member server), use the Windows 11 sections for users and local policy, then come back for roles.

    5. On a DC, record the starting health so you can tell later what you broke:

      dcdiag /q

    #Check if the server is a domain controller

    Run this in any PowerShell window. It needs no extra modules:

    (Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).DomainRole
    Value Meaning Where users and policy live
    0 Standalone workstation Local
    1 Member workstation Local, plus domain GPOs
    2 Standalone server Local (lusrmgr.msc, secpol.msc)
    3 Member server Local users exist, but domain GPOs override local policy
    4 Backup domain controller (any DC that is not the PDC emulator) Active Directory and domain GPOs
    5 Primary domain controller (holds the PDC emulator role) Active Directory and domain GPOs

    Other confirmations if you want a second opinion. On a DC this returns the DC's details; elsewhere it errors:

    Get-ADDomainController

    The NTDS service exists only on a DC:

    Get-Service NTDS

    From cmd, dcdiag /q prints only errors, net user /domain lists domain users, and nltest finds the DC for a domain:

    dcdiag /q
net user /domain
nltest /dsgetdc:<domain-name>

    On a non-domain server, net user /domain fails with "System error 1355 has occurred. The specified domain either does not exist or could not be contacted."

    In the GUI, Server Manager > Dashboard shows an AD DS tile on a DC, and Server Manager > Tools lists Active Directory Users and Computers. Opening lusrmgr.msc on a DC shows an error saying the snap-in cannot be used on a domain controller.

    AD DS installed does not mean promoted

    Get-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services showing Installed only proves the role binaries are there. A server can have the role installed and never have been promoted. Trust DomainRole or Get-Service NTDS.

    Member servers

    DomainRole 3 means the server is joined to a domain but is not a DC. Local users still exist (use Windows 11 users), but GPOs from the domain override local policy. In CyberPatriot the Server image is usually standalone (2) or a DC (4 or 5).

    #What changes on a DC

    Area Windows 11 Server 2022 standalone Server 2022 domain controller
    Users lusrmgr.msc, netplwiz Same as Windows 11 dsa.msc or AD PowerShell; no local users
    Password and lockout policy secpol.msc secpol.msc Default Domain Policy GPO in gpmc.msc
    Audit, user rights, security options secpol.msc secpol.msc Default Domain Controllers Policy GPO
    Optional software optionalfeatures.exe Server Manager roles and features, Get-WindowsFeature Same as standalone
    Settings app Windows 11 layout Windows 10 layout: Settings > Update & Security Same as standalone
    Admin console Settings, Control Panel Server Manager (opens at logon), sconfig Same, plus AD consoles
    Browser Edge Edge, plus Internet Explorer 11 with IE Enhanced Security Configuration Same as standalone
    Defender Always present Removable feature Windows-Defender, automatic role exclusions Same as standalone
    Microsoft Store and consumer apps Present Not present Not present
    Built-in Administrator Disabled by default Enabled, usually the logon account Domain Administrator, usually the logon account

    #Server Manager

    Open it from Start > Server Manager (it also opens at every logon).

    • Local Server shows firewall state, Remote management (WinRM), Remote Desktop, IE Enhanced Security Configuration, Windows Update, Microsoft Defender Antivirus and time zone. Click a value to open that setting.
    • Manage > Add Roles and Features and Manage > Remove Roles and Features install and remove roles.
    • Tools launches every admin console: ADUC, DNS, DHCP, Group Policy Management, IIS Manager, Services, Event Viewer.
    • The flag icon at the top shows pending tasks and post-deployment warnings.

    #Roles and features

    A role is a server job: AD DS, DNS Server, DHCP Server, Web Server (IIS), File and Storage Services, Remote Access, Fax Server. A feature is supporting software: Telnet Client, SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support, Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine, SNMP Service, RSAT tools. Get-WindowsFeature lists both and Uninstall-WindowsFeature removes both (removal).

    #No local users on a domain controller

    Promoting a server to DC replaces the local accounts database with Active Directory, so every user is a domain user. The only local account left is the DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) administrator, which is used only when you boot into DSRM (DSRM). Do all user work in ADUC or AD PowerShell (AD users).

    #Why secpol.msc changes do not stick on a DC

    Group Policy applies Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU, and the later one wins. secpol.msc and gpedit.msc edit only the Local policy, so any domain GPO that sets the same thing overrides them.

    • Password, lockout and Kerberos policy for domain accounts come only from a GPO linked at the domain root, normally the Default Domain Policy. Setting them in secpol.msc on a DC changes nothing useful.
    • User rights and many security options on DCs come from the Default Domain Controllers Policy (linked to the Domain Controllers OU).
    • A setting that no domain GPO defines does take effect from local policy, but on a DC edit the GPOs anyway so the scoring engine and gpresult agree (GPO guide).

    #Defender on Server

    • Microsoft Defender Antivirus is the removable feature Windows-Defender. If it is gone, reinstall it (how).
    • Server roles get automatic exclusions (AD database, SYSVOL, DNS, DHCP, IIS paths). They do not show in Get-MpPreference and they are normal. Remove only exclusions that Get-MpPreference lists.
    • Defender on Server does not switch itself to passive mode when another antivirus is installed.

    Everything else (real-time protection, scans, policy keys) works as on Windows 11 (Defender).

    #What IE Enhanced Security Configuration does

    Server Manager > Local Server > IE Enhanced Security Configuration. Keep it On for both Administrators and Users; turning it off is a classic planted weakness. It only affects Internet Explorer, so download any tool you need with Edge (how).

    #sconfig menu on Server 2022

    Run sconfig in an elevated PowerShell or command prompt. It starts by itself only on Server Core; on Desktop Experience you type it. Server 2019 uses the same option numbers, but its update prompts use letters instead of the numbered sub-menu (2019 differences).

    Option Does
    1 Domain or workgroup membership
    2 Computer name
    3 Add local administrator (not used on a DC)
    4 Remote management (WinRM)
    5 Update setting: A Automatic, D Download only, M Manual
    6 Install updates: 1 all quality updates, 2 recommended quality updates, 3 feature updates
    7 Remote desktop
    8 Network settings
    9 Date and time
    10 Telemetry setting
    11 Windows activation
    12 Log off user
    13 Restart server
    14 Shut down server
    15 Exit to command line (PowerShell)

    #Server-only services you will see

    Service name Display name Belongs to
    NTDS Active Directory Domain Services DC
    Kdc Kerberos Key Distribution Center DC
    Netlogon Netlogon DC (also runs on members)
    ADWS Active Directory Web Services DC; AD PowerShell and ADAC need it
    DFSR DFS Replication DC; replicates SYSVOL
    Dfs DFS Namespace DC; serves the \\<domain-name>\SYSVOL path
    IsmServ Intersite Messaging DC
    DNS DNS Server DNS role
    DHCPServer DHCP Server DHCP role
    W3SVC and WAS World Wide Web Publishing Service, Windows Process Activation Service IIS
    ftpsvc Microsoft FTP Service IIS FTP
    WMSVC Web Management Service IIS remote management
    CertSvc Active Directory Certificate Services AD CS
    RemoteAccess Routing and Remote Access Remote Access role

    #Ports a domain controller needs open

    The AD DS and DNS roles create firewall rules for these. If you tighten the firewall on a DC, keep these inbound rules and do not delete the role rule groups.

    Port Protocol Use
    53 TCP and UDP DNS
    88 TCP and UDP Kerberos
    123 UDP Time (W32Time)
    135 TCP RPC endpoint mapper
    389 TCP and UDP LDAP
    445 TCP SMB (SYSVOL, NETLOGON, GPOs)
    464 TCP and UDP Kerberos password change
    636 TCP LDAPS
    3268 and 3269 TCP Global Catalog and Global Catalog over SSL
    9389 TCP AD Web Services
    49152-65535 TCP Dynamic RPC (replication, management)
    67 UDP DHCP (DHCP role only)
    80 and 443 TCP IIS (web role only)
    21 TCP FTP (FTP role only, plus its passive range)
    3389 TCP RDP (only if required)
    5985 and 5986 TCP WinRM HTTP and HTTPS

    Everything else about the firewall works as on Windows 11 (firewall). Never block outbound traffic.

    PreviousServer master checklistNextAD users and groups
    SRV

    AD users and groups

    jump:srv-ad-users

    This applies on a DC (or a member server with the RSAT AD tools). On a standalone server use Windows 11 users.

    The README is the only list that counts

    Remove or disable exactly the users the README does not authorize, and follow its wording ("remove" or "disable"). Never delete krbtgt, the built-in Administrator you are logged in as, or computer accounts. If the README says someone is a standard user, take them out of every admin group and keep the account.

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator and load the AD module:

      Import-Module ActiveDirectory

    2. List every domain user and compare with the README:

      Get-ADUser -Filter * | Sort-Object SamAccountName | Format-Table Name,SamAccountName,Enabled -AutoSize

    3. Disable a user the README does not list (or remove them if it says remove):

      Disable-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    4. List Domain Admins and remove anyone the README does not name as an admin:

      Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Select-Object SamAccountName

      Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members <username> -Confirm:$false

    5. Check the other privileged groups (table).

    6. Disable Guest and clear the risky account flags (flags).

    #Open the ADUC and ADAC consoles

    • Active Directory Users and Computers: Win+R, type dsa.msc (or Server Manager > Tools > Active Directory Users and Computers).
    • In ADUC turn on View > Advanced Features. Without it you cannot see the Attribute Editor tab, the System container or the Object tab with deletion protection.
    • Active Directory Administrative Center: Win+R, type dsac.exe. It has a global search box and a PowerShell History pane at the bottom that shows the cmdlet behind every GUI action.
    • Users and groups live mostly in the Users and Builtin containers, but attackers also create OUs. Expand every OU.

    #List every domain user

    Get-ADUser -Filter * | Sort-Object SamAccountName | Format-Table Name,SamAccountName,Enabled -AutoSize

    All properties of one user (description, logon script, flags, group memberships):

    Get-ADUser -Identity <username> -Properties *

    Risky flags for every user in one table:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNeverExpires,PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption,CannotChangePassword,AdminCount | Format-Table SamAccountName,Enabled,PasswordNeverExpires,PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption,CannotChangePassword,AdminCount -AutoSize

    #Read the description and logon script fields

    Attackers and Forensics Questions hide passwords in the Description field and malicious logon scripts in ScriptPath (they run from \\<domain-name>\NETLOGON). List every user that has either:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description,ScriptPath | Where-Object { $_.Description -or $_.ScriptPath } | Select-Object SamAccountName,Description,ScriptPath

    Open a script it names from C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol\<domain-name>\scripts.

    #Compare AD users to the README

    Save the authorized usernames (sAMAccountName, one per line) as authorized.txt on the desktop, then list every account that is not on it. Built-in accounts are skipped:

    $authorized = Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\authorized.txt" | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } | Where-Object { $_ }
$builtin = 'Administrator','Guest','krbtgt'
Get-ADUser -Filter * | Where-Object { $authorized -notcontains $_.SamAccountName -and $builtin -notcontains $_.SamAccountName } | Select-Object SamAccountName,Name,Enabled

    Every name it prints is not in the README. Do the same for admins with admins.txt:

    $admins = Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\admins.txt" | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } | Where-Object { $_ }
Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Where-Object { $admins -notcontains $_.SamAccountName -and $_.SamAccountName -ne 'Administrator' } | Select-Object SamAccountName,objectClass

    #Check privileged group membership

    This loop prints the members of every privileged group. -Recursive expands nested groups, so a user hidden inside another group still shows up:

    $groups = 'Domain Admins','Enterprise Admins','Schema Admins','Administrators','Account Operators','Backup Operators','Server Operators','Print Operators','DnsAdmins','Group Policy Creator Owners','Remote Desktop Users','Remote Management Users','Protected Users'
foreach ($g in $groups) {
  "=== $g ==="
  try { Get-ADGroupMember -Identity $g -Recursive -ErrorAction Stop | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SamAccountName }
  catch { "  (error or group not present: $($_.Exception.Message))" }
}

    -Recursive flattens groups, so Builtin Administrators shows users only. To see which groups are nested directly inside it, drop -Recursive:

    Get-ADGroupMember -Identity Administrators | Select-Object SamAccountName,objectClass

    Expected defaults on a fresh Server 2022 domain:

    Group Container Expected members Why it matters
    Domain Admins Users Administrator plus README admins Full control of the domain
    Enterprise Admins Users (forest root only) Administrator Full control of the forest
    Schema Admins Users (forest root only) Administrator Can change the AD schema
    Administrators Builtin Administrator, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins Full control of every DC
    Account Operators Builtin Empty Can create and change most users and groups
    Backup Operators Builtin Empty Can back up ntds.dit, which holds every password hash
    Server Operators Builtin Empty Can log on to DCs, change services, back up
    Print Operators Builtin Empty Can log on to DCs and load printer drivers
    DnsAdmins Users (exists only with the DNS role) Empty Can make the DNS service load a DLL as SYSTEM on the DC
    Group Policy Creator Owners Users Administrator Can create GPOs
    Remote Desktop Users Builtin Empty, or README RDP users RDP access
    Remote Management Users Builtin Empty WinRM and PowerShell remoting access
    Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access Builtin Authenticated Users Everyone or ANONYMOUS LOGON here allows anonymous users to read AD (fix)
    Protected Users Users Empty (optional hardening) Details

    In the GUI: dsa.msc > Users (or Builtin) > double-click the group > Members tab.

    #Remove a user from a privileged group

    Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members <username> -Confirm:$false

    GUI: dsa.msc > Users > Domain Admins > Members tab > select the user > Remove > OK.

    Check Domain Admins and Builtin Administrators

    A user added directly to Builtin\Administrators is a full admin on every DC but does not appear in Domain Admins. Check Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins as well. Group changes take effect at that user's next logon.

    #Find users hidden through primary group

    A user whose primary group is Domain Admins (RID 512) does not appear in the group's member attribute. Get-ADGroupMember and ADUC still show them, but list every user whose primary group is not Domain Users to be sure:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PrimaryGroupID | Where-Object { $_.PrimaryGroupID -ne 513 -and $_.SamAccountName -ne 'Guest' } | Select-Object SamAccountName,PrimaryGroupID
    PrimaryGroupID Group
    513 Domain Users (normal)
    514 Domain Guests (normal for Guest)
    512 Domain Admins
    518 Schema Admins
    519 Enterprise Admins

    To fix one: dsa.msc > user > Member Of tab > select Domain Users > Set Primary Group, then remove the admin group.

    #Add a README-required admin

    Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members <username>

    If the README says "administrator" without naming a group, Domain Admins is the normal choice on a DC; it is already nested in Builtin Administrators.

    #Disable or remove an unauthorized user

    Disable the account:

    Disable-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    Or delete it, if the README says remove:

    Remove-ADUser -Identity <username> -Confirm:$false

    dsa.msc > right-click the user > Disable Account, or Delete.

    Check the result. Enabled should be False, or you get "Cannot find an object" after removal:

    Get-ADUser -Identity <username>

    If Remove-ADUser fails with "Access is denied" even as Domain Admin, the object is protected from accidental deletion. Clear the protection, then delete again:

    Get-ADUser -Identity <username> | Set-ADObject -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $false

    In ADUC (with Advanced Features on): user > Properties > Object tab > clear Protect object from accidental deletion.

    #Disable the domain Guest account

    Disable-ADAccount -Identity Guest
Get-ADUser -Identity Guest | Select-Object Name,Enabled

    Enabled should read False.

    #The domain Administrator account

    • Do not disable the built-in Administrator if you are logged in as it or the README names it as your account.
    • Give it a strong password if the README allows changing it.
    • Rename it only if the README asks, with the GPO setting Accounts: Rename administrator account in the Default Domain Policy. You must then log in with the new name.

    #Reset a user's password

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity <username> -Reset -NewPassword $pw

    GUI: dsa.msc > right-click the user > Reset Password. Use the team password unless the README gives one.

    #Reset every user's password at once

    Run this only if the README or scoring points at weak passwords. It skips you and the built-in accounts, and prints each name it changes:

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
Get-ADUser -Filter 'Enabled -eq $true' | Where-Object { $_.SamAccountName -notin @($env:USERNAME,'Administrator','krbtgt','Guest') } | ForEach-Object { Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity $_ -Reset -NewPassword $pw; $_.SamAccountName }

    The policy can reject the reset

    "The password does not meet the length, complexity, or history requirement" means the new password breaks the domain policy. An admin reset still has to meet the minimum length and complexity (minimum age and history are not checked on a reset). Use a longer password.

    #Fix dangerous account flags

    These are the Account options on dsa.msc > user > Properties > Account tab.

    Property Checkbox in ADUC Want Fix
    PasswordNeverExpires Password never expires False Set-ADUser <username> -PasswordNeverExpires $false
    PasswordNotRequired No checkbox (userAccountControl flag 32) False Set-ADUser <username> -PasswordNotRequired $false
    CannotChangePassword User cannot change password False Set-ADUser <username> -CannotChangePassword $false
    AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption Store password using reversible encryption False Set-ADUser <username> -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $false
    DoesNotRequirePreAuth Do not require Kerberos preauthentication False Set-ADAccountControl <username> -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false
    UseDESKeyOnly Use only Kerberos DES encryption types for this account False Set-ADAccountControl <username> -UseDESKeyOnly $false
    AccountNotDelegated Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated True for admins Set-ADUser <username> -AccountNotDelegated $true
    TrustedForDelegation Delegation tab: Trust this user for delegation to any service False for users Set-ADAccountControl <username> -TrustedForDelegation $false

    Set-ADUser has no preauth or DES switch, which is why those two rows use Set-ADAccountControl.

    Fix every user at once. The block reads all users once, then clears each flag only where it is set. Guest and krbtgt are skipped where it matters:

    $all = Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNeverExpires,PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption,CannotChangePassword,UseDESKeyOnly
$all | Where-Object PasswordNotRequired | Set-ADUser -PasswordNotRequired $false
$all | Where-Object DoesNotRequirePreAuth | Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false
$all | Where-Object AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption | Set-ADUser -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $false
$all | Where-Object UseDESKeyOnly | Set-ADAccountControl -UseDESKeyOnly $false
$all | Where-Object { $_.CannotChangePassword -and $_.SamAccountName -ne 'Guest' } | Set-ADUser -CannotChangePassword $false
$all | Where-Object { $_.PasswordNeverExpires -and $_.SamAccountName -notin @('krbtgt','Guest') } | Set-ADUser -PasswordNeverExpires $false

    Verify

    Both commands should print nothing except accounts you deliberately left alone (Guest, a README service account):

    Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly | Select-Object SamAccountName

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption | Where-Object { $_.PasswordNotRequired -or $_.DoesNotRequirePreAuth -or $_.AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption } | Select-Object SamAccountName

    Before clearing Password never expires on your own account

    If your logon account's password is older than the maximum password age, you will be forced to change it at next logon. Know its password (or reset it to the team password) first. A README-listed service account may legitimately need a non-expiring password.

    Clearing PasswordNotRequired only stops future blank passwords. A user who already has a blank password keeps it, so reset the password of every user that had the flag.

    Why these flags are scored

    With DoesNotRequirePreAuth set, anyone can request an encrypted blob for that user and crack it offline (AS-REP roasting). Reversible encryption stores a recoverable password. Accounts with a service principal name (SPN) can be Kerberoasted: anyone can request a service ticket and crack it offline, so they need long passwords. DES keys are trivially broken.

    #Find accounts with SPNs (Kerberoastable)

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'ServicePrincipalName -like "*"' -Properties ServicePrincipalName | Select-Object SamAccountName,@{n='SPNs';e={$_.ServicePrincipalName -join '; '}}
    • krbtgt always has kadmin/changepw. That is normal.
    • Any other user with an SPN is a service account. If the README does not mention it, remove the SPN or at least give the account a long password:
    Set-ADUser <username> -ServicePrincipalNames @{Remove='<spn>'}

    #Find accounts that were once admins (AdminCount)

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'AdminCount -eq 1' | Select-Object SamAccountName

    AdminCount=1 is stamped on members of protected groups (Domain Admins, Administrators, Account, Backup, Server and Print Operators and others) and is not cleared when the user leaves the group. Use the list to find former admins and confirm they are out of every privileged group.

    Clearing it is optional. Clear the attribute, then turn permission inheritance back on in dsa.msc > user > Security tab > Advanced > Enable inheritance:

    Set-ADUser <username> -Clear adminCount

    #Search-ADAccount quick finds

    Find Command
    Passwords that never expire Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly
    Disabled users Search-ADAccount -AccountDisabled -UsersOnly
    Locked-out users Search-ADAccount -LockedOut -UsersOnly
    Expired passwords Search-ADAccount -PasswordExpired -UsersOnly
    No logon in 90 days Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -UsersOnly
    Expired accounts Search-ADAccount -AccountExpired -UsersOnly

    Clear the lockout on an authorized user:

    Unlock-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    Enable an authorized user who is disabled:

    Enable-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    #Create users and groups the README asks for

    Create the user with the team password, enabled. Without -Path it lands in the Users container:

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
New-ADUser -Name "<username>" -SamAccountName "<username>" -UserPrincipalName "<username>@<domain-name>" -AccountPassword $pw -Enabled $true

    To put it in an OU, add -Path "<ou-dn>", where the OU's distinguished name looks like OU=Staff,DC=corp,DC=local.

    Create a global security group and add members:

    New-ADGroup -Name "<groupname>" -GroupScope Global -GroupCategory Security
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "<groupname>" -Members <username>

    Check it: Get-ADGroupMember "<groupname>" | Select-Object SamAccountName.

    GUI: dsa.msc > right-click Users > New > User (or Group, with scope Global and type Security).

    Copy names exactly

    Scoring checks the exact sAMAccountName and group name from the README. Copy and paste them.

    #Check computer accounts, SIDHistory and logon scripts

    List computer objects. Remove an unknown one only if it is clearly rogue (rarely scored) and never delete the DC:

    Get-ADComputer -Filter * | Select-Object Name,Enabled

    SIDHistory is an advanced backdoor and should be empty in a fresh domain:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory | Where-Object SIDHistory | Select-Object SamAccountName,SIDHistory

    Users with a logon script. Inspect each script in C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol\<domain-name>\scripts:

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'ScriptPath -like "*"' -Properties ScriptPath | Select-Object SamAccountName,ScriptPath
    PreviousHow Server differs from Windows 11NextGroup Policy on a domain
    SRV

    Group Policy on a domain

    jump:srv-gpo

    On a DC the domain GPOs hold password, lockout, Kerberos, audit, user rights and security options. secpol.msc on a DC edits only local policy, which domain GPOs override (why).

    Back up GPOs before editing

    One wrong user right in the Default Domain Controllers Policy can lock everyone out of the DC. Back up first (how) and keep an elevated PowerShell window open while you edit.

    Fast path

    1. Back up every GPO from an elevated PowerShell window:

      New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\GPOBackup -Force | Out-Null
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\GPOBackup

    2. Run gpmc.msc and open Forest > Domains > your domain. Right-click Default Domain Policy > Edit.

    3. Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies and set Password Policy and Account Lockout Policy from the tables below.

    4. Apply and check the result:

      gpupdate /force
Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

    5. Set audit policy, user rights and security options in the Default Domain Controllers Policy instead (how).

    6. List every GPO and its links and look for planted ones (how).

    #Which GPO holds which setting

    Setting Edit it in Linked at
    Password policy, account lockout, Kerberos policy Default Domain Policy (or another GPO linked at the domain root) Domain root
    Audit policy, user rights assignment Default Domain Controllers Policy Domain Controllers OU
    DC security options (LDAP signing, SMB signing, NTLM) Default Domain Controllers Policy Domain Controllers OU
    Security options for every computer in the domain Default Domain Policy Domain root
    Administrative Templates (Defender, Windows Update, RDP) for DCs Default Domain Controllers Policy, or the GPO already setting it Domain Controllers OU

    Account policies set in an OU-linked GPO or in the Default Domain Controllers Policy do nothing for domain accounts. They only work from a GPO linked at the domain root.

    #Back up and restore GPOs

    Back up all GPOs (create the folder first):

    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\GPOBackup -Force | Out-Null
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\GPOBackup

    Restore one GPO from that backup:

    Restore-GPO -Name "<gpo-name>" -Path C:\GPOBackup

    #Open the Group Policy Management console

    Run gpmc.msc (or Server Manager > Tools > Group Policy Management) and expand Forest > Domains > your domain.

    • GPOs linked directly under the domain node (for example Default Domain Policy) apply to every user and computer in the domain.
    • The Domain Controllers OU has Default Domain Controllers Policy linked, which applies to DCs only.
    • The Group Policy Objects container lists every GPO, linked or not.

    To edit, right-click the GPO or its link > Edit. Every security setting is under Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings.

    #Set the domain password policy

    Path: gpmc.msc > Default Domain Policy > Edit > Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy.

    Setting Recommended Default in a new domain
    Enforce password history 24 passwords remembered 24
    Maximum password age 60 days (30-90 is fine) 42
    Minimum password age 1 day 1
    Minimum password length 14 characters (at least 10) 7
    Password must meet complexity requirements Enabled Enabled
    Store passwords using reversible encryption Disabled Disabled

    The editor accepts at most 14 for minimum length unless Relax minimum password length limits (same folder) is Enabled. 14 is enough for CyberPatriot. Never set a length your own team password does not meet.

    #Set the domain lockout policy

    Path: same GPO > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy.

    Setting Recommended Default
    Account lockout threshold 5 to 10 invalid attempts (never 0) 0 (no lockout)
    Account lockout duration 30 minutes or more Not defined
    Reset account lockout counter after 30 minutes (no longer than the duration) Not defined

    Setting the threshold makes the editor offer values for the other two; accept them, then change them to the table values. Fully updated builds may also show Allow Administrator account lockout, which applies to local Administrator accounts; leave it at its default unless the README mentions it.

    #Check the Kerberos policy

    Path: same GPO > Account Policies > Kerberos Policy. These settings exist only in domain GPOs. The defaults are already secure, so scoring checks that nobody weakened them.

    Setting Secure value (default)
    Enforce user logon restrictions Enabled
    Maximum lifetime for service ticket 600 minutes
    Maximum lifetime for user ticket 10 hours
    Maximum lifetime for user ticket renewal 7 days
    Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization 5 minutes

    #Apply and verify the domain password policy

    gpupdate /force
net accounts

    Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

    On a DC, net accounts shows the domain values. Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy reads them straight from the domain object. If they disagree, run gpupdate /force again after a minute.

    #Set the domain password policy with PowerShell

    This writes the domain object directly. Time spans use days.hours:minutes:seconds, so 60.00:00:00 is 60 days and 00:30:00 is 30 minutes. The observation window must not be longer than the lockout duration.

    Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy -Identity (Get-ADDomain).DNSRoot -MinPasswordLength 14 -PasswordHistoryCount 24 -MaxPasswordAge 60.00:00:00 -MinPasswordAge 1.00:00:00 -ComplexityEnabled $true -ReversibleEncryptionEnabled $false -LockoutThreshold 5 -LockoutDuration 00:30:00 -LockoutObservationWindow 00:30:00
Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

    The GPO overwrites the PowerShell change

    The next time the Default Domain Policy is processed (an edit to the GPO, gpupdate /force, or the periodic security refresh), its values overwrite what Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy wrote. Make the GPO match, or the change silently reverts.

    #Find and fix fine-grained password policies

    Fine-grained password policies (Password Settings Objects, PSOs) override the domain policy for the users and groups they apply to. Attackers plant weak ones (length 0, no complexity, no lockout) on Domain Users or on one admin.

    List every PSO with its settings:

    Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Filter * | Format-List Name,Precedence,MinPasswordLength,ComplexityEnabled,PasswordHistoryCount,MaxPasswordAge,MinPasswordAge,LockoutThreshold,LockoutDuration,ReversibleEncryptionEnabled,AppliesTo

    See which PSO actually applies to one user. No output means the domain policy applies:

    Get-ADUserResultantPasswordPolicy -Identity <username>

    Strengthen a PSO the README wants kept:

    Set-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Identity "<pso-name>" -MinPasswordLength 14 -ComplexityEnabled $true -PasswordHistoryCount 24 -LockoutThreshold 5 -ReversibleEncryptionEnabled $false

    Delete a PSO the README does not mention. Clear its deletion protection first:

    Set-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Identity "<pso-name>" -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $false
