    #Ubuntu 24.04 starts SSH from a socket

    On Ubuntu 24.04, ssh.socket owns port 22 and starts ssh.service when the first connection arrives. Until then systemctl is-active ssh can print inactive even though SSH works, and ss -tlnp shows systemd (not sshd) on port 22. Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian use the plain ssh.service.

    Check both units:

    systemctl status ssh.socket ssh.service --no-pager
    Task Ubuntu 24.04 command
    Apply a normal sshd_config change sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh
    Apply a Port or ListenAddress change sudo systemctl daemon-reload then sudo systemctl restart ssh.socket
    Turn SSH off without removing it sudo systemctl disable --now ssh.socket ssh.service
    Turn SSH on (README requires it) sudo systemctl enable --now ssh.socket

    On 24.04 a systemd generator reads Port and ListenAddress from sshd_config, so the daemon-reload is what makes a port change take effect. Disabling only ssh.service leaves the socket listening, and the next connection starts SSH again.

    When SSH is a critical service, you can make ssh.service run all the time so a status check always shows active. This is the revert procedure from Ubuntu's announcement:

    sudo systemctl disable --now ssh.socket
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/ssh.service.d/00-socket.conf
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/ssh.socket.d/addresses.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now ssh.service

    Check with systemctl is-active ssh (prints active) and sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':22 ' (shows sshd).

    #Review authorized_keys

    List and print every authorized_keys file on the disk:

    sudo find / -xdev \( -name authorized_keys -o -name authorized_keys2 \) -exec ls -la {} \; -exec cat {} \; 2>/dev/null

    Check whether the key file location was changed:

    sudo grep -ri AuthorizedKeysFile /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
    • Remove keys the README did not authorize, especially in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys and for unauthorized users. Note the key comment for Forensics first.
    • Look for unexpected command= or from= options at the start of a key line.
    • An AuthorizedKeysFile pointing at an odd path (for example /tmp/keys) is a backdoor.
    • ~/.ssh should be 700 and authorized_keys 600, owned by the user.

    Fix the permissions for one user:

    sudo chmod 700 /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R <username>:<username> /home/<username>/.ssh

    #Check other SSH files

    • /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key must be 600 root:root, and the *.pub files 644.
    • /etc/hosts.equiv, ~/.rhosts and ~/.shosts should not exist.
    • /etc/ssh/sshrc and ~/.ssh/rc run at every login and should not exist unless you know why.
    • ~/.ssh/environment is only used with PermitUserEnvironment yes; delete planted ones.

    Pair SSH with the firewall: allow it before enabling ufw, consider sudo ufw limit OpenSSH (firewall), and set up fail2ban (how).

    #Remove SSH when it is not required

    Scored as "OpenSSH service is disabled or removed" on a Mint image (R2) where the README did not list SSH. When the README does list SSH, removing it is a penalty ("OpenSSH service has been stopped or removed", K6).

    Answer any Forensics Question about SSH keys or logins first, then purge the server. The openssh-client package (the ssh command) can stay:

    sudo apt purge openssh-server

    Check that nothing listens on port 22: sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':22 ' prints nothing. Purging removes ssh.socket on Ubuntu 24.04 too; if you only disable instead, disable both ssh.socket and ssh.service.

    Verify

    sudo sshd -T | grep -iE 'permitrootlogin|permitemptypasswords|x11forwarding|maxauthtries' prints permitrootlogin no, permitemptypasswords no, x11forwarding no and maxauthtries 3, and systemctl is-active ssh prints active (on Ubuntu 24.04, systemctl is-active ssh.socket).

    PreviousServices and open portsNextHardening required services (FTP, Apache, Samba, MySQL, PHP, nginx, mail)
    LNX

    Hardening required services (FTP, Apache, Samba, MySQL, PHP, nginx, mail)

    jump:lin-required-services

    Never remove a service the README calls critical

    A required service that stops, gets purged or fails its functional check costs points every scoring cycle. Harden it in place, test the config, and confirm it is still running after every change.

    Fast path

    1. Find which server services are installed and running:

      systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | grep -E 'vsftpd|proftpd|pure-ftpd|apache2|nginx|smbd|nmbd|mysql|mariadb|php|postfix|dovecot'

    2. Compare with the README. Keep and harden the ones it requires; the rest belong in Services and open ports.

    3. Back up the service's config folder (paths in the table below):

      sudo cp -a <path> /root/

    4. Set the values from that service's subsection on this page.

    5. Run the service's syntax test from the table, then restart it:

      sudo systemctl restart <service-name>

    6. Confirm it is running and still works:

      systemctl is-active <service-name>

    This page is the short version for each service. Deeper checks, the README decision (remove or harden), Debian and Fedora paths, and update steps are in Web servers, PHP and WordPress, Databases, FTP, Samba and NFS and Mail, DNS and other daemons.

    #Config files and test commands

    Service systemd unit Main config Syntax test
    vsftpd vsftpd /etc/vsftpd.conf none; read journalctl -u vsftpd after restart
    ProFTPD proftpd /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf sudo proftpd -t
    Pure-FTPd pure-ftpd /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/ (one file per option) read journalctl -u pure-ftpd
    Apache apache2 /etc/apache2/ sudo apache2ctl configtest
    nginx nginx /etc/nginx/ sudo nginx -t
    PHP 8.1 apache2 or php8.1-fpm /etc/php/8.1/ php -l <file> for scripts
    Samba smbd, nmbd /etc/samba/smb.conf testparm -s
    MySQL 8.0 mysql /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf sudo mysqld --validate-config
    MariaDB 10.6 mariadb /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf read journalctl -u mariadb
    Postfix postfix /etc/postfix/main.cf sudo postfix check
    Dovecot dovecot /etc/dovecot/conf.d/ sudo doveconf -n

    Ubuntu 22.04 ships PHP 8.1, MySQL 8.0, MariaDB 10.6, Samba 4.15, Apache 2.4.52, nginx 1.18, vsftpd 3.0.5 and Postfix 3.6. Mint 21 uses the same packages.

    #Harden vsftpd (FTP)

    Back up and open the config:

    sudo cp -a /etc/vsftpd.conf /root/vsftpd.conf.bak
sudo nano /etc/vsftpd.conf

    Set these lines (change the existing line if it is there, add it if not):

    anonymous_enable=NO
anon_upload_enable=NO
anon_mkdir_write_enable=NO
local_enable=YES
write_enable=NO
chroot_local_user=YES
xferlog_enable=YES
ssl_enable=YES
allow_anon_ssl=NO
force_local_logins_ssl=YES
force_local_data_ssl=YES
rsa_cert_file=/etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem
rsa_private_key_file=/etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key
    Setting Why
    anonymous_enable=NO No anonymous FTP (already NO in the Ubuntu default file, but planted images flip it)
    write_enable YES only if the README says users upload files; otherwise NO
    chroot_local_user=YES Users are locked into their home directory
    allow_writeable_chroot=YES Add only if chroot plus a writable home is needed (see "If it fails" below)
    ssl_enable=YES and the two force_local_* lines Encrypt logins and data with TLS
    rsa_cert_file / rsa_private_key_file The snakeoil certificate from the ssl-cert package; these two lines are already in the default file
    xferlog_enable=YES Log transfers to /var/log/vsftpd.log

    To allow only listed users, also add userlist_enable=YES, userlist_deny=NO and userlist_file=/etc/vsftpd.userlist, then put one username per line in that file.

    /etc/ftpusers is the opposite list: users who may never use FTP. It is read through PAM (/etc/pam.d/vsftpd) and root is in it by default; keep it there. The same PAM file also requires the user's shell to be listed in /etc/shells, so an FTP user whose shell you set to nologin can no longer log in to FTP.

    Check that the certificate exists before turning on TLS:

    ls -l /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key

    If either file is missing, install the package and generate it:

    sudo apt install ssl-cert
sudo make-ssl-cert generate-default-snakeoil --force-overwrite

    Restart and confirm:

    sudo systemctl restart vsftpd
systemctl is-active vsftpd

    If it fails: 500 OOPS: vsftpd: refusing to run with writable root inside chroot() means the user's home is writable while chroot_local_user=YES. Add allow_writeable_chroot=YES and restart. If ssl_enable=YES makes the README's FTP clients fail, set it back to NO (one lost item is better than a broken required service).

    "FTP users may log in with SSL" was scored on a Mint 21 Round 2 image (R2) where vsftpd was required. "Vsftpd has been updated" appeared on the same image: sudo apt install --only-upgrade vsftpd.

    #Fix permissions on the FTP root directory

    Scored in a past Mint key (R2). Find the folder vsftpd serves:

    grep -E '^\s*(local_root|anon_root|user_sub_token)' /etc/vsftpd.conf
getent passwd ftp

    With no local_root line, local users land in their home folder; anonymous users land in the ftp user's home (/srv/ftp on Ubuntu, Mint and Debian). Check the mode:

    stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' <path>

    A mode ending in 7, 6, 3 or 2 (for example 777) is world-writable. Remove world write and give the folder to root:

    sudo chmod 755 <path>
sudo chown root:root <path>

    If users must upload, give them a subfolder they own instead of a writable root. Full walkthrough in FTP, Samba and NFS.

    #Other FTP servers

    ProFTPD: in /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf keep the <Anonymous ~ftp> block commented out or deleted, and set:

    DefaultRoot ~
ServerIdent off
RequireValidShell on

    Test with sudo proftpd -t, then sudo systemctl restart proftpd. TLS settings live in /etc/proftpd/tls.conf.

    Pure-FTPd keeps one option per file. Turn off anonymous logins and lock users into their homes:

    echo yes | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/NoAnonymous
echo yes | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/ChrootEveryone
sudo systemctl restart pure-ftpd

    #Harden Apache2

    Scored in past keys: "Apache server tokens set to least" and "Apache trace requests disabled" (Hivestorm wording), "Apache has been updated" (G1). When Apache is not required, "Apache2 service has been disabled or removed" (R1, SR2) is the item instead; see Web servers.

    Back up the whole config folder:

    sudo cp -a /etc/apache2 /root/apache2.bak

    Open /etc/apache2/conf-available/security.conf (it is enabled by default) and set these three lines. The Ubuntu defaults are ServerTokens OS and ServerSignature On.

    ServerTokens Prod
ServerSignature Off
TraceEnable Off

    In /etc/apache2/apache2.conf, find the <Directory /var/www/> block. Ubuntu ships it with Options Indexes FollowSymLinks, which lists folder contents to anyone. Change it to:

    <Directory /var/www/>
    Options -Indexes +FollowSymLinks
    AllowOverride None
    Require all granted
</Directory>

    Leave AllowOverride None unless the site needs .htaccess files. The <Directory /> block above it must stay Require all denied; a planted image may have changed it to granted.

    Optional security headers go in security.conf. They need the headers module:

    sudo a2enmod headers

    Header set X-Content-Type-Options: "nosniff"
Header set X-Frame-Options: "sameorigin"

    Enable the security config (it is on by default; this puts it back if someone disabled it):

    sudo a2enconf security

    Disable modules the site does not use. autoindex and status are on by default; -f skips the "essential module" prompt for autoindex:

    sudo a2dismod -f autoindex status

    If the README's site is a different virtual host, disable the default one:

    sudo a2dissite 000-default

    Test, then restart. The test must print Syntax OK:

    sudo apache2ctl configtest
sudo systemctl restart apache2

    #Clean up the web root

    After answering forensics questions, remove files in /var/www/html that are not part of the site (phpinfo.php, info.php, shell.php, backup.zip, a .git folder). Past keys scored "phpinfo file removed" (/var/www/html/info.php, G1) and a PHP web shell (/var/www/html/r57.php, G1). The engine also checked that wp-login.php still existed, so delete only the bad file, never the folder. Search for web shells:

    sudo grep -rlE 'eval\(|base64_decode|system\(|shell_exec|passthru' /var/www

    Make the site files owned by root, so www-data can read them but not change them. Skip this if the README says the site accepts uploads into a folder; that folder must stay writable by www-data.

    sudo chown -R root:root /var/www/html
sudo find /var/www/html -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +
sudo find /var/www/html -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +

    Apache must run as www-data, never root. Check /etc/apache2/envvars:

    grep -E 'APACHE_RUN_(USER|GROUP)' /etc/apache2/envvars

    You should see www-data on both lines. To turn on HTTPS when the README asks for it:

    sudo a2enmod ssl
sudo a2ensite default-ssl
sudo systemctl reload apache2

    #Harden nginx

    In /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, inside the http { block, the Ubuntu file has server_tokens off; commented out. Uncomment it or add these lines:

    server_tokens off;
autoindex off;

    Remove any autoindex on; lines:

    sudo grep -rn 'autoindex on' /etc/nginx/

    Optional headers, inside the same http { block or a server { block:

    add_header X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN;
add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;

    Test and reload:

    sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

    #Harden PHP

    Scored in past keys: "PHP expose_php disabled" (G1), "PHP does not display errors" and "PHP display errors has been disabled" (Hivestorm). The Ubuntu defaults are already Off, so a scored image has had them switched On; check the exact file the web server loads.

    Each way of running PHP has its own php.ini. Edit the one the web server uses:

    Used by File
    Apache module (libapache2-mod-php8.1) /etc/php/8.1/apache2/php.ini
    PHP-FPM (usual with nginx) /etc/php/8.1/fpm/php.ini
    Command line only /etc/php/8.1/cli/php.ini 
    ls /etc/php/*/

    Set these values:

    Setting Value Ubuntu default
    expose_php Off Off
    display_errors Off Off
    log_errors On On
    allow_url_fopen Off if the site does not fetch URLs On
    allow_url_include Off Off
    file_uploads Off if the site has no upload form On
    disable_functions exec,passthru,shell_exec,system,proc_open,popen,pcntl_exec empty
    session.cookie_httponly 1 empty
    session.use_strict_mode 1 0

    Test the site after setting disable_functions; some applications call exec.

    Restart whichever runs PHP:

    sudo systemctl restart apache2

    sudo systemctl restart php8.1-fpm

    #Harden Samba

    Back up and edit:

    sudo cp -a /etc/samba/smb.conf /root/smb.conf.bak
sudo nano /etc/samba/smb.conf

    In [global] set these. Ubuntu's file ships with map to guest = bad user and usershare allow guests = yes, both of which you are replacing:

    map to guest = never
restrict anonymous = 2
server min protocol = SMB2
usershare allow guests = no
server signing = mandatory
server smb encrypt = required

    "Samba SMB1 protocol is disabled" and "Samba encryption is required" are Hivestorm items fixed with exactly these two lines. server smb encrypt is the current name; older guides and the key write smb encrypt, which Samba 4.15 and later still accept as a synonym. required refuses clients that cannot encrypt (anything older than SMB3, such as Windows 7); if the README names such a client, use desired and accept the lost item. server min protocol already defaults to SMB2_02 on this Samba version, but writing it out satisfies checks that read the file.

    In each share the README requires (for example [shared]):

    guest ok = no
browseable = yes
read only = yes
valid users = @<groupname> <username>
create mask = 0660
directory mask = 0770

    Use read only = no only if the README says users write to the share.

    Check the config and restart:

    testparm -s
sudo systemctl restart smbd nmbd

    #Remove extra shares and Samba users

    • Delete shares the README does not mention, and any share of /, /etc, /root or a home directory with write access.
    • [printers] and [print$] are in the default file; remove them if printing is not required. [homes] is commented out by default; remove or restrict it if someone enabled it.

    • Look for shares users created themselves:

      ls -la /var/lib/samba/usershares/

    Samba keeps its own password database. List Samba users:

    sudo pdbedit -L

    Remove an unauthorized one, or set a password for an authorized one:

    sudo smbpasswd -x <username>

    sudo smbpasswd -a <username>

    #Harden the MySQL or MariaDB server

    Run the secure installation script with sudo (without sudo it cannot log in, because root uses socket authentication):

    sudo mysql_secure_installation

    Answers, in order:

    1. VALIDATE PASSWORD component: y, then 1 (MEDIUM). It only checks passwords set from now on.
    2. On current Ubuntu 22.04 builds the script prints Skipping password set for root as authentication with auth_socket is used by default. That is correct; root logs in through sudo mysql and has no password to set.
    3. Remove anonymous users: y.
    4. Disallow root login remotely: y.
    5. Remove test database: y.
    6. Reload privilege tables: y.
    sudo mariadb-secure-installation

    sudo mysql_secure_installation runs the same script. Answers:

    1. Current root password: press Enter.
    2. Switch to unix_socket authentication: n (root already uses it on Ubuntu).
    3. Change the root password: y, then the team password unless the README gives one.
    4. Remove anonymous users, disallow root login remotely, remove test database, reload privilege tables: y to each.

    Older MySQL builds loop on the root password

    MySQL 8.0 builds from mid 2022 (around 8.0.29) loop forever on SET PASSWORD has no significance for user 'root'@'localhost'. Press Ctrl+C and do the same cleanup with the SQL commands below. Updating the package fixes the script.

    #Check database accounts by hand

    List every account and how it logs in:

    sudo mysql -e "SELECT user,host,plugin FROM mysql.user;"

    Expected on a clean MySQL 8.0: root@localhost with auth_socket, plus debian-sys-maint, mysql.infoschema, mysql.session and mysql.sys, all on localhost. Leave those system accounts alone.

    Remove anonymous accounts and remote root:

    sudo mysql -e "DROP USER IF EXISTS ''@'localhost';"
sudo mysql -e "DROP USER IF EXISTS ''@'<hostname>';"
sudo mysql -e "DROP USER IF EXISTS 'root'@'%';"

    Remove an account the README does not mention:

    sudo mysql -e "DROP USER '<username>'@'localhost';"

    See what an application account can do:

    sudo mysql -e "SHOW GRANTS FOR '<username>'@'localhost';"

    GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* or WITH GRANT OPTION on an application account is too much. Changing an application account's password breaks the site unless you also update the password in the site's config file, so only do it when the README asks.

    #Set the server options

    "MySQL remote access disabled" was scored in G1, which accepted either bind-address = 127.0.0.1 or skip-networking in the config. In /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf (MySQL) or /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf (MariaDB), under [mysqld]:

    bind-address = 127.0.0.1
local-infile = 0

    Ubuntu already sets bind-address = 127.0.0.1 (and mysqlx-bind-address = 127.0.0.1 for MySQL); check nobody changed it to 0.0.0.0. Leave it alone if the README says other machines connect to the database.

    Restart:

    sudo systemctl restart mysql

    sudo systemctl restart mariadb

    #Harden the Postfix and Dovecot mail servers

    When the README does not mention mail, the scored items are "SMTP service has been disabled or removed" and "POP3 service has been disabled or removed" (Hivestorm). Removal steps are in Mail, DNS and other daemons.

    Postfix settings go in /etc/postfix/main.cf:

    smtpd_banner = $myhostname ESMTP
disable_vrfy_command = yes
smtpd_helo_required = yes
mynetworks = 127.0.0.0/8 [::1]/128
inet_interfaces = loopback-only

    Use inet_interfaces = loopback-only only if the machine does not need to receive mail from other hosts. Otherwise keep inet_interfaces = all and confirm it is not an open relay:

    smtpd_relay_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated defer_unauth_destination

    Apply:

    sudo postfix check
sudo systemctl restart postfix

    Dovecot: set disable_plaintext_auth = yes in /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-auth.conf and ssl = required in /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-ssl.conf. Apply:

    sudo doveconf -n >/dev/null
sudo systemctl restart dovecot

    Verify every required service at the end

    systemctl is-active <service-name> prints active for each one, and a quick functional test works: open http://localhost in Firefox, run ftp localhost, or list shares with smbclient -L localhost -U <username>.

    Why services are scored this way

    Scoring checks a required service two ways: is it still running and reachable, and are specific insecure settings gone (anonymous FTP, directory listing, guest shares, anonymous database users). Losing the service costs more than any single setting earns, which is why every edit above ends with a syntax test and is-active.

    PreviousSSH server hardeningNextUnwanted software and hacking tools
    LNX

    Unwanted software and hacking tools

    jump:lin-software

    Read apt's removal list before typing Y

    Only remove software the README does not require. If apt purge lists mint-meta-*, cinnamon*, lightdm, slick-greeter, xserver-*, python3*, ubuntu-minimal or dozens of unrelated packages, answer n. Losing a meta-package looks harmless, but the next apt autoremove then strips the desktop.

    Fast path

    1. List installed packages that match known tools, games and P2P clients:

      dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Package}\n' | awk '$1=="ii" {print $2}' | grep -xE 'john|john-data|hydra|hydra-gtk|nmap|ndiff|zenmap|ncat|netcat-traditional|socat|aircrack-ng|wireshark|wireshark-qt|wireshark-gtk|tshark|ophcrack|ophcrack-cli|nikto|sqlmap|medusa|ncrack|ettercap-common|ettercap-graphical|ettercap-text-only|kismet|fcrackzip|pdfcrack|rarcrack|crack|crack-common|crack-md5|hashcat|dsniff|yersinia|macchanger|hping3|p0f|masscan|zmap|dirb|gobuster|wfuzz|bettercap|wifite|reaver|weevely|logkeys|rfdump|transmission-gtk|transmission-common|deluge|qbittorrent|ktorrent|amule|amule-daemon|amule-utils|amule-common|aisleriot|gnome-mines|gnome-sudoku|gameconqueror|scanmem|manaplus|manaplus-data|zangband|zangband-data|freeciv|freeciv-client-gtk|freeciv-client-gtk3|freeciv-client-qt|freeciv-server|freeciv-data|minetest|minetest-server|wesnoth|supertux|supertuxkart|openarena|0ad'

    2. Cross out anything the README requires.

    3. Purge the rest, reading the list apt prints before you answer:

      sudo apt purge <package>

    4. Clean up leftover dependencies (read this list too):

      sudo apt autoremove --purge

    5. Look for tools that apt does not know about (portable tools).

    The GUI route: Menu > Administration > Synaptic Package Manager, search the name, right-click > Mark for Complete Removal > Apply. Software Manager (Menu > Administration > Software Manager) also shows installed apps, including Flatpaks.

    #Catch renamed or unusual tools

    The exact-name list above misses tools with odd package names. A looser search catches more, with false positives:

    dpkg -l | grep -iE 'crack|sniff|scan|brute|keylog|torrent|exploit|game|backdoor'

    libcrack2 and cracklib-runtime will match crack. They are the password dictionary that libpam-pwquality uses, not hacking tools. Purging libcrack2 also removes libpwquality1, libpam-pwquality, gnome-disk-utility and seahorse, which breaks the password policy and can pull a Mint meta-package with it.

    #Common planted packages

    Packages seen in past Linux keys as "Prohibited software removed": Game Conqueror and ManaPlus (K6), aisleriot and ophcrack (R1), aMule, Wireshark and Zangband (R2), Kismet, ophcrack and Freeciv (SR2), John the Ripper and Nikto (G1), and Nmap, john, fcrackzip, dsniff and rfdump (Hivestorm). Wireshark was required software in other images, so read the README first.

    Names checked against the Ubuntu 22.04 (jammy) archive. "Multiverse" means the package is in jammy's multiverse component, which Mint enables. "Not in jammy" means apt cannot install it from the normal repositories; if it is on the image, someone installed it from a downloaded .deb, a third-party repository or source, and apt purge of that exact name only works if dpkg -l shows it.

    Tool Package name(s) on jammy Category
    John the Ripper john, john-data Password cracker
    Hydra hydra, hydra-gtk Login brute forcer
    Nmap nmap, ndiff Port scanner
    Zenmap not in jammy (Python 2 era GUI) Port scanner GUI
    ncat ncat Netcat clone, backdoor capable
    Wireshark wireshark, wireshark-qt, tshark, wireshark-common; wireshark-gtk is a dummy that pulls in wireshark-qt Sniffer
    Aircrack-ng aircrack-ng Wi-Fi cracker
    Ophcrack ophcrack, ophcrack-cli Password cracker
    Nikto nikto (multiverse) Web scanner
    sqlmap sqlmap SQL injection
    Medusa, Ncrack, Patator medusa, ncrack, patator Brute forcers
    Ettercap ettercap-graphical, ettercap-text-only, ettercap-common Man in the middle
    Bettercap bettercap Man in the middle
    Kismet not in jammy (vendor repository only) Wireless sniffer
    fcrackzip, pdfcrack, rarcrack same names File password crackers
    Crack crack, crack-common, crack-md5 Password cracker
    hashcat hashcat Password cracker
    dsniff dsniff Sniffer suite
    rfdump rfdump RFID sniffer
    Game Conqueror gameconqueror, scanmem Game memory cheat tool
    Wifite, Reaver wifite, reaver, pixiewps, cowpatty Wi-Fi attack
    masscan, zmap masscan, zmap Fast scanners
    dirb, gobuster, wfuzz same names Web content brute forcers
    Weevely weevely PHP web shell
    netcat (traditional) netcat-traditional Supports -e, so it can serve a shell
    socat socat Relay; remove unless required
    yersinia yersinia Layer 2 attacks
    macchanger macchanger MAC spoofing
    p0f, hping3, arpwatch, dnsrecon, netdiscover same names Recon
    RainbowCrack not packaged; look for rcrack in /opt and home folders Cracker
    Burp Suite not packaged; look for burpsuite*.jar or an install in /opt Web proxy
    Metasploit not in jammy; /opt/metasploit-framework, msfconsole Exploit framework
    logkeys, lkl not in jammy; look for the binaries and a logkeys service Keyloggers
    Torrent clients transmission-gtk, transmission-common, deluge, qbittorrent, ktorrent P2P (Mint ships Transmission; remove it if policy forbids P2P)
    aMule amule, amule-daemon, amule-utils, amule-common P2P (eDonkey)
    Games aisleriot, gnome-mines, gnome-sudoku, freeciv-client-gtk3, freeciv-server, freeciv-data, manaplus, manaplus-data, zangband and zangband-data (multiverse), minetest, minetest-server, wesnoth, supertux, supertuxkart, openarena, 0ad Games (policy). A game server such as minetest-server is also a service (other daemons)
    Remote access x11vnc, tigervnc-standalone-server, tightvncserver, xrdp, vino; teamviewer and anydesk are vendor .debs Remote control

    Old insecure servers such as telnetd, inetutils-telnetd, telnetd-ssl, rsh-server, rsh-redone-server, talkd, nis, tftpd-hpa, xinetd and openbsd-inetd all exist in jammy. Remove them unless the README needs them (Services and open ports).

    netcat: remove the right package

    netcat-openbsd is part of the base install, and ubuntu-minimal depends on it. Purging it removes that meta-package, and autoremove then removes much more. Remove netcat-traditional and ncat instead, then see what nc points to with readlink -f "$(command -v nc)". If it resolves to /bin/nc.openbsd, leave it.

    Disable printing and network discovery instead of purging them when the README does not need them, sockets included (otherwise the next connection starts them again):

    sudo systemctl disable --now cups.service cups.socket cups.path cups-browsed.service avahi-daemon.service avahi-daemon.socket

    cups, cups-daemon and avahi-daemon are recommended by much of the desktop, and libcups2 and libavahi-client3 are linked into GTK and Cinnamon, so purging them can take desktop packages with them.

    #Find software by other means

    Search installed packages for a name:

    apt list --installed 2>/dev/null | grep -i <package>

    Every installed package, one per line:

    dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ {print $2}' | less

    Packages installed recently, newest last (useful for spotting what the image builder added):

    grep ' install ' /var/log/dpkg.log | tail -50
zgrep ' install ' /var/log/dpkg.log.*.gz | less

    The apt history log also shows the command line that installed each package:

    grep -A2 'Start-Date' /var/log/apt/history.log | less

    Packages someone asked for by name (the rest came in as dependencies):

    apt-mark showmanual | less

    Flatpak apps (Mint supports Flatpak out of the box) and their removal:

    flatpak list --app
sudo flatpak uninstall <app-id>

    Snap is disabled by default on Mint 21, so this usually prints nothing:

    snap list 2>/dev/null

    Python tools installed with pip:

    pip3 list 2>/dev/null
sudo pip3 list 2>/dev/null

    #Check for portable tools and scripts

    List the folders where hand-installed software lives:

    ls -la /opt /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin /usr/local/share

    Find executables, scripts, Java archives and installers in user and temp folders:

    sudo find /home /root /opt /tmp /var/tmp -type f \( -perm -u+x -o -iname '*.sh' -o -iname '*.py' -o -iname '*.jar' -o -iname '*.deb' -o -iname '*.AppImage' \) 2>/dev/null

    Files changed after the system was installed, outside the noisy folders:

    sudo find / -xdev -type f -newer /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys|run|var/lib|var/cache|var/log)' | head -100

    Nothing in /usr/local/bin comes from a package, so dpkg -S <file> finds nothing there. Suspicious names include nc, john, hydra, keylogger and backdoor, or scripts that run nc -e or bash -i >& /dev/tcp/.... Record the path for forensics, then delete the file:

    sudo rm <file>

    Verify

    Re-run the dpkg-query line from the fast path. Only README-approved packages should print, and systemctl status lightdm still shows active (running).

    PreviousHardening required services (FTP, Apache, Samba, MySQL, PHP, nginx, mail)NextFiles, media and permissions
    LNX

    Files, media and permissions

    jump:lin-files

    Fast path

    1. Check permissions on the account and config files:

      stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/sudoers /etc/ssh/sshd_config /boot/grub/grub.cfg /root

    2. Fix anything that differs from the permissions table.

    3. Find SUID programs and compare them with the normal list:

      sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

    4. Find media files in user folders (full command) and delete prohibited ones after forensics.

    5. Find world-writable files:

      sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 2>/dev/null

    6. Set home folders to 750 with the home folder loop.

    #Find prohibited media files

    Scored on almost every past Linux image (K3, K6, R1, R2, SR2, G1). The music sat in a user's Music or Downloads folder, and one forensics question asked for that folder's absolute path (/home/benjamin/Music/ in R1), so record the path before deleting. Delete the files, never the user's folder: the engine checks that the home folder still exists.

    sudo find /home /root /srv /opt /var/www /tmp -type f \( -iname '*.mp3' -o -iname '*.mp4' -o -iname '*.wav' -o -iname '*.flac' -o -iname '*.ogg' -o -iname '*.m4a' -o -iname '*.aac' -o -iname '*.wma' -o -iname '*.avi' -o -iname '*.mkv' -o -iname '*.mov' -o -iname '*.wmv' -o -iname '*.flv' -o -iname '*.webm' -o -iname '*.mpg' -o -iname '*.mpeg' -o -iname '*.jpg' -o -iname '*.jpeg' -o -iname '*.png' -o -iname '*.gif' \) 2>/dev/null | grep -v '/\.cache/'

    Pictures are often legitimate (wallpapers, avatars). Remove media that is clearly personal or prohibited (music, movies) per the README. Renamed media still shows up by content:

    sudo find /home -type f -size +1M -exec file {} + 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'audio|video|MPEG|ISO Media'

    Delete after answering forensics questions, quoting the path:

    sudo rm '<path>'

    #Find files containing plaintext passwords

    Files that mention passwords:

    sudo grep -rilIE 'password|passwd|pwd|credential' /home /root /opt /var/www /srv 2>/dev/null | grep -v '/\.mozilla/' | head -50

    Files named like password stores:

    sudo find /home /root -type f \( -iname '*pass*' -o -iname '*cred*' -o -iname '*.kdbx' -o -iname '*secret*' \) 2>/dev/null

    Delete files that store real user passwords after forensics, unless the README says they are needed. A web application's config file (for example wp-config.php) holds its database password legitimately; leave it.

    #Fix world-writable files and folders

    World-writable files:

    sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 2>/dev/null

    World-writable folders without the sticky bit:

    sudo find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 2>/dev/null

    Take away world write on a file:

    sudo chmod o-w <file>

    If a folder must stay world-writable, give it the sticky bit so users cannot delete each other's files:

    sudo chmod +t <path>

    /tmp, /var/tmp and /dev/shm are normally 1777 (world-writable with the sticky bit). Leave those.

    #Find SUID and SGID programs

    SUID programs run as their owner (usually root). List them:

    sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -la {} + 2>/dev/null

    SGID programs:

    sudo find / -xdev -perm -2000 -type f -exec ls -la {} + 2>/dev/null

    Normal SUID on Mint 21:

    Path From
    /usr/bin/sudo, /usr/bin/su, /usr/bin/passwd, /usr/bin/chsh, /usr/bin/chfn, /usr/bin/gpasswd, /usr/bin/newgrp sudo, util-linux, passwd, login
    /usr/bin/mount, /usr/bin/umount, /usr/bin/fusermount3 mount, fuse3
    /usr/bin/pkexec, /usr/libexec/polkit-agent-helper-1 (/usr/lib/policykit-1/polkit-agent-helper-1 on images that were never updated) pkexec, polkitd (policykit-1)
    /usr/lib/dbus-1.0/dbus-daemon-launch-helper dbus
    /usr/lib/openssh/ssh-keysign openssh-client
    /usr/lib/xorg/Xorg.wrap xserver-xorg-legacy
    /usr/sbin/pppd ppp
    /usr/bin/vmware-user-suid-wrapper open-vm-tools-desktop (VMware images)
    /usr/sbin/mount.nfs, /usr/bin/at, /usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine only if nfs-common, at or snapd is installed

    Normal SGID: /usr/bin/chage and /usr/bin/expiry (group shadow), /usr/sbin/unix_chkpwd and /usr/sbin/pam_extrausers_chkpwd (shadow), /usr/bin/crontab (crontab), /usr/bin/wall and /usr/bin/write.ul (tty), /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/utempter/utempter (utmp), /usr/bin/dotlockfile (mail), /usr/bin/plocate or /usr/bin/mlocate (locate database), /usr/bin/ssh-agent on some releases, and Xorg.wrap.

    Suspicious SUID: bash, sh, dash, find, vim, vi, nano, less, more, python3*, perl, cp, env, tar, nmap, awk, ntfs-3g (Ubuntu 22.04 installs it without SUID), or any binary in /tmp, /home or /var.

    Check whether a package owns the file:

    dpkg -S <path>

    A file no package owns, with SUID set, is planted. A packaged binary such as /usr/bin/find or /usr/bin/vim.basic with SUID was changed by hand; remove the bit. Judge by the normal list, because dpkg --verify only compares file contents (md5sums) and does not report permission changes. Mint 21 has a merged /usr, and many packages still register /bin/... paths. If dpkg -S /usr/bin/su says "no path found", try dpkg -S /bin/su before deciding a binary is planted (this applies to su, mount, umount, fusermount3 and ntfs-3g).

    Remove SUID or SGID from a binary that should not have it:

    sudo chmod u-s <path>

    sudo chmod g-s <path>

    #Correct permissions for system files

    Scored in past keys: "Insecure permissions on shadow file fixed" (K3 Ubuntu 22, plus Hivestorm) and "GRUB configuration is not world readable" (Hivestorm). A planted /etc/shadow is usually 644 or 666. The GRUB password and boot settings are in Advanced hardening.

    File Mode Owner:Group
    /etc/passwd, /etc/group 644 root:root
    /etc/shadow, /etc/gshadow 640 root:shadow
    /etc/passwd-, /etc/group- (backups) 644 root:root
    /etc/shadow-, /etc/gshadow- (backups) 640 root:shadow
    /etc/sudoers 440 root:root
    /etc/sudoers.d/* 440 root:root
    /etc/ssh/sshd_config 600 (Ubuntu ships 644, which is also accepted) root:root
    /boot/grub/grub.cfg 400 or 600 (Ubuntu ships 444) root:root
    /etc/crontab 600 root:root
    /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly, /etc/cron.monthly 700 root:root
    /etc/security/opasswd 600 root:root
    /etc/hosts 644 root:root
    /root 700 root:root
    /home/<username> 750 or 700 owner:owner's group
    /var/log 775 (Ubuntu default; never world-writable) root:syslog
    /tmp 1777 root:root

    Fix the account files:

    sudo chown root:root /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/passwd- /etc/group-
sudo chmod 644 /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/passwd- /etc/group-
sudo chown root:shadow /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/shadow- /etc/gshadow-
sudo chmod 640 /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/shadow- /etc/gshadow-

    Fix sudoers:

    sudo chown root:root /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*
sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*

    Fix the others:

    sudo chmod 600 /etc/ssh/sshd_config /boot/grub/grub.cfg /etc/crontab
sudo chmod 700 /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.weekly /etc/cron.monthly /root
sudo chmod o-w /var/log
sudo chmod 1777 /tmp

    update-grub writes the new menu into the existing grub.cfg, so the mode you set survives later kernel updates. If the file is ever deleted and recreated, it comes back as 444.

    #Fix home directory permissions

    The loop sets each home folder that belongs to a real account to 750, owned by that user and the user's primary group, and prints folders with no matching account:

    for d in /home/*/; do
  u=$(basename "$d")
  if id "$u" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    sudo chown "$u": "$d"
    sudo chmod 750 "$d"
    echo "fixed $d"
  else
    echo "ORPHAN home: $d (no such user)"
  fi
done

    Do not chmod -R home folders; it breaks .ssh and application files. Ubuntu 22.04 already creates new homes as 750: HOME_MODE 0750 is set in /etc/login.defs for useradd, and adduser uses DIR_MODE in /etc/adduser.conf. Check both, because an image built from an older release may have 755:

    grep -E '^\s*HOME_MODE' /etc/login.defs
grep -E '^\s*DIR_MODE' /etc/adduser.conf

    Files with no valid owner (left behind by deleted users):

    sudo find / -xdev \( -nouser -o -nogroup \) 2>/dev/null

    #Remove immutable and append-only flags

    If even root gets "Operation not permitted" when editing a file, check its attributes:

    sudo lsattr /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/sudoers /etc/hosts /etc/resolv.conf

    Search all of /etc for immutable files:

    sudo lsattr -R /etc 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^\S*i\S* '

    An i in the flags means immutable and an a means append-only. Attackers use both to protect backdoors from deletion. Clear them:

    sudo chattr -i -a <file>

    #Set the default umask

    UMASK in /etc/login.defs is applied at login by pam_umask. Ubuntu ships 022, which makes new files readable by everyone. Some checklists want 027:

    sudo sed -i -E 's/^\s*UMASK\s.*/UMASK\t\t027/' /etc/login.defs
grep -E '^\s*UMASK' /etc/login.defs

    It takes effect at the next login. Skip it if the README describes users sharing files through group or world permissions.

    Verify

    Re-run the stat line from the fast path: every value matches the table. The SUID find shows only paths from the normal list.

    PreviousUnwanted software and hacking toolsNextPersistence, backdoors and malware
    LNX

    Persistence, backdoors and malware

    jump:lin-malware

    Record before you remove

    Write down every finding (path, content, user, port) before deleting it. Forensics questions often ask about the backdoor.

    Fast path

    1. Show every user's crontab:

      for u in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do out=$(sudo crontab -l -u "$u" 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)'); [ -n "$out" ] && printf '== %s ==\n%s\n' "$u" "$out"; done

    2. Read the system cron files and folders (details).

    3. List hand-made systemd units (files that are not symlinks):

      sudo find /etc/systemd/system /etc/systemd/user -type f \( -name '*.service' -o -name '*.timer' -o -name '*.socket' -o -name '*.path' -o -name '*.conf' \)

    4. Check the preload file, which must not exist:

      cat /etc/ld.so.preload

    5. Look for listening backdoors:

      sudo ss -tulpn

    6. Find system files that were modified (takes a minute or two):

      sudo dpkg --verify 2>/dev/null | grep -v ' c /'

    7. Remove what you find, then remove whatever restarts it (cron, systemd, shell startup files, autostart).

    For rarer hiding places (udev rules, generators, motd scripts, PATH hijacks, SUID shell copies, web shells, kernel rootkits) continue with Rootkit and persistence hunting.

    #Check user crontabs

    The loop in the fast path prints every non-comment crontab line, per user. The files themselves live in one folder:

    sudo ls -la /var/spool/cron/crontabs/

    Edit one user's crontab, or remove all of it:

    sudo crontab -e -u <username>

    sudo crontab -r -u <username>

    #Check system cron

    In the Ubuntu 22 Training Round 2 key (K3), the scored malware was a netcat listener on port 1 started from a line in /etc/crontab.

    grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.weekly /etc/cron.monthly
sudo grep -rvhE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/cron.d/

    Normal contents on Mint 21: /etc/crontab has four run-parts lines (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly). /etc/cron.d/ has e2scrub_all and anacron, maybe popularity-contest. /etc/cron.daily/ has items like apt-compat, dpkg, logrotate and man-db.

    Suspicious: anything calling nc, bash -i, /dev/tcp/, curl ... | bash, wget, python3 -c, chmod u+s or useradd, anything that runs a file in /tmp, and anything that runs every minute (* * * * *).

    Remove a bad system job after noting it:

    sudo rm /etc/cron.d/<file>
    Which files in cron.daily actually run

    The cron.hourly, cron.daily, cron.weekly and cron.monthly folders are run by run-parts (from /etc/crontab, or from anacron on Mint). Debian's run-parts only runs files that are executable and whose names contain nothing but letters, digits, underscores and hyphens. backdoor.sh in /etc/cron.daily is skipped because of the dot; backdoor runs. A planted script with a dot is still worth removing (it may be scored), but it is not what ran. Files in /etc/cron.d/ are different: they are crontab-format files with a user field, and their names follow the same no-dot rule.

    Optional: only root and listed users may use crontab once /etc/cron.allow exists. Root is always allowed.

    echo root | sudo tee /etc/cron.allow

    #Check at jobs

    sudo atq

    Show a job's commands (the end of the output is the actual script), then remove it:

    sudo at -c <job-number> | tail -20
sudo atrm <job-number>

    atq reports "command not found" if the at package is not installed, which is normal on Mint.

    #Check systemd units and timers

    All timers, including disabled ones:

    systemctl list-timers --all

    Places a malicious unit can hide on Mint 21:

    Location What
    /etc/systemd/system/ and its *.wants/ folders Admin-created units and enable links. Real files here (not symlinks) are worth reading
    /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/*.conf Drop-ins that override a packaged unit, for example a new ExecStart
    /usr/lib/systemd/system/ (same as /lib/systemd/system/) Packaged units; a file here that no package owns is planted
    /run/systemd/system/ Runtime units, gone after reboot
    /etc/systemd/user/, /usr/lib/systemd/user/, /home/*/.config/systemd/user/ Per-user units that start at login
    /etc/systemd/system-generators/, /usr/lib/systemd/system-generators/ Programs that create units at boot

    Every unit that overrides or extends a packaged one, in one list:

    systemd-delta --type=extended,overridden,redirected

    User-level units:

    ls -la /etc/systemd/user/ /home/*/.config/systemd/user/ 2>/dev/null

    Read a suspicious unit, including its drop-ins:

    systemctl cat <service-name>

    Look for ExecStart pointing at scripts in /tmp, home folders, /dev/shm or /opt. Check which package owns a unit; "no path found" means it was made by hand:

    dpkg -S /lib/systemd/system/<service-name>.service

    Remove a malicious unit:

    sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/<service-name>.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

    #Check rc.local and init scripts

    /etc/rc.local does not exist on a clean Mint 21. If it exists and is executable, rc-local.service runs it as root at every boot:

    ls -l /etc/rc.local
cat /etc/rc.local

    Remove anything that is not required, or the whole file after noting it. Also look at the legacy init scripts; anything there that no package owns is suspicious:

    ls -la /etc/init.d/

    #Check shell startup files and aliases

    sudo grep -nE 'alias|nc |/dev/tcp|curl|wget|base64|export (PATH|LD_)' /etc/bash.bashrc /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/* /etc/environment /root/.bashrc /root/.profile /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.profile /home/*/.bash_profile /home/*/.bash_login /home/*/.bash_logout /home/*/.bash_aliases 2>/dev/null

    Red flags:

    • alias sudo=..., alias ls=..., alias passwd=... or alias apt=... that run something extra.
    • export PATH=/tmp:$PATH, or a home folder ahead of /usr/bin (a fake sudo earlier in the path).
    • export LD_PRELOAD=....
    • Lines that download and run code.

    The default Ubuntu .bashrc aliases (ll, la, l, ls --color=auto, grep --color=auto, alert) are fine. Compare a user's file with the clean template:

    diff /etc/skel/.bashrc /home/<username>/.bashrc

    #Check /etc/ld.so.preload

    cat /etc/ld.so.preload

    Expected output on a clean system:

    cat: /etc/ld.so.preload: No such file or directory

    A library listed in this file loads into every program, which is a classic rootkit trick. Note the library path, then delete the file and the library:

    sudo rm /etc/ld.so.preload
sudo rm <path>

    Also check /etc/ld.so.conf.d/ for unknown library folders:

    cat /etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.conf

    #Check /etc/hosts for tampering

    cat /etc/hosts

    A clean Mint file looks like this, plus one comment line above the IPv6 entries:

    127.0.0.1   localhost
127.0.1.1   <hostname>

::1     ip6-localhost ip6-loopback
fe00::0 ip6-localnet
ff00::0 ip6-mcastprefix
ff02::1 ip6-allnodes
ff02::2 ip6-allrouters

    Remove entries that redirect update servers (archive.ubuntu.com, security.ubuntu.com, packages.linuxmint.com), search engines or banks. Two related files:

    • /etc/resolv.conf should point to nameserver 127.0.0.53 (the systemd-resolved stub on Mint 21).
    • The hosts: line in /etc/nsswitch.conf should start with files and include dns.

    #Find listening backdoors and odd processes

    Scored in past keys: "Malware removed" (netcat on port 1, K3), a python listener on port 1337 living in /usr/share/zod (K8 forensics, Mint 21), and "Removed netcat backdoor", "Removed python backdoor" and "Removed perl owl-shell backdoor" (Hivestorm). Each was found with ss -tlnp and ps, then removed together with whatever started it.

    Listening ports with the owning program:

    sudo ss -tulpn

    Process tree:

    ps auxf | less

    Common reverse shell and listener patterns:

    ps aux | grep -E '[n]c |[n]cat|[s]ocat|[b]ash -i|/dev/tcp|[p]ython.*socket'

    Programs running from temp folders or from deleted files:

    sudo ls -l /proc/*/exe 2>/dev/null | grep -E '/tmp|/dev/shm|/var/tmp|deleted'

    Details of one process (open files and sockets, working folder, full command line):

    sudo lsof -p <pid>
sudo ls -l /proc/<pid>/cwd /proc/<pid>/exe
sudo cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '

    Kill it, then find and remove what starts it again (cron, systemd, rc.local, bashrc, autostart):

    sudo kill -9 <pid>

    Also look for scripts and binaries in the temp folders:

    ls -la /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm

    #Remove a netcat backdoor started from cron

    1. Note the port, PID and command line:

      sudo ss -tlnp

    2. Delete the line that starts it from /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/ or the user's crontab (system cron).

    3. Kill the listener by the PID from step 1 (the key used pkill -f nc, which also matches unrelated names such as rsync):

      sudo kill <pid>

    4. Find out what the nc binary is before deleting anything:

      readlink -f "$(command -v nc)"
dpkg -S "$(readlink -f "$(command -v nc)")"

    5. If no package owns it, or it is netcat-traditional, remove it (sudo rm <path> or sudo apt purge netcat-traditional). The K3 key deleted /usr/bin/nc. If it resolves to /usr/bin/nc.openbsd from netcat-openbsd, deleting the /usr/bin/nc link is enough; do not purge netcat-openbsd (why).

    6. Run sudo ss -tlnp again after a minute: the port must stay closed. If it comes back, another cron line, unit or startup file restarts it.

    #Find modified system files and PAM backdoors

    Packaged files whose contents changed (config files, marked c, are filtered out):

    sudo dpkg --verify 2>/dev/null | grep -v ' c /'

    A line like ??5?????? /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_unix.so means the file's checksum no longer matches the package. A replaced PAM module is a backdoor that accepts a secret password. Find the owning package and reinstall it:

    dpkg -S <path>
sudo apt install --reinstall <package>

    For pam_unix.so the package is libpam-modules. debsums does the same check and can include config files:

    sudo apt install debsums
sudo debsums -s 2>/dev/null
sudo debsums -as 2>/dev/null | grep -i pam

    #Check the PAM stack for backdoor lines

    The deep PAM checks (pam-configs profiles, pam_exec password loggers, module files no package owns) are in Advanced hardening.

    grep -nE 'pam_permit|pam_exec|pam_succeed_if|sufficient' /etc/pam.d/* | grep -v ':\s*#'

    Unknown module files (real files, not symlinks) in the PAM module folder:

    ls -la /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/ | grep -v '^l'

    Normal on Mint 21, leave these alone:

    File Normal line
    common-auth, common-account, common-password requisite pam_deny.so followed by required pam_permit.so
    common-session, common-session-noninteractive first line session [default=1] pam_permit.so, then requisite pam_deny.so, required pam_permit.so
    lightdm auth sufficient pam_succeed_if.so user ingroup nopasswdlogin (the nopasswdlogin group must be empty; see Login screen)
    lightdm-autologin auth required pam_permit.so (this file is only used for automatic login)

    Backdoors: auth sufficient pam_permit.so near the top of any file (accepts any password), pam_exec.so running an unknown script, or pam_succeed_if.so with sufficient on a group or user you do not recognize. Compare a file with the package original:

    dpkg -S /etc/pam.d/<file>

    Then restore it from your backup or from a teammate's clean image. Changing the common files is covered in Password policy and Account lockout.

    #Check kernel modules

    lsmod | less
lsmod | grep -iE 'rootkit|diamorphine|reptile|hide'
cat /etc/modules
ls /etc/modules-load.d/ /etc/modprobe.d/

    Unknown modules loaded from /etc/modules or /etc/modules-load.d/*.conf deserve a look:

    modinfo <module>

    Ubuntu's own modules sit under /lib/modules/<kernel-version>/kernel/ (uname -r prints the version). Modules under updates/dkms/ were built locally; VirtualBox or VMware guest drivers there are normal. A filename: anywhere else, such as /tmp or a home folder, means the module was planted.

    #Check autostart entries

    ls -la /etc/xdg/autostart/ /home/*/.config/autostart/ /root/.config/autostart/ 2>/dev/null
grep -h '^Exec' /etc/xdg/autostart/*.desktop /home/*/.config/autostart/*.desktop 2>/dev/null

    GUI: Menu > Preferences > Startup Applications. Remove entries that run scripts or unknown programs. A system entry that no package owns was added by hand:

    dpkg -S /etc/xdg/autostart/<file>

    #Check apt hooks

    grep -rnE 'Invoke|Pre-Install-Pkgs|Post-Invoke-Success' /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/

    Normal hooks exist (20packagekit, 50appstream, 70debconf, 99update-notifier-style entries, Mint's mintupdate hooks). A hook that runs /tmp/..., nc, curl | sh or a hidden script runs as root every time apt runs. Remove that file after noting it.

    #Other persistence spots

    • /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow edits: compare with the automatic backups, diff /etc/passwd- /etc/passwd.
    • /etc/sudoers.d/ and /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/ (sudoers and sudo rights).
    • ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and /root/.ssh/ (SSH server hardening).
    • /etc/update-motd.d/ scripts run as root at every SSH or console login: ls -la /etc/update-motd.d/.
    • /etc/profile.d/*.sh runs at every login shell.
    • /etc/skel/: everything there is copied into new users' homes.
    • Git hooks, .vimrc and scripts under .config/ in home folders (lower priority).
    • Unknown files in /usr/local/bin, /usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/lib and /opt.

    #Run rootkit and malware scanners

    Use these when the internet works and you have time. Install them:

    sudo apt install rkhunter chkrootkit clamav

    rkhunter (skip rkhunter --update: Ubuntu's config sets WEB_CMD="/bin/false", so the update fails with an error):

    sudo rkhunter --propupd
sudo rkhunter -c --sk --rwo

    chkrootkit:

    sudo chkrootkit -q

    ClamAV (stop the updater service so freshclam can take its lock, update, start it again, then scan):

    sudo systemctl stop clamav-freshclam
sudo freshclam
sudo systemctl start clamav-freshclam
sudo clamscan -r -i /home /tmp /var/tmp /opt /usr/local

    rkhunter --propupd records the current files as good, so run it only after removing obvious problems, or skip it and read the warnings carefully. All three scanners produce false positives; treat their output as leads. An installed scanner is sometimes a scored item, but it is never required.

    Verify

    Run the recon script again and compare it with the first run: no unexpected crontab lines, units, preload file, listeners or modified PAM files remain.

    PreviousFiles, media and permissionsNextKernel hardening (sysctl) and core dumps
    LNX

    Kernel hardening (sysctl) and core dumps

    jump:lin-kernel

    Fast path

    1. Write the hardening file with the block below.

    2. Apply every sysctl file:

      sudo sysctl --system

    3. Find lines elsewhere that override yours. Fix the ones in /etc/sysctl.conf, /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf or a file that sorts after 99-cp.conf; stock lines such as rp_filter=2 in 10-network-security.conf and 50-default.conf load earlier and can stay:

      grep -rnE 'ip_forward|randomize|syncookies|redirects|source_route|rp_filter|martians|suid_dumpable' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/ /run/sysctl.d/ /usr/lib/sysctl.d/ /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf 2>/dev/null

    4. Make ufw's own sysctl file log martian packets too (details):

      sudo sed -i -E 's/^(net\/ipv4\/conf\/(all|default)\/log_martians)=0/\1=1/' /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf

    5. Check the result:

      sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians kernel.randomize_va_space fs.suid_dumpable

    #Write the sysctl hardening file

    Scored in past keys: SYN cookies (K3, R2, G1 and Hivestorm), IPv4 forwarding disabled (K3), Magic SysRq disabled and TIME-WAIT assassination protection (G1), and martian logging, broadcast and bogus ICMP, ICMP redirects and dmesg_restrict (Hivestorm). Every one of them is in this file.

    Run as one block. It creates /etc/sysctl.d/99-cp.conf and loads it:

    sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-cp.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_rfc1337 = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians = 1
net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1
net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra = 0
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2
kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2
kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1
kernel.sysrq = 0
fs.protected_hardlinks = 1
fs.protected_symlinks = 1
fs.suid_dumpable = 0
EOF
sudo sysctl --system

    Set net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 instead only if the README says the machine routes traffic.

    /etc/sysctl.conf wins over this file

    Delete or correct conflicting lines in /etc/sysctl.conf (fast path step 3 finds them). sysctl --system reads every *.conf in /etc/sysctl.d/, /run/sysctl.d/, /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/, /usr/lib/sysctl.d/ and /lib/sysctl.d/, sorted by file name, then /etc/sysctl.conf last. The last value read wins. Ubuntu also links /etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf to /etc/sysctl.conf, which sorts after 99-cp.conf. So a planted net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 in /etc/sysctl.conf beats your file. Some scoring checks read /etc/sysctl.conf itself; if an item does not score from 99-cp.conf, put the same line in /etc/sysctl.conf as well.

    #Fix the ufw sysctl file

    Every time ufw starts (including at boot, after the sysctl files load), it applies /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf. On Mint 21 that file sets:

    net/ipv4/conf/all/log_martians=0
net/ipv4/conf/default/log_martians=0

    That silently undoes log_martians = 1. The rest of the file (redirects off, broadcast pings ignored) agrees with the hardening file. Change both lines to 1 and reload ufw:

    sudo sed -i -E 's/^(net\/ipv4\/conf\/(all|default)\/log_martians)=0/\1=1/' /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf
sudo ufw reload

    The alternative is pointing ufw at the main file: set IPT_SYSCTL=/etc/sysctl.conf in /etc/default/ufw. Also check that nobody uncommented net/ipv4/ip_forward=1 in /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf.

    #What each setting does

    Setting Value Ubuntu default Why
    net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies 1 1 SYN flood protection
    net.ipv4.tcp_rfc1337 1 0 TIME-WAIT assassination protection (RFC 1337)
    net.ipv4.ip_forward 0 0 Not a router
    net.ipv4.conf.*.accept_redirects 0 1 (ufw sets 0) Ignore ICMP redirects (man in the middle)
    net.ipv4.conf.*.secure_redirects 0 1 Ignore redirects even from listed gateways
    net.ipv4.conf.*.send_redirects 0 1 Do not send redirects
    net.ipv4.conf.*.accept_source_route 0 0 Drop source-routed packets
    net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter 1 2 (loose) Strict reverse path filter (anti-spoofing)
    net.ipv4.conf.*.log_martians 1 0 Log packets with impossible addresses
    net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts 1 1 Smurf attack protection
    net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses 1 1 Ignore bogus ICMP errors
    net.ipv6.conf.*.accept_redirects 0 1 (ufw sets 0) IPv6 redirects
    net.ipv6.conf.*.accept_ra 0 1 Ignore router advertisements; only safe if IPv6 autoconfiguration is not needed
    kernel.randomize_va_space 2 2 Full ASLR
    kernel.dmesg_restrict 1 1 Only root reads the kernel log
    kernel.kptr_restrict 2 1 Hide kernel pointers from everyone
    kernel.yama.ptrace_scope 1 1 Processes cannot attach to unrelated processes
    kernel.sysrq 0 176 Disable the magic SysRq keys
    fs.protected_hardlinks, fs.protected_symlinks 1 1 Block link attacks in /tmp
    fs.suid_dumpable 0 0 (2 while apport runs) No core dumps from SUID programs

    Optional extras, if a checklist asks:

    Setting Value Note
    net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6, net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6 1 Only if the README does not need IPv6. Rarely breaks anything on the image
    fs.protected_fifos, fs.protected_regular 2 Ubuntu defaults are 1 for fifos and 2 for regular
    kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled 1 Cannot be set back to 0 without a reboot

    #Disable core dumps

    Add a hard limit of zero for everyone:

    echo '* hard core 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/security/limits.conf
grep -n core /etc/security/limits.conf

    It applies from the next login. Two more places can turn dumps back on:

    • apport, Ubuntu's crash reporter, sets fs.suid_dumpable to 2 whenever its service starts. If systemctl is-enabled apport says enabled and the README does not need it, run sudo systemctl disable --now apport.
    • If systemd-coredump is installed, set Storage=none and ProcessSizeMax=0 in /etc/systemd/coredump.conf.

    #Disable USB storage

    Only do this if the README or a checklist asks for it. How to check that the block really works, and other modules worth blocking, are in Advanced hardening.

    echo 'install usb-storage /bin/false' | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/disable-usb-storage.conf
echo 'blacklist usb-storage' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/disable-usb-storage.conf
sudo modprobe -r usb-storage

    The same install <module> /bin/false line disables unused filesystems (cramfs, freevxfs, jffs2, hfs, hfsplus, udf) and protocols (dccp, sctp, rds, tipc). Low priority.

    #Other boot and kernel items

    • Shared memory: add tmpfs /dev/shm tmpfs defaults,noexec,nodev,nosuid 0 0 to /etc/fstab, then test with sudo mount -o remount /dev/shm. "Shared memory secured" was scored in G1 (Ubuntu 14, where the path was /run/shm). Details and /tmp in Advanced hardening.
    • GRUB password: possible, but easy to lock yourself out of the boot menu. Skip it unless the README asks; the safe method is in Advanced hardening.
    • /etc/fstab should not mount anything unusual (network shares, a second mount of /).
    • AppArmor must not be turned off on the kernel command line (AppArmor).

    Verify

    sudo sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'accept_redirects|send_redirects|accept_source_route|log_martians' shows = 0 for redirects and source routes and = 1 for martians. Run it again after sudo ufw reload to prove ufw did not change anything.

    PreviousPersistence, backdoors and malwareNextLogin screen, guest and screen lock
    LNX

    Login screen, guest and screen lock

    jump:lin-login

    Fast path

    1. Open Menu > Administration > Login Window and go to the Users tab.
    2. Turn off guest sessions (if the option is shown) and clear Automatic login.
    3. Turn on "Hide the user list" and "Allow manual login" unless the README objects.

    4. Check every LightDM file for overrides:

      sudo grep -rnEi 'guest|autologin|hide-users|manual-login|allow-tcp|xdmcp' /etc/lightdm/ /usr/share/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d/ /etc/xdg/lightdm/ 2>/dev/null

    5. Check that the nopasswdlogin group (members log in without a password) is empty; the output must end in a colon with nothing after it:

      getent group nopasswdlogin

    6. Set the screen to lock (screen lock).

    7. Do not restart LightDM now; changes apply at the next login screen.

    #Set the login options

    Scored in past keys: "Guest account is disabled" (R2, SR2, and G1, which read allow-guest=false from the LightDM files), "Greeter does not enumerate user accounts" (greeter-hide-users=true) and "X Server does not allow TCP connections" (xserver-allow-tcp=false), both Hivestorm.

    Menu > Administration > Login Window (the lightdm-settings tool), Users tab:

    Setting Value
    Allow guest sessions Off (only shown when guest support is installed)
    Hide the user list On, unless the README objects
    Allow manual login On (needed when the list is hidden)
    Automatic login Username empty

    The tool writes these to /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf and saves appearance options to /etc/lightdm/slick-greeter.conf. Wording shifts a little between Mint 21.x releases. Always confirm with the terminal check, because a planted file can override the GUI.

    Open the main file:

    sudo nano /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf

    Make it contain this section (create the file if it does not exist; Mint 21 does not ship one):

    [Seat:*]
allow-guest=false
greeter-allow-guest=false
autologin-guest=false
greeter-hide-users=true
greeter-show-manual-login=true
xserver-allow-tcp=false

    Then delete every autologin-user= and autologin-user-timeout= line in all LightDM files (fast path step 4 finds them). The fix script does the guest and autologin part in one go.

    #Where LightDM reads its settings

    LightDM reads these in order, and a later file overrides an earlier one:

    Order Location What is there on Mint 21
    1 /usr/share/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d/*.conf Package defaults: 50-disable-guest.conf (allow-guest=false), 50-slick-greeter.conf (greeter-session=slick-greeter) and wrapper settings
    2 /etc/xdg/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d/*.conf Usually nothing
    3 /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d/*.conf 70-linuxmint.conf ([SeatDefaults] with user-session=cinnamon)
    4 /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf Written by the Login Window tool; read last, so it wins

    A planted autologin-user= in any of these files works unless a later file overrides it. Delete such lines wherever they are, rather than counting on order.

    Key Safe value Meaning
    allow-guest false No guest account (already false by package default, but scoring often checks the line)
    greeter-allow-guest false Greeter does not offer a guest button
    autologin-user absent or empty No automatic login
    autologin-user-timeout absent Delay before automatic login
    autologin-guest false No automatic guest login
    greeter-hide-users true Hide the user list
    greeter-show-manual-login true Allow typing a username
    xserver-allow-tcp false X server starts with -nolisten tcp (already the default; write it out because checks read the file)
    xdmcp-manager, [XDMCPServer] enabled absent, false XDMCP turns TCP back on for the X server

    [SeatDefaults] is the old section name and [Seat:*] is the current one; LightDM 1.30 accepts both.

    #Check the effective LightDM config

    lightdm --show-config 2>&1 | grep -iE 'guest|autologin|hide-users|manual'

    Each line shows the value LightDM will use and a letter for the file it came from (the legend is at the bottom of the full output). You should see allow-guest=false and no autologin-user line with a name.

    Do not restart LightDM while logged in

    systemctl restart lightdm ends your desktop session and loses unsaved work. The new settings apply the next time the login screen appears; reboot at a calm moment if you need to test them.

    #Stop the X server from accepting TCP connections

    Check whether X is listening on the network (port 6000 and up):

    sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':60[0-9][0-9]\b'

    No output is correct. Add xserver-allow-tcp=false to [Seat:*] in /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf (block above) and delete any xserver-allow-tcp=true or xdmcp-manager= line elsewhere. It applies at the next login screen. GDM, Fedora and the running-process check are in Advanced hardening.

    #Block passwordless and root logins at the greeter

    Ubuntu's /etc/pam.d/lightdm contains auth sufficient pam_succeed_if.so user ingroup nopasswdlogin. Any member of the nopasswdlogin group logs in at the greeter without a password. The group must list nobody:

    getent group nopasswdlogin

    Remove a member:

    sudo gpasswd -d <username> nopasswdlogin

    Root should not be able to log in at the greeter. Root's password must be locked, which sudo passwd -S root shows as L (Users and groups). With root locked, greeter-show-manual-login=true does not let root in.

    Also look for planted lines such as auth sufficient pam_permit.so in /etc/pam.d/lightdm and /etc/pam.d/login. /etc/pam.d/lightdm-autologin normally contains auth required pam_permit.so; that is how automatic login skips the password, and it is harmless once automatic login is off.

    #Lock the screen in Cinnamon

    Menu > Preferences > Screensaver (also in System Settings):

    • "Delay before starting the screensaver": 5 minutes, or what the README asks.
    • "Lock the computer after the screensaver starts": On, with a short delay (0 to 1 minute).
    • "Lock the computer when put to sleep": On, if shown here or under Power Management.

    Menu > Preferences > Power Management: require a password on wake.

    Run as the logged-in user, without sudo (these settings are per user):

    gsettings set org.cinnamon.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled true
gsettings set org.cinnamon.desktop.screensaver lock-delay 0
gsettings set org.cinnamon.desktop.session idle-delay 300

    Check:

    gsettings get org.cinnamon.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled

    To change the default for every user who has not changed it themselves, create /usr/share/glib-2.0/schemas/90-cp.gschema.override with:

    [org.cinnamon.desktop.screensaver]
lock-enabled=true
lock-delay=uint32 0

[org.cinnamon.desktop.session]
idle-delay=uint32 300

    Then compile the schemas:

    sudo glib-compile-schemas /usr/share/glib-2.0/schemas/

    #Other display and login files

    • /etc/lightdm/users.conf: old hidden-users list, only used when AccountsService is missing.
    • /var/lib/AccountsService/users/<username>: SystemAccount=true hides a user from the greeter (Users and groups).
    • /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net: optional legal banner for console and network logins.

    • /etc/gdm3/ exists only if GNOME's display manager was installed; Mint uses LightDM. If gdm3 is installed and the README does not need it, keep LightDM active. This should print /usr/sbin/lightdm:

      cat /etc/X11/default-display-manager

    Verify

    lightdm --show-config 2>&1 | grep -iE 'guest|autologin' shows allow-guest=false and no autologin user, and getent group nopasswdlogin ends in a colon with nothing after it.

    PreviousKernel hardening (sysctl) and core dumpsNextAppArmor, auditd, logging and fail2ban
    LNX

    AppArmor, auditd, logging and fail2ban

    jump:lin-apparmor-audit

    Fast path

    1. Check AppArmor is loaded and enforcing:

      sudo aa-status

    2. If it is disabled, turn it on:

      sudo systemctl enable --now apparmor

    3. Install and start auditd:

      sudo apt install auditd audispd-plugins
sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

    4. Add the audit rules and load them.

    5. Confirm system logging runs:

      systemctl is-active rsyslog systemd-journald

    6. If SSH is a required service, set up fail2ban.

    #Check AppArmor

    aa-status is in the apparmor package. The tools that change profile modes are in apparmor-utils:

    sudo apt install apparmor-utils apparmor-profiles

    Check the service:

    systemctl is-enabled apparmor
systemctl is-active apparmor

    sudo aa-status should say apparmor module is loaded. and list profiles in enforce mode. Put a complain-mode profile into enforce mode one at a time, then check the related service still works (enforcing everything at once can break programs):

    sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/<profile>

    Check that AppArmor was not turned off at boot. This must not show apparmor=0 or security=none:

    grep GRUB_CMDLINE /etc/default/grub

    If it does, remove that word from the line, then rebuild the boot menu (it takes effect at the next reboot):

    sudo update-grub

    Disabled profiles are symlinks in /etc/apparmor.d/disable/. An unexpected one (for example for a required service) can be removed, then reload the profile:

    ls -la /etc/apparmor.d/disable/
sudo rm /etc/apparmor.d/disable/<profile>
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/<profile>

    #Turn on auditd

    sudo apt install auditd audispd-plugins
sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

    Check that auditing is on; the output must include enabled 1:

    sudo auditctl -s

    #Add audit rules

    Rule files go in /etc/audit/rules.d/ and must end in .rules. This block writes a basic set that watches account, sudo, SSH, cron and PAM files for writes and attribute changes, then loads it:

    sudo tee /etc/audit/rules.d/cp.rules >/dev/null <<'EOF'
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/group -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/security/opasswd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k scope
-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k scope
-w /etc/ssh/sshd_config -p wa -k sshd
-w /etc/crontab -p wa -k cron
-w /etc/cron.d/ -p wa -k cron
-w /etc/pam.d/ -p wa -k pam
-w /etc/login.defs -p wa -k login
EOF
sudo augenrules --load

    List the active rules:

    sudo auditctl -l

    Search events by key, with readable names:

    sudo ausearch -k identity -i

    Do not add -e 2 mid-round. It locks the rules until the next reboot, so later fixes cannot change them.

    #Logs to know

    Log What it holds
    /var/log/auth.log Logins, sudo, su, SSH, PAM failures
    /var/log/syslog General system messages
    /var/log/ufw.log Firewall blocks
    /var/log/apt/history.log apt installs and removals with dates and the command used (forensics)
    /var/log/dpkg.log Every package change
    /var/log/audit/audit.log auditd events (read with ausearch)
    /var/log/apache2/access.log, error.log Web server
    /var/log/vsftpd.log FTP transfers
    journalctl -u ssh SSH service log (-f follows, -b limits to this boot)
    journalctl -xe Latest errors with explanations
    last Login history from /var/log/wtmp
    sudo lastb Failed logins from /var/log/btmp
    lastlog Last login of each user

    Failed logins and sudo use, most recent last:

    sudo grep -iE 'failed|invalid|sudo:' /var/log/auth.log | tail -40

    #Keep logging running

    systemctl is-active rsyslog || sudo systemctl enable --now rsyslog
systemctl is-active systemd-journald

    Optional persistent journal: set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, then:

    sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald

    Log files must not be world-writable. This should print nothing:

    sudo find /var/log -type f -perm -0002

    #Set up fail2ban for SSH

    Only when SSH is a required service:

    sudo apt install fail2ban

    Ubuntu's package already turns on the sshd jail in /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/defaults-debian.conf. Put your own settings in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local, which overrides jail.conf (never edit jail.conf; updates replace it):

    sudo nano /etc/fail2ban/jail.local

    [DEFAULT]
bantime = 15m
findtime = 10m
maxretry = 5

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = ssh

    Start it and read the jail status:

    sudo systemctl enable fail2ban
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

    Unban an address that got caught by mistake:

    sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip <ip-address>

    Verify

    sudo aa-status shows profiles in enforce mode, sudo auditctl -l lists your rules, and sudo fail2ban-client status sshd (if used) shows the jail with Currently failed and Currently banned counters.

    PreviousLogin screen, guest and screen lockNextFirefox on Mint
    LNX

    Firefox on Mint

    jump:lin-firefox

    Fast path

    1. Update Firefox through apt:

      sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade firefox

    2. In Firefox open about:preferences#privacy and set the options in the settings table.

    3. Open about:addons and remove extensions nobody needs.

    4. Look for existing policy files (read them before changing anything):

      cat /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json /usr/lib/firefox/distribution/policies.json 2>/dev/null

    5. Write the system policy file so the settings apply to every user.

    6. Restart Firefox and open about:policies. It should show "Active" with no errors.

    #Update Firefox

    On Mint 21, Firefox is a normal .deb from the Mint repository (not a snap). It does not update itself; apt does.

    sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade firefox
firefox --version

    Or open Update Manager, select firefox and click Install Updates. Close and reopen Firefox afterwards. Help > About Firefox shows the version.

    #Set the privacy and security options

    Do this in each user account that uses Firefox, or use the policy file below for all of them at once. Open about:preferences (Menu > Settings):

    Where Setting
    Privacy & Security > Enhanced Tracking Protection Strict (Standard at minimum)
    Privacy & Security > Website Privacy Preferences "Tell websites not to sell or share my data" On. Recent Firefox versions removed the Do Not Track checkbox; turn it on if your version still has it
    Privacy & Security > Passwords Uncheck "Ask to save passwords"; remove saved passwords if policy says so
    Privacy & Security > Permissions "Block pop-up windows" On, "Warn you when websites try to install add-ons" On
    Privacy & Security > Security "Block dangerous and deceptive content", "Block dangerous downloads" and "Warn you about unwanted and uncommon software" all On
    Privacy & Security > HTTPS-Only Mode "Enable HTTPS-Only Mode in all windows"
    Privacy & Security > Firefox Data Collection and Use Off (optional)
    General > Downloads "Always ask you where to save files" (optional)

    Labels change slightly between versions. The search box at the top of Settings finds them: type pop-ups, HTTPS, dangerous or passwords.

    #Remove bad extensions and settings

    • about:addons > Extensions: remove anything not required (crypto miners, "free VPN", unknown names). Check Themes and Plugins too.
    • about:preferences#home: the homepage and new tab page must not point to a strange site.
    • about:preferences#search: the default search engine should be a normal one; remove odd engines.
    • about:config, only if needed: browser.safebrowsing.malware.enabled and browser.safebrowsing.phishing.enabled should be true.

    • Profile folders are in /home/<username>/.mozilla/firefox/. A user.js file in a profile folder rewrites preferences at every start. Read it, record it for forensics, then delete it:

      ls /home/*/.mozilla/firefox/*/user.js 2>/dev/null

    #Enforce settings with policies.json

    Firefox on Linux reads enterprise policies from /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json, or from distribution/policies.json next to the program (/usr/lib/firefox/distribution/policies.json on Mint). It uses only one file: when the /etc file exists, the distribution file is ignored. So if Mint's package ships a distribution file, copy any entries you want to keep into the /etc file.

    Create the folder and file:

    sudo mkdir -p /etc/firefox/policies
sudo nano /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json

    Contents:

    {
  "policies": {
    "DisableTelemetry": true,
    "DisableFirefoxStudies": true,
    "PasswordManagerEnabled": false,
    "OfferToSaveLogins": false,
    "PopupBlocking": { "Default": true, "Locked": true },
    "HttpsOnlyMode": "force_enabled",
