    "EnableTrackingProtection": { "Value": true, "Locked": true, "Cryptomining": true, "Fingerprinting": true },
    "Preferences": {
      "browser.safebrowsing.malware.enabled": { "Value": true, "Status": "locked" },
      "browser.safebrowsing.phishing.enabled": { "Value": true, "Status": "locked" },
      "browser.safebrowsing.downloads.enabled": { "Value": true, "Status": "locked" }
    }
  }
}

    Leave out PasswordManagerEnabled if the README says users keep saved passwords. Check the JSON before restarting Firefox; a single missing comma disables every policy:

    python3 -m json.tool /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json >/dev/null && echo OK

    Malicious policies

    A planted policies.json can force a proxy (Proxy), install extensions (ExtensionSettings or Extensions), set a homepage (Homepage) or block about pages. Remove those entries unless the README requires them. DisableAppUpdate is harmless on Mint, because apt does the updating.

    Verify

    Restart Firefox and open about:policies: the status is Active, the Errors tab is empty, and about:preferences#privacy shows the locked settings greyed out.

    PreviousAppArmor, auditd, logging and fail2banNextRecon and fix scripts (bash)
    LNX

    Recon and fix scripts (bash)

    jump:lin-scripts

    None of these scripts delete users

    The recon script only reads. The fix snippets change settings but never delete users, files or packages. Deleting is always a manual decision after checking the README and answering forensics questions.

    Fast path

    1. Open a terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) and create the script file:

      nano ~/recon.sh

    2. Copy the recon script from this page and paste it with Ctrl+Shift+V. Save with Ctrl+O, Enter, and exit with Ctrl+X.

    3. Run it with sudo (it takes 2 to 4 minutes):

      sudo bash ~/recon.sh

    4. Open the report:

      xed ~/Desktop/recon.txt

    5. Work through the report section by section. Use the fix snippets below for common changes; paste each one straight into the terminal.

    #How to run a snippet

    Short snippets can be pasted directly into a terminal; they call sudo themselves and ask for your password once. Longer ones can be saved like the recon script (nano ~/fix.sh, paste, save) and run with sudo bash ~/fix.sh. You never need chmod +x when you run a file with bash.

    #Read-only recon script

    What it does:

    1. Refuses to run without sudo, because it reads /etc/shadow and other root-only files.
    2. Works out the Desktop of the user who typed sudo and writes the report to ~/Desktop/recon.txt (or ~/recon.txt if there is no Desktop folder). Give a path as the first argument to write somewhere else.
    3. Collects users and groups, password and PAM settings, sudoers, firewall, ports, services, timers, cron and at jobs, startup files, preload and rc.local, SUID files, suspicious packages, media files, SSH keys and settings, LightDM, hosts, apt sources, sysctl values, file permissions, immutable files, AppArmor, auditd, Firefox policies and modified package files.
    4. Changes nothing on the system apart from creating the report file and giving it to you.

    How to run it: save it as ~/recon.sh (see the fast path), then run sudo bash ~/recon.sh. To compare before and after later, run it again with a new output path, for example sudo bash ~/recon.sh ~/Desktop/recon2.txt, then compare the two with diff ~/Desktop/recon.txt ~/Desktop/recon2.txt | less.

    if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then echo "Run with sudo: sudo bash $0"; exit 1; fi
REALUSER="${SUDO_USER:-root}"
REALHOME=$(getent passwd "$REALUSER" | cut -d: -f6)
OUT="$REALHOME/Desktop/recon.txt"
[ -d "$REALHOME/Desktop" ] || OUT="$REALHOME/recon.txt"
[ -n "$1" ] && OUT="$1"
HUMANS=$(awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd)
sec() { printf '\n========== %s ==========\n' "$1"; }
echo "Writing $OUT (this takes a few minutes)"

{
sec "Generated $(date) on $(hostname)"
grep -E 'DESCRIPTION|CODENAME' /etc/linuxmint/info 2>/dev/null
uname -r

sec "Human users (UID 1000-65533)"
awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {printf "%-16s uid=%-6s gid=%-6s home=%-22s shell=%s\n",$1,$3,$4,$6,$7}' /etc/passwd

sec "UID 0 accounts (only root expected)"
awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd

sec "Duplicate UIDs or user names"
cut -d: -f3 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -d
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -d

sec "System accounts (UID below 1000) with a login shell (only root expected)"
awk -F: '$3<1000 && $7 !~ /(nologin|false|sync)$/ {print $1, $3, $7}' /etc/passwd

sec "Admin-type groups"
for g in sudo admin adm lpadmin sambashare root shadow nopasswdlogin wheel; do getent group "$g"; done
echo "-- users whose primary group is sudo (GID 27):"
awk -F: '$4==27 {print $1}' /etc/passwd

sec "Accounts with an EMPTY password field in /etc/shadow"
awk -F: '$2=="" {print $1}' /etc/shadow
echo "-- /etc/passwd entries without x in the password field:"
awk -F: '$2!="x" {print $1}' /etc/passwd

sec "Password status: user P/L/NP lastchange min max warn inactive"
for u in root $HUMANS; do passwd -S "$u"; done

sec "sudoers (non-comment lines)"
grep -HnvE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null
grep -Hn 'includedir' /etc/sudoers
echo "-- sudo rights per human user:"
for u in $HUMANS; do echo "[$u]"; sudo -l -U "$u" 2>/dev/null | sed -n '/may run the following/,$p'; done

sec "polkit local rules"
ls -la /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/50-local.d/ /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ 2>/dev/null

sec "login.defs"
grep -E '^\s*(PASS_MAX_DAYS|PASS_MIN_DAYS|PASS_WARN_AGE|ENCRYPT_METHOD|UMASK|HOME_MODE)' /etc/login.defs

sec "pwquality.conf (non-comment)"
grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/security/pwquality.conf 2>/dev/null

sec "faillock.conf (non-comment)"
grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/security/faillock.conf 2>/dev/null

sec "PAM common files (non-comment)"
for f in common-auth common-account common-password common-session; do
  echo "-- $f"; grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' "/etc/pam.d/$f"
done
echo "-- pam_permit / pam_exec / nullok anywhere in /etc/pam.d:"
grep -HnE 'pam_permit|pam_exec|nullok' /etc/pam.d/* | grep -v ':\s*#'

sec "ufw"
ufw status verbose 2>&1

sec "Listening ports"
ss -tulpn

sec "Enabled services"
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled --no-pager --no-legend

sec "Running services"
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager --no-legend

sec "Timers"
systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager

sec "Real unit files and drop-ins in /etc/systemd"
find /etc/systemd/system /etc/systemd/user -type f \( -name '*.service' -o -name '*.timer' -o -name '*.socket' -o -name '*.path' -o -name '*.conf' \) -ls 2>/dev/null
echo "-- systemd-delta (overridden or extended units):"
systemd-delta --no-pager --type=extended,overridden,redirected 2>/dev/null
echo "-- per-user units:"
ls -la /home/*/.config/systemd/user/ 2>/dev/null

sec "User crontabs"
for u in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do
  c=$(crontab -l -u "$u" 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)')
  [ -n "$c" ] && printf -- '-- %s\n%s\n' "$u" "$c"
done

sec "System cron"
grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.weekly /etc/cron.monthly
grep -HvE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/cron.d/* 2>/dev/null
echo "-- cron.allow / cron.deny:"; cat /etc/cron.allow /etc/cron.deny 2>/dev/null
echo "-- at jobs:"; atq 2>/dev/null

sec "rc.local and ld.so.preload"
if [ -e /etc/rc.local ]; then ls -l /etc/rc.local; cat /etc/rc.local; else echo "no /etc/rc.local"; fi
if [ -e /etc/ld.so.preload ]; then echo "LD.SO.PRELOAD EXISTS:"; cat /etc/ld.so.preload; else echo "no /etc/ld.so.preload"; fi
echo "-- ld.so.conf.d:"; cat /etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null

sec "Aliases and suspicious lines in shell startup files"
grep -HnE 'alias |/dev/tcp|nc |ncat|curl|wget|base64|LD_PRELOAD|PATH=' /etc/bash.bashrc /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/*.sh /etc/environment /root/.bashrc /root/.profile /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.profile /home/*/.bash_aliases /home/*/.bash_login /home/*/.bash_profile 2>/dev/null

sec "Autostart entries"
grep -H '^Exec' /etc/xdg/autostart/*.desktop /home/*/.config/autostart/*.desktop /root/.config/autostart/*.desktop 2>/dev/null

sec "update-motd.d and apt hooks"
ls -la /etc/update-motd.d/ 2>/dev/null
grep -rnE 'Invoke|Pre-Install-Pkgs' /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/ 2>/dev/null

sec "Files in /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm changed in the last 30 days"
find /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm -type f -mtime -30 -ls 2>/dev/null | head -100

sec "Processes running from temp folders or deleted files"
ls -l /proc/[0-9]*/exe 2>/dev/null | grep -E '/tmp|/dev/shm|/var/tmp|deleted'

sec "Loaded kernel modules not from the kernel package"
for m in $(lsmod | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}'); do f=$(modinfo -n "$m" 2>/dev/null); case "$f" in /lib/modules/*/kernel/*|/usr/lib/modules/*/kernel/*|"") ;; *) echo "$m $f";; esac; done
cat /etc/modules 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)'

sec "SUID files NOT in the usual Mint list"
KNOWN='^(/usr/bin/(sudo|su|passwd|chsh|chfn|gpasswd|newgrp|mount|umount|pkexec|fusermount3?|at|vmware-user-suid-wrapper)|/usr/sbin/(pppd|mount\.nfs|mount\.cifs)|/usr/lib/(dbus-1\.0/dbus-daemon-launch-helper|openssh/ssh-keysign|policykit-1/polkit-agent-helper-1|polkit-1/polkit-agent-helper-1|xorg/Xorg\.wrap|snapd/snap-confine)|/usr/libexec/polkit-agent-helper-1)$'
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -vE "$KNOWN"

sec "Installed packages of interest (compare with README)"
TOOLS='john|john-data|hydra|hydra-gtk|nmap|ndiff|zenmap|ncat|netcat-traditional|socat|aircrack-ng|wireshark|wireshark-qt|wireshark-gtk|wireshark-common|tshark|ophcrack|ophcrack-cli|nikto|sqlmap|medusa|ncrack|patator|ettercap-common|ettercap-graphical|ettercap-text-only|bettercap|kismet|fcrackzip|pdfcrack|rarcrack|crack|crack-common|crack-md5|hashcat|dsniff|yersinia|macchanger|hping3|p0f|masscan|zmap|dirb|gobuster|wfuzz|wifite|reaver|weevely|logkeys|telnetd|inetutils-telnetd|telnetd-ssl|telnet|rsh-server|rsh-redone-server|rsh-client|talkd|vsftpd|proftpd-basic|proftpd-core|pure-ftpd|tftpd-hpa|xinetd|openbsd-inetd|snmpd|nis|x11vnc|vino|tigervnc-standalone-server|tightvncserver|xrdp|apache2|nginx|lighttpd|samba|nfs-kernel-server|rpcbind|openssh-server|mysql-server|mariadb-server|postgresql|postfix|dovecot-core|bind9|isc-dhcp-server|squid|cups|avahi-daemon|transmission-gtk|deluge|qbittorrent|ktorrent|aisleriot|gnome-mines|gnome-sudoku|freeciv-client-gtk3|minetest|wesnoth|supertux|supertuxkart|openarena|0ad'
dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Package}\n' 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="ii" {print $2}' | grep -xE "$TOOLS"
echo "-- flatpak apps:"; flatpak list --app 2>/dev/null
echo "-- snaps:"; snap list 2>/dev/null
echo "-- /opt, /usr/local/bin, /usr/local/sbin:"; ls -la /opt /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin 2>/dev/null

sec "Media files under /home, /root, /srv, /var/www"
find /home /root /srv /var/www -type f \( -iname '*.mp3' -o -iname '*.mp4' -o -iname '*.wav' -o -iname '*.flac' -o -iname '*.ogg' -o -iname '*.m4a' -o -iname '*.avi' -o -iname '*.mkv' -o -iname '*.mov' -o -iname '*.wmv' -o -iname '*.flv' -o -iname '*.webm' \) 2>/dev/null

sec "authorized_keys files"
find / -xdev -name 'authorized_keys*' -type f 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do echo "-- $f"; cat "$f"; done

sec "sshd effective settings (if installed)"
if command -v sshd >/dev/null; then sshd -T 2>/dev/null | grep -iE '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|permitemptypasswords|x11forwarding|maxauthtries|pubkeyauthentication|allowusers|allowgroups|usepam)'; else echo "openssh-server not installed"; fi
ls -la /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ 2>/dev/null

sec "LightDM settings in every config folder"
grep -rHnEi 'guest|autologin|hide-users|manual' /etc/lightdm/ /etc/xdg/lightdm/ /usr/share/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d/ 2>/dev/null

sec "/etc/hosts, resolv.conf, nsswitch hosts line"
grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/hosts
grep -E '^nameserver' /etc/resolv.conf
grep -E '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf

sec "APT sources (non-comment)"
grep -HvE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/* 2>/dev/null
echo "-- apt.conf.d proxy or insecure settings:"
grep -HniE 'proxy|unauth|insecure|AllowDowngrade' /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/* 2>/dev/null
echo "-- held packages:"; apt-mark showhold
echo "-- 20auto-upgrades:"; cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades 2>/dev/null

sec "sysctl values"
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians kernel.randomize_va_space kernel.dmesg_restrict kernel.kptr_restrict kernel.sysrq fs.suid_dumpable 2>/dev/null
echo "-- sysctl lines in /etc/sysctl.conf, /etc/sysctl.d and ufw:"
grep -HvE '^\s*(#|;|$)' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf 2>/dev/null

sec "File permissions"
stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* /etc/ssh/sshd_config /boot/grub/grub.cfg /etc/crontab /root /home/* 2>/dev/null
echo "-- world-writable files outside /proc, /sys, /tmp:"
find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys|tmp|var/tmp|dev)/' | head -50

sec "Immutable or append-only files in /etc"
lsattr -R /etc 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^\S*[ia]\S* '

sec "AppArmor and auditd"
aa-status 2>/dev/null | head -8
grep -E 'apparmor=0|security=none' /etc/default/grub
auditctl -s 2>/dev/null | head -3
systemctl is-active rsyslog auditd fail2ban 2>/dev/null

sec "Firefox policies and user.js"
cat /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json /usr/lib/firefox/distribution/policies.json 2>/dev/null
ls /home/*/.mozilla/firefox/*/user.js 2>/dev/null

sec "Packaged files whose contents changed (dpkg --verify, config files excluded)"
dpkg --verify 2>/dev/null | grep -vE ' c /|/usr/share/(doc|man|locale|help)/' | head -300
} > "$OUT" 2>&1

chown "$REALUSER": "$OUT" 2>/dev/null
echo "Wrote $OUT"

    #Read the recon report

    Report section What to look for Where to fix it
    Human users, UID 0, admin groups Names not in the README, extra admins, a second UID 0 Users and groups
    Empty password field, password status Any name listed; NP in the status column Users and groups
    sudoers, polkit NOPASSWD, !authenticate, unknown files sudoers and sudo rights
    login.defs, pwquality, faillock, PAM Defaults left in place, nullok, pam_permit in the wrong place Password policy, Account lockout
    ufw, listening ports, services Firewall inactive, unknown listeners, unneeded services Firewall, Services
    Units, cron, rc.local, preload, startup files, autostart Anything calling scripts in odd places Persistence and backdoors
    SUID, packages, media, permissions, immutable files Unknown SUID, hacking tools, music, wrong modes Software, Files
    sshd, LightDM, sysctl, AppArmor, Firefox Unsafe values SSH, Login screen, Kernel, AppArmor, Firefox
    dpkg --verify Changed binaries or PAM modules Modified system files

    #Snippet to enable ufw

    1. Sets the default policy to deny incoming and allow outgoing (never block outgoing; the scoring client needs it).
    2. Turns on logging and enables the firewall without the yes/no prompt.
    3. Prints the result.

    Run it by pasting into a terminal. Afterwards allow each service the README requires, for example sudo ufw allow OpenSSH or sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp.

    sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw logging on
sudo ufw --force enable
sudo ufw status verbose

    #Snippet to set login.defs aging values

    1. Backs up /etc/login.defs to /root.
    2. Sets PASS_MAX_DAYS 90, PASS_MIN_DAYS 1 and PASS_WARN_AGE 7. These only apply to accounts created afterwards; use the aging snippet for existing users.
    3. Prints the three lines so you can check them.

    Paste into a terminal.

    sudo cp -a /etc/login.defs /root/login.defs.bak
sudo sed -i -E 's/^\s*PASS_MAX_DAYS.*/PASS_MAX_DAYS\t90/; s/^\s*PASS_MIN_DAYS.*/PASS_MIN_DAYS\t1/; s/^\s*PASS_WARN_AGE.*/PASS_WARN_AGE\t7/' /etc/login.defs
grep -E '^PASS_(MAX|MIN|WARN)' /etc/login.defs

    #Snippet to age passwords of all human users

    1. Finds every account with a UID from 1000 to 65533.
    2. Sets maximum age 90, minimum age 1 and warning 7 days on each.

    Run it only after setting new passwords: an account whose password was last changed more than 90 days ago expires the moment this runs, and that includes your own. Paste into a terminal.

    for u in $(awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd); do
  sudo chage -M 90 -m 1 -W 7 "$u" && echo "aged $u"
done

    #Snippet to lock root

    1. Locks root's password so nobody can log in as root with a password (sudo keeps working).
    2. Prints root's status, which should show L.
    sudo passwd -l root && sudo passwd -S root

    #Snippet to set passwords from a list

    1. Sets the team password in a variable.
    2. For each name in the list, sets that password if the account exists; missing names are skipped and never created.

    Before running, replace <team-password> (keep the single quotes) and <user-list> with the README's users separated by spaces. Leave out your own account unless the README says to change it. Paste into a terminal.

    PW='<team-password>'
for u in <user-list>; do
  if id "$u" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf '%s:%s\n' "$u" "$PW" | sudo chpasswd && echo "password set: $u"
  else
    echo "SKIP (no such user): $u"
  fi
done

    #Snippet to remove nullok

    1. Backs up /etc/pam.d to /root with the time in the folder name.
    2. Removes nullok from the two PAM files that use it, so empty passwords stop working.
    3. Prints any nullok left in the common files.

    First give every account a password: anyone with an empty password is locked out after this. This prints accounts with an empty password and should print nothing:

    sudo awk -F: '$2==""' /etc/shadow

    Keep a root shell open (sudo -i in a second terminal) while changing PAM, then paste:

    sudo cp -a /etc/pam.d /root/pam.d.bak.$(date +%H%M)
sudo sed -i -E 's/[[:space:]]+nullok(_secure)?\b//g' /etc/pam.d/common-auth /etc/pam.d/common-password
grep -n nullok /etc/pam.d/common-* || echo "nullok removed"

    sudo pam-auth-update --force regenerates common-auth and puts nullok back (it also drops faillock and history lines). Without --force it leaves hand-edited files alone. Run this snippet again if anyone forces it.

    #Snippet to turn off LightDM guest and autologin

    1. Backs up /etc/lightdm to /root.
    2. Deletes every guest and autologin line from all LightDM files under /etc.
    3. Creates /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf if needed and adds allow-guest=false, greeter-allow-guest=false and autologin-guest=false under [Seat:*].
    4. Prints the settings LightDM will use.

    Paste into a terminal. It does not restart LightDM; the change applies at the next login screen.

    sudo cp -a /etc/lightdm /root/lightdm.bak.$(date +%H%M)
sudo find /etc/lightdm /etc/xdg/lightdm -name '*.conf' -exec sed -i -E '/^\s*(allow-guest|greeter-allow-guest|autologin-user|autologin-user-timeout|autologin-guest|autologin-session)\s*=/d' {} + 2>/dev/null
sudo touch /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf
grep -q '^\[Seat:\*\]' /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf || echo '[Seat:*]' | sudo tee -a /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf >/dev/null
sudo sed -i '0,/^\[Seat:\*\]/s//[Seat:*]\nallow-guest=false\ngreeter-allow-guest=false\nautologin-guest=false/' /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf
lightdm --show-config 2>&1 | grep -iE 'guest|autologin'

    #Snippet to turn off SSH root login

    Only when SSH is a required service.

    1. Backs up the whole /etc/ssh folder, drop-ins included, to /root.
    2. Sets PermitRootLogin no, PermitEmptyPasswords no and X11Forwarding no in the main file and in any drop-in under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (Ubuntu reads drop-ins first, and the first value wins). Indented lines inside Match blocks are left alone. If the main file has no line for a setting, it adds one at the top.
    3. Tests the config, restarts SSH only if the test passes, and prints the effective values.

    Paste into a terminal. More settings are in SSH server hardening.

    sudo cp -a /etc/ssh /root/ssh.bak.$(date +%H%M)
for k in PermitRootLogin PermitEmptyPasswords X11Forwarding; do
  sudo sed -i -E "s/^#?$k\s.*/$k no/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null
  grep -qE "^$k\s" /etc/ssh/sshd_config || sudo sed -i "1i $k no" /etc/ssh/sshd_config
done
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh
sudo sshd -T | grep -E '^(permitrootlogin|permitemptypasswords|x11forwarding) '

    #Snippet to write the sysctl hardening file

    1. Writes /etc/sysctl.d/99-cp.conf with the network and kernel settings explained in Kernel hardening.
    2. Changes ufw's log_martians=0 lines to 1 so ufw stops undoing that setting.
    3. Loads all sysctl files and reloads ufw.
    4. Prints lines in /etc/sysctl.conf and ufw's file that could still override yours.

    Paste the whole block into a terminal.

    sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-cp.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians = 1
net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1
net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_rfc1337 = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2
kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2
kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1
kernel.sysrq = 0
fs.protected_hardlinks = 1
fs.protected_symlinks = 1
fs.suid_dumpable = 0
EOF
sudo sed -i -E 's/^(net\/ipv4\/conf\/(all|default)\/log_martians)=0/\1=1/' /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf
sudo sysctl --system >/dev/null
sudo ufw reload
grep -nE 'ip_forward|randomize_va_space|redirects|source_route|martians|syncookies' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf | grep -v ':\s*#'

    #Snippet to fix permissions on account files

    1. Sets /etc/passwd and /etc/group (and their - backups) to 644 root:root.
    2. Sets /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow (and backups) to 640 root:shadow.
    3. Sets /etc/sudoers and everything in /etc/sudoers.d to 440 root:root.
    4. Prints the result.
    sudo chown root:root /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/passwd- /etc/group-
sudo chmod 644 /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/passwd- /etc/group-
sudo chown root:shadow /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/shadow- /etc/gshadow-
sudo chmod 640 /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/shadow- /etc/gshadow-
sudo chown root:root /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*
sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*
stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' /etc/passwd /etc/group /etc/shadow /etc/gshadow /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/*

    #Snippet to fix home directory permissions

    1. Goes through every folder in /home.
    2. If an account with that name exists, sets the folder to 750 and prints it; folders without an account are left alone.
    for d in /home/*/; do
  u=$(basename "$d")
  id "$u" >/dev/null 2>&1 && sudo chmod 750 "$d" && echo "750 $d"
done

    #Snippet to preview removing hacking tools

    1. Lists installed packages from a list of known hacking tools.
    2. Asks apt to simulate purging them (-s), which removes nothing and prints every package that would go, including collateral damage.

    Read the output. If it contains mint-meta, cinnamon or other desktop packages, take those tools out of your list. Then purge the rest yourself with sudo apt purge <package>.

    TOOLS='john|john-data|hydra|hydra-gtk|nmap|ndiff|ncat|netcat-traditional|socat|aircrack-ng|wireshark|wireshark-qt|wireshark-gtk|tshark|ophcrack|ophcrack-cli|nikto|sqlmap|medusa|ncrack|patator|ettercap-common|ettercap-graphical|ettercap-text-only|bettercap|fcrackzip|pdfcrack|rarcrack|crack|crack-common|crack-md5|hashcat|dsniff|yersinia|macchanger|hping3|p0f|masscan|zmap|dirb|gobuster|wfuzz|wifite|reaver|weevely'
PKGS=$(dpkg-query -W -f='${db:Status-Abbrev} ${Package}\n' | awk '$1=="ii" {print $2}' | grep -xE "$TOOLS" | tr '\n' ' ')
echo "Installed tools: ${PKGS:-none}"
[ -n "$PKGS" ] && apt-get -s purge $PKGS | grep -E '^(Purg|Remv) '

    Verify

    Run the recon script again to a new file and diff it with the first report. Every change you made should appear, and nothing you did not intend.

    PreviousFirefox on MintNextLinux command quick reference
    LNX

    Linux command quick reference

    jump:lin-cmd-ref

    Commands that change the system need sudo, shown where required. Placeholders such as <username> fill in when you click them.

    #Terminal and system basics

    Task Command
    Open a terminal Ctrl+Alt+T
    Root shell (keep one open while changing PAM or sudoers) sudo -i
    Re-run the last command with sudo sudo !!
    Edit a file sudo nano <file> or sudo xed <file>
    Back up a file before editing sudo cp -a <file> <file>.bak
    Mint and Ubuntu version cat /etc/linuxmint/info, lsb_release -a
    Running kernel uname -r
    Reboot sudo reboot

    #Users, groups and passwords

    Task Command
    List human users awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd
    A user's groups id <username>
    Members of a group getent group <groupname>
    Add a user sudo adduser <username>
    Delete a user, keep home sudo deluser <username>
    Delete a user and home sudo deluser --remove-home <username>
    Add a user to a group sudo usermod -aG <groupname> <username>
    Remove a user from a group sudo gpasswd -d <username> <groupname>
    Create a group sudo groupadd <groupname>
    Set a password sudo passwd <username>
    Set a password without a prompt printf '%s:%s\n' '<username>' '<team-password>' | sudo chpasswd
    Lock an account's password, or remove the lock sudo passwd -l <username>, sudo passwd -u <username>
    Password status of every account sudo passwd -S -a
    Change a login shell sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <username>
    Accounts with UID 0 awk -F: '$3==0' /etc/passwd
    Accounts with an empty password sudo awk -F: '$2==""' /etc/shadow
    Set password aging for a user sudo chage -M 90 -m 1 -W 7 <username>
    Show password aging sudo chage -l <username>
    Clear a faillock lockout sudo faillock --user <username> --reset

    #sudo and permissions

    Task Command
    Edit sudoers safely sudo visudo
    Check sudoers syntax sudo visudo -c
    A user's sudo rights sudo -l -U <username>
    Permissions in numbers stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' <file>
    Change permissions sudo chmod 640 <file>
    Change owner sudo chown root:root <file>
    Show and clear the immutable flag lsattr <file>, sudo chattr -i <file>
    SUID files sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
    World-writable files sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 2>/dev/null

    #Packages

    Task Command
    Refresh package lists sudo apt update
    Upgrade everything sudo apt full-upgrade -y
    Install a package sudo apt install <package>
    Remove a package and its config sudo apt purge <package>
    Remove unused dependencies sudo apt autoremove --purge
    Is a package installed dpkg -l | grep -i <package>
    Which package owns a file dpkg -S <path>
    Files in a package dpkg -L <package>
    Finish an interrupted install sudo dpkg --configure -a
    Check package files for changes sudo dpkg --verify <package>
    Reinstall a package sudo apt install --reinstall <package>

    #Services, ports and processes

    Task Command
    Listening ports with programs sudo ss -tulpn
    Running services systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
    Enabled services systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled
    Service status systemctl status <service-name>
    Stop and disable sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>
    Start and enable sudo systemctl enable --now <service-name>
    Restart sudo systemctl restart <service-name>
    Block a service from starting at all sudo systemctl mask <service-name>
    Service log journalctl -u <service-name> -n 50 --no-pager
    Latest errors journalctl -xe
    Process tree ps auxf
    Kill a process sudo kill -9 <pid>
    Which process uses a port sudo lsof -i :<port>
    Firewall on sudo ufw enable
    Firewall status sudo ufw status verbose
    Allow a port sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp
    Delete a firewall rule sudo ufw status numbered, then sudo ufw delete <rule-number>

    #Scheduled jobs

    Task Command
    A user's crontab sudo crontab -l -u <username>
    Remove a user's crontab sudo crontab -r -u <username>
    at jobs sudo atq
    systemd timers systemctl list-timers --all

    #Searching and forensics

    Task Command
    Find a file by name sudo find / -iname '*<name>*' 2>/dev/null
    Search text inside files sudo grep -rniI '<text>' <path>
    Hash a file sha256sum <file>
    Decode base64 echo '<text>' | base64 -d
    Login history last, sudo lastb
    Recent authentication events sudo tail -50 /var/log/auth.log

    #Hardening checks

    Task Command
    Read a kernel setting sysctl <key>
    Reload all sysctl files sudo sysctl --system
    Test the SSH config sudo sshd -t
    Effective SSH config sudo sshd -T
    AppArmor status sudo aa-status
    Effective LightDM config lightdm --show-config

    LNX

    Linux troubleshooting and recovery

    jump:lin-troubleshoot

    Fast path

    1. Stop making changes. Open your changelog and undo the most recent change first.

    2. If sudo still works, find the error:

      journalctl -xe

    3. If sudo is broken, use the root shell you kept open, or pkexec (sudo is broken).

    4. If a service will not start, read its status and run its config test (service will not start).
    5. If nothing else works, use recovery mode.
    6. Wait a minute or two for the score to refresh before undoing anything else.

    #sudo is broken

    Symptoms: "is not in the sudoers file", "parse error in /etc/sudoers", or sudo asks for a password and then fails.

    1. Use the root shell you kept open (prompt ends in #) and fix the file with visudo. For a drop-in, visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/<file>.

    2. No root shell? Use polkit, which does not read sudoers. pkexec shows a password dialog and works if you are still in the sudo group:

      pkexec visudo

      For a drop-in file, or for a full root shell:

      pkexec visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/<file>

      pkexec bash

    3. If you removed yourself from the sudo group, pkexec fails too. Use recovery mode.

    visudo points at the broken line, for example >>> /etc/sudoers: syntax error near line 25 <<<. A broken drop-in can also be deleted: pkexec rm /etc/sudoers.d/<file>.

    #Locked out by a PAM change

    • From the root shell you kept open, restore the backup folder, then test with su - <username> in a new terminal. The backup from the Password policy steps is in /root/cp-backup/pam.d:

      cp -a /root/cp-backup/pam.d/. /etc/pam.d/

      The nullok snippet makes time-stamped copies instead (ls -d /root/pam.d.bak.* lists them):

      cp -a /root/pam.d.bak.<time>/. /etc/pam.d/

    • If no root shell remains and sudo fails because of PAM, pkexec probably fails as well: /etc/pam.d/polkit-1 includes common-auth. Use recovery mode; its root shell does not ask for a password while root is locked.

    • Most common causes: a wrong success=N jump count in common-auth, a typo in a module name, pwquality settings so strict that no password passes, nullok removed while your account has an empty password, or faillock locking your account (faillock --user <username> --reset from a root shell).

    #Boot into recovery mode

    Last resort: rebooting costs a few minutes, but the scoring engine keeps its state.

    1. Reboot. While the machine starts, hold Shift (BIOS) or tap Esc (UEFI) to show the GRUB menu.
    2. Choose Advanced options for Linux Mint, then the entry ending in "(recovery mode)".
    3. Choose root (Drop to root shell prompt) and press Enter at "Press Enter for maintenance".

    4. Make the disk writable:

      mount -o remount,rw /

    5. Fix the file (visudo, restore /etc/pam.d from /root, gpasswd -a <username> sudo).

    6. Reboot:

      reboot

    #apt or dpkg is locked or interrupted

    Check whether apt, dpkg, unattended-upgrades or Update Manager is still running. If something is, wait for it:

    ps aux | grep -E '[a]pt|[d]pkg|[u]nattended|[m]intupdate'

    Finish an interrupted install and repair broken dependencies:

    sudo dpkg --configure -a
sudo apt --fix-broken install

    Remove the lock files only when the ps line above prints nothing:

    sudo rm -f /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend /var/lib/dpkg/lock /var/cache/apt/archives/lock /var/lib/apt/lists/lock
sudo dpkg --configure -a

    #ufw blocks SSH or a required service

    Work on the image's own console, not over SSH. List the rules, allow the service and reload:

    sudo ufw status numbered
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw reload

    Replace OpenSSH with the required port (sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp) for other services. In an emergency, sudo ufw disable, fix the rules, then sudo ufw enable straight away: a disabled firewall loses points.

    #A service will not start

    systemctl status <service-name> --no-pager -l
journalctl -u <service-name> -n 50 --no-pager

    Then run the service's own config test:

    Service Test command
    ssh sudo sshd -t
    apache2 sudo apache2ctl configtest
    nginx sudo nginx -t
    samba testparm -s
    vsftpd no test; read journalctl -u vsftpd. Common: 500 OOPS: vsftpd: refusing to run with writable root inside chroot(), fixed with allow_writeable_chroot=YES
    mysql sudo mysqld --validate-config
    postfix sudo postfix check
    sudoers sudo visudo -c

    If the service is masked, unmask and start it:

    sudo systemctl unmask <service-name>
sudo systemctl enable --now <service-name>

    If the package was purged by mistake, reinstall it and restore its config from your backup:

    sudo apt install <package>

    #Score dropped after a change

    1. Open your changelog and undo the most recent change: restore the .bak, reinstall the package, re-add the user to the group, or re-enable the service.
    2. Wait a minute or two for the score to refresh before undoing anything else.
    3. Usual causes: an authorized user or admin removed, a required service or package removed, a required file deleted, a required service's config broken, or a password changed that the README said to leave alone.

    #Permission denied

    • Add sudo, or use the root shell.
    • Redirects run as you, not as root. Use echo <text> | sudo tee <file> instead of sudo echo <text> > <file>.
    • Run scripts with sudo bash <file>; no chmod +x needed.
    • Still denied as root: the file is immutable (next heading) or the disk is mounted read-only (mount | grep ' / ' shows ro).

    #Operation not permitted even as root

    The file has the immutable or append-only attribute:

    lsattr <file>
sudo chattr -i -a <file>

    #Find which change broke things

    • Keep a changelog from the start: time, file or command, old value, new value.

    • Files in /etc changed in the last 60 minutes:

      sudo find /etc -mmin -60 -type f 2>/dev/null

    • Compare with a backup:

      diff /root/pam.d.bak.<time>/common-auth /etc/pam.d/common-auth

    • Package changes:

      grep -E ' (install|remove|purge) ' /var/log/dpkg.log | tail -30
tail -50 /var/log/apt/history.log

    • Your own commands: history | tail -100 in each terminal. The root shell has its own history.

    #Desktop froze or you logged out by accident

    • Switch to a text console with Ctrl+Alt+F2, log in, fix the problem, then return to the desktop with Ctrl+Alt+F7 (or Ctrl+Alt+F1 if F7 is blank).
    • Restart the Cinnamon shell without logging out: Ctrl+Alt+Esc, or Alt+F2, type r and press Enter.

    #No network or apt cannot resolve hosts

    Test the raw connection, then name lookup:

    ping -c 2 8.8.8.8
ping -c 2 archive.ubuntu.com

    If the first works and the second fails, DNS is the problem. Check for tampering and the resolver service:

    cat /etc/hosts /etc/resolv.conf
systemctl status systemd-resolved --no-pager
nmcli general status

    Verify

    After any recovery: sudo -v returns without an error, sudo visudo -c reports the files parsed OK, and systemctl --failed lists no required service.

    PreviousLinux command quick referenceNextLinux distro differences (Mint, Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, FreeBSD)
    LNX

    Linux distro differences (Mint, Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, FreeBSD)

    jump:lin-distro-diff

    Fast path

    1. Print the distro name and version:

      cat /etc/os-release

    2. If that file is missing or uname -s prints FreeBSD, go to FreeBSD.

    3. Find your column in the differences table and note the firewall, update tool, login screen and SSH unit.
    4. Open the distro notes: Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora. Mint is the default everywhere else in the Linux area.
    5. Work the master checklist; every item is the same on the Debian family unless it names a distro.

    CyberPatriot 19 scored rounds use Linux Mint 21 (Round 1, Round 2, State, Semifinals) and Ubuntu 24.04 (State). Training rounds use Ubuntu 22.04. Debian 11 appeared in CP-16 and Fedora 36 at CP-15 Semifinals (Platinum). One unofficial guide claims Debian 12 and FreeBSD at CP-19 Semifinals; the official round table does not list them, so treat them as possible, not expected.

    #Tell which distro and version you are on

    Run these in order until one answers:

    cat /etc/os-release

    hostnamectl

    cat /etc/linuxmint/info /etc/debian_version /etc/fedora-release 2>/dev/null

    On FreeBSD, /etc/os-release exists on recent releases too, and these always work:

    uname -a
freebsd-version -kru

    How to read the result:

    You see You are on Codename
    ID=linuxmint, VERSION_ID="21.3", UBUNTU_CODENAME=jammy Linux Mint 21.x (built on Ubuntu 22.04) vanessa, vera, victoria, virginia
    ID=ubuntu, VERSION_ID="22.04" Ubuntu 22.04 LTS jammy
    ID=ubuntu, VERSION_ID="24.04" Ubuntu 24.04 LTS noble
    ID=debian, VERSION_ID="11" Debian 11 bullseye
    ID=debian, VERSION_ID="12" Debian 12 bookworm
    ID=fedora, VERSION_ID=40 (any number) Fedora none
    ID=freebsd or uname -s prints FreeBSD FreeBSD none

    Find the desktop and the login screen, because the guest, user-list and screen-lock fixes depend on them:

    echo "$XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP"

    systemctl status display-manager --no-pager

    lightdm means the LightDM section applies. gdm or gdm3 means the GDM3 section. sddm (KDE) is covered in Debian login screens.

    #Differences table

    Item Mint 21 Ubuntu 22.04 Ubuntu 24.04 Debian 12 (11) Fedora FreeBSD
    Package manager apt, dpkg apt, dpkg, snap apt, dpkg, snap apt, dpkg dnf, rpm pkg (packages), freebsd-update (base)
    Firewall ufw (off), gufw GUI ufw (off), no GUI ufw (off), no GUI none; install ufw firewalld (on) pf or ipfw (off)
    Display manager LightDM (slick-greeter) GDM3 GDM3 GDM3 (GNOME), LightDM (XFCE, Cinnamon, MATE), SDDM (KDE) GDM none by default
    Update GUI Update Manager (mintupdate) Software Updater, Software & Updates Software Updater, Software & Updates GNOME Software or none GNOME Software none
    Automatic updates mintupdate-automation, unattended-upgrades unattended-upgrades (installed) unattended-upgrades (installed) unattended-upgrades (install it) dnf-automatic (dnf5 on 41+) freebsd-update cron
    Admin group sudo sudo (and legacy admin) sudo (and legacy admin) sudo, often empty when root has a password wheel wheel (for su)
    Root account locked locked locked locked, or has a password locked unless set at install password set at install, plus toor
    PAM files /etc/pam.d/common-* /etc/pam.d/common-* /etc/pam.d/common-* /etc/pam.d/common-* system-auth, password-auth through authselect /etc/pam.d/*, /etc/login.conf
    Lockout module pam_faillock (by hand) pam_faillock (by hand) pam_faillock (by hand) pam_faillock (by hand) authselect with-faillock none built in
    Password hash yescrypt yescrypt yescrypt yescrypt yescrypt sha512 (login.conf)
    SSH unit ssh.service ssh.service ssh.socket + ssh.service ssh.service sshd.service sshd rc script
    Auth log /var/log/auth.log /var/log/auth.log /var/log/auth.log journal only on 12 (journalctl); /var/log/auth.log on 11 journal, /var/log/audit/audit.log /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/security
    MAC framework AppArmor AppArmor AppArmor AppArmor SELinux (enforcing) securelevel, optional MAC modules
    Apt source file sources.list.d/official-package-repositories.list sources.list sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources (deb822) sources.list /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo /etc/pkg/FreeBSD.conf
    Web server unit apache2 apache2 apache2 apache2 httpd apache24
    Text editor GUI xed gedit gnome-text-editor gnome-text-editor or mousepad gnome-text-editor none
    What stays the same across the Debian family

    Mint, Ubuntu and Debian share /etc/login.defs, the common-* PAM files, /etc/security/pwquality.conf and faillock.conf, /etc/sudoers with the sudo group, /etc/ssh/sshd_config with sshd_config.d, sysctl.d, systemctl, ufw, cron, AppArmor, and every check in users, password policy, lockout, kernel, files and malware. Only the login screen, the update GUI, the SSH socket on 24.04, snaps on Ubuntu and the missing sudo and firewall on Debian differ.

    PreviousLinux troubleshooting and recoveryNextUbuntu 22.04 and 24.04 specifics
    LNX

    Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 specifics

    jump:lin-ubuntu

    Fast path

    1. Open Software & Updates > Updates and set: security updates checked, "Automatically check for updates" Daily, "When there are security updates" Download and install automatically (details).

    2. Install updates, then refresh the snaps (close Firefox first):

      sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo snap refresh

    3. Turn off automatic login and hide the user list in GDM3 (details):

      sudo nano /etc/gdm3/custom.conf

    4. Turn on the screen lock as your desktop user (details):

      gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled true

    5. On 24.04, check SSH with systemctl status ssh.socket (details).

    6. Work the rest of the master checklist; users, PAM, sudo, ufw, kernel and files are the same as on Mint.

    Past Ubuntu keys (K3 Ubuntu 22 Training, K6 Ubuntu 20 Practice, G1 Ubuntu 14 State) scored the same families as Mint: users, login.defs, PAM length and lockout, sysctl, ufw, shadow permissions, FTP removal, daily update checks, security updates, Firefox update, MP3 files, hacking tools, a cron netcat backdoor and SSH root login. The CP-18 State Ubuntu 24 image had 26 items, with Account Policy 2, Local Policy 3, Forensics 3 and Unwanted Software 2.

    #Set automatic updates in Software & Updates

    Scored in past keys as "The system automatically checks for updates daily" (K3, K6, SR2) and "Install updates from important security updates" (R1, R2, G1).

    1. Press Super, type Software & Updates, and open it (or run software-properties-gtk). Enter your password when asked.

    2. Open the Updates tab and set:

      Setting Value
      Install updates from: Important security updates (jammy-security or noble-security) checked
      Install updates from: Recommended updates (-updates) checked
      Automatically check for updates Daily
      When there are security updates Download and install automatically
      When there are other updates Display immediately (or weekly)
      Notify me of a new Ubuntu version For long-term support versions

    3. Click Close. If it offers Reload, click it.

    4. On the Ubuntu Software tab, check that main, universe, restricted and multiverse are ticked and the download server is a normal Ubuntu mirror.

    The GUI writes the APT::Periodic keys into a file in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/. Check the result from the terminal:

    apt-config dump | grep -i periodic

    You should see:

    APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1";
APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";

    If a value stays "0", another file in apt.conf.d overrides it. Find it with grep -rn 'APT::Periodic' /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/, fix that file, and set 20auto-upgrades by hand.

    The security checkbox adds or removes the -security suite in the source file. If it will not stay checked, read the sources directly (22.04, 24.04).

    Verify

    apt-config dump | grep -i periodic shows Update-Package-Lists "1" and Unattended-Upgrade "1", systemctl is-enabled unattended-upgrades prints enabled, and grep -rn security /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ shows an active security line.

    #Read deb822 sources on Ubuntu 24.04

    Ubuntu 24.04 keeps its repositories in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources, and /etc/apt/sources.list holds only a comment pointing there. Show the file:

    cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources

    A clean file has two stanzas (the mirror hostname may differ, for example us.archive.ubuntu.com):

    Types: deb
URIs: http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/
Suites: noble noble-updates noble-backports
Components: main restricted universe multiverse
Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/ubuntu-archive-keyring.gpg

Types: deb
URIs: http://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/
Suites: noble-security
Components: main restricted universe multiverse
Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/ubuntu-archive-keyring.gpg

    Red flags in deb822 files:

    • The noble-security stanza is missing, or its Suites: line lacks noble-security.
    • Enabled: no inside a stanza turns that repository off.
    • Trusted: yes skips signature checks (the deb822 form of [trusted=yes]).
    • Another codename (jammy, focal), a Debian or Kali URI, or an unknown .sources or .list file in the folder.

    Edit with sudo nano /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources, then run sudo apt update and read it for errors. Stanzas are separated by one blank line.

    #Update and check snaps

    Firefox (22.04 and 24.04), Thunderbird (24.04) and Chromium are snaps on Ubuntu, so apt does not update them.

    List the snaps and what has a pending update:

    snap list
snap refresh --list

    Close the app, then refresh one snap or all of them:

    sudo snap refresh firefox

    sudo snap refresh

    If it says the snap "has running apps", close every window of that app (check with pgrep -a firefox) and run it again.

    A refresh hold stops updates. Show the schedule and any hold, then clear holds:

    snap refresh --time

    sudo snap refresh --unhold

    Remove an unauthorized snap (games and hacking tools also come as snaps):

    sudo snap remove --purge <package>

    Snap services can listen on ports too. List them with snap services.

    #Harden the GDM3 login screen

    Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 (and Debian GNOME, Fedora) use GDM, not LightDM, so the lightdm.conf fixes in LightDM do not apply. The equivalents:

    Scoring idea LightDM setting GDM3 setting
    No automatic login autologin-user= empty AutomaticLoginEnable=false and TimedLoginEnable=false in [daemon]
    Greeter does not enumerate user accounts greeter-hide-users=true disable-user-list=true in [org/gnome/login-screen]
    X Server does not allow TCP connections xserver-allow-tcp=false DisallowTCP=true in [security] (the default)
    Guest account is disabled allow-guest=false GDM has no guest session
    No remote XDMCP logins [XDMCPServer] enabled=false Enable=false in [xdmcp]

    The guest scoring items in past keys (R2, SR2, G1) were all on LightDM images. On a GDM3 image, check that no account named guest exists with getent passwd | grep -i guest, and if lightdm is installed and running, use the LightDM fix instead.

    #Turn off automatic login in custom.conf

    The file is /etc/gdm3/custom.conf on Ubuntu and /etc/gdm3/daemon.conf on Debian. Fedora uses /etc/gdm/custom.conf.

    sudo nano /etc/gdm3/custom.conf

    Set these lines, each under its section header (create the header if it is missing):

    [daemon]
AutomaticLoginEnable=false
TimedLoginEnable=false

[security]
DisallowTCP=true

[xdmcp]
Enable=false

    Delete any AutomaticLogin=<username> or TimedLogin= line. In the GUI the same switch is Settings > Users > Automatic Login.

    #Hide the user list

    Open the greeter defaults file:

    sudo nano /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults

    Under [org/gnome/login-screen], remove the # from the disable-user-list line so it reads:

    [org/gnome/login-screen]
disable-user-list=true

    Optional lines in the same section are banner-message-enable=true and banner-message-text='Authorized users only'.

    GDM reads both files when it starts, so the change shows at the next reboot. sudo systemctl restart gdm3 applies it at once but ends your desktop session, including your root terminal; do it only at the final reboot.

    The dconf method from the CIS benchmark

    CIS uses a dconf profile instead. Both work; use one. Create /etc/dconf/profile/gdm:

    user-db:user
system-db:gdm
file-db:/usr/share/gdm/greeter-dconf-defaults

    Create /etc/dconf/db/gdm.d/00-login-screen:

    [org/gnome/login-screen]
disable-user-list=true

    Create the folder before the file with sudo mkdir -p /etc/dconf/db/gdm.d. Then compile the database:

    sudo dconf update

    Check with grep -r disable-user-list /etc/dconf/db/gdm.d/.

    Verify

    grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/gdm3/custom.conf shows AutomaticLoginEnable=false, and grep -n disable-user-list /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults shows the line without #. After the reboot the login screen asks for a username.

    #Lock the screen in GNOME

    Ubuntu 22.04: Settings > Privacy > Screen. Ubuntu 24.04: Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Lock. Set Blank Screen Delay to 5 minutes, turn Automatic Screen Lock on, and set the lock delay to "Screen Turns Off".

    Run these as your normal desktop user, without sudo. gsettings changes only the account that runs it:

    gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay 300
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled true
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-delay 0

    Ubuntu also has a lock-on-suspend key. If it prints "No such key", skip it:

    gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.screensaver ubuntu-lock-on-suspend true

    Check with gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled, which prints true.

    #Check AppArmor and user namespaces on Ubuntu

    AppArmor is on by default on Ubuntu, as on Mint. Show its state:

    sudo aa-status

    You should see "apparmor module is loaded" and a list of profiles in enforce mode. A profile switched to complain mode for a network service (for example /usr/sbin/cupsd or a planted name) is suspicious; put it back with sudo aa-enforce <path> (from apparmor-utils). The full AppArmor section is here.

    Ubuntu 24.04 also restricts unprivileged user namespaces through AppArmor. The value should be 1:

    sysctl kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns

    #Check netplan and network files

    Ubuntu writes network settings through netplan. The desktop file is usually /etc/netplan/01-network-manager-all.yaml, which hands everything to NetworkManager. List the files and their permissions:

    sudo ls -la /etc/netplan/

    The files should be 600 and owned by root; netplan warns "Permissions for /etc/netplan/... are too open" otherwise. Fix it with sudo chmod 600 /etc/netplan/*.yaml. A planted file that sets odd nameservers sends DNS to an attacker; check the active DNS servers with resolvectl status. Do not run sudo netplan apply unless you changed something on purpose, because it can drop the network for a moment.

    #Other Ubuntu differences

    Topic Ubuntu detail Where it is covered
    Users GUI Settings > Users (24.04: Settings > System > Users) users
    Editor gedit (22.04), gnome-text-editor (24.04) terminal
    Firewall GUI gufw is not installed (sudo apt install gufw) firewall
    SSH ssh.socket on 24.04 SSH
    polkit JavaScript rules in /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ on 24.04 sudo
    Pro and ESM pro status shows Ubuntu Pro; esm source files appear only when Pro is attached this section
    Crash reports apport and whoopsie are stock services

    LNX

    Debian 11 and 12 specifics

    jump:lin-debian

    Fast path

    1. Confirm the release with cat /etc/debian_version.
    2. Test sudo with sudo -v. If it fails, become root with su - and install sudo.
    3. Check /etc/apt/sources.list for the security line and comment out any deb cdrom: line (details).

    4. Install updates:

      sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y

    5. Install and enable the firewall, which Debian does not ship. Add the allow rules for README services before ufw enable:

      sudo apt install ufw
sudo ufw enable

    6. Set up automatic updates with the Debian-Security origin (details).

    7. Fix the login screen for your desktop (details), then work the master checklist.

    Debian 11 was a CP-16 image (Practice, Round 2, Semifinals). Debian 12 is rumored, not confirmed, for CP-19. Hivestorm 2020 and 2021 (Debian 9 and Ubuntu images) scored the same families as the CyberPatriot Ubuntu keys, plus PostgreSQL and Samba settings, dmesg_restrict, insecure sudo, GRUB config permissions and the password hashing algorithm.

    #Get sudo working on Debian

    The Debian installer decides this. If the root password was left blank, sudo is installed, root is locked and the first user is in sudo, as on Ubuntu. If a root password was set, sudo may be missing and nobody is in the sudo group.

    1. Become root with the root password from the README (the - matters, see why):

      su -

    2. Install sudo:

      apt install sudo

    3. Add each README administrator to the sudo group:

      usermod -aG sudo <username>

    4. Group membership applies at the next login. Keep using the root shell for now, or open a fresh login shell for your user with su - <username> and test sudo -v there.

    Keep root usable until sudo is proven. Only then decide about locking root: if the README gives a root password and lists root as used, set a strong password instead of locking it.

    #Check Debian apt sources

    Show the active lines:

    grep -rvE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/

    A clean Debian 12 /etc/apt/sources.list:

    deb http://deb.debian.org/debian bookworm main non-free-firmware
deb http://deb.debian.org/debian bookworm-updates main non-free-firmware
deb http://security.debian.org/debian-security bookworm-security main non-free-firmware

    A clean Debian 11 file uses bullseye, bullseye-updates and bullseye-security, without non-free-firmware (that component started with Debian 12). contrib and non-free may also appear; they are fine.

    • A deb cdrom: line from the install DVD makes apt update fail. Put # in front of it.
    • A missing -security line means no security updates. Add it back.
    • Old forms such as buster/updates, another codename, Kali, Ubuntu or an IP address are planted.
    • If /etc/apt/sources.list.d/debian.sources exists, it is in deb822 format; read it the way the Ubuntu 24.04 file is read.

    The proxy, trusted=yes, held-package and apt hook checks are the same as on Mint (how).

    #Turn on automatic updates on Debian

    Debian may not have unattended-upgrades installed. Install it and turn it on (answer Yes):

    sudo apt install unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges
sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

    That writes /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades. It must contain:

    APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1";
APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";

    Debian's 50unattended-upgrades uses Origins-Pattern instead of Ubuntu's Allowed-Origins. Open it and check that the security line is present and not commented out with //:

    sudo nano /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades

    Unattended-Upgrade::Origins-Pattern {
        "origin=Debian,codename=${distro_codename},label=Debian";
        "origin=Debian,codename=${distro_codename},label=Debian-Security";
        "origin=Debian,codename=${distro_codename}-security,label=Debian-Security";
};

    Test it:

    sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug 2>&1 | grep -iE 'allowed origins|pattern'

    Make sure the timers run: systemctl is-enabled unattended-upgrades apt-daily.timer apt-daily-upgrade.timer.

    #Debian login screens

    Debian's login screen depends on the desktop chosen at install. Check with cat /etc/X11/default-display-manager.

    Desktop Display manager File Fix
    GNOME (default) GDM3 /etc/gdm3/daemon.conf and /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults Same keys as Ubuntu GDM3; only the first file name differs
    XFCE, Cinnamon, MATE, LXDE LightDM (gtk-greeter or slick-greeter) /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf and /usr/share/lightdm/lightdm.conf.d/ Same keys as Mint LightDM under [Seat:*]
    KDE Plasma SDDM /etc/sddm.conf or /etc/sddm.conf.d/*.conf Empty User= under [Autologin]

    Debian's own LightDM drop-in sets greeter-hide-users=false, so put your greeter-hide-users=true and allow-guest=false in /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf under [Seat:*], which is read after it. Confirm the effective value with lightdm --show-config (how).

    For SDDM, check the autologin section in every file:

    grep -rn -A3 '\[Autologin\]' /etc/sddm.conf /etc/sddm.conf.d/ 2>/dev/null

    #Debian logs without rsyslog

    From Debian 12, rsyslog is not installed by default, so /var/log/auth.log and /var/log/syslog do not exist. Read the journal instead:

    Old file Debian 12 command
    /var/log/auth.log sudo journalctl _COMM=sshd _COMM=sudo _COMM=su or sudo journalctl -t sudo
    /var/log/syslog sudo journalctl -b
    One service sudo journalctl -u <service-name>
    Follow live sudo journalctl -f

    Install rsyslog with sudo apt install rsyslog only if a README or a tool needs the text files; it is not a scored default. Debian 11 still has rsyslog and the text logs.

    #Other Debian defaults that trip people up

    Topic Debian behavior What to do
    PATH for root su without - leaves out /usr/sbin Always su -
    Firewall No ufw or gufw installed sudo apt install ufw (firewall)
    pwquality libpam-pwquality not installed Install it (password policy)
    PAM files Same common-* files, yescrypt, nullok in common-auth Same fixes as Mint
    su restriction /etc/pam.d/su has pam_wheel.so commented out Optional hardening, not seen in keys
    Firefox Package is firefox-esr sudo apt install --only-upgrade firefox-esr
    AppArmor On by default since Debian 10 sudo aa-status (install apparmor-utils for aa-enforce)
    polkit Debian 12 uses JavaScript rules sudo
    Admin GUI Depends on the desktop (GNOME Settings > Users, or none) Use the terminal commands
    adduser Present, same as Ubuntu users
    PreviousUbuntu 22.04 and 24.04 specificsNextFedora and RHEL family (dnf, firewalld, SELinux)
    LNX

    Fedora and RHEL family (dnf, firewalld, SELinux)

    jump:lin-fedora

    Fast path

    1. Confirm the release with cat /etc/fedora-release.

    2. List admins and compare with the README; remove extras with sudo gpasswd -d <username> wheel:

      getent group wheel

    3. Start the updates in their own terminal:

      sudo dnf upgrade --refresh -y

    4. Make sure firewalld runs and remove services the README does not need (details):

      sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all

    5. Check SELinux is enforcing; fix with sudo setenforce 1 and the config file (details):

      getenforce

    6. Turn on lockout and password history through authselect (details).

    7. Harden /etc/ssh/sshd_config as on Mint and restart with sudo systemctl restart sshd.

    Fedora 36 was a CP-15 Semifinals Platinum image. No Fedora answer key has been found, so the items below are the Fedora way of doing what the Ubuntu and Mint keys scored.

    #Map Debian commands to Fedora

    Task Debian family Fedora
    Update everything sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade sudo dnf upgrade --refresh
    Remove a package sudo apt purge <package> sudo dnf remove <package>
    List installed packages dpkg -l rpm -qa
    Which package owns a file dpkg -S <path> rpm -qf <path>
    Verify package files sudo debsums -s sudo rpm -Va
    Repository files /etc/apt/sources.list* /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo
    Undo a package change none sudo dnf history undo <id>
    Admin group sudo wheel
    Firewall ufw firewall-cmd
    MAC AppArmor (aa-status) SELinux (getenforce, sestatus)
    PAM policy files /etc/pam.d/common-* authselect writes system-auth and password-auth
    Web server apache2 httpd (config in /etc/httpd/)
    Samba units smbd, nmbd smb, nmb
    DNS server named (bind9) named (bind)
    SSH unit ssh sshd
    Auth log /var/log/auth.log sudo journalctl -u sshd, /var/log/audit/audit.log

    #Manage users and the wheel group

    The user checks in users all work on Fedora (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, UID 0, empty hashes, nologin shells). The differences:

    • Admins are members of wheel, and sudoers grants %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL.

    • adduser is only a link to useradd; it does not prompt. Create a user and set the password:

      sudo useradd -m <username>
sudo passwd <username>

    • Delete a user (after Forensics) and remove the home folder:

      sudo userdel -r <username>

    • Promote and demote:

      sudo usermod -aG wheel <username>

      sudo gpasswd -d <username> wheel

    • Check /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ with sudo visudo exactly as on Mint (sudo). Fedora's file has a commented %wheel ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL line; an uncommented one is planted.

    #Install updates with dnf

    sudo dnf upgrade --refresh -y

    List what is waiting, and update one package:

    dnf check-update
sudo dnf upgrade <package>

    Check the repositories for planted ones. gpgcheck=0 or an unknown baseurl is a red flag:

    dnf repolist
grep -nE 'baseurl|metalink|gpgcheck|enabled' /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo

    Kernel updates need a reboot. sudo dnf history lists every transaction, and sudo dnf history undo <id> reverses one if an update broke a required service.

    #Turn on automatic updates with dnf-automatic

    Install the plugin and turn on installing:

    sudo dnf install dnf5-plugin-automatic
sudo nano /etc/dnf/automatic.conf

    Put these lines in the file:

    [commands]
apply_updates = yes
upgrade_type = default

    Start the timer:

    sudo systemctl enable --now dnf5-automatic.timer

    sudo dnf install dnf-automatic
sudo nano /etc/dnf/automatic.conf

    Under [commands] set apply_updates = yes, then:

    sudo systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic.timer

    Open Software > menu > Preferences and turn on Automatic Updates. It downloads updates and installs them at the next restart.

    Check with systemctl list-timers | grep -i automatic.

    #Turn on firewalld

    firewalld is on by default on Fedora. A planted image may have stopped it or opened extra services. Do not install ufw next to it.

    sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld
sudo firewall-cmd --state

    Show the default zone and what it allows:

    sudo firewall-cmd --get-default-zone
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all

    Fedora Workstation's default zone FedoraWorkstation allows TCP and UDP ports 1025-65535 from anywhere. Switch to the stricter public zone, then add back only the README services:

    sudo firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=public

    sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

    Remove a service or port the README does not need, then reload:

    sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=<service-name>
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-port=<port>/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

    --permanent writes the config; without it the change is lost at the next reload. Common service names are ssh, http, https, ftp, samba, mysql, postgresql, dns, smtp and cockpit. Outgoing traffic is allowed by default; leave it that way.

    Verify

    sudo firewall-cmd --state prints running, systemctl is-enabled firewalld prints enabled, and sudo firewall-cmd --list-all shows only the README services.

    #Keep SELinux enforcing

    getenforce
    Output Meaning Fix
    Enforcing Correct none
    Permissive Logs but does not block sudo setenforce 1 and set the config file
    Disabled Off in the config or on the kernel command line Set the config file, relabel, reboot

    Set the config file for the next boot:

    sudo sed -i 's/^SELINUX=.*/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config
grep -E '^SELINUX(TYPE)?=' /etc/selinux/config

    Expect SELINUX=enforcing and SELINUXTYPE=targeted. If SELinux was Disabled, files have no labels; request a relabel before the reboot (it adds several minutes to the boot):

    sudo touch /.autorelabel

    A selinux=0 kernel argument also disables it. Remove it from every kernel entry:

    sudo grubby --update-kernel ALL --remove-args selinux

    If a required service breaks after you enforce, read the denials instead of turning SELinux off:

    sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent

    The usual fixes are restoring labels on moved web or FTP files with sudo restorecon -Rv <path>, or turning on the boolean the service needs (list them with getsebool -a | grep -E 'httpd|ftp|samba', set one with sudo setsebool -P <boolean> on). Booleans that are on but not needed, such as ftpd_anon_write or httpd_enable_cgi, can be turned off the same way.

    #Set password policy and lockout with authselect

    On Fedora, /etc/pam.d/system-auth and password-auth are links into /etc/authselect/. Do not edit them by hand; authselect overwrites them. Show the profile and features:

    sudo authselect current

    Fresh Fedora 40 and later use the local profile; older installs use sssd. Turn on lockout, history and the nullok removal, then apply:

    sudo authselect enable-feature with-faillock
sudo authselect enable-feature with-pwhistory
sudo authselect enable-feature without-nullok
sudo authselect apply-changes

    Set the values in the same files the Debian family uses. Append to each with sudo nano:

    /etc/security/faillock.conf:

    deny = 5
fail_interval = 900
unlock_time = 900

    /etc/security/pwquality.conf (pam_pwquality is already in Fedora's stack):

    minlen = 12
ucredit = -1
lcredit = -1
dcredit = -1
ocredit = -1
dictcheck = 1
enforce_for_root

    /etc/security/pwhistory.conf:

    remember = 5
enforce_for_root

    Aging is in /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS 90, PASS_MIN_DAYS 1, PASS_WARN_AGE 7) and chage, as on Mint (aging).

    If authselect current says "No existing configuration detected" or authselect check reports changes, the PAM files were edited by hand, possibly with a backdoor. Reset them to a clean profile with the features on (use sssd instead of local on Fedora 39 and older):

    sudo authselect select local with-faillock with-pwhistory without-nullok --force

    Test a login with su - <username> in a second terminal before closing your root shell.

    #Harden SSH on Fedora

    The settings are the same as on Mint (SSH), including the drop-in folder /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ (Fedora ships 50-redhat.conf there). The unit is sshd:

    sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart sshd

    SSH is off by default on Fedora Workstation. If the README does not need it, sudo systemctl disable --now sshd; if it does, allow it with sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh and reload. A changed Port also needs the SELinux port label: sudo semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp <port>.

    #Find modified packages with rpm -Va

    sudo rpm -Va

    Each line shows what changed and the file. Example output:

    S.5....T.  c /etc/ssh/sshd_config
..5....T.    /usr/bin/passwd
    Letter Changed
    S size
    5 file contents (digest)
    M permissions or type
    U, G owner, group
    T modification time
    c before the path config file (changes are normal)

    A config file with 5 is usually your own hardening. A binary in /usr/bin, /usr/sbin or /usr/lib with 5 and no c was replaced. Note it for Forensics, then reinstall the owner:

    rpm -qf <path>
sudo dnf reinstall <package>

    #Services and logs on Fedora

    The service names differ from Ubuntu: httpd, mariadb or mysqld, smb and nmb, named, vsftpd, postfix, dovecot, cups, avahi-daemon, rpcbind, nfs-server, telnet.socket, and on Fedora Server cockpit.socket (web admin on port 9090). Disable with sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name> and remove with sudo dnf remove <package>.

    Fedora keeps logs in the journal and auditd's /var/log/audit/audit.log; /var/log/secure exists only if rsyslog was installed. Useful queries:

    sudo journalctl -u sshd --since today
sudo ausearch -m USER_LOGIN -ts today
    PreviousDebian 11 and 12 specificsNextFreeBSD essentials
    LNX

    FreeBSD essentials

    jump:lin-freebsd

    Fast path

    1. Become root (su -; your user must be in wheel) and confirm the release with freebsd-version -kru.

    2. List users, wheel members and UID 0 accounts (details):

      pw groupshow wheel
awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/master.passwd

    3. List listening ports and enabled services:

      sockstat -46l
service -e

    4. Disable each unneeded service with service <service-name> stop and sysrc <service-name>_enable=NO.

    5. Install updates:

      freebsd-update fetch install
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y

    6. Turn on pf with a default-deny inbound rule set (details).

    7. Set PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and run service sshd restart.

    FreeBSD has never appeared in an official CyberPatriot round list; one unofficial CP-19 guide mentions it for Semifinals. No FreeBSD key exists, so this section maps the Linux scoring families to FreeBSD commands. Commands are run as root; FreeBSD has no sudo unless the sudo or doas package was installed.

    #Learn the FreeBSD layout

    Linux habit FreeBSD equivalent
    /etc/shadow /etc/master.passwd (edit with vipw, which rebuilds the databases)
    systemctl enable/disable sysrc <service-name>_enable=YES or NO in /etc/rc.conf
    systemctl start/stop/status service <service-name> start, stop, status
    ss -tulpn sockstat -46l
    apt pkg (third-party software), freebsd-update (base system)
    /etc/pam.d/common-password /etc/pam.d/passwd and /etc/login.conf
    ufw pf (/etc/pf.conf) or ipfw
    /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf /etc/sysctl.conf
    Config for added software /usr/local/etc/ (sudoers, nginx, apache24, samba)
    /var/log/auth.log /var/log/auth.log, plus /var/log/security (firewall) and /var/log/messages
    lsattr, chattr ls -lo, chflags

    #Manage users with pw

    List human accounts (FreeBSD users start at UID 1001) and admins:

    awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1, $3, $7}' /etc/passwd
pw groupshow wheel
    Task Command
    Add a user with a home folder pw useradd -n <username> -m -s /bin/sh, then passwd <username>
    Add a user interactively adduser
    Delete a user and home folder pw userdel -n <username> -r
    Add to wheel (admin) pw groupmod wheel -m <username>
    Remove from wheel pw groupmod wheel -d <username>
    Add to any group pw groupmod <groupname> -m <username>
    Set a password passwd <username>
    Lock an account pw lock <username>
    Remove a login shell pw usermod <username> -s /usr/sbin/nologin

    Two accounts have UID 0 on a stock system: root and toor. toor is a standard spare root account whose password field is * (no login). Any other UID 0 account is planted. Check for empty passwords:

    awk -F: '$2=="" {print "EMPTY:", $1}' /etc/master.passwd

    #Set password policy on FreeBSD

    Password aging and the hash format live in the default class of /etc/login.conf. Open it with nano or ee and add or change these lines inside the default: entry (each line ends with :\):

        :passwd_format=sha512:\
    :passwordtime=90d:\
    :warnpassword=7d:\

    Rebuild the database, or the change does nothing:

    cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf

    passwordtime and passwd_format apply the next time each password is changed, so set the passwords again afterwards with passwd <username>. minpasswordlen in login.conf is no longer implemented; length and complexity come from pam_passwdqc. In /etc/pam.d/passwd, add this line above the pam_unix.so password line (a commented example is usually already there):

    password    requisite   pam_passwdqc.so min=disabled,disabled,16,12,12 similar=deny retry=3 enforce=users

    The five min= values are the minimum lengths for, in order: passwords with one character class, two classes, passphrases, three classes and four classes. disabled forbids that kind, so this line rejects one- and two-class passwords, and needs 16 characters for a passphrase and 12 for a mixed password. With enforce=users, root can still set any password, so the team password goes through.

    FreeBSD has no pam_faillock. Limit guessing over SSH with MaxAuthTries 3 and, if time allows, blacklistd (sysrc blacklistd_enable=YES, UseBlacklist yes in sshd_config). FreeBSD 15 renamed it to blocklistd (sysrc blocklistd_enable=YES, UseBlocklist yes).

    #Install updates on FreeBSD

    Update the base system, then packages:

    freebsd-update fetch
freebsd-update install

    pkg update
pkg upgrade -y

    List installed packages with known vulnerabilities:

    pkg audit -F

    freebsd-version -kru shows the kernel, running kernel and userland versions; a kernel update needs a reboot. For automatic checks, add this line to /etc/crontab, which downloads updates daily and mails root:

    @daily  root    freebsd-update cron

    #Turn on the pf firewall

    Write /etc/pf.conf (add a port inside the braces for each README service):

    set skip on lo0
block in all
pass out all keep state
pass in proto tcp to port { 22 } keep state

    Check the syntax, enable pf at boot and start it:

    pfctl -nf /etc/pf.conf
sysrc pf_enable=YES
sysrc pflog_enable=YES
service pf start

    Show the loaded rules and status:

    pfctl -sr
pfctl -si

    pfctl -si prints Status: Enabled. After editing the file later, reload with pfctl -f /etc/pf.conf.

    The built-in workstation rule set allows outgoing traffic and blocks unsolicited incoming traffic:

    sysrc firewall_enable=YES
sysrc firewall_type=workstation
sysrc firewall_myservices="22/tcp"
sysrc firewall_allowservices="any"
service ipfw start

    List the rules with ipfw list. Use pf or ipfw, not both.

    Starting a firewall can cut an SSH session; work from the console.

    #Disable services in rc.conf

    service -e
sockstat -46l

    Stop a service, then turn it off at boot:

    service <service-name> stop
sysrc <service-name>_enable=NO

    Remove the software if it is a package: pkg delete <package>. Settings to check in /etc/rc.conf (and /etc/rc.conf.local, which overrides it):

    sendmail_enable="NONE"
inetd_enable="NO"
clear_tmp_enable="YES"
syslogd_flags="-ss"

    syslogd_flags="-ss" stops syslogd listening on the network. If inetd is required, read /etc/inetd.conf and keep only the needed lines.

    #Harden SSH on FreeBSD

    The file is /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the settings are the same. FreeBSD ships PermitRootLogin no as the default, so a yes anywhere is planted. Test and restart:

    sshd -t && service sshd restart

    Turn SSH off when not required:

    service sshd stop
sysrc sshd_enable=NO

    Check /root/.ssh/authorized_keys and every user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as on Linux.

    #Set security sysctls and securelevel

    These are the values the FreeBSD installer's hardening menu writes, plus network ones. Append them to /etc/sysctl.conf:

    security.bsd.see_other_uids=0
security.bsd.see_other_gids=0
security.bsd.unprivileged_read_msgbuf=0
security.bsd.unprivileged_proc_debug=0
security.bsd.hardlink_check_uid=1
security.bsd.hardlink_check_gid=1
kern.randompid=1
net.inet.tcp.blackhole=2
net.inet.udp.blackhole=1
net.inet.ip.forwarding=0

    Apply the file now:

    sysctl -f /etc/sysctl.conf

    The securelevel raises kernel protection at boot. Set it in rc.conf as the last change of the round:

    sysrc kern_securelevel_enable=YES
sysrc kern_securelevel=1

    Securelevel 1 cannot be lowered without a reboot

    At level 1 nobody, including root, can clear the schg immutable flag, load kernel modules, or write to /dev/mem. Remove planted immutable flags (ls -lo <file>, then chflags noschg <file>) before the reboot that turns it on. Check the running level with sysctl kern.securelevel.

    #Hunt persistence on FreeBSD

    Place Command
    System and user cron cat /etc/crontab, ls -la /var/cron/tabs/
    Startup scripts ls -la /etc/rc.d/ /usr/local/etc/rc.d/, cat /etc/rc.local
    Boot loader settings cat /boot/loader.conf /boot/loader.conf.local
    Kernel modules kldstat
    Shell startup files ls -la /root /home/* and read .profile, .shrc, .cshrc, .login
    Listening programs sockstat -46l
    Package file integrity pkg check -s -a
    Base system integrity freebsd-update IDS

    pkg check -s -a reports package files whose checksum changed; freebsd-update IDS does the same for the base system and lists config files you edited too.

    PreviousFedora and RHEL family (dnf, firewalld, SELinux)NextLinux items scored in past answer keys
    LNX

    Linux items scored in past answer keys

    jump:lin-answer-key

    Every Linux item seen in a real CyberPatriot key, scoring report or decrypted scoring config, grouped by scoring category. The scoring-report wording is in quotes. Items marked Hivestorm come from the Hivestorm competition, which uses the same scoring engine wording; they have not been seen in a CyberPatriot key but are cheap to fix. Sources: K3 (Ubuntu 22 Training 2, CP17), K6 (Ubuntu 20 Practice, CP-XV), K8 (Mint 21 Training 2), R1 and R2 (Mint 21 Rounds 1 and 2, CP-18), SR2 (Linux Round 1 report), G1 (Ubuntu 14 State config, CP-IX), N1 (student practice notes).

    Not every item appears on every image, and a fix that is not scored can still be good practice. The README overrides everything here.

    #Forensics

    #User auditing

    #Account policy

    #Local policy

    #Defensive countermeasures

    #Uncategorized OS settings

    #Service auditing

    #Operating system updates

    #Application updates

    #Prohibited files

    #Unwanted software

    #Malware

    #Application security

    How many items to expect

    Category counts from the CP-18 State Gold round: Mint 21 had 32 items (Account Policy 3, Application Updates 3, Local Policy 3, Forensics 2, Service Auditing 2, Unwanted Software 2, Defensive Countermeasures 1, Malware 1, Prohibited Files 1, no Uncategorized), and Ubuntu 24 had 26 (Forensics 3, Local Policy 3, Account Policy 2, Unwanted Software 2, and one each for Application Updates, Defensive Countermeasures, Malware, Prohibited Files and Service Auditing). User Auditing, OS Updates and Application Security made up the rest (14 on Mint, 11 on Ubuntu). Expect most points from users, PAM, updates and required-service settings.

    PreviousFreeBSD essentialsNextPenalties on Linux images and how to undo them
    LNX

    Penalties on Linux images and how to undo them

    jump:lin-penalties

    Fast path

    1. Open the scoring report and read the penalty line; it names the problem (for example "OpenSSH service has been stopped or removed").
    2. Find the matching change in your changelog ~/cp-changes.txt.
    3. Undo it with the command in the undo table.
    4. Refresh the scoring report after a minute; the penalty disappears once the check passes again.

    Penalties are recoverable: the engine re-runs every check, so undoing the change removes the penalty. The penalty wording seen on a Linux key is "OpenSSH service has been stopped or removed" (K6).
