    #Penalties seen on Linux and similar images

    Penalty Points How it happens Source
    Critical service stopped or removed (OpenSSH, Apache, MySQL, PHP, WordPress) -5 Purging or disabling a service the README lists, or breaking its config so it will not start K3, K6, G1
    Required software removed (Firefox, Thunderbird, Perl on Linux) -5 each apt purge or apt autoremove taking a README program with it K3
    Authorized user deleted, including root -5 to -10 Deleting a README user, or deleting root G1
    Authorized user's home folder deleted -5 to -10 deluser --remove-home on the wrong user, or deleting a whole folder to get rid of MP3s G1
    Authorized administrator demoted -5 Removing a README admin from sudo Windows configs G2, G3
    Lockout threshold below 5 -2 to -4 Setting deny to 1-4 (seen on Windows keys; keep Linux at 5 or more too) Windows keys

    How the engine tests these (from the decrypted configs): removal items also check that the parent folder still exists, so a user's home folder must remain when you delete their MP3s, and wp-login.php must remain when you delete info.php or a web shell.

    #Avoid the common Linux penalties

    • Read apt's removal list before answering Y. If it lists a README program, perl, python3, ubuntu-desktop, mint-meta-*, cinnamon or xserver, answer n. K3's README listed Perl as required, and many packages depend on it.
    • Delete files, not folders. Remove /home/<username>/Music/song.mp3, never /home/<username>/Music or the home folder.
    • Harden a required service instead of removing it. Run sudo sshd -t or sudo apache2ctl configtest before a restart, and check systemctl is-active <service-name> after every restart.
    • On Ubuntu 24.04, systemctl is-active ssh can print inactive while SSH works through the socket (why). Do not "fix" that by removing the socket when SSH is required.
    • Never delete root, change root's UID, or delete your own account.
    • Keep the outgoing firewall default at allow and never stop anything named CyberPatriot or CCS.
    • Change one thing at a time and refresh the score, so a penalty points at one change.

    #Undo a penalty

    Penalty Undo
    Service stopped or disabled sudo systemctl unmask <service-name>, then sudo systemctl enable --now <service-name>
    Service package purged sudo apt install <package>, then restore your hardened config from /root/cp-backup/ and restart
    Service will not start after a config edit sudo systemctl status <service-name> and sudo journalctl -u <service-name> -n 30 show the bad line; restore the backup (troubleshooting)
    Required program removed sudo apt install <package> (on Ubuntu, sudo snap install firefox for Firefox)
    Authorized user deleted sudo adduser <username>, set the README password, re-add the groups
    Home folder deleted Recreate it with sudo mkhomedir_helper <username>; the files are gone, so the penalty may stay
    Admin demoted sudo usermod -aG sudo <username>
    SSH removed when required sudo apt install openssh-server, re-apply your settings, sudo systemctl enable --now ssh (24.04: ssh.socket)
    Firewall blocks a required service sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp (firewall)

    If a purge removed many packages at once, find them in the apt history and reinstall the list:

    grep -A3 'Purge\|Remove' /var/log/apt/history.log | tail -n 20
    PreviousLinux items scored in past answer keysNextWeb servers, PHP and WordPress
    LNX

    Web servers, PHP and WordPress

    jump:lin-services-web

    A required website must keep working

    G1 (a decrypted Ubuntu scoring config) penalized 5 points each for Apache, MySQL, PHP or WordPress no longer working. Back up before editing, run the syntax test, and load the site in Firefox after every restart.

    Fast path

    1. See which web software is installed and listening:

      sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(80|443|8080|8443)\b'
dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(apache2|nginx|php|libapache2-mod-php|tomcat|phpmyadmin|wordpress)/ {print $2}'

    2. Read the README. If it does not mention a website, web server, WordPress or LAMP, remove the web stack.

    3. If it is required, apply the basics in Hardening required services, then the deeper items on this page.
    4. Remove phpinfo files and web shells, deleting only the bad file (how).

    5. Test and restart:

      sudo apache2ctl configtest && sudo systemctl restart apache2

    6. Update the web packages (how).

    #Decide whether the web server is required

    Look at what the server actually serves before deciding:

    ls -la /var/www/ /var/www/html/
sudo apache2ctl -S 2>/dev/null
grep -rh 'DocumentRoot\|root ' /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/ /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ 2>/dev/null
    What you find README says Action
    Only the default "It works" or "Welcome to nginx" page Nothing about a website Remove. "Apache2 service has been disabled or removed" was scored in R1 and SR2
    A WordPress or custom site in /var/www Website, WordPress, LAMP, intranet Keep and harden. G1 had WordPress as the critical service
    A site, but the README is silent Nothing Ask the team. Leave it running while you decide; disabling it later is quick
    Apache and nginx both installed One named Keep the named one, remove the other

    #Remove Apache, nginx or PHP when not required

    Stopping and disabling is enough for the engine (it accepts a stopped service or a missing binary). Purging also removes the attack surface.

    sudo systemctl disable --now apache2
sudo apt purge apache2 apache2-bin apache2-data apache2-utils

    sudo systemctl disable --now nginx
sudo apt purge nginx nginx-common nginx-core

    List every PHP package first, then purge the list:

    dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(php|libapache2-mod-php)/ {print $2}'
sudo apt purge $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(php|libapache2-mod-php)/ {print $2}')

    sudo systemctl disable --now httpd
sudo dnf remove httpd php-fpm

    Read apt's list before answering Y; it must not include desktop packages. Then clean up with sudo apt autoremove --purge. The files in /var/www stay behind, which is fine.

    #Check what Apache is serving

    Virtual hosts and the files they load:

    sudo apache2ctl -S

    Loaded modules:

    sudo apache2ctl -M

    Everything enabled by hand, which is where a planted setting usually sits:

    ls -la /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/ /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/ /etc/apache2/mods-enabled/
grep -rnE 'Options|AllowOverride|Require all granted|server-status|server-info|ScriptAlias|php_(admin_)?(flag|value)' /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/ /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/

    Red flags: Options Indexes or ExecCGI on the web root, <Location /server-status> or /server-info with Require all granted, Require all granted on <Directory />, and php_admin_flag display_errors on in a virtual host.

    #Harden Apache beyond the basics

    Do the three security.conf lines and the Indexes fix first. Those two items are the ones seen in keys.

    Disable modules that expose information or run code, unless the site uses them. A module that is already off prints a notice and is skipped:

    sudo a2dismod -f status info autoindex userdir cgi cgid dav dav_fs

    Hide version control folders and other dot files. Add to /etc/apache2/conf-available/security.conf (Ubuntu ships a commented .svn example in the same file):

    <DirectoryMatch "/\.(git|svn|hg)">
    Require all denied
</DirectoryMatch>

    If HTTPS is enabled, allow only TLS 1.2 and 1.3. In /etc/apache2/mods-available/ssl.conf change SSLProtocol all -SSLv3 to:

    SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3

    Test and restart:

    sudo apache2ctl configtest
sudo systemctl restart apache2

    Check the response headers (wget is on every Mint, Ubuntu and Debian desktop):

    wget -q -S -O /dev/null http://localhost 2>&1 | grep -iE 'server:|x-powered-by'

    You should see Server: Apache with no version and no X-Powered-By line.

    #Harden nginx beyond the basics

    Set server_tokens off; and remove autoindex on; first (basics). Then check the virtual hosts:

    grep -rnE 'autoindex|root |location|fastcgi_pass|ssl_protocols|server_tokens' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ /etc/nginx/conf.d/

    Ubuntu 22.04's nginx.conf ships ssl_protocols TLSv1 TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;. Change it to:

    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

    Deny dot files (.git, .env, .htpasswd) inside each server { block:

    location ~ /\.(?!well-known) {
    deny all;
}

    user www-data; must be the first line of nginx.conf, never user root;. Test and reload:

    sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

    #Find the php.ini the web server uses

    php --ini reports the command-line file only. The web server's file depends on the PHP version and how PHP runs:

    OS PHP Apache module file PHP-FPM file and service
    Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 8.1 /etc/php/8.1/apache2/php.ini /etc/php/8.1/fpm/php.ini, php8.1-fpm
    Ubuntu 24.04 8.3 /etc/php/8.3/apache2/php.ini /etc/php/8.3/fpm/php.ini, php8.3-fpm
    Debian 12 8.2 /etc/php/8.2/apache2/php.ini /etc/php/8.2/fpm/php.ini, php8.2-fpm
    Fedora current none (Fedora uses FPM) /etc/php.ini, php-fpm

    List what exists:

    ls /etc/php/*/*/php.ini

    Settings can also be overridden after php.ini, so search the override spots:

    sudo grep -rnE 'display_errors|expose_php|allow_url|disable_functions' /etc/php/*/apache2/conf.d/ /etc/php/*/fpm/conf.d/ /etc/php/*/fpm/pool.d/ /etc/apache2/ /var/www/ 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^\S*php.ini:'

    A php_admin_value[display_errors] = on line in pool.d/www.conf, or php_flag display_errors on in a virtual host or .htaccess, beats php.ini. Delete those lines.

    #Set the scored PHP options

    The two items seen in keys are expose_php = Off (G1) and display_errors = Off (Hivestorm). Set both in the Apache module file with one command. Change 8.1 to the version from the table:

    sudo cp -a /etc/php/8.1/apache2/php.ini /root/php.ini.bak
sudo sed -i -E 's/^\s*;?\s*(expose_php|display_errors)\s*=.*/\1 = Off/' /etc/php/8.1/apache2/php.ini
grep -nE '^\s*(expose_php|display_errors)\s*=' /etc/php/8.1/apache2/php.ini

    Expected output (line numbers vary):

    400:expose_php = Off
503:display_errors = Off

    The other recommended values (allow_url_include, disable_functions, session cookies) are in the PHP table. Restart whatever runs PHP: sudo systemctl restart apache2, or sudo systemctl restart php8.1-fpm for nginx.

    #Remove phpinfo files and web shells

    phpinfo pages print the whole server configuration. Find them by content, since the name varies:

    sudo grep -rlE 'phpinfo\s*\(' /var/www /srv /usr/share/wordpress 2>/dev/null

    Web shells use a few telltale functions. List candidates, then read each one:

    sudo grep -rlE 'eval\s*\(\s*(base64_decode|gzinflate|str_rot13|\$_(GET|POST|REQUEST|COOKIE))|(system|shell_exec|passthru|proc_open|popen)\s*\(\s*\$_' /var/www /srv 2>/dev/null

    PHP files have no business in an uploads folder:

    sudo find /var/www -path '*uploads*' -name '*.php*' 2>/dev/null

    Record each path (forensics questions ask), then delete only that file:

    sudo rm '<path>'

    G1 checked that wp-login.php still existed after info.php and r57.php were removed. Known shell names include r57.php, c99.php, wso.php, b374k.php, shell.php and cmd.php, but a shell can have any name. More patterns are in Rootkit and persistence hunting.

    #Harden WordPress

    #Find the WordPress install and its database

    sudo find / -xdev -name wp-config.php 2>/dev/null

    A hand install lives in /var/www/html or a subfolder. The Ubuntu and Debian wordpress package puts code in /usr/share/wordpress and the config in /etc/wordpress/config-<hostname>.php. Read the database name, user and table prefix:

    sudo grep -nE "DB_NAME|DB_USER|DB_HOST|table_prefix" <path>/wp-config.php

    #Check the version and update WordPress

    G1 scored "WordPress has been updated" by reading $wp_version from wp-includes/version.php:

    grep "wp_version =" <path>/wp-includes/version.php

    Log in at http://localhost/wp-admin with an administrator from the README, then Dashboard > Updates > Update now. It needs internet and write access to the files, so update before you lock down permissions.

    1. Download and unpack the current release:

      wget -P /tmp https://wordpress.org/latest.tar.gz
tar -xzf /tmp/latest.tar.gz -C /tmp

    2. Back up the site, then replace wp-admin, wp-includes and the top-level PHP files. wp-config.php is not in the download and wp-content is not copied, so the site's settings, themes, plugins and uploads are left alone:

      sudo cp -a <path> /root/wordpress-backup
sudo rm -rf <path>/wp-admin <path>/wp-includes
sudo cp -r /tmp/wordpress/wp-admin /tmp/wordpress/wp-includes <path>/
sudo cp /tmp/wordpress/*.php <path>/

    3. Open http://localhost/wp-admin/upgrade.php and click the database update button if one appears.

    sudo apt install --only-upgrade wordpress

    #Remove unauthorized WordPress administrators

    GUI: Dashboard > Users, filter "Administrator". Change the role of anyone the README does not list as a WordPress admin to Subscriber, or delete them and attribute their content to an authorized user.

    Terminal, assuming the table prefix is wp_ and <db-name> is the DB_NAME value:

    sudo mysql -e "SELECT u.ID, u.user_login, u.user_email, m.meta_value FROM <db-name>.wp_users u JOIN <db-name>.wp_usermeta m ON m.user_id = u.ID AND m.meta_key = 'wp_capabilities';"

    Rows whose meta_value contains administrator are admins. To set a weak WordPress password to the team password (WordPress accepts an MD5 hash and upgrades it at the next login):

    sudo mysql -e "UPDATE <db-name>.wp_users SET user_pass = MD5('<team-password>') WHERE user_login = '<username>';"

    #Lock down wp-config.php

    Add above the line /* That's all, stop editing! */:

    define( 'DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG', false );

    DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT removes the theme and plugin editors, which attackers use to plant code. Also delete define( 'AUTOMATIC_UPDATER_DISABLED', true ); if present, and add define( 'FORCE_SSL_ADMIN', true ); only when HTTPS works. If the keys and salts still read put your unique phrase here, replace them with a fresh set from https://api.wordpress.org/secret-key/1.1/salt/ (everyone gets logged out).

    #Remove risky plugins and themes

    ls -la <path>/wp-content/plugins/ <path>/wp-content/themes/ <path>/wp-content/mu-plugins/ 2>/dev/null

    mu-plugins (must-use) load automatically and do not appear as normal plugins; anything there that the README does not explain is suspect. File manager, shell and "backup" plugins the README does not mention can go: deactivate them in Dashboard > Plugins, then delete. Deleting a plugin folder from the terminal also disables it.

    #Block xmlrpc.php

    xmlrpc.php allows password guessing in bulk. Block it unless the README mentions the mobile app or Jetpack.

    Create /etc/apache2/conf-available/wp-hardening.conf with:

    <Files xmlrpc.php>
    Require all denied
</Files>

    Enable it and reload:

    sudo a2enconf wp-hardening
sudo apache2ctl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2

    Inside the site's server { block:

    location = /xmlrpc.php {
    deny all;
}

    Then sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx.

    #Set WordPress file permissions

    Folders 755, files 644, owned by root so the web server cannot rewrite code. wp-config.php must stay readable by www-data, and wp-content/uploads must stay writable by it:

    sudo chown -R root:root <path>
sudo find <path> -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +
sudo find <path> -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +
sudo chown root:www-data <path>/wp-config.php
sudo chmod 640 <path>/wp-config.php
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data <path>/wp-content/uploads

    Dashboard updates and plugin installs stop working with root ownership. Do updates first, or hand ownership back to www-data for the update and lock it again afterwards.

    #Lock down phpMyAdmin

    Not in the README: remove it, which also removes /phpmyadmin from Apache:

    sudo apt purge phpmyadmin

    Required: forbid empty passwords and root logins with a drop-in file, which config.inc.php loads from conf.d:

    sudo tee /etc/phpmyadmin/conf.d/99-cp.php >/dev/null <<'EOF'
<?php
$cfg['Servers'][1]['AllowNoPassword'] = false;
$cfg['Servers'][1]['AllowRoot'] = false;
EOF

    To allow it only from the machine itself, add Require local inside the <Directory /usr/share/phpmyadmin> block of /etc/phpmyadmin/apache.conf, then sudo systemctl reload apache2.

    #Harden Tomcat

    OS Package and service Config Web apps
    Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 tomcat9 /etc/tomcat9/ /var/lib/tomcat9/webapps/
    Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 12 tomcat10 /etc/tomcat10/ /var/lib/tomcat10/webapps/

    Not required: sudo systemctl disable --now tomcat9, then sudo apt purge tomcat9 tomcat9-admin tomcat9-examples tomcat9-docs.

    Required:

    1. Read the users file. Any <user> with manager-gui, manager-script or admin-gui can deploy code:

      sudo grep -n '<user' /etc/tomcat9/tomcat-users.xml

    2. Delete users the README does not name, and give the rest a strong password.

    3. Remove the manager, examples and docs apps unless the README needs them:

      sudo apt purge tomcat9-admin tomcat9-examples tomcat9-docs

    4. List deployed apps. An unknown .war file or folder is a likely web shell:

      ls -la /var/lib/tomcat9/webapps/

    5. In /etc/tomcat9/server.xml, Debian and Ubuntu ship <Server port="-1" shutdown="SHUTDOWN">, which disables the shutdown port. Put -1 back if someone set 8005. To hide version details on error pages, add this inside the <Host> element:

      <Valve className="org.apache.catalina.valves.ErrorReportValve" showReport="false" showServerInfo="false" />

    6. Restart and check:

      sudo systemctl restart tomcat9
systemctl is-active tomcat9

    #Update the web stack

    Upgrade every installed web package in one command. Packages that are not installed are skipped:

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install --only-upgrade $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(apache2|nginx|php|libapache2-mod-php|tomcat|phpmyadmin|wordpress)/ {print $2}')

    G1 scored "Apache has been updated", "MySQL has been updated" and "PHP has been updated" by checking that the binary's hash had changed, so the package update is what counts. Restart the service afterwards.

    Verify

    systemctl is-active apache2 (or nginx) prints active, the site loads in Firefox, the header check shows no version, and the phpinfo and web shell searches print nothing.

    Fedora and Debian differences
    Item Ubuntu, Mint, Debian Fedora
    Apache package and service apache2 httpd
    Apache config /etc/apache2/apache2.conf, sites-enabled/, conf-enabled/ /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf, /etc/httpd/conf.d/
    Apache user www-data apache
    Syntax test apache2ctl configtest apachectl configtest
    Enable a module a2enmod, a2dismod edit /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d/*.conf
    php.ini /etc/php/<php-version>/<sapi>/php.ini /etc/php.ini
    Extra on Fedora SELinux booleans such as httpd_can_network_connect_db must stay as the site needs them; list them with getsebool -a

    Debian 12 ships Apache 2.4, PHP 8.2, nginx 1.22 and Tomcat 10. Ubuntu 24.04 ships Apache 2.4.58, PHP 8.3, nginx 1.24 and Tomcat 10.

    PreviousPenalties on Linux images and how to undo themNextDatabases (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL)
    LNX

    Databases (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL)

    jump:lin-services-db

    The website logs in with an application account

    WordPress and other apps connect with the user in their config file (DB_USER in wp-config.php). Changing that account's password, dropping it or binding the server so the app cannot reach it takes the site down and costs the critical-service penalty.

    Fast path

    1. Find which database runs and where it listens:

      sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(3306|33060|5432)\b'
systemctl list-units --type=service | grep -E 'mysql|mariadb|postgresql'

    2. Check the README and the web app config. Not needed: remove it.

    3. MySQL or MariaDB: run the secure installation script and the account checks, then confirm bind-address = 127.0.0.1.
    4. PostgreSQL: remove trust from pg_hba.conf, empty pg_ident.conf and fix the file permissions.
    5. Restart and confirm the site still loads.
    6. Update the server package (how).

    #Remove a database server that is not required

    G1 scored "PostgreSQL disabled" and accepted a stopped service as well as a removed package. Purging asks whether to delete the databases; answer yes only after forensics questions are done.

    sudo systemctl disable --now mysql
sudo apt purge mysql-server mysql-server-8.0 mysql-server-core-8.0

    sudo systemctl disable --now mariadb
sudo apt purge mariadb-server

    sudo systemctl disable --now postgresql
sudo apt purge $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^postgresql/ {print $2}')

    Client libraries (mysql-client, libmysqlclient21, libpq5) are used by other programs; leave them.

    #Check MySQL and MariaDB accounts

    Run the secure installation script first. It removes anonymous users, remote root and the test database. Then check what it does not touch.

    Every account, where it may connect from, and how it logs in:

    sudo mysql -e "SELECT user, host, plugin FROM mysql.user;"

    Accounts with no password (socket-authenticated accounts are fine):

    sudo mysql -e "SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE authentication_string = '' AND plugin NOT IN ('auth_socket', 'unix_socket');"

    Accounts with dangerous global rights:

    sudo mysql -e "SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE Super_priv = 'Y' OR File_priv = 'Y' OR Grant_priv = 'Y';"

    root, debian-sys-maint and the mysql.* system accounts are expected there. An application or personal account is not.

    Finding Fix
    User '' (anonymous) sudo mysql -e "DROP USER ''@'localhost';" (repeat for each host shown)
    root with host % or an IP sudo mysql -e "DROP USER 'root'@'%';"
    Account not in the README or app config sudo mysql -e "DROP USER '<username>'@'<hostname>';"
    App account with ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* Revoke and grant only its database (below)
    Empty password on a needed account sudo mysql -e "ALTER USER '<username>'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '<team-password>';" and update the app config to match

    Cut an application account down to its own database:

    sudo mysql -e "REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES, GRANT OPTION FROM '<username>'@'localhost'; GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <db-name>.* TO '<username>'@'localhost';"

    Remove the sample database if the script did not:

    sudo mysql -e "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS test;"

    #Set MySQL and MariaDB server options

    "MySQL remote access disabled" (G1) passed with bind-address = 127.0.0.1 or skip-networking. Look for planted settings in every config file first:

    sudo grep -rnE 'bind.address|skip.networking|skip.grant.tables|local.infile|secure.file.priv|^\s*port' /etc/mysql/

    skip-grant-tables turns off password checks for everyone. Delete that line wherever it is.

    OS File to edit, under [mysqld]
    Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 (MySQL 8.0) /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf
    Ubuntu with MariaDB, Debian 12 (MariaDB 10.11) /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf
    Fedora /etc/my.cnf.d/mariadb-server.cnf or /etc/my.cnf.d/mysql-server.cnf 
    bind-address = 127.0.0.1
mysqlx-bind-address = 127.0.0.1
local_infile = 0

    mysqlx-bind-address exists only in MySQL; leave it out on MariaDB or the server will not start. Do not set secure_file_priv to an empty value (SQL could then read and write files anywhere); the Ubuntu default is /var/lib/mysql-files. Use skip-networking only if every client connects through the socket (WordPress with DB_HOST set to localhost does).

    Restart and check the values the server actually uses:

    sudo systemctl restart mysql
sudo mysql -e "SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('bind_address', 'skip_networking', 'local_infile', 'secure_file_priv');"

    On MariaDB the service is mariadb.

    #Harden PostgreSQL

    Find the cluster version and its config folder:

    pg_lsclusters
ls -l /etc/postgresql/*/main/
    OS Version Config folder
    Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 14 /etc/postgresql/14/main/
    Debian 12 15 /etc/postgresql/15/main/
    Ubuntu 24.04 16 /etc/postgresql/16/main/
    Fedora current /var/lib/pgsql/data/ (config and data together)

    #Require authentication in pg_hba.conf

    Scored in Hivestorm as "PostgreSQL requires authentication for all connections". Show the active lines:

    sudo grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/postgresql/*/main/pg_hba.conf

    trust in the last column means no password at all. Also bad: a host line with 0.0.0.0/0 or all as the address when the README does not need remote access. A clean Ubuntu file looks like this:

    local   all             postgres                                peer
local   all             all                                     peer
host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
host    all             all             ::1/128                 scram-sha-256
local   replication     all                                     peer
host    replication     all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
host    replication     all             ::1/128                 scram-sha-256

    Edit the file, change each trust to peer on local lines and scram-sha-256 on host lines, then reload:

    sudo nano /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main/pg_hba.conf
sudo systemctl reload postgresql

    If an app stops connecting after the change, its role still has an old MD5 password. Reset it with sudo -u postgres psql -c "\password <username>" and put the same password in the app's config, or use md5 instead of scram-sha-256 on that one line.

    Check the rules the server loaded (an error column means a typo):

    sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT line_number, type, database, user_name, address, auth_method, error FROM pg_hba_file_rules;"

    #Remove user maps to the postgres account

    Scored in Hivestorm. pg_ident.conf can let an ordinary Linux user log in as the postgres superuser:

    sudo grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/postgresql/*/main/pg_ident.conf
sudo grep -n 'map=' /etc/postgresql/*/main/pg_hba.conf

    A clean install prints nothing for both. Delete any line such as admins bob postgres and any map= option, then sudo systemctl reload postgresql.

    #Fix permissions on PostgreSQL configuration files

    Scored in Hivestorm. pg_createcluster creates the files with these modes, all owned by postgres:postgres:

    File Mode
    postgresql.conf, start.conf, pg_ctl.conf, environment 644
    pg_hba.conf, pg_ident.conf 640
    The main folder and conf.d 755
    Data folder /var/lib/postgresql/<pg-version>/main 700

    Restore them:

    sudo chown -R postgres:postgres /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main
sudo chmod 644 /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main/*.conf /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main/environment
sudo chmod 640 /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main/pg_hba.conf /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main/pg_ident.conf
sudo chmod 700 /var/lib/postgresql/<pg-version>/main

    #Set the server options in postgresql.conf

    In /etc/postgresql/<pg-version>/main/postgresql.conf:

    listen_addresses = 'localhost'
password_encryption = scram-sha-256
ssl = on

    localhost is the default, so a commented-out line is already safe; a planted listen_addresses = '*' is not. scram-sha-256 has been the default since PostgreSQL 14. Changing listen_addresses needs a restart (sudo systemctl restart postgresql), not a reload.

    #Review PostgreSQL roles

    sudo -u postgres psql -c "\du"

    Only postgres should have Superuser. Remove it from anyone else, or drop a role the README does not mention:

    sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER ROLE <username> NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEROLE NOCREATEDB;"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "DROP ROLE <username>;"

    DROP ROLE fails if the role owns objects; run REASSIGN OWNED BY <username> TO postgres; and DROP OWNED BY <username>; in that database first. For forensics, sudo -u postgres psql -c "\l" lists databases and /var/lib/postgresql/.psql_history holds the postgres user's past queries (a Hivestorm question asked for exactly this).

    #Update the database server

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install --only-upgrade $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(mysql-server|mysql-client|mariadb-server|mariadb-client|postgresql)/ {print $2}')

    "MySQL has been updated" (G1) and "PostgreSQL has been updated" (Hivestorm) were scored this way. The upgrade restarts the service; check the site afterwards.

    Verify

    sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(3306|5432)\b' shows 127.0.0.1 or [::1] only (unless the README needs remote access), the anonymous and empty-password queries return no rows, pg_hba.conf contains no trust, and the website still loads.

    Fedora and Debian differences

    Debian 12 has no mysql-server; default-mysql-server installs MariaDB 10.11, and its root account uses socket login like Ubuntu. On Fedora, PostgreSQL needs sudo postgresql-setup --initdb before first start, its files live in /var/lib/pgsql/data/, and a fresh MariaDB root account has no socket login until mysql_secure_installation is run.

    PreviousWeb servers, PHP and WordPressNextFTP, Samba and NFS file sharing
    LNX

    FTP, Samba and NFS file sharing

    jump:lin-services-files

    Keep the README's share and its files

    Past keys penalized disabling the authorized share and deleting a business file from it (K7, G3). Remove extra shares and fix permissions, but leave the named share and its contents in place.

    Fast path

    1. Find file-sharing servers that are running or listening:

      sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(20|21|111|139|445|2049)\b'
systemctl list-units --type=service | grep -E 'ftp|smbd|nmbd|nfs|rpcbind'

    2. Compare with the README. Remove the ones it does not need (FTP, Samba, NFS).

    3. FTP required: turn off anonymous access, turn on TLS and fix the FTP root permissions.
    4. Samba required: disable SMB1, require encryption and remove guest access (details).
    5. NFS required: remove no_root_squash, insecure and wildcard clients from /etc/exports.
    6. Restart and test with a client.

    #Decide which file services are required

    Server Package systemd unit Port Seen in keys
    vsftpd vsftpd vsftpd 21 Removed when not needed (K3, K6, H1); hardened and updated when required (R2)
    Pure-FTPd pure-ftpd, pure-ftpd-common pure-ftpd 21 Removed (H1)
    ProFTPD proftpd-basic (Ubuntu 22.04), proftpd-core proftpd 21 not seen
    Samba samba smbd, nmbd 139, 445 "Samba (smbd) disabled" (G1); SMB1 and encryption when required (H2)
    NFS server nfs-kernel-server nfs-server 2049, plus rpcbind on 111 not seen
    TFTP tftpd-hpa tftpd-hpa 69/udp Windows OpenTFTP was scored as unwanted software (K4)

    A README that mentions "file server", "shared folder", "FTP" or a named share means keep that one.

    #Remove an FTP server that is not required

    Record the FTP banner and any FTP users first; forensics questions have asked for the banner (R2: "220 Welcome to AFA").

    sudo systemctl disable --now vsftpd
sudo apt purge vsftpd

    sudo systemctl disable --now pure-ftpd
sudo apt purge pure-ftpd pure-ftpd-common

    sudo systemctl disable --now proftpd
sudo apt purge $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^proftpd/ {print $2}')

    An FTP or TFTP server can also be started by a super-server. Check, then delete or comment the line and restart the super-server:

    grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/inetd.conf 2>/dev/null
ls /etc/xinetd.d/ 2>/dev/null

    Confirm port 21 is closed: sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':21\b' prints nothing.

    #Harden vsftpd completely

    Apply the base settings first. These are the full set of options worth checking in /etc/vsftpd.conf:

    Setting Safe value Default on Ubuntu, Mint and Debian Notes
    anonymous_enable NO NO Planted images flip it to YES
    anon_upload_enable, anon_mkdir_write_enable, anon_other_write_enable NO NO (built in) Only matter if anonymous is on
    local_enable YES YES Needed for README users to log in
    write_enable NO unless users upload commented out (so NO)
    chroot_local_user YES commented out (so NO) Locks users in their home
    allow_writeable_chroot YES only if needed NO See the 500 OOPS error in the base section
    hide_ids YES NO Listings show ftp instead of real owners
    ls_recurse_enable NO NO
    ssl_enable YES NO "FTP users may log in with SSL" (R2)
    force_local_logins_ssl, force_local_data_ssl YES YES once ssl_enable=YES
    allow_anon_ssl NO NO
    xferlog_enable YES YES
    ftpd_banner any text without version details not set Forensics questions read it

    Find lines that appear twice (vsftpd uses the last one, so a planted duplicate at the bottom wins):

    grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/vsftpd.conf | cut -d= -f1 | sort | uniq -d

    vsftpd refuses to start on an option name it does not know, so check spelling. Restart and test a TLS login (-k accepts the snakeoil certificate; install curl if it is missing):

    sudo systemctl restart vsftpd
curl --ssl-reqd -k -u <username> ftp://localhost/

    If a client such as FileZilla fails on data transfers after TLS is on, add require_ssl_reuse=NO and restart.

    #Fix the FTP root directory permissions

    Scored on a Mint 21 Round 2 image (R2). Work out which folder is the FTP root:

    Server Where the root is set Default
    vsftpd, local users local_root= in /etc/vsftpd.conf Each user's home folder
    vsftpd, anonymous anon_root= Home of the ftp user, /srv/ftp
    ProFTPD DefaultRoot and <Anonymous ~ftp> User homes; ~ftp
    Pure-FTPd ChrootEveryone User homes; ~ftp for anonymous 
    grep -E '^\s*(local_root|anon_root)' /etc/vsftpd.conf
getent passwd ftp | cut -d: -f6

    Check the root and anything world-writable under it:

    stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' <path>
sudo find <path> -perm -0002 -ls

    Fix the root and remove world write below it:

    sudo chown root:root <path>
sudo chmod 755 <path>
sudo chmod -R o-w <path>

    Use 555 for an anonymous root; vsftpd refuses to run with a writable anonymous root. When README users upload, create a folder inside the root owned by that user or group (sudo install -d -o <username> -g <groupname> -m 775 <path>/upload) rather than making the root writable. Restart the FTP server and log in once to prove it still works.

    #Harden ProFTPD

    In /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf: keep the <Anonymous ~ftp> block commented out or deleted, and set:

    DefaultRoot ~
ServerIdent off
RequireValidShell on
RootLogin off

    TLS needs the module package first (on Ubuntu and Debian mod_tls is not in proftpd-core):

    sudo apt install proftpd-mod-crypto

    Then three edits. In /etc/proftpd/modules.conf, uncomment LoadModule mod_tls.c. In proftpd.conf, uncomment Include /etc/proftpd/tls.conf. In /etc/proftpd/tls.conf, inside <IfModule mod_tls.c>:

    TLSEngine on
TLSRequired on
TLSProtocol TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3
TLSRSACertificateFile /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem
TLSRSACertificateKeyFile /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key

    Test and restart:

    sudo proftpd -t
sudo systemctl restart proftpd

    #Harden Pure-FTPd

    Debian's wrapper reads one file per option from /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/; the file name is the option and its content is the value. NoAnonymous must read yes; check what the image has:

    grep -H . /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/*

    Lock users in their homes and require TLS (2 means TLS only):

    echo yes | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/NoAnonymous
echo yes | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/ChrootEveryone
echo 2 | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/TLS

    TLS needs a combined key and certificate at /etc/ssl/private/pure-ftpd.pem:

    sudo openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -subj "/CN=<hostname>" -keyout /etc/ssl/private/pure-ftpd.pem -out /etc/ssl/private/pure-ftpd.pem
sudo chmod 600 /etc/ssl/private/pure-ftpd.pem
sudo systemctl restart pure-ftpd

    #Harden Samba completely

    Start with the base settings: they include the two scored lines, server min protocol = SMB2 and server smb encrypt = required. Then look for dangerous options in every share:

    testparm -s 2>/dev/null | grep -nE '^\[|guest ok|public|writ|read only|force user|force group|admin users|wide links|path|hosts allow|usershare'
    Option Problem Fix
    guest ok = yes or public = yes Anyone connects without a password guest ok = no
    force user = root Every file action runs as root Delete the line, or force an ordinary user the README names
    admin users = <username> That user acts as root on the share Delete the line
    path = /, /etc, /root Exposes the system Delete the share
    writable = yes / read only = no Users can change files Only if the README says they write
    wide links = yes Symlinks escape the share Delete the line (default no)
    map to guest = bad user Typos become guest logins map to guest = never

    Check single values the way the server sees them:

    testparm -s --parameter-name='server min protocol' 2>/dev/null
testparm -s --parameter-name='server smb encrypt' 2>/dev/null

    Samba users with their flags (an N in the flags means no password):

    sudo pdbedit -L -v | grep -E 'Unix username|Account Flags'

    Restart and test as a README user:

    sudo systemctl restart smbd nmbd
smbclient -L localhost -U <username>

    smbstatus shows who is connected right now. On Mint, users in the sambashare group can create shares from the file manager; those appear in /var/lib/samba/usershares/.

    #Remove Samba when not required

    sudo systemctl disable --now smbd nmbd
sudo apt purge samba

    Purge only samba. smbclient, samba-libs and libsmbclient are used by the file manager to browse Windows shares, and purging them can pull desktop packages with them.

    #Lock down NFS exports

    See what is exported and to whom:

    cat /etc/exports
ls /etc/exports.d/ 2>/dev/null
sudo exportfs -v
    Option or entry Problem
    * or 0.0.0.0/0 as the client Any host can mount
    no_root_squash Root on the client is root on the share
    insecure Allows client ports above 1024 (any user can mount)
    rw Clients can write; use ro unless the README needs writing
    Exporting /, /etc or /home Exposes the system or every user

    A safe line, limited to one subnet and read-only:

    /srv/share 192.168.1.0/24(ro,sync,root_squash,no_subtree_check)

    Apply without restarting:

    sudo exportfs -ra

    Not required: stop the server and its port mapper, then purge the server package (keep nfs-common if the machine mounts NFS shares listed in /etc/fstab):

    sudo systemctl disable --now nfs-server rpcbind.service rpcbind.socket
sudo apt purge nfs-kernel-server

    #Update file sharing servers

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install --only-upgrade $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(vsftpd|pure-ftpd|proftpd|samba|smbclient|nfs-kernel-server)/ {print $2}')

    Only installed packages are named, so the command works whichever servers the image has. "Vsftpd has been updated" (R2) and "Samba has been updated" (Hivestorm) were scored this way.

    Verify

    sudo ss -tlnp shows only the README's file services, curl --ssl-reqd -k -u <username> ftp://localhost/ or smbclient -L localhost -U <username> logs in, stat on the FTP root shows no world write, and sudo exportfs -v has no no_root_squash.

    Fedora differences

    vsftpd's config is /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf and its user lists are /etc/vsftpd/user_list and /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers. Samba's units are smb and nmb. SELinux controls what FTP and Samba may touch: getsebool -a | grep -E 'ftp|samba' lists booleans such as ftpd_full_access and samba_enable_home_dirs, which should be off unless the README needs them. Open services with firewall-cmd, not ufw.

    PreviousDatabases (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL)NextMail, DNS and other daemons
    LNX

    Mail, DNS and other daemons

    jump:lin-services-mail

    Fast path

    1. List every listening port and the program behind it:

      sudo ss -tulpn

    2. Match unknown ports with the port table.

    3. For each daemon the README does not need, stop it and purge its server package (how):

      sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>
sudo apt purge <package>

    4. Harden the ones it does need, using the subsection for that daemon.

    5. Run sudo ss -tulpn again: removed ports are gone, required ones still listen.

    #Match a listening port to a daemon

    Port Daemon Server package Unit Wording seen in keys
    25, 587 Postfix (Exim on some Debian images) postfix (exim4-daemon-light) postfix (exim4) "SMTP service has been disabled or removed" (Hivestorm)
    110, 995 Dovecot POP3 dovecot-pop3d dovecot "POP3 service has been disabled or removed" (Hivestorm)
    143, 993 Dovecot IMAP dovecot-imapd dovecot
    53 BIND9 bind9 named (alias bind9) "DNS service is disabled or removed" (Hivestorm)
    6667, 6697 IRC server ngircd, inspircd, ircd-hybrid, ircd-irc2 same names "IRC daemon has been disabled or removed" (Hivestorm)
    30000/udp Minetest server minetest-server minetest-server "Minetest service has been disabled or removed" (Hivestorm)
    161/udp SNMP agent snmpd snmpd "SNMP service has been stopped and disabled" (Hivestorm, Windows image)
    631 CUPS printing cups, cups-daemon cups
    3128 Squid proxy squid squid
    2375, 2376 Docker API docker.io or docker-ce docker

    127.0.0.53:53 is systemd-resolved, part of the OS; leave it. If a port is not in the table, sudo ss -tulpn names the process, and dpkg -S "$(readlink -f /proc/<pid>/exe)" names its package.

    #Remove a daemon the README does not need

    The engine accepts a stopped and disabled service or a removed package. Do both:

    sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>
sudo apt purge <package>

    Purge only the server package. These client packages share names with servers and are part of the desktop or of other tools:

    Remove Keep
    bind9 bind9-host, bind9-dnsutils, bind9-libs (the dig and host commands)
    snmpd libsnmp40 and similar libraries
    postfix nothing else needed; bsd-mailx and mailutils go with it, which is fine
    dovecot-pop3d, dovecot-imapd, dovecot-core
    cups, cups-daemon libcups2 (do not purge it; see planted packages)

    #Harden Postfix

    postconf -e writes main.cf for you, without opening an editor:

    sudo postconf -e 'disable_vrfy_command = yes'
sudo postconf -e 'smtpd_helo_required = yes'
sudo postconf -e 'smtpd_banner = $myhostname ESMTP'
sudo postconf -e 'smtpd_relay_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated defer_unauth_destination'
sudo postconf -e 'mynetworks = 127.0.0.0/8 [::ffff:127.0.0.0]/104 [::1]/128'

    If the machine only sends local mail, also run sudo postconf -e 'inet_interfaces = loopback-only'. Check the values in effect:

    postconf mynetworks inet_interfaces smtpd_relay_restrictions disable_vrfy_command

    A wide mynetworks such as 0.0.0.0/0 makes an open relay. /etc/aliases can hide persistence: a line like support: "|/tmp/run.sh" runs a command for every message to that address.

    grep -n '|' /etc/aliases

    Delete such lines, then rebuild the alias database, check and restart:

    sudo newaliases
sudo postfix check
sudo systemctl restart postfix

    #Harden Dovecot or remove POP3

    Dovecot enables a protocol when its package is installed. To drop POP3 and keep IMAP:

    sudo apt purge dovecot-pop3d

    Show the settings in effect (only non-default values):

    sudo doveconf -n

    Set disable_plaintext_auth = yes in /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-auth.conf (already the default in Dovecot 2.3, which all target distros ship) and ssl = required in /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-ssl.conf (Ubuntu ships ssl = yes). Restart:

    sudo systemctl restart dovecot

    #Harden the BIND9 DNS server

    If the README does not mention DNS, remove it (Hivestorm scored this):

    sudo systemctl disable --now named
sudo apt purge bind9

    If it is required, edit /etc/bind/named.conf.options. For a server that answers only for its own zones:

    options {
    directory "/var/cache/bind";
    version "not disclosed";
    recursion no;
    allow-transfer { none; };
    dnssec-validation auto;
    listen-on-v6 { any; };
};

    If it is the LAN's resolver, use recursion yes; with allow-recursion { localhost; localnets; }; instead of recursion no;. Zone transfers can also be opened per zone in /etc/bind/named.conf.local; look for allow-transfer { any; }; there.

    Check the syntax, a zone file, and restart:

    sudo named-checkconf
sudo named-checkzone <domain-name> /etc/bind/db.<domain-name>
sudo systemctl restart named

    Test (needs dig from bind9-dnsutils). The first should answer, the second should be refused:

    dig @127.0.0.1 <domain-name>
dig @127.0.0.1 <domain-name> axfr

    #Remove IRC servers

    Packaged IRC servers on Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04: ngircd, inspircd, ircd-hybrid and ircd-irc2. Remove the one that is listening:

    sudo systemctl disable --now ngircd
sudo apt purge ngircd

    UnrealIRCd is not packaged. It is usually unpacked in a home folder and started by cron or a user unit, so find it by process:

    ps aux | grep -iE '[i]rcd|[u]nreal'

    Kill it, delete its folder after recording the path, and remove the cron line or unit that starts it (persistence). Hivestorm also scored "Disabled shell login for user irc": the irc system account must have /usr/sbin/nologin as its shell (how).

    #Remove the Minetest server

    sudo systemctl disable --now minetest-server
sudo apt purge minetest-server

    The server runs as the Debian-minetest user and reads /etc/minetest/minetest.conf. The minetest package is the game client, which counts as unwanted software. Check that nothing still listens on UDP 30000: sudo ss -ulnp | grep 30000.

    #Harden or remove SNMP

    Not required: sudo systemctl disable --now snmpd, then sudo apt purge snmpd.

    Required: show the active lines:

    sudo grep -vhE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null

    Ubuntu's default listens on 127.0.0.1,[::1] only and allows read-only community public limited to the systemonly view. Bad signs: any rwcommunity line, agentaddress udp:161 or 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) when the README does not need remote monitoring, and rocommunity public without -V systemonly. Delete rwcommunity lines, change public to a long random string the README monitoring tool is told about, or use the SNMPv3 rouser line instead. Restart:

    sudo systemctl restart snmpd

    #Lock down CUPS printing

    If printing is not needed, disable it with its socket and path units (how). If it is needed, turn off sharing and remote administration:

    sudo cupsctl --no-remote-admin --no-remote-any --no-share-printers
cupsctl

    The second command prints the current settings; _remote_admin=0, _remote_any=0 and _share_printers=0 are correct. /etc/cups/cupsd.conf should keep Listen localhost:631 (not Port 631, which listens on every interface). Members of the lpadmin group manage printers; check getent group lpadmin against the README admins.

    #Lock down the Squid proxy

    Not required: sudo systemctl disable --now squid, then sudo apt purge squid squid-common.

    Required: list the access rules in order. Squid uses the first rule that matches:

    sudo grep -nE '^\s*(http_access|http_port|include)' /etc/squid/squid.conf /etc/squid/conf.d/*.conf

    http_access allow all makes an open proxy; delete it. The Ubuntu default order is: deny unsafe ports, deny CONNECT to non-SSL ports, allow localhost manager, deny manager, the conf.d include, allow localhost, then http_access deny all. If the README says the LAN uses the proxy, add http_access allow localnet just above http_access deny all. Optional privacy lines:

    via off
forwarded_for delete
httpd_suppress_version_string on

    Check and restart:

    sudo squid -k parse
sudo systemctl restart squid

    #Secure Docker

    Find out whether Docker runs and what it runs:

    systemctl is-active docker
sudo docker ps -a
sudo docker images
getent group docker

    Not required: stop it with its socket (otherwise the socket starts it again) and purge it:

    sudo systemctl disable --now docker.service docker.socket containerd.service
sudo apt purge docker.io

    On Docker's own repository the packages are docker-ce, docker-ce-cli and containerd.io.

    Required:

    1. Remove unauthorized users from the docker group. Membership is equal to root, because a member can mount / into a container:

      sudo gpasswd -d <username> docker

    2. Check that the API is not on the network. Port 2375 is unencrypted, unauthenticated root access:

      sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':237[56]\b'
systemctl cat docker | grep ExecStart
cat /etc/docker/daemon.json 2>/dev/null

      Remove any -H tcp://... from a drop-in in /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/ and any tcp:// entry in the "hosts" list of daemon.json, then sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart docker.

    3. Find containers with dangerous settings:

      sudo docker ps -q | xargs -r sudo docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} privileged={{.HostConfig.Privileged}} net={{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}} binds={{.HostConfig.Binds}}'

      privileged=true, net=host or a bind of / or /etc gives the container control of the host. Remove containers the README does not need with sudo docker rm -f <container-name>.

    4. The socket must be 660 root:docker:

      stat -c '%a %U:%G' /run/docker.sock

    Docker writes its own iptables rules ahead of ufw, so a published container port is reachable even when ufw denies it. Bind published ports to 127.0.0.1 unless the README needs them from outside.

    #Other network daemons

    Telnet, rsh, TFTP, xinetd, VNC, xrdp, Avahi, rpcbind and NIS are covered in Commonly planted services. The removal steps above apply to them too.

    #Update mail, DNS and other daemons

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install --only-upgrade $(dpkg -l | awk '/^ii/ && $2 ~ /^(postfix|dovecot|bind9|snmpd|cups|squid|docker|exim4|ngircd|inspircd|ircd|minetest-server)/ {print $2}')

    Only installed packages are named. A full sudo apt full-upgrade covers all of them at once when time allows (Updates).

    Verify

    sudo ss -tulpn lists only the README's services plus the OS defaults (systemd-resolved on 127.0.0.53, and CUPS on localhost if printing is kept). Every required daemon still answers its own test (dig, postconf, doveconf -n, squid -k parse, docker ps).

    Fedora and Debian differences

    Fedora's BIND config is /etc/named.conf with zones under /var/named/, the package is bind, and the unit is named. Fedora uses dnf remove and opens ports with firewall-cmd. Debian 12 may run Exim (exim4) as its mail server instead of Postfix; remove it with sudo apt purge exim4-daemon-light exim4-base exim4-config if the README does not need mail. Debian 12 ships Postfix 3.7, Dovecot 2.3.19 and BIND 9.18; Ubuntu 24.04 ships Postfix 3.8, Dovecot 2.3.21 and BIND 9.18.

    PreviousFTP, Samba and NFS file sharingNextAdvanced hardening for later rounds (PAM, sudo, boot, mounts, kernel)
    LNX

    Advanced hardening for later rounds (PAM, sudo, boot, mounts, kernel)

    jump:lin-advanced

    Finish the basics first

    Everything here comes after users, password policy, firewall, updates, services and malware. Several items (PAM, GRUB, mount options) can lock you out or stop the image from booting, so back up each file and keep a root terminal open while you test.

    Fast path

    1. Audit PAM for backdoors and verify the PAM packages (details):

      grep -nE 'pam_exec|pam_permit|pam_succeed_if|pam_rootok' /etc/pam.d/* | grep -v ':\s*#'
sudo dpkg --verify libpam-modules libpam-modules-bin libpam-runtime

    2. Hunt insecure sudo rules, including env_keep and NOPASSWD (details):

      sudo grep -rnE 'env_keep|!env_reset|NOPASSWD|!authenticate|secure_path|timestamp_timeout' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/

    3. List password hashes that are not yescrypt or SHA-512:

      sudo awk -F: '$2 ~ /^\$/ && $2 !~ /^\$(y|6)\$/ {print $1, substr($2,1,4)}' /etc/shadow

    4. Give system accounts a nologin shell, and set xserver-allow-tcp=false and greeter-hide-users=true for LightDM.

    5. Fix /boot/grub/grub.cfg permissions (600) and set /dev/shm to nodev,nosuid,noexec.

    6. Check file capabilities and immutable files:

      sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

    7. Block usb-storage, mask ctrl-alt-del.target and confirm debug-shell.service is disabled.

    #Audit PAM for backdoors

    PAM decides who can log in, so it is the favorite place for a backdoor. Four kinds turn up:

    Backdoor How to spot it
    auth sufficient pam_permit.so above pam_unix Any password works. grep below shows it
    pam_exec.so expose_authtok <script> The script receives every password typed (a password logger). Read the script and note where it writes
    A replaced pam_unix.so with a built-in master password dpkg --verify shows 5 in the third column for the module
    A planted profile in /usr/share/pam-configs/ Every pam-auth-update run writes the backdoor back into common-*

    Show every active line that grants access without a password check:

    grep -nE 'pam_exec|pam_permit|pam_succeed_if|pam_rootok|pam_listfile|pam_wheel' /etc/pam.d/* | grep -v ':\s*#'

    Normal results are listed in the PAM table. auth sufficient pam_rootok.so is normal in su, chfn, chsh and runuser (root can use them without a password); anywhere else it is suspicious.

    Verify the module packages against their checksums. Any output line for a .so file means the file was replaced:

    sudo dpkg --verify libpam-modules libpam-modules-bin libpam-runtime libpam0g

    List PAM module files and pam-auth-update profiles that no package installed. Mint and Ubuntu register some files under /lib instead of /usr/lib, so the loop tries both:

    for f in /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/*.so /usr/share/pam-configs/*; do dpkg -S "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || dpkg -S "${f#/usr}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "NOT PACKAGED: $f"; done

    pam_faillock profiles you created yourself (Account lockout) and pam_pwquality from libpam-pwquality are expected. Anything else printed is suspect: record it, then delete it and run sudo pam-auth-update.

    Restore a replaced module and the stock files:

    sudo apt install --reinstall libpam-modules libpam-modules-bin libpam-runtime

    Also read the files PAM modules load at login:

    File Watch for
    /etc/security/pam_env.conf, /etc/environment LD_PRELOAD or a PATH with /tmp
    /etc/security/group.conf Lines that hand out the sudo or adm group at login (used with pam_group)
    /etc/security/access.conf Extra + rules that let a user in
    /etc/security/limits.conf, /etc/security/limits.d/ Nothing that raises core limits after you set them to 0

    Keep a root shell open while editing PAM

    Open sudo -i in a second terminal before editing any file in /etc/pam.d/, and test sudo -k; sudo true from a third before closing it. Recovery steps are in Locked out by a PAM change.

    On Fedora, PAM is managed by authselect: authselect current shows the profile, authselect check reports hand edits, and rpm -V pam verifies the modules.

    #Find insecure sudo configurations

    "Insecure sudo configuration fixed" was scored in G1 (ALL ALL=NOPASSWD: ALL in /etc/sudoers.d/apollo) and Hivestorm. The basics are in sudoers and sudo rights. The less obvious problems:

    Line Why it is dangerous
    Defaults env_keep += "LD_PRELOAD" (or LD_LIBRARY_PATH, PYTHONPATH, PERL5LIB) Any allowed sudo command loads the user's library or module as root
    Defaults !env_reset The user's whole environment reaches root
    Defaults !authenticate, Defaults:<username> !authenticate No password for sudo
    Defaults timestamp_timeout=-1 One password unlocks sudo until reboot
    Defaults secure_path= with /tmp, /home or . A planted apt or systemctl earlier in the path runs as root
    <username> ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim (or less, find, awk, python3, tar, nano, cp, bash, env) Each of these can start a root shell; see GTFOBins
    /usr/bin/cat /var/log/* style wildcards * also matches ../../etc/shadow and extra arguments
    %users ALL=... or %<groupname> ALL=(ALL) ALL for a group the README does not mention Every member becomes an admin

    Search every sudoers file at once:

    sudo grep -rnE 'env_keep|!env_reset|NOPASSWD|!authenticate|secure_path|timestamp_timeout|%users|ALL ALL' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/

    Show what each human user may run, which catches rules that come in through groups and aliases:

    for u in $(getent passwd | awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}'); do echo "== $u"; sudo -l -U "$u" 2>/dev/null | sed -n '/may run/,$p'; done

    Fix lines with sudo visudo (main file) or sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/<file>, then validate every file:

    sudo visudo -c

    Two quieter spots: /etc/sudo.conf can load a replacement policy plugin (a clean file has only comments, or Plugin sudoers_policy sudoers.so lines), and files in /etc/sudoers.d/ whose names contain a . or end in ~ are ignored by sudo. A planted 90-admins is read; 90-admins.bak is not.

    #Use a secure password hash algorithm

    "Password for <x> is hashed with a secure algorithm" was scored in Hivestorm. The hash type is the prefix of the second field in /etc/shadow:

    Prefix Algorithm Verdict
    $y$ yescrypt Default on Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, Debian 11 and 12, Fedora 35 and later
    $6$ SHA-512 Good
    $5$ SHA-256 Weak, replace
    $2b$, $2y$ bcrypt Acceptable, but not the distro default
    $1$ MD5 Insecure, replace
    13 characters, no $ DES Insecure, replace
    ! or * at the start Locked, no password login Fine for system accounts

    List users whose hash is not yescrypt or SHA-512:

    sudo awk -F: '$2 ~ /^\$/ && $2 !~ /^\$(y|6)\$/ {print $1, substr($2,1,4)}' /etc/shadow
sudo awk -F: 'length($2) == 13 {print $1, "DES"}' /etc/shadow

    Fix in this order:

    1. Check the hash option on the pam_unix line of /etc/pam.d/common-password. It must say yescrypt or sha512; md5 or bigcrypt there is the planted change, and a line with no hash word should get yescrypt added:

      grep -n pam_unix /etc/pam.d/common-password

    2. Edit the line so it ends in yescrypt (the stock line is in Password policy).

    3. Set ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512 in /etc/login.defs. It is used by tools that hash outside PAM (newusers, chpasswd -c). YESCRYPT is also accepted on Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12; the shadow version on Mint 21 and Ubuntu 22.04 does not list it, so use SHA512 there.

    4. Reset the password of each listed user so it is hashed again with the new algorithm:

      sudo passwd <username>

    5. Run the awk check again; it should print nothing.

    #Disable login for system accounts

    Hivestorm scored "Disabled shell login for user irc" and "Disabled password login for user bin". The basic check and fix are in Fix system accounts with login shells. The two scored items need different fixes:

    Wording Fix
    Disabled shell login for user <x> sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <username>
    Disabled password login for user <x> sudo passwd -l <username> (puts ! in front of the hash)

    List system accounts (UID below 1000, except root) that have a real hash, which means a password could be used:

    sudo awk -F: 'NR==FNR {uid[$1]=$3; next} uid[$1] > 0 && uid[$1] < 1000 && $2 !~ /^[!*]/ {print $1}' /etc/passwd /etc/shadow

    Lock each one printed with sudo passwd -l <username>. Also check /etc/shells: it should list only real shells (/bin/sh, /bin/bash, /bin/dash, /usr/bin/bash and the like, plus rbash, tmux or screen if installed). A path in /tmp or a home folder there is planted.

    #Stop X from listening on TCP

    Scored in Hivestorm as "X Server does not allow TCP connections". Check the running X server's command line and its ports:

    ps -o args= -C Xorg
sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':60[0-9][0-9]\b'

    You want -nolisten tcp in the first output and nothing from the second.

    In [Seat:*] of /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf:

    xserver-allow-tcp=false

    Remove any xdmcp-manager= line, and enabled=true under [XDMCPServer]. Full LightDM settings are in Login screen.

    In /etc/gdm3/custom.conf (Debian: /etc/gdm3/daemon.conf):

    [security]
DisallowTCP=true

[xdmcp]
Enable=false

    DisallowTCP=true is the default; the file only matters if someone set it to false.

    Same keys in /etc/gdm/custom.conf.

    For startx sessions, Debian's /etc/X11/xinit/xserverrc contains exec /usr/bin/X -nolisten tcp "$@"; make sure -nolisten tcp is still there. Changes apply at the next login screen.

    #Hide the user list at the greeter

    Scored in Hivestorm as "Greeter does not enumerate user accounts".

    greeter-hide-users=true and greeter-show-manual-login=true in [Seat:*] of /etc/lightdm/lightdm.conf (Login screen).

    In /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults, under [org/gnome/login-screen], uncomment or add:

    disable-user-list=true

    GDM reads this file when it starts, so the list disappears after the next reboot. Do not restart gdm3 from inside your session; it logs you out.

    #Set a GRUB password

    Make normal boot unrestricted or the image may not start

    With a GRUB superuser set and no --unrestricted, every boot stops at a password prompt. Do this only if the README or a checklist asks, and do step 4 before running update-grub.

    1. Create the hash. Type the team password twice:

      grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2

      Copy everything after PBKDF2 hash of your password is (it starts with grub.pbkdf2.sha512.).

    2. Back up the GRUB scripts:

      sudo cp -a /etc/grub.d /root/grub.d.bak

    3. Append the superuser to /etc/grub.d/40_custom, pasting the hash in place of the placeholder:

      printf 'set superusers="root"\npassword_pbkdf2 root %s\n' '<grub-hash>' | sudo tee -a /etc/grub.d/40_custom

    4. Let the menu entries boot without the password, so only editing an entry and the GRUB command line are protected (the recovery mode entries also become unrestricted):

      sudo sed -i 's/^CLASS="--class gnu-linux --class gnu --class os"$/CLASS="--class gnu-linux --class gnu --class os --unrestricted"/' /etc/grub.d/10_linux
grep -n '^CLASS=' /etc/grub.d/10_linux

    5. Rebuild the menu and lock the file:

      sudo update-grub
sudo chmod 600 /boot/grub/grub.cfg

    update-grub prints done when the scripts are valid. On Fedora, sudo grub2-setpassword does the whole thing and stores the hash in /boot/grub2/user.cfg.

    #Protect grub.cfg

    Hivestorm scored "GRUB configuration is not world readable". Ubuntu creates grub.cfg as 444. Fix it:

    sudo chown root:root /boot/grub/grub.cfg
sudo chmod 600 /boot/grub/grub.cfg
stat -c '%a %U:%G' /boot/grub/grub.cfg

    On Ubuntu and Mint, update-grub writes into the existing file, so the mode stays 600 after kernel updates. Also check /etc/default/grub: GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT should not contain apparmor=0, security=none, init=/bin/bash or systemd.debug_shell.

    #Secure /tmp and /dev/shm mount options

    G1 scored "Shared memory secured" when /etc/fstab mounted shared memory noexec,nosuid. Check the current options:

    findmnt -no TARGET,OPTIONS /dev/shm /tmp /var/tmp

    /dev/shm can be changed live. Add the fstab line and remount:

    echo 'tmpfs /dev/shm tmpfs defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo mount -o remount /dev/shm
findmnt -no OPTIONS /dev/shm

    The output must include nosuid,nodev,noexec. Check that the fstab has only one /dev/shm line: grep -n shm /etc/fstab.

    Skip /tmp unless a key or the README asks for it

    No CyberPatriot key in this guide's research scored a /tmp mount. A noexec or size-limited /tmp can stop installers and may interfere with the scoring client, and the change only shows after a reboot, when it is hardest to undo. On competition images, secure /dev/shm (scored in past keys) and leave /tmp alone.

    /tmp is a plain folder on the root filesystem on Mint 21, Ubuntu and Debian 12 (Debian 13 and Fedora mount it as tmpfs). Giving it its own tmpfs mount takes effect at the next boot; do not mount over /tmp in a running desktop session, because it hides files programs are using:

    echo 'tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec,size=2G 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo findmnt --verify

    noexec on /tmp can break installers

    Some package scripts and installers run programs from /tmp. If apt or an installer fails with "Permission denied" after a reboot, remount it temporarily with sudo mount -o remount,exec /tmp, finish, and remount noexec.

    #Restrict cron and at with allow files

    When /etc/cron.allow exists, only users listed in it (and root) may run crontab; cron.deny is then ignored. The same rule applies to at.allow and at.deny.

    echo root | sudo tee /etc/cron.allow /etc/at.allow
sudo chown root:crontab /etc/cron.allow
sudo chown root:daemon /etc/at.allow
sudo chmod 640 /etc/cron.allow /etc/at.allow

    On Ubuntu, Mint and Debian crontab runs with the crontab group and at runs as the daemon user and group, so those groups must be able to read the allow files (Debian ships at.deny as root:daemon 640). On Fedora use root:root.

    Add a README user on its own line if they need cron. Remove an old cron.deny or at.deny that lists nobody, so the intent is clear. System cron files in /etc/cron.d/ are not affected.

    #Log out idle shells with TMOUT

    TMOUT closes an idle shell after the given number of seconds. Create /etc/profile.d/tmout.sh:

    printf 'TMOUT=900\nreadonly TMOUT\nexport TMOUT\n' | sudo tee /etc/profile.d/tmout.sh

    This closes your own idle terminals too

    Terminal windows opened after the next login close after 15 idle minutes, including teammates' root shells. Set it near the end of the round.

    #Set a restrictive umask

    UMASK in /etc/login.defs reaches login sessions through pam_umask, which Ubuntu, Mint and Debian list in common-session (how to set it). Check that nothing overrides it later:

    grep -rnE '^\s*umask' /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/ /etc/bash.bashrc /etc/login.defs /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.profile 2>/dev/null

    A planted umask 000 or umask 002 in one of these files makes new files world-writable. Delete it. 027 is the common hardened value; services set their own umask in their unit files.

    #Find dangerous file capabilities

    A file capability gives a program part of root's power without SUID, so the SUID search misses it. List them all:

    sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

    Normal on Mint 21 and Ubuntu:

    /usr/bin/ping cap_net_raw=ep
/usr/bin/mtr-packet cap_net_raw=ep
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/gstreamer1.0/gstreamer-1.0/gst-ptp-helper cap_net_bind_service,cap_net_admin=ep

    /usr/bin/arping with cap_net_raw is also normal if iputils-arping is installed. Red flags are cap_setuid, cap_setgid, cap_dac_override, cap_dac_read_search, cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, cap_sys_module or cap_chown, especially on python3*, perl, vim, tar, gdb, node or a copy in /tmp or a home folder. Record it, then remove it:

    sudo setcap -r <path>

    #Find and clear immutable files

    An attacker can make a backdoor or a bad config file immutable so even root cannot change it. The /etc search is in Remove immutable and append-only flags. Search the other places persistence hides:

    sudo lsattr -Ra /root /home /usr/local /opt /var/spool /var/www /etc/systemd /etc/cron.d 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^\S*[ia]\S*\s'

    Clear the flag, then fix or delete the file:

    sudo chattr -i -a <path>

    #Blacklist kernel modules including usb-storage

    blacklist <module> only stops automatic loading; a user or script can still run modprobe on it. install <module> /bin/false blocks both. Write both lines for each module:

    sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/cp-blacklist.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
install usb-storage /bin/false
blacklist usb-storage
install uas /bin/false
blacklist uas
install cramfs /bin/false
install freevxfs /bin/false
install jffs2 /bin/false
install hfs /bin/false
install hfsplus /bin/false
install dccp /bin/false
install sctp /bin/false
install rds /bin/false
install tipc /bin/false
EOF
sudo modprobe -r uas usb-storage 2>/dev/null
sudo update-initramfs -u

    uas is the faster USB storage driver and depends on usb-storage, so block both. Leave squashfs (snaps and live media use it) and udf (DVDs) alone unless a checklist names them. Do not block usb-storage if the README mentions USB drives.

    Check what modprobe would do now and that nothing is loaded:

    modprobe -n -v usb-storage
lsmod | grep -E 'usb_storage|uas'

    Expected output of the first command:

    install /bin/false

    The same /etc/modprobe.d/ files work on Fedora; rebuild its initramfs with sudo dracut -f.

    #Harden systemd

    Turn off two root shortcuts. debug-shell.service opens a root shell with no password on tty9; it must not be enabled:

    systemctl is-enabled debug-shell.service
sudo systemctl disable --now debug-shell.service

    Stop Ctrl+Alt+Del on a text console from rebooting the machine:

    sudo systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target

    Rate how exposed each running service is (higher numbers are worse; most stock services score high, so use it to compare, not as a target):

    systemd-analyze security --no-pager

    For a required network service, a drop-in can add sandboxing. Open one with sudo systemctl edit <service-name> and add:

    [Service]
NoNewPrivileges=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ProtectSystem=full

    Then sudo systemctl restart <service-name> and test the service. Do not add ProtectHome=yes to a service that serves home folders (Samba [homes], vsftpd local users, Apache userdir). Remove the drop-in with sudo systemctl revert <service-name> if anything breaks.

    Keep logs across reboots so forensics has history: set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and run sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald.

    #Find root-equivalent group memberships

    Some groups give root power without sudo. Check each against the README's admins:

    getent group sudo admin wheel root adm shadow disk docker lxd libvirt lpadmin
awk -F: '$4 == 0 {print $1, "has primary group root"}' /etc/passwd
    Group What a member can do
    sudo, admin (old Ubuntu), wheel (Fedora) Run anything as root
    docker, lxd, libvirt Start a container or VM with the host's / mounted: root equivalent
    disk Read and write raw disks, including /etc/shadow
    shadow Read password hashes
    root (GID 0) Write any group-writable root file
    adm Read system logs (normal for the first Mint user)
    lpadmin Manage printers (normal for the first Mint user)

    Remove a member with sudo gpasswd -d <username> <groupname>.

    #Other checks top teams make

    • Lock accounts that stay unused: sudo useradd -D -f 30 makes new accounts lock 30 days after their password expires; sudo chage --inactive 30 <username> does the same for an existing one.
    • Restrict su to admins: add auth required pam_wheel.so group=sudo near the top of /etc/pam.d/su (the line is there, commented, on Ubuntu, Mint and Debian).
    • Check root's PATH for writable or relative entries: sudo -i printenv PATH must not contain ., /tmp or a home folder.
    • Check polkit rules, which can grant admin actions without a password: Check polkit rules. Ubuntu 22.04 and Mint 21 use .pkla files; Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12 use JavaScript .rules files in /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ (Ubuntu 24.04 also still reads .pkla).
    • Record everything you change in a team note, so a penalty can be traced back and undone.

    Verify

    The fast path commands print only expected lines: no PAM backdoor lines or unpackaged modules, no env_keep or NOPASSWD surprises, no weak hashes, findmnt /dev/shm shows noexec, getcap shows only the normal three, modprobe -n -v usb-storage prints install /bin/false, and systemctl is-enabled debug-shell prints disabled.

    PreviousMail, DNS and other daemonsNextLinux forensics question playbook
    LNX

    Linux forensics question playbook

    jump:lin-forensics

    Answer forensics questions before you fix anything

    Removing a user, a backdoor or a package destroys the evidence a question asks about (K5, K6). Read every question at the start, answer the ones you can, and note what each one depends on.

    Fast path

    1. Open each Forensics Question N.txt on the Desktop and read the question and the answer format.
    2. Find the question type in the technique table and run the command it points to.
    3. Copy the exact value (path, name, number) from the output; do not retype it.

    4. Put only the answer after ANSWER:, keeping the line format, and save:

      nano '/home/<username>/Desktop/Forensics Question 1.txt'

    5. Check the scoring report a minute later. A wrong answer costs nothing, so try another format (trailing slash, case, full path) if it did not score.

    #Match the question to a technique

    Question asks for Seen in Go to
    Path of the folder with prohibited MP3 files K3, K6, R1 (/home/benjamin/Music/) Find files
    UID of a user, members of a group K6, K4 Users and groups
    Port a backdoor listens on, or the path of the program K8 (python on 1337 in /usr/share/zod), H1 (netcat on 5102) Network ports
    A config value or banner R2 (vsftpd banner "220 Welcome to AFA") Find files
    Decode base64, then follow the hint K3 (pointed to a file in the Trash), K8 (passphrase for steghide) Decode, Trash
    Hidden message in an image K8 (steghide extract, then md5sum) Images
    Hash of a file K2, K5, K8 Hashes
    Credentials or an IP in a pcap K1, K8 (two FTP passwords) Packet capture
    Who ran a command, logged in, or was added general practice Logs, History
    When or why a package was installed general practice Package history
    Data in a database H2 (PostgreSQL users and history) Databases

    Basic decoding and search commands are also in README and Forensics on Linux.

    #Find files by name, content, owner and time

    By name, ignoring case:

    sudo find / -xdev -iname '*<text>*' 2>/dev/null

    By content, in the places users and attackers leave things (-I skips binaries, -l lists file names):

    sudo grep -rIil '<text>' /home /root /etc /opt /srv /var/www /tmp /var/tmp /usr/local 2>/dev/null

    Inside compressed logs too:

    sudo zgrep -il '<text>' /var/log/*.gz 2>/dev/null

    By owner, and files whose owner was deleted:

    sudo find / -xdev -user <username> -type f 2>/dev/null
sudo find / -xdev \( -nouser -o -nogroup \) 2>/dev/null

    By time (<start-date> and <end-date> as 2026-10-01 or 2026-10-01 14:30), or within the last hour:

    sudo find / -xdev -type f -newermt '<start-date>' ! -newermt '<end-date>' 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys|run|var/lib|var/cache)'
sudo find /home /etc /tmp /opt /var/www -xdev -type f -mmin -60 2>/dev/null

    Timestamps of one file, including when it was created (Birth, shown by stat on ext4):

    stat <file>

    Media by real type, even when renamed:

    sudo find /home -type f -exec file {} + 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'audio|video|image|zip|PDF'

    locate is fast but uses a database that may be old; refresh it first with sudo updatedb. Give paths exactly as the question shows: absolute, with or without the trailing slash.

    #Answer questions about users and groups

    UID, primary group and all groups:

    id <username>
getent passwd <username>

    Members of a group. The first command shows listed members; the second adds users whose primary group it is:

    getent group <groupname>
awk -F: -v g="$(getent group <groupname> | cut -d: -f3)" '$4 == g {print $1}' /etc/passwd

    Account changes recorded in the logs (who was added, deleted or given a group, and when):

    sudo zgrep -hE 'useradd|userdel|usermod|groupadd|groupdel|gpasswd|new user|delete user' /var/log/auth.log* 2>/dev/null

    The same from the journal, which is the only place on Debian 12 (it does not install rsyslog, so there is no auth.log):

    sudo journalctl _COMM=useradd _COMM=userdel _COMM=usermod _COMM=gpasswd --no-pager

    Earlier copies of the account files show what changed: /etc/passwd- and /etc/group- (previous version) and /var/backups/passwd.bak, group.bak and shadow.bak (daily copies on Ubuntu, Mint and Debian):

    sudo diff /var/backups/passwd.bak /etc/passwd
sudo diff /etc/group- /etc/group

    Last password change and expiry for one user: sudo chage -l <username>.

    #Read authentication logs and the journal

    OS Authentication log
    Mint 21, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 /var/log/auth.log (older ones rotate to auth.log.1, auth.log.2.gz)
    Debian 12 journal only (journalctl)
    Fedora the journal (/var/log/secure only if rsyslog is installed)

    SSH logins, failed and successful:

    sudo zgrep -hE 'Failed password|Accepted (password|publickey)|Invalid user' /var/log/auth.log* 2>/dev/null

    Commands run with sudo, with the user and working folder:

    sudo zgrep -h 'COMMAND=' /var/log/auth.log* 2>/dev/null

    Journal equivalents (the SSH unit is ssh on Ubuntu, Mint and Debian, sshd on Fedora):

    sudo journalctl -u ssh --since '<start-date>' --no-pager
sudo journalctl _COMM=sudo --no-pager

    Login history and boots:

    last -x | head -40
sudo lastb | head -20
lastlog | grep -v 'Never logged in'
journalctl --list-boots

    last reads /var/log/wtmp; older months are in /var/log/wtmp.1 (last -f /var/log/wtmp.1). lastb needs root because it reads /var/log/btmp. sudo faillock --user <username> lists recent failed logins counted toward lockout.

    #Read shell and application history

    Every user's shell history, including root's:

    sudo ls -la /root/.bash_history /home/*/.bash_history
sudo cat /home/<username>/.bash_history

    A history file that is a link to /dev/null, empty, or missing for an active user means someone hid their tracks; say so to the team. Lines like #1760000000 are timestamps (set by HISTTIMEFORMAT); convert one with date -d @1760000000.

    Other history files worth reading:

    File (in a home folder) Records
    .python_history Python prompt input
    .mysql_history, .psql_history, .sqlite_history Database commands (PostgreSQL's own is /var/lib/postgresql/.psql_history)
    .lesshst, .viminfo Searches and files opened in less and vim
    .local/share/recently-used.xbel Files opened from the desktop, with times
    .wget-hsts Sites downloaded from with wget
    .ssh/known_hosts Hosts this user connected to

    Firefox history. Copy the database first (Firefox locks it), then query it with Python's built-in SQLite. On Ubuntu with the snap Firefox the profile is under /home/<username>/snap/firefox/common/.mozilla/firefox/:

    sudo cp /home/<username>/.mozilla/firefox/*.default*/places.sqlite /tmp/places.sqlite
python3 - <<'EOF'
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect('/tmp/places.sqlite')
q = "SELECT datetime(v.visit_date/1000000, 'unixepoch'), p.url FROM moz_historyvisits v JOIN moz_places p ON p.id = v.place_id ORDER BY v.visit_date DESC LIMIT 50"
for row in db.execute(q):
    print(*row)
EOF

    If cp complains about several profiles, list them with ls /home/<username>/.mozilla/firefox/ and copy from one.

    #Find what cron ran and when

    cron logs every job it starts with the user and the command:

    sudo zgrep -h 'CRON' /var/log/syslog* 2>/dev/null | grep CMD | tail -50
sudo journalctl -u cron --no-pager | grep CMD | tail -50
