    The unit is cron on Ubuntu, Mint and Debian and crond on Fedora. A job that runs every minute fills this log, which makes the backdoor's command and start time easy to read. Where jobs are defined is in Persistence, backdoors and malware.

    #Find when a package was installed

    apt's history keeps the command line, the user (Requested-By) and the date for each run:

    zcat -f /var/log/apt/history.log* | grep -E 'Start-Date|Commandline|Requested-By|Install:|Remove:' | less

    dpkg's log has one line per package action, sortable by time:

    zcat -f /var/log/dpkg.log* | grep -E ' (install|remove|purge) ' | sort | less
zcat -f /var/log/dpkg.log* | grep ' install <package>'

    The base install date is the oldest entry, or the date of /var/log/installer/. Which package a file came from, and which files a package installed:

    dpkg -S <path>
dpkg -L <package>

    On Fedora, dnf history lists transactions, dnf history info <id> shows one, and rpm -qa --last | head lists the newest packages.

    #Find which program uses a network port

    sudo ss -tulpn
sudo ss -tunap state established

    For one port:

    sudo ss -tlnp 'sport = :<port>'
sudo lsof -i :<port>

    Then the program's real path, working folder and full command line:

    sudo readlink -f /proc/<pid>/exe
sudo readlink -f /proc/<pid>/cwd
sudo cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '; echo

    For a script, exe is the interpreter (/usr/bin/python3.10); the script's path is in the command line or relative to cwd. That is how K8's answer (the listener's folder under /usr/share) was found. ss shows users:(("nc",pid=812,fd=3)); the number after pid= is the PID.

    #Decode, decrypt and unpack

    base64, hex, ROT13 and binary are covered in Decode base64, hex, ROT13 and binary. More formats:

    echo '<text>' | base32 -d
python3 -c 'import sys, urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.unquote(sys.argv[1]))' '<text>'

    All 25 Caesar shifts at once; read down the list for the one that makes sense:

    python3 -c 'import sys; t = sys.argv[1]; [print(k, "".join(chr((ord(c) - b + k) % 26 + b) if c.isalpha() else c for c in t for b in [65 if c.isupper() else 97])) for k in range(1, 26)]' '<text>'

    XOR or one-time pad, with the ciphertext and key both given as hex (K1 gave an OTP this way). The key repeats if it is shorter:

    python3 -c 'import sys; c = bytes.fromhex(sys.argv[1]); k = bytes.fromhex(sys.argv[2]); print(bytes(a ^ k[i % len(k)] for i, a in enumerate(c)))' '<cipher-hex>' '<key-hex>'

    Files encrypted with a password:

    Kind (from file <file>) Command
    openssl enc'd data with salted password openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in <file> -out /tmp/out -k '<passphrase>' (try without -pbkdf2 and with -md md5 for older files)
    PGP symmetric key encrypted data gpg -d <file>
    Zip archive data unzip -P '<passphrase>' <file>
    7-zip archive data 7z x -p'<passphrase>' <file>

    The internet is allowed during rounds, so CyberChef (gchq.github.io/CyberChef) and its "Magic" operation are fine for unknown encodings.

    #Hash a file or a string

    md5sum <file>
sha1sum <file>
sha256sum <file>
sha512sum <file>

    Hash a string without the trailing newline that echo adds (the newline changes the hash):

    printf '%s' '<text>' | sha256sum

    RIPEMD-160 (an N1 practice item). OpenSSL older than 3.0.7, as on Mint 21 and Ubuntu 22.04, keeps it in the legacy provider:

    openssl dgst -ripemd160 <file> || openssl dgst -provider legacy -provider default -ripemd160 <file>

    Find which file has a given hash:

    sudo find /home /root /opt /tmp -type f -exec sha256sum {} + 2>/dev/null | grep -i '<hash>'

    #Examine images and hidden data

    Start with what the file really is and any readable text:

    file <file>
strings -n 6 <file> | less

    Metadata (author, GPS, comments), from libimage-exiftool-perl:

    sudo apt install libimage-exiftool-perl
exiftool <file>

    Data appended or embedded (a zip after the JPEG, another image):

    unzip -l <file>
sudo apt install binwalk
binwalk <file>
binwalk -e <file>

    steghide hides data in JPEG and BMP files with a passphrase. K8 (Mint 21) gave the passphrase in base64, then asked for the MD5 of the extracted file:

    sudo apt install steghide
steghide info <file>
steghide extract -sf <file> -p '<passphrase>' -xf /tmp/steg-out
md5sum /tmp/steg-out

    QR codes: sudo apt install zbar-tools, then zbarimg <file>. Purge the tools you installed once the question is answered, if the README's software policy is strict:

    sudo apt purge steghide binwalk libimage-exiftool-perl zbar-tools

    #Read a packet capture

    tcpdump reads captures without installing anything on most images:

    tcpdump -nn -r <file> | head -50
tcpdump -nn -A -r <file> | grep -E 'USER|PASS'

    The second line pulls FTP usernames and passwords, which K8 asked for. tshark gives more control. Wireshark is required software on some images and prohibited on others, so install it only if the README allows, and purge it afterwards if it does not:

    sudo apt install tshark
tshark -r <file> -q -z conv,ip
tshark -r <file> -Y 'ftp.request.command == "PASS"' -T fields -e ip.src -e ftp.request.arg
tshark -r <file> -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,0
tshark -r <file> --export-objects http,/tmp/pcap-objects

    conv,ip lists who talked to whom (the attacker's IP is usually the busiest unknown address). Change the 0 in follow,tcp,ascii,0 to read other streams. Exported files land in /tmp/pcap-objects.

    #Recover deleted and deleted-but-open files

    Files deleted from the desktop go to the user's Trash, with the original path and date in a matching .trashinfo file. K3's answer was in a trashed file:

    sudo ls -la /home/*/.local/share/Trash/files/ /root/.local/share/Trash/files/ 2>/dev/null
sudo cat /home/<username>/.local/share/Trash/info/*.trashinfo

    A file deleted while a program still has it open stays readable through /proc. Backdoors often delete their own binary or log after starting:

    sudo lsof +L1
sudo find /proc/[0-9]*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' -printf '%p -> %l\n' 2>/dev/null

    Copy it out before you kill the process (the fd number is the last part of the /proc path):

    sudo cp /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd-number> /root/recovered-file

    Files removed with rm and not open are usually gone. Look for copies instead: editor backups (*~, .*.swp), /var/backups/, mail spools in /var/mail/, and old versions in the user's .cache or the package cache.

    #Query application databases

    PostgreSQL roles, databases and the postgres user's command history (H2 asked about these):

    sudo -u postgres psql -c '\du'
sudo -u postgres psql -c '\l'
sudo cat /var/lib/postgresql/.psql_history

    Run a query in one database:

    sudo -u postgres psql -d <db-name> -c 'SELECT * FROM <table-name> LIMIT 20;'

    MySQL or MariaDB:

    sudo mysql -e 'SHOW DATABASES;'
sudo mysql -e 'SELECT * FROM <db-name>.<table-name> LIMIT 20;'

    An SQLite file (file reports SQLite 3.x database), without installing anything:

    python3 -c 'import sqlite3, sys; db = sqlite3.connect(sys.argv[1]); [print(r) for r in db.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type=\"table\"")]' <file>

    WordPress users are in the wp_users table (query).

    Check it worked

    The scoring report lists "Forensics Question N correct" within a few minutes of saving. The file must still be named as it was, in the same place, with ANSWER: intact.

    PreviousAdvanced hardening for later rounds (PAM, sudo, boot, mounts, kernel)NextRootkit and persistence hunting
    LNX

    Rootkit and persistence hunting

    jump:lin-rootkits

    Record before you remove

    Note each finding's path, contents and owner first. Forensics questions ask about planted files, and you need the list to explain a score drop.

    Fast path

    1. Verify package files against their checksums (a minute or two):

      sudo dpkg --verify 2>/dev/null | grep -v ' c /'

    2. Check preloading, which every rootkit in user space needs:

      cat /etc/ld.so.preload 2>/dev/null; grep -rn LD_PRELOAD /etc/environment /etc/security/pam_env.conf /etc/profile.d/ /etc/systemd/ 2>/dev/null

    3. List kernel modules that did not come from the kernel's own folder (details).

    4. List SUID files outside /usr, which should print nothing:

      sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f ! -path '/usr/*' 2>/dev/null

    5. Run the persistence location sweep and the web shell search.

    6. Run rkhunter and chkrootkit last and read their warnings as leads.

    #Verify package files with debsums and dpkg

    dpkg --verify compares every installed file with the checksum its package recorded. The output format:

    ??5??????   /usr/bin/ls
??5?????? c /etc/ssh/sshd_config

    A 5 in the third column means the contents changed. Lines marked c are config files, which you and the image builder change legitimately. A changed binary in /usr/bin, /usr/sbin or a library folder is a trojan. Find its package and reinstall it:

    dpkg -S <path>
sudo apt install --reinstall <package>

    debsums (universe package) does the same and lists packages that have no checksums to compare:

    sudo apt install debsums
sudo debsums -s
sudo debsums -l

    A careful attacker can also edit the checksum lists in /var/lib/dpkg/info/. For a binary that matters (ls, ps, ss, sudo, login, sshd), compare with a fresh copy from the archive. dpkg -L shows the path inside the package, which may start with /bin on Mint 21:

    cd /tmp && apt download <package>
dpkg-deb -x /tmp/<package>_*.deb /tmp/pkg-check
cmp /tmp/pkg-check<path> <path>

    No output from cmp means identical. On Fedora, sudo rpm -Va does the same check; a 5 in its third column means the same thing.

    #Check LD_PRELOAD and ld.so.preload

    /etc/ld.so.preload must not exist (details). The same trick works through environment variables. Check where they are set:

    sudo grep -rn 'LD_PRELOAD\|LD_LIBRARY_PATH' /etc/environment /etc/security/pam_env.conf /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/ /etc/bash.bashrc /root/.bashrc /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.profile /etc/systemd/ /home/*/.ssh/environment 2>/dev/null

    And in running processes:

    sudo grep -la 'LD_PRELOAD' /proc/[0-9]*/environ 2>/dev/null

    A library that every program loads shows up in ldd of any binary:

    ldd /usr/bin/ls

    Normal output lists only linux-vdso.so.1, libselinux.so.1, libc.so.6, libpcre2-8.so.0 and /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2. An extra library, especially from /tmp, /usr/local/lib or a hidden folder, is the rootkit. Also list the extra library folders:

    cat /etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.conf

    Clean folders are /usr/local/lib, the x86_64-linux-gnu multiarch folders and ones added by real packages (fakeroot, libc). After removing a bad entry, run sudo ldconfig.

    #Check kernel modules and kernel taint

    Modules loaded from anywhere other than the kernel's own folder:

    for m in $(lsmod | awk 'NR > 1 {print $1}'); do f=$(modinfo -n "$m" 2>/dev/null); case "$f" in /lib/modules/*|/usr/lib/modules/*) ;; *) echo "$m $f";; esac; done

    No output is clean. Modules under /lib/modules/<kernel-version>/updates/dkms/ were built locally; VirtualBox and VMware drivers there are normal.

    Modules present in /sys/module but hidden from lsmod:

    comm -13 <(lsmod | awk 'NR > 1 {print $1}' | sort) <(for d in /sys/module/*; do [ -f "$d/initstate" ] && basename "$d"; done | sort)

    The taint value is 0 on a kernel that only loaded signed, in-tree modules:

    cat /proc/sys/kernel/tainted
sudo dmesg | grep -iE 'taint|module verification failed'

    module verification failed: signature and/or required key missing names an unsigned module; guest drivers built by DKMS cause it too, so check the name. Where modules are loaded at boot:

    cat /etc/modules
ls -la /etc/modules-load.d/ /usr/lib/modules-load.d/ /etc/modprobe.d/

    Remove a planted module: delete its line from those files, delete the .ko file, run sudo depmod -a and sudo update-initramfs -u, then reboot. sudo rmmod <module> may refuse, because rootkits block unloading.

    #Check systemd generators, timers and user units

    Generators are programs systemd runs at every boot, before any unit, to create units. Only packaged ones belong here:

    ls -la /etc/systemd/system-generators/ /usr/local/lib/systemd/system-generators/ /etc/systemd/user-generators/ 2>/dev/null

    A clean Mint or Ubuntu system has nothing in these three folders. Units and timers that no package installed:

    for f in /usr/lib/systemd/system/*.service /usr/lib/systemd/system/*.timer /etc/systemd/system/*.service /etc/systemd/system/*.timer; do [ -L "$f" ] && continue; dpkg -S "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || dpkg -S "${f#/usr}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "NOT PACKAGED: $f"; done

    Files in /etc/systemd/system/ are often made by setup tools, so read each one (systemctl cat <service-name>) rather than deleting the list. A unit in /usr/lib/systemd/system/ that no package owns is planted.

    User units start when that user logs in, or at boot if the user has lingering enabled:

    ls -la /etc/systemd/user/ /home/*/.config/systemd/user/ 2>/dev/null
ls /var/lib/systemd/linger/ 2>/dev/null

    A file in /var/lib/systemd/linger/ named after a user keeps that user's units running without a login. Turn it off with sudo loginctl disable-linger <username>. Timers and unit removal are covered in Check systemd units and timers.

    #Check udev rules

    A udev rule with RUN+= runs a program as root whenever a matching device appears, including at every boot:

    ls -la /etc/udev/rules.d/
grep -rn 'RUN' /etc/udev/rules.d/ 2>/dev/null

    On a clean Mint 21 the folder is empty or holds only a VMware or VirtualBox rule. Packaged rules live in /usr/lib/udev/rules.d/; check any you doubt with dpkg -S. Delete a planted rule, then reload:

    sudo udevadm control --reload

    #Check motd, login and shell startup scripts

    These run as root or as the user at every login:

    Location Runs when
    /etc/update-motd.d/* As root, at every SSH or console login
    /etc/profile, /etc/profile.d/*.sh, /etc/bash.bashrc Every login or interactive shell, any user
    ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.bash_logout That user's shells
    /etc/X11/Xsession.d/, ~/.xsessionrc, ~/.xprofile Desktop login

    Files in update-motd.d and profile.d that no package installed:

    for f in /etc/update-motd.d/* /etc/profile.d/* /etc/X11/Xsession.d/*; do dpkg -S "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "NOT PACKAGED: $f"; done

    Your own tmout.sh from TMOUT is expected. Then search the per-user files for commands that run quietly:

    sudo grep -nE 'PROMPT_COMMAND|trap |nc |ncat|/dev/tcp|curl|wget|base64|python3? -c|LD_PRELOAD|alias (sudo|su|ls|passwd)' /root/.bashrc /root/.profile /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.profile /home/*/.bash_profile /home/*/.bash_logout /home/*/.xsessionrc /home/*/.xprofile 2>/dev/null

    PROMPT_COMMAND and trap ... DEBUG run a command before every prompt or every command. The basic alias checks are in Check shell startup files and aliases.

    #Check SSH keys and sshd settings used for persistence

    Every authorized_keys file on the system, wherever it is:

    sudo find / -xdev -name 'authorized_keys*' -exec ls -la {} \; 2>/dev/null

    Then the settings that change where sshd looks for keys or what it runs:

    sudo sshd -T | grep -iE 'authorizedkeysfile|authorizedkeyscommand|permituserenvironment|permitrootlogin|forcecommand'
    Finding Problem
    A key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys Root login with no password
    authorizedkeysfile with an extra path (default is .ssh/authorized_keys .ssh/authorized_keys2) Keys hidden in another file
    authorizedkeyscommand set A program decides which keys work
    permituserenvironment yes ~/.ssh/environment can set LD_PRELOAD
    command="..." or environment="..." at the start of a key line The key runs a hidden command

    Remove keys the README does not explain (Review authorized_keys), fix the setting in sshd_config or its drop-in folder, then sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh.

    #Find PATH hijacks

    A program in an earlier PATH folder replaces the real one. /usr/local/bin and /usr/local/sbin come before /usr/bin in the default PATH, so a planted /usr/local/bin/sudo or ls runs instead of the real one. List names there that shadow a system command:

    for f in /usr/local/bin/* /usr/local/sbin/*; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; n=$(basename "$f"); for d in /usr/bin /usr/sbin; do [ -e "$d/$n" ] && echo "$f shadows $d/$n"; done; done

    PATH folders anyone can write to:

    for d in $(echo "$PATH" | tr ':' ' '); do [ -d "$d" ] && find "$d" -maxdepth 0 -perm -0002 -print; done

    Also check secure_path in sudoers (insecure sudo) and PATH= lines in /etc/environment and the startup files above. Delete a shadowing file after recording it; run hash -r in open shells.

    #Find SUID shell copies

    A copy of a shell with the SUID bit gives any user a root shell (/tmp/.x -p). On Mint 21 and current Ubuntu and Debian, every legitimate SUID program is under /usr (merged /usr), so anything else is planted:

    sudo find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f ! -path '/usr/*' -exec ls -la {} \; 2>/dev/null

    Copies hidden inside /usr under another name are caught by comparing hashes with the real shells:

    h=$(sha256sum /usr/bin/bash /usr/bin/dash /usr/bin/python3* 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}' | paste -sd'|')
sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -exec sha256sum {} + 2>/dev/null | grep -E "$h"

    No output is clean. Remove the file, or the bit if it is a real system binary that someone modified (SUID list).

    #Find web shells

    G1 scored "PHP web shell removed" (/var/www/html/r57.php). The function-pattern search is in Remove phpinfo files and web shells. Deeper checks:

    PHP code hidden in image files (-a makes grep read binary files as text):

    sudo grep -rla --include='*.jpg' --include='*.jpeg' --include='*.png' --include='*.gif' --include='*.ico' '<?php' /var/www 2>/dev/null

    Server settings that make other files run as PHP, or prepend a script to every page:

    sudo grep -rnE 'AddType|AddHandler|SetHandler|auto_prepend_file|auto_append_file' /var/www /etc/apache2 /etc/php 2>/dev/null

    Code files that were changed recently or that the web server owns (it should only own upload folders):

    sudo find /var/www -type f \( -name '*.php' -o -name '*.phtml' -o -name '*.jsp' \) -mtime -30 2>/dev/null
sudo find /var/www -type f -user www-data -name '*.php' 2>/dev/null

    Requests that used a shell, from the access log:

    sudo zgrep -hE '\.php\?(cmd|c|exec|e|q)=|whoami|/etc/passwd' /var/log/apache2/access.log* /var/log/nginx/access.log* 2>/dev/null | tail -20

    Tomcat shells are .jsp files or .war archives under /var/lib/tomcat9/webapps/. Record the path and the first lines of each shell, delete only that file, and confirm the site still loads.

    #Find hidden processes and files

    A rootkit that hides processes from ps usually cannot hide every trace in /proc. unhide compares several sources:

    sudo apt install unhide
sudo unhide quick

    Names designed to be overlooked:

    sudo find / -xdev \( -name '...' -o -name '.. *' -o -name '. *' -o -name ' *' \) 2>/dev/null
sudo find /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm /home /root -name '.*' -type f -newer /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null

    Regular files in /dev (devices are not regular files, so a clean system prints nothing outside /dev/shm):

    sudo find /dev -type f ! -path '/dev/shm/*' 2>/dev/null

    #Sweep the persistence locations

    The common spots (cron, systemd, rc.local, bashrc, ld.so.preload, autostart, apt hooks) are in Persistence, backdoors and malware. The rarer ones:

    Location Runs Check
    /etc/NetworkManager/dispatcher.d/ As root whenever a network connection changes ls -la, then dpkg -S each file
    /etc/logrotate.d/* (postrotate blocks) As root daily grep -n -A3 postrotate /etc/logrotate.d/*
    /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/*.pth, /usr/local/lib/python3*/dist-packages/*.pth Lines starting with import run with every Python program grep -n '^import' <file>; distutils-precedence.pth from setuptools is normal
    /etc/binfmt.d/, /proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/ An interpreter for a file type Only packaged entries such as python3.10 or Wine
    /etc/aliases Pipes to commands for mail Postfix
    /etc/initramfs-tools/scripts/, /etc/initramfs-tools/hooks/ At boot, before the real system Should be empty unless a package uses it
    .git/hooks/ in repositories When someone runs git there Hooks without .sample are active
    /etc/skel/ Copied into every new user's home ls -la /etc/skel

    #Run rkhunter and chkrootkit

    Install and run them as shown in Run rootkit and malware scanners. Read only the warnings:

    sudo grep -E 'Warning|Possible rootkit' /var/log/rkhunter.log
sudo chkrootkit -q

    Known false positives on Mint and Ubuntu:

    Scanner Warning Why it is harmless
    rkhunter /usr/bin/lwp-request replaced by a script It is a Perl script in libwww-perl
    rkhunter Hidden file /etc/.updated systemd writes it after updates
    chkrootkit PACKET SNIFFER on dhclient or NetworkManager DHCP uses raw sockets
    chkrootkit Hidden files such as .gitignore or .build-id under /usr/lib Normal package files

    Anything else names a real file: check it with dpkg -S and dpkg --verify.

    Verify

    dpkg --verify shows no changed binaries, /etc/ld.so.preload does not exist, ldd /usr/bin/ls lists only the normal libraries, the module, SUID and unpackaged-file loops print nothing unexplained, and rkhunter's warnings are all on the false-positive list.

    PreviousLinux forensics question playbookNextHow to take the networking quiz fast
    NET

    How to take the networking quiz fast

    jump:net-quiz-strategy

    Fast path

    1. Read the question count and time limit on the quiz start screen and write down the finish time.
    2. Open the Tools section in a second tab. It has the number converter and the subnet calculator.
    3. First pass: answer every question you know in under 20 seconds. Write down the numbers of the rest.
    4. Second pass: search one keyword from each skipped question in the search box, or find it in the keyword table.
    5. Send every binary, hex or decimal question to the converter in Tools instead of converting by hand.
    6. With 2 minutes left, answer anything still blank. A blank scores nothing.

    #Which modules each round tests

    CP-19 high school Networking Quiz ranges from the official challenge table. Module numbers are the CyberPatriot Content Course numbers. Modules 1-17 line up with CCNA ITN v7 modules 1-17. Modules 18-23 are extra modules beyond ITN; their pages in this guide are the SRWE topic pages, which also explain why the mapping is a best guess.

    Round (CP-19 dates) Quiz modules (points) Read these pages
    Practice Round (Oct 7-20) 1-2 (unscored) Modules 1 and 2
    Round 1 (Oct 22-25) 3-7 (10) Module 3, Module 4, Module 5, Module 6, Module 7, cram 3-7, flashcards 3-7
    Round 2 (Nov 12-15) 8-11 and 21-22 (10) Module 8, Module 9, Module 10, Module 11, modules 21-22 on the SRWE pages (likely WLAN and DHCP topics), cram 8-17, flashcards 8-17
    State (Dec 10-13) 12-17 (30) Module 12, Module 13, Module 14, Module 15, Module 16, Module 17, cram 8-17, flashcards 8-17
    Semifinals (Jan 21-23) 18-20 and 23 (72 Platinum, 30 Gold and Silver) SRWE overview, cram, flashcards

    Earlier modules are still fair game for background: a Module 11 subnetting question assumes the Module 5 binary skills, and State questions on ICMP assume Module 8 headers. Packet Tracer covers every module up to the round (1-7, then 1-11 and 21-22, then 1-17, then 1-23), see Packet Tracer strategy.

    Where the module ranges come from

    The CP-19 Competition Challenges table lists the quiz and Packet Tracer module ranges for each round. CP-18 used the same ranges. No public source lists the Content Course module titles, so the ITN mapping for 1-17 is an inference from the ranges and the course order. Check the real titles on the Coach Dashboard Content Course if you can.

    #Set up before you start

    #Where to look for each question type

    Question looks like Look here
    Names a PDU, layer, standard number, cable, frame field Search box, one keyword (fragment-free, LLC, goodput, rollover)
    "Which layer" or "which sublayer" does something Keyword table, then the cram sheet
    Binary, hex or decimal number Converter in Tools, or Module 5
    "Which term describes" Glossary
    Module 1-2 or Networking Basics wording Modules 1 and 2 and the Networking Basics map
    Subnet, mask, prefix, "how many hosts", "which address is the broadcast" Subnet calculator in Tools, method in Module 11
    IPv6 address, compress, expand, EUI-64, SLAAC, link-local Module 12
    Port number, TCP flag, handshake, window Module 14 and Common ports
    show command output, ping symbols, troubleshooting step Module 17 and Module 10
    Any Module 8-17 keyword Keyword table for 8-17

    #Answer format rules that cost points

    Question wording What to do
    "Which two" or "Choose two" Select exactly two. Count your selections before you move on.
    "Which three" Select exactly three.
    "Best describes" Several options may be partly true. Pick the most complete and most specific one.
    "What is the purpose of" Pick the option that states the main job, not a side effect.
    "Which statement is true" One option is fully correct. Options with "always", "only" or "never" are usually the wrong ones.
    "Which is NOT" or "except" Read the question twice, then find the one option that does not fit.
    Matching or drag and drop Place the pairs you are sure of first. The leftovers narrow down the hard ones.
    Exhibit or topology picture Read device labels and cable styles first. In Packet Tracer drawings a solid black line is straight-through, a dashed line is crossover, and a light blue line is console.

    #Keyword to answer table

    If the question contains the keyword on the left, the answer is almost always on the right.

    Keyword in the question Likely answer
    bits, signals, voltage, light pulses, connector, encoding, signaling, hub, repeater Layer 1 Physical
    frame, MAC address, NIC-to-NIC, same network, media access, FCS, CRC, switch Layer 2 Data Link
    packet, IP address, logical address, across networks, best path, routing, router Layer 3 Network (TCP/IP Internet layer)
    segment, port number, reliability, flow control, TCP, UDP, sequencing Layer 4 Transport
    dialog, organize the dialogue, manage data exchange Layer 5 Session
    common representation of data, compression, encryption, JPEG, ASCII Layer 6 Presentation
    process-to-process, interface to applications, HTTP, DNS, DHCP, FTP Layer 7 Application
    identifies which network layer protocol is in the frame, IEEE 802.2 LLC sublayer
    frame encapsulation and media access, implemented in hardware MAC sublayer (IEEE 802.3, 802.11, 802.15)
    ARP in the TCP/IP model Network Access layer
    develops RFCs, maintains internet and TCP/IP technologies IETF
    promotes open development and use of the internet ISOC
    overall management and development of internet standards IAB
    long-term research on internet and TCP/IP protocols IRTF
    coordinates IP address allocation and domain names, based in the US ICANN
    oversees and manages IP addresses, domain names, protocol identifiers for ICANN IANA
    802 standards, Ethernet, WLAN IEEE
    electrical wiring, connectors, 19-inch racks EIA
    radio equipment, cellular towers, VoIP devices, satellite TIA
    video compression, IPTV, DSL ITU-T
    data link layer standards bodies IEEE, ITU, ISO, ANSI (not the IETF)
    immune to EMI and RFI, longest distance, light pulses Fiber optic
    cancellation, twisted pairs UTP limiting crosstalk
    laser, very small core, hundreds of km Single-mode fiber (SMF)
    LED, larger core, up to 550 m Multimode fiber (MMF)
    PC serial port to console port Rollover (console) cable
    like devices (switch-switch, PC-PC, router-router) Crossover (legacy; auto-MDIX makes either cable work)
    unlike devices (host to switch, switch to router) Straight-through
    capacity of the medium Bandwidth
    actual measured transfer of bits Throughput
    usable data, throughput minus overhead Goodput
    time including delays Latency
    whole frame, checks CRC, needed for QoS analysis Store-and-forward
    forwards right after the destination MAC, lowest latency Cut-through fast-forward
    checks the first 64 bytes Cut-through fragment-free
    one busy port delays the whole queue Port-based memory buffering
    ports of different speeds, common buffer Shared memory buffering (asymmetric switching)
    switch learns from Source MAC address
    switch forwards using Destination MAC address
    unknown destination MAC, broadcast, multicast Flood out all ports except the incoming port
    detects straight-through or crossover cable Auto-MDIX (mdix auto)
    wireless access, avoid collisions CSMA/CA
    legacy hub or bus Ethernet, detect collisions CSMA/CD
    each node takes its turn, deterministic Controlled access (legacy Token Ring, ARCNET)
    frame under 64 bytes Runt or collision fragment (discarded)
    more than 1500 bytes of data Jumbo or baby giant frame
    Gigabit port duplex Full-duplex only

    #Time budget

    • Divide the time limit by the question count. About 1 minute per question is typical, and one-fact questions should take far less.
    • First pass: answer everything you know in under 20 seconds each.
    • Second pass: look up the skipped questions.
    • Last 2 minutes: every question gets an answer, even a guess.

    Answer with the course value

    The quiz grades against NetAcad wording, and the textbook answer wins over real-world exceptions. Real 802.11ac gear can exceed 1.3 Gbps, but the course says 450 Mbps to 1.3 Gbps. Where this guide marks a fact as a course value, answer with that.

    Options that mix layers are usually wrong. "A switch forwards packets based on IP address" is wrong because switches forward frames by MAC address. Options that pair a PDU with the wrong layer are also wrong ("the transport layer encapsulates frames").

    PreviousRootkit and persistence huntingNextCram sheet for modules 3 to 7
    NET

    Cram sheet for modules 3 to 7

    jump:net-cram

    #Module 3 protocols and models cram

    • Message rules: encoding, formatting and encapsulation, size, timing, delivery options.
    • Message timing: flow control (how much and how fast), response timeout (how long to wait for a reply), access method (when a device may send).
    • Delivery options: unicast (one to one), multicast (one to a group), broadcast (one to all). IPv6 does not use broadcast.
    • Protocol functions: addressing, reliability, flow control, sequencing, error detection, application interface.
    • Web page example: HTTP (request and response format) over TCP (reliable conversation) over IP (sender to receiver across networks) over Ethernet (NIC to NIC on the LAN).
    • OSI layers 7 to 1: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.
    • TCP/IP layers: Application (OSI 5-7), Transport (4), Internet (3), Network Access (1-2).
    • OSI is a reference model. TCP/IP is a protocol model.
    • PDUs from the top: data, segment, packet, frame, bits. A UDP PDU is called a datagram.
    • Encapsulation adds headers on the way down. De-encapsulation removes them on the way up. Only the data link layer adds a trailer.
    • ARP sits in the TCP/IP Network Access layer in the course table. NAT, ICMP and routing protocols sit in the Internet layer.
    • IP addresses are end to end and do not change. MAC addresses are NIC to NIC and are rewritten at every router.
    • Remote destination: destination MAC = default gateway MAC, destination IP = final host IP.
    • Segmentation benefits: speed (multiplexing many conversations) and efficiency (only lost segments are resent).
    Organization One-line job
    ISOC Promotes open development and use of the internet
    IAB Overall management and development of internet standards
    IETF Develops and maintains internet and TCP/IP technologies, publishes RFCs
    IRTF Long-term research on internet and TCP/IP protocols
    ICANN Coordinates IP address allocation and domain names (US based)
    IANA Oversees and manages IP addresses, domain names and protocol identifiers for ICANN
    IEEE 802 standards (802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 WLAN)
    EIA Electrical wiring, connectors, 19-inch racks
    TIA Radio equipment, cellular towers, VoIP devices, satellite communications
    ITU-T Video compression, IPTV, broadband such as DSL

    #Module 4 physical layer cram

    • Physical layer standards cover physical components, encoding and signaling.
    • Media: copper (electrical signals), fiber (light pulses), wireless (microwave signals).
    • Bandwidth = capacity. Throughput = measured rate. Goodput = throughput minus overhead. Latency = time including delays.
    • Units: Kbps 10^3, Mbps 10^6, Gbps 10^9, Tbps 10^12 bits per second.
    • Copper problems: attenuation, EMI/RFI, crosstalk. UTP limits crosstalk by cancellation (twisted pairs with different twist rates).
    • UTP: 100 m maximum, RJ-45 connector, TIA/EIA-568 standard, electrical ratings by the IEEE.
    • Course category speeds: Cat5 100 Mbps, Cat5e 1000 Mbps (minimum acceptable today), Cat6 up to 10 Gbps (separator between pairs), Cat7 10 Gbps, Cat8 40 Gbps.
    • T568B pin 1-2: white/orange, orange. T568A pin 1-2: white/green, green. The two standards swap the orange and green pairs.
    • Straight-through: same standard both ends, host to network device. Crossover: A on one end, B on the other, like devices, now legacy. Rollover: Cisco proprietary console cable.
    • Coax: cable internet and antenna connections; BNC, N-type, F-type connectors.
    • Fiber: completely immune to EMI and RFI, longest distance, highest cost and installation skill.
    • SMF: very small core, laser, hundreds of km, yellow jacket. MMF: larger core, LED, up to 10 Gbps over 550 m, orange or aqua jacket.
    • Fiber connectors: ST (twist-on bayonet), SC (square push-pull), LC (small), duplex LC.
    • Wireless concerns: coverage area, interference, security, shared half-duplex medium.
    • Wireless standards: Wi-Fi 802.11, Bluetooth 802.15, WiMAX 802.16, Zigbee 802.15.4.

    #Module 5 number systems cram

    • Binary place values: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. One octet holds 0-255. IPv4 is 32 bits.
    • Mask octets: 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255 (1 to 8 leading ones).
    • One hex digit = 4 bits. Two hex digits = one byte (00-FF). A-F = 10-15.
    • IPv6 = 128 bits = 8 hextets of 16 bits = 32 hex digits. MAC = 48 bits = 12 hex digits.
    • 0xFF = 255, 0xC0 = 192, 0x80 = 128, 0xA = 10, 0x10 = 16.

    #Module 6 data link layer cram

    • Data link layer: accepts Layer 3 packets, encapsulates them into frames, controls media access, detects errors and rejects corrupt frames.
    • LLC (IEEE 802.2) identifies the network layer protocol. MAC (802.3, 802.11, 802.15) does encapsulation and media access in hardware.
    • Data link standards come from IEEE, ITU, ISO and ANSI.
    • Routers strip and rebuild the Layer 2 frame at every hop. The Layer 3 packet stays the same.
    • WAN topologies: point-to-point (simplest and most common), hub and spoke, mesh (high availability, high cost). Hybrid = a mix, such as partial mesh.
    • LAN topologies: star and extended star today. Bus and ring are legacy.
    • Half-duplex: one direction at a time (WLANs, hubs). Full-duplex: both directions at once (switches).
    • Contention-based access: CSMA/CD (legacy Ethernet hubs and bus), CSMA/CA (WLANs). Controlled access: legacy Token Ring and ARCNET.
    • Generic frame fields: frame start, addressing, type, control, data, error detection, frame stop. The trailer holds error detection (FCS with a CRC value) and frame stop.
    • Layer 2 protocols: Ethernet, 802.11 wireless, PPP, HDLC, Frame Relay.

    #Module 7 Ethernet switching cram

    • Ethernet: IEEE 802.2 and 802.3, works at Layers 1 and 2.
    • Frame fields: Preamble 7, SFD 1, Destination MAC 6, Source MAC 6, Type/Length 2, Data 46-1500, FCS 4 (bytes).
    • Frame size 64 to 1518 bytes, counted from Destination MAC through FCS. Under 64 = runt or collision fragment. Over 1500 bytes of data = jumbo or baby giant.
    • Type values: 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP.
    • MAC: 48 bits. First 24 bits = OUI (vendor, assigned by IEEE). Broadcast FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. IPv4 multicast 01-00-5E. IPv6 multicast 33-33.
    • Switch learns the source MAC and forwards by the destination MAC. Unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast are flooded out all ports except the incoming one.
    • MAC table entries age out after 5 minutes by default.
    • Store-and-forward checks the whole frame and is required for QoS analysis. Fast-forward has the lowest latency. Fragment-free checks the first 64 bytes.
    • Port-based memory: per-port queues. Shared memory: common buffer, allows asymmetric switching.
    • Gigabit ports run full-duplex only. Best practice for duplex: configure both switch ports as full-duplex.
    • Auto-MDIX is on by default from IOS 12.2(18)SE; re-enable it with mdix auto.
    PreviousHow to take the networking quiz fastNextModules 1 and 2 networking today and basic IOS
    NET

    Modules 1 and 2 networking today and basic IOS

    jump:net-m1-2

    #Clients, servers and peer-to-peer

    Term Meaning
    Host or end device Any device that sends or receives messages directly (PC, server, phone, printer, IP camera). Every host has an IP address.
    Server Runs software that provides information to other hosts (email, web, file server)
    Client Runs software that requests and displays information from a server (web browser, email client)

    One computer can be a client and a server at the same time.

    Peer-to-peer Client/server
    Setup Easy, less complex, lower cost Needs dedicated servers
    Administration No central administration Centralized
    Security Weaker Stronger
    Scalability Not scalable Scales well
    Performance Slower when a device serves and works at once Better
    Typical use Small networks, sharing files and printers Businesses, larger networks

    #Network components

    Component Examples Role
    End devices PCs, laptops, servers, printers, VoIP phones, TelePresence, security cameras, phones Source or destination of a message
    Intermediary devices Switches, wireless access points, routers, firewalls Connect end devices and move data between them
    Network media Copper wires, glass or plastic fiber, wireless Channel that carries the signal

    #What intermediary devices do

    • Regenerate and retransmit data signals.
    • Keep information about which pathways exist through the network.
    • Notify other devices of errors and communication failures.
    • Direct data along alternate paths when a link fails.
    • Classify and direct messages by priority (QoS).
    • Permit or deny traffic based on security settings.

    #Choosing network media

    Four criteria: maximum distance the signal can travel, the installation environment, the amount of data and speed needed, and the cost of media and installation.

    #NIC, port and interface

    Term Meaning
    NIC (network interface card) Gives a device its physical connection to the network
    Physical port Connector on a device where media plugs in
    Interface Specialized port on a networking device that connects to a network (routers and switches call their ports interfaces)

    #Physical and logical topology diagrams

    Diagram Shows
    Physical topology diagram Physical location of intermediary devices and cable installation (building, room, rack)
    Logical topology diagram Devices, ports and the IP addressing scheme

    #Network types

    Type Meaning Traits
    LAN Network in a small area (home, school, office building) Usually one organization or person administers it; high-speed bandwidth to end devices
    WAN Connects LANs over a wide geographic area Usually administered by one or more service providers; typically slower links between LANs
    MAN Spans a city or campus Larger than a LAN, smaller than a WAN
    WLAN Wireless LAN (802.11) Like a LAN but uses radio
    SAN Storage area network Supports file servers, storage, retrieval and replication
    PAN Devices around one person Bluetooth range

    #Network sizes

    Size Meaning
    Small home network A few computers connected to each other and the internet
    SOHO (small office/home office) A home or remote office connected to a corporate network
    Medium to large Hundreds or thousands of hosts
    World wide The internet, connecting hundreds of millions of computers

    #Internet, intranet and extranet

    Term Meaning
    Internet Worldwide collection of interconnected networks, owned by no single person or group
    Intranet Private collection of LANs and WANs inside an organization, open only to its members
    Extranet Secure, controlled access to an organization's network for outside people such as suppliers, customers and contractors

    Nobody owns the internet. Groups such as the IETF, ICANN and the IAB develop and maintain its standards and structure.

    #Internet connection types

    #Home and small office connections

    Connection How it works
    Cable Cable TV provider's coaxial line; high bandwidth, always on
    DSL Telephone line; high bandwidth, always on; ADSL (download faster than upload) is common for homes
    Cellular Cell phone network; limited by coverage and data plan
    Satellite Rural areas without cable or DSL; needs a clear line of sight to the satellite
    Dial-up telephone Phone line and modem; cheap, very low bandwidth

    #Business connections

    Connection How it works
    Dedicated leased line Reserved circuits in the provider's network connecting distant offices; rented monthly or yearly
    Metro Ethernet (Ethernet WAN) Extends LAN access technology into the WAN
    Business DSL Several formats; SDSL (symmetric DSL) gives the same upload and download speed
    Satellite Used when wired options are not available

    #Converged networks

    A traditional network design ran separate networks for phone, TV and data, each with its own rules and standards. A converged network carries voice, video and data over one infrastructure with the same rules and standards.

    #Reliable network characteristics

    Characteristic Meaning Achieved by
    Fault tolerance Limits the devices affected by a failure and recovers quickly Redundancy (multiple paths) and packet switching (packets can take different routes)
    Scalability Grows without degrading service for existing users Following standards and good design
    Quality of Service (QoS) Manages congestion so voice and live video get priority QoS policies
    Security Protects devices and data Network infrastructure security (physical access) and information security

    Information security goals (CIA):

    Goal Meaning
    Confidentiality Only intended, authorized recipients can read the data
    Integrity Data is not altered in transit
    Availability Timely, reliable access for authorized users

    #Network trends

    Trend What to know
    BYOD (bring your own device) Users reach company information and resources from their own devices, anytime and anywhere
    Online collaboration Working together on projects with tools such as Cisco Webex
    Video communications Video calls and conferencing
    Cloud computing Store files and run applications on servers over the internet
    Smart home technology Appliances connected to and controlled over the network
    Powerline networking Uses existing electrical wiring; adapters plug into outlets where Wi-Fi cannot reach
    Wireless broadband A WISP (wireless internet service provider) connects subscribers to an access point or hotspot, often in rural areas; cellular broadband to homes is another option

    #Cloud types

    Cloud Who uses it
    Public Anyone, over the internet (free or pay-per-use)
    Private One organization, such as a government
    Hybrid Two or more cloud types connected but kept separate
    Community Organizations with a shared need, such as healthcare groups under the same compliance rules

    #Network security threats and solutions

    External threat What it is
    Viruses, worms and Trojan horses Malicious code that runs on a device
    Spyware and adware Software that collects information or shows ads without consent
    Zero-day (zero-hour) attacks Exploit a vulnerability on the day it becomes known
    Threat actor attacks A person attacks devices or resources
    Denial of service (DoS) Slows or crashes applications and processes
    Data interception and theft Captures private information
    Identity theft Steals login credentials to reach private data

    Internal threats are lost or stolen devices, accidental misuse by employees, and malicious employees. Insiders already have access, so internal threats can do more damage.

    Network size Security solutions
    Home or small office Antivirus and antispyware, firewall filtering
    Larger or corporate All of the above plus dedicated firewall systems, access control lists (ACLs), intrusion prevention systems (IPS), virtual private networks (VPNs)

    #Cisco IOS access methods

    Method Type Notes
    Console Out-of-band physical port Initial configuration; works with no network configured; console (rollover) cable or USB console
    SSH In-band, over the network Encrypted and recommended; the device needs an IP address (an SVI on a switch)
    Telnet In-band, over the network Sends everything in plaintext; avoid it
    AUX Out-of-band, legacy Remote CLI through a dial-up telephone modem on some older routers

    Terminal emulation programs: PuTTY, Tera Term, SecureCRT. SSH setup steps are in Securing device access and SSH.

    #IOS command modes and prompts

    Mode Prompt Enter with Leave with
    User EXEC Switch> Log in logout or exit
    Privileged EXEC Switch# enable disable
    Global configuration Switch(config)# configure terminal exit, end or Ctrl+Z
    Line configuration Switch(config-line)# line console 0 or line vty 0 15 exit (to global) or end
    Interface configuration Switch(config-if)# interface vlan 1 or interface fa0/1 exit (to global) or end

    User EXEC allows only limited monitoring commands. Privileged EXEC allows all show and debug commands, copy and reload, and is the way into configuration mode. exit goes back one level. end or Ctrl+Z goes straight to privileged EXEC.

    #IOS help and hotkeys

    Key or command Action
    ? Context-sensitive help: lists commands or the next parameters
    sh? Lists commands that start with "sh"
    Tab Completes a partially typed command or keyword
    Ctrl+A / Ctrl+E Cursor to the start / end of the line
    Ctrl+B or Left arrow / Ctrl+F or Right arrow Cursor one character left / right
    Esc then B / Esc then F Cursor back / forward one word
    Ctrl+R Redisplays the line
    Up arrow or Ctrl+P / Down arrow or Ctrl+N Previous / next command in history
    Ctrl+Z Leaves configuration mode for privileged EXEC
    Ctrl+C Leaves configuration mode for privileged EXEC; in setup mode, aborts to the prompt
    Ctrl+Shift+6 Break sequence: stops DNS lookups, traceroutes and pings
    Enter at --More-- Next line
    Space at --More-- Next screen
    Any other key at --More-- Ends the output and returns to the prompt

    Commands can be shortened to the shortest unique prefix (conf t, sh run).

    Error message Meaning
    % Ambiguous command Not enough letters to identify the command
    % Incomplete command Required parameters are missing
    % Invalid input detected at '^' marker Typo at the caret position

    #Basic device configuration

    Fast path

    1. Enter privileged EXEC and then global configuration:

      enable
configure terminal

    2. Name the device and set the encrypted privileged EXEC password:

      hostname <hostname>
enable secret <password>

    3. Password-protect the console and vty lines (commands below).

    4. Encrypt plaintext passwords, add a banner, and save. Press Enter when asked Destination filename [startup-config]?:

      service password-encryption
banner motd #Authorized access only#
end
copy running-config startup-config

    Hostname rules: start with a letter, no spaces, end with a letter or digit, only letters, digits and dashes, fewer than 64 characters.

    #Secure the console and vty lines

    Set a console password, from global configuration:

    line console 0
password <password>
login
exit

    Set a password on the 16 remote (vty) lines:

    line vty 0 15
password <password>
login
exit

    #Running config and startup config

    running-config startup-config
    Stored in RAM (volatile) NVRAM (non-volatile)
    Lost on reboot Yes No
    Changes Take effect immediately Used at boot
    View with show running-config show startup-config

    Save the running config so it survives a reboot (privileged EXEC):

    copy running-config startup-config

    Discard unsaved changes by reloading without saving. Answer no if asked System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]:, then press Enter at [confirm]:

    reload

    Erase the saved config (the device boots with no config on the next reload):

    erase startup-config

    Verify

    After saving, show startup-config shows the same settings as show running-config.

    #Give a switch an IP address with an SVI

    A Layer 2 switch needs an IP address only for remote management (SSH or Telnet). The address goes on a switch virtual interface (SVI), VLAN 1 by default, and the SVI must be enabled with no shutdown. From privileged EXEC:

    configure terminal
interface vlan 1
ip address <ip-address> <subnet-mask>
no shutdown
exit
ip default-gateway <default-gateway>
end

    ip default-gateway is needed only to manage the switch from another network. End devices get addresses statically or from DHCP, and their default gateway is the router interface they send remote traffic to.

    Verify

    show ip interface brief shows Vlan1 with the address and status up/up. The SVI comes up only when at least one port in VLAN 1 is connected.

    NET

    Module 3 protocols, standards and the OSI and TCP/IP models

    jump:net-m3-models

    #Message rules

    Every communication has a source (sender), a destination (receiver) and a channel (the media between them).

    Rule Meaning Example
    Message encoding Converts information into a form that can be transmitted (bits into voltage, light or radio waves); decoding reverses it A NIC turns bits into electrical signals
    Message formatting and encapsulation The message follows a set format; encapsulation places it inside an envelope with addressing A frame header carries source and destination addresses
    Message size Long messages are broken into smaller pieces Ethernet data field holds at most 1500 bytes
    Message timing Flow control, response timeout, access method See below
    Message delivery options Unicast, multicast, broadcast See below
    Human protocol requirements the course compares this to

    Human communication needs an identified sender and receiver, a common language and grammar, agreed speed and timing of delivery, and confirmation or acknowledgment requirements. Network protocols cover the same needs.

    #Message timing: flow control, response timeout, access method

    Term Meaning
    Flow control Manages the rate of data transmission: how much can be sent and how fast it can be delivered
    Response timeout How long a host waits for a reply and what it does when the reply does not arrive
    Access method Decides when a device can send; two devices sending at once on shared media cause a collision

    #Message delivery options: unicast, multicast, broadcast

    Option Delivery Note
    Unicast One to one Single destination
    Multicast One to a group Group of destinations
    Broadcast One to all on the local network IPv4 only; IPv6 does not use broadcast

    In course diagrams, a round node icon stands for any device.

    #Network protocol functions

    Function Meaning Example protocols
    Addressing Identifies the sender and the intended receiver Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6
    Reliability Guaranteed delivery if messages are lost or corrupted TCP
    Flow control Data flows at an efficient rate between two hosts TCP
    Sequencing Labels each segment so it can be reassembled in order TCP
    Error detection Determines whether data was corrupted in transit Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, TCP
    Application interface Process-to-process communication between network applications HTTP, HTTPS

    #Types of protocols

    Type Job Examples
    Network communications Devices communicate across one or more networks IP, TCP, HTTP
    Network security Authentication, data integrity, encryption SSH, SSL, TLS
    Routing Routers exchange route information and pick the best path OSPF, BGP
    Service discovery Automatic detection of devices or services DHCP (addressing), DNS (name to IP)

    #Protocol interaction when loading a web page

    Protocol TCP/IP layer Job in the example
    HTTP Application Content and format of requests and responses between web client and server
    TCP Transport Manages each conversation, guarantees reliable delivery, flow control
    IP Internet Delivers messages from sender to receiver; routers use it across networks
    Ethernet Network Access Delivers frames from one NIC to another on the same Ethernet LAN

    #Protocol suites

    A protocol suite is a group of inter-related protocols that work together.

    Suite Notes
    TCP/IP (Internet Protocol Suite) Used by the internet today; open standard, free to use, maintained by the IETF through RFCs
    OSI Developed in 1977 by ISO and ITU; its protocols lost out to TCP/IP, but the OSI reference model is used everywhere
    AppleTalk Proprietary Apple suite (1985); Apple adopted TCP/IP in 1995
    Novell NetWare Proprietary Novell suite and network OS (1983) using IPX; moved to TCP/IP in 1995
    Why open standards matter

    Open standards encourage interoperability, competition and innovation. Any vendor's device can talk to any other's: a Windows PC can browse a web server on Linux through any brand of router.

    #TCP/IP protocols by layer

    TCP/IP layer Category Protocols
    Application Name system DNS (domain names to IP addresses)
    Application Host configuration DHCPv4, DHCPv6, SLAAC (IPv6 addressing without a DHCPv6 server)
    Application Email SMTP (send), POP3 (download), IMAP (access mail kept on the server)
    Application File transfer FTP (reliable, acknowledged), SFTP (extension of SSH), TFTP (simple, connectionless, unacknowledged)
    Application Web and web service HTTP, HTTPS, REST (web service using APIs and HTTP requests)
    Transport Connection-oriented TCP (reliable, acknowledged)
    Transport Connectionless UDP (no delivery confirmation)
    Internet Internet Protocol IPv4 (32-bit), IPv6 (128-bit), NAT (private IPv4 to public IPv4)
    Internet Messaging ICMPv4, ICMPv6 (error feedback, ping), ICMPv6 ND (address resolution and duplicate address detection)
    Internet Routing OSPF (link-state, open standard), EIGRP (Cisco proprietary), BGP (open standard, between ISPs)
    Network Access Address resolution ARP (IPv4 address to MAC address)
    Network Access Data link Ethernet, WLAN (802.11)

    Where ARP goes

    The course's TCP/IP table puts ARP in the Network Access layer. Outside the course it is often described as working between Layers 2 and 3. When the question uses the TCP/IP model, answer Network Access.

    Common port numbers for context
    Port Protocol Transport
    20, 21 FTP data, control TCP
    22 SSH, SFTP TCP
    23 Telnet TCP
    25 SMTP TCP
    53 DNS UDP and TCP
    67, 68 DHCPv4 server, client UDP
    69 TFTP UDP
    80 HTTP TCP
    110 POP3 TCP
    143 IMAP TCP
    443 HTTPS TCP

    The full list is in Common ports and services.

    #Standards organizations

    #Internet standards organizations

    Organization Full name Job (course wording)
    ISOC Internet Society Promotes the open development, evolution and use of the internet worldwide
    IAB Internet Architecture Board Overall management and development of internet standards
    IETF Internet Engineering Task Force Develops, updates and maintains internet and TCP/IP technologies; publishes RFCs
    IRTF Internet Research Task Force Long-term research on internet and TCP/IP protocols (anti-spam, crypto forum and peer-to-peer research groups)
    ICANN Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers US based; coordinates IP address allocation, domain name management and other TCP/IP identifiers
    IANA Internet Assigned Numbers Authority Oversees and manages IP address allocation, domain names and protocol identifiers for ICANN

    ICANN or IANA

    "Coordinates" with "based in the United States" points to ICANN. "Oversees and manages ... for ICANN" or "protocol identifiers" points to IANA.

    #Electronic and communications standards organizations

    Organization Full name Job (course wording)
    IEEE ("I triple E") Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Standards for power and energy, healthcare, telecommunications and networking; the 802 family (802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 WLAN)
    EIA Electronic Industries Alliance Electrical wiring, connectors, and the 19-inch racks that hold network equipment
    TIA Telecommunications Industry Association Communication standards for radio equipment, cellular towers, VoIP devices, satellite communications
    ITU-T International Telecommunication Union, Telecommunication Standardization Sector One of the largest and oldest; video compression, IPTV, broadband such as DSL

    ISO (International Organization for Standardization) developed the OSI model with the ITU. Physical layer bodies are listed in Module 4.

    #OSI model layers

    # Layer Course description PDU Examples Devices
    7 Application Protocols for process-to-process communication Data HTTP, DNS, DHCP, FTP, SMTP, SSH, Telnet Hosts, servers
    6 Presentation Common representation of data: formatting, compression, encryption Data JPEG, GIF, MPEG, ASCII Hosts
    5 Session Organizes the dialogue and manages data exchange Data Session setup and teardown Hosts
    4 Transport Segments, transfers and reassembles data for individual communications Segment TCP, UDP Hosts, firewalls
    3 Network Exchanges pieces of data across the network between identified end devices Packet IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, OSPF Routers, multilayer switches
    2 Data Link Exchanges frames between devices over a common media Frame Ethernet, 802.11, PPP, HDLC Switches, NICs, wireless APs
    1 Physical Mechanical, electrical, functional and procedural means to activate, maintain and deactivate physical connections for bit transmission Bits Cables, connectors, signaling Hubs, repeaters, cables

    Mnemonics: top down (7 to 1) "All People Seem To Need Data Processing". Bottom up (1 to 7) "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".

    #TCP/IP model and OSI mapping

    TCP/IP layer OSI layers Course description Protocols
    Application 7, 6, 5 Represents data to the user, plus encoding and dialog control HTTP, DNS, DHCP, FTP, SMTP
    Transport 4 Supports communication between devices across diverse networks TCP, UDP
    Internet 3 Determines the best path through the network IP, ICMP, routing protocols
    Network Access 2, 1 Controls the hardware devices and media that make up the network Ethernet, WLAN, ARP

    OSI is a reference model: it describes what must happen at each layer without naming protocols. TCP/IP is a protocol model: it matches the structure of an actual protocol suite.

    Benefits of a layered model
    • Helps protocol design: each layer has defined information it acts on and a defined interface to the layers above and below.
    • Fosters competition, because products from different vendors work together.
    • Stops technology or capability changes in one layer from affecting the layers above and below.
    • Gives a common language for networking functions and capabilities.

    #PDUs and encapsulation

    Layer PDU
    Application (OSI 7-5) Data
    Transport (4) Segment (a UDP PDU is called a datagram)
    Network (3) Packet
    Data Link (2) Frame
    Physical (1) Bits

    Encapsulation on the sending host:

    1. The application creates the data.
    2. The transport layer adds a TCP or UDP header with port numbers, making a segment.
    3. The network layer adds an IP header with source and destination IP addresses, making a packet.
    4. The data link layer adds a header with MAC addresses and a trailer with the FCS, making a frame.
    5. The physical layer sends the frame as bits on the media.
    Data
[TCP hdr][Data]                          = Segment
[IP hdr][TCP hdr][Data]                  = Packet
[Eth hdr][IP hdr][TCP hdr][Data][FCS]    = Frame
0101011010101...                         = Bits

    The receiving host de-encapsulates from the bottom up: it checks the FCS and removes the frame header and trailer, then the IP header, then the TCP header, and hands the data to the application.

    Only one layer adds a trailer

    The data link layer is the only layer that adds a trailer (the FCS). Every other layer adds only a header.

    #Segmentation, multiplexing and sequencing

    Term Meaning
    Segmentation Dividing a data stream into smaller pieces for transmission
    Speed benefit Many conversations interleave on the network (multiplexing) instead of one large stream tying up the link
    Efficiency benefit Only a lost segment is retransmitted, not the whole stream
    Sequencing TCP numbers each segment so the receiver can reassemble them in order and detect missing ones

    #Network addresses and data link addresses

    Network layer address (IP) Data link address (MAC)
    Scope End to end: original source to final destination, across networks NIC to NIC on the same network
    Changes on the way No (except with NAT) Yes, rewritten at every router
    Parts Network portion (prefix) and host portion OUI and vendor-assigned part
    Size IPv4 32 bits, IPv6 128 bits 48 bits

    #Destination on the same network

    • Packet: source IP = sender, destination IP = receiver.
    • Frame: source MAC = sender's NIC, destination MAC = receiver's NIC.
    • The sender finds the receiver's MAC with ARP (IPv4) or Neighbor Discovery (IPv6).

    #Destination on a remote network

    • Packet: source IP = sender, destination IP = the final remote host (unchanged end to end).
    • Frame: source MAC = sender's NIC, destination MAC = the default gateway router interface.
    • Each router strips the frame, reads the packet, picks the next hop, and builds a new frame with new MAC addresses.

    Classic trap

    When PC1 sends to a server on another network, the destination MAC in PC1's frame is its default gateway's MAC. It is not the server's MAC.

    #Role of the default gateway

    • It is the router interface IP address on the local network that hosts send remote traffic to.
    • It must be in the same network as the host.
    • A host with a wrong or missing default gateway can reach local hosts but not remote networks.
