    • A host's default gateway is the IP address of the router interface on the same LAN (for example 192.168.10.1 for a host in 192.168.10.0/24).
    • A Layer 2 switch only needs a default gateway to be managed (SSH, Telnet, ping) from another network. User traffic passing through the switch does not use it.

    Set the switch's gateway in global configuration mode:

    ip default-gateway <default-gateway>

    #Set the default gateway on a switch

    The switch also needs an SVI with an IP address in the same network (see SVI setup). Check it with show running-config | include default-gateway.

    Verify

    From a host, ping the default gateway first, then a host on another network. If the gateway ping fails, check the host's IP and mask, the cable and the router interface status. If only the remote ping fails, check the host's default gateway setting.

    Why router interfaces start shut down

    A router connects networks, so an interface coming up by itself could join two networks that should stay apart. Switch ports exist to connect end devices to one LAN, so they come up automatically.

    PreviousModule 9 address resolution, ARP and IPv6 neighbor discoveryNextModule 11 IPv4 addressing, subnetting and VLSM
    NET

    Module 11 IPv4 addressing, subnetting and VLSM

    jump:net-m11-ipv4-addressing

    Fast path: subnet any address

    1. If the quiz allows it, paste the address and prefix into the subnet calculator in Tools and read the answers.
    2. By hand: find the interesting octet, the one where the mask is not 255 and not 0 (mask table).
    3. Block size = 256 minus the mask value in that octet.
    4. Network = the largest multiple of the block size that is at or below the address's value in that octet. Octets to the right become 0.
    5. Broadcast = next network minus 1 (the interesting octet becomes network + block - 1, octets to the right become 255).
    6. First host = network + 1. Last host = broadcast - 1. Usable hosts = 2^h - 2, where h = 32 minus the prefix.

    #IPv4 address structure

    • An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal octets (0-255) separated by dots.
    • The left part is the network portion, shared by every device on that network. The right part is the host portion, unique per device.
    • The subnet mask (or prefix length) says where the split is. A 1 bit in the mask marks a network bit, a 0 bit marks a host bit.
    • The prefix length is the number of 1 bits in the mask: 255.255.255.0 is /24.

    #Network, host and broadcast addresses

    Address Host bits Can a host use it?
    Network address All 0 No. It names the network.
    First usable host All 0 except the last bit = 1 Yes
    Last usable host All 1 except the last bit = 0 Yes
    Broadcast address All 1 No. It reaches every host on the network.

    Usable hosts = 2^h - 2. The minus 2 removes the network and broadcast addresses.

    #Subnet mask and prefix table

    Prefix Mask Block size (interesting octet) Usable hosts
    /8 255.0.0.0 1 in octet 1 (octet boundary) 16,777,214
    /9 255.128.0.0 128 in octet 2 8,388,606
    /10 255.192.0.0 64 in octet 2 4,194,302
    /12 255.240.0.0 16 in octet 2 1,048,574
    /16 255.255.0.0 1 in octet 2 (octet boundary) 65,534
    /17 255.255.128.0 128 in octet 3 32,766
    /18 255.255.192.0 64 in octet 3 16,382
    /19 255.255.224.0 32 in octet 3 8,190
    /20 255.255.240.0 16 in octet 3 4,094
    /21 255.255.248.0 8 in octet 3 2,046
    /22 255.255.252.0 4 in octet 3 1,022
    /23 255.255.254.0 2 in octet 3 510
    /24 255.255.255.0 1 in octet 3 (octet boundary) 254
    /25 255.255.255.128 128 in octet 4 126
    /26 255.255.255.192 64 in octet 4 62
    /27 255.255.255.224 32 in octet 4 30
    /28 255.255.255.240 16 in octet 4 14
    /29 255.255.255.248 8 in octet 4 6
    /30 255.255.255.252 4 in octet 4 2
    /31 255.255.255.254 2 in octet 4 0 in the course formula (special point-to-point use)
    /32 255.255.255.255 1 Single host route

    Mask octet values in order: 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255.

    #Find the network address by ANDing

    A host finds the network address by ANDing each bit of its address with the mask: 1 AND 1 = 1, everything else = 0.

    Worked example, 192.168.10.75/27 (mask 255.255.255.224). Only the fourth octet is interesting:

    Address octet 4:   75  = 0100 1011
Mask octet 4:     224  = 1110 0000
AND result:             0100 0000  = 64
Broadcast (host bits set to 1): 0101 1111 = 95

    Network 192.168.10.64, first host .65, last host .94, broadcast 192.168.10.95, 30 usable hosts.

    #Subnet any network in four steps

    Worked example in the third octet, 172.16.77.10/20:

    1. The mask is 255.255.240.0, so octet 3 is interesting.
    2. Block size = 256 - 240 = 16. Networks in octet 3 go 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80 and so on.
    3. 77 falls between 64 and 80, so the network is 172.16.64.0.
    4. Next network is 172.16.80.0, so the broadcast is 172.16.79.255.

    Result: hosts 172.16.64.1 to 172.16.79.254, 2^12 - 2 = 4,094 usable.

    #Borrow bits to make subnets

    Formula Meaning
    Subnets = 2^n n = number of host bits borrowed
    Hosts per subnet = 2^h - 2 h = host bits left

    Worked example: divide 192.168.1.0/24 into 4 subnets.

    1. 2^2 = 4, so borrow 2 bits. The prefix becomes /26 (mask 255.255.255.192).
    2. Block size 64. Subnets: 192.168.1.0, .64, .128, .192.
    3. Each subnet has 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable hosts.
    Subnet Network Host range Broadcast
    0 192.168.1.0/26 .1 to .62 .63
    1 192.168.1.64/26 .65 to .126 .127
    2 192.168.1.128/26 .129 to .190 .191
    3 192.168.1.192/26 .193 to .254 .255

    Borrowing more bits gives more subnets with fewer hosts each. The same idea works on a /16 or /8: borrowing 8 bits from a /16 gives 256 subnets of /24.

    #Pick a prefix from a host count

    Find the smallest h where 2^h - 2 is at least the host count, then prefix = 32 - h.

    Hosts needed Host bits Prefix Usable
    2 2 /30 2
    3 to 6 3 /29 6
    7 to 14 4 /28 14
    15 to 30 5 /27 30
    31 to 62 6 /26 62
    63 to 126 7 /25 126
    127 to 254 8 /24 254
    255 to 510 9 /23 510
    511 to 1,022 10 /22 1,022

    A count of exactly 2^h needs one more bit: 32 hosts do not fit in a /27 (30 usable), so use a /26.

    #VLSM

    VLSM gives each subnet a mask sized for its own host count instead of one size for all, which wastes fewer addresses. A point-to-point WAN link needs 2 addresses, so it gets a /30.

    Method:

    1. Sort the subnets from most hosts to fewest.
    2. Give the largest one the smallest prefix that fits, starting at the first address of the block.
    3. Start the next subnet at the address right after the previous broadcast.
    4. Repeat. Each new subnet must start on a multiple of its own block size, which allocating largest first does automatically.

    Worked example, 10.10.0.0/24 for 100, 50 and 20 hosts plus one WAN link:

    Need Prefix Network Host range Broadcast
    100 hosts /25 10.10.0.0 .1 to .126 .127
    50 hosts /26 10.10.0.128 .129 to .190 .191
    20 hosts /27 10.10.0.192 .193 to .222 .223
    WAN link /30 10.10.0.224 .225 to .226 .227

    Addresses 10.10.0.228 to 10.10.0.255 stay free for growth.

    #Structured design and address assignment

    Plan from the requirements: how many subnets, how many hosts in each, and room for growth.

    Device Usual assignment
    End-user clients DHCP
    Servers and peripherals (printers) Static, so the address is predictable
    Servers reachable from the internet Public address (often through NAT)
    Intermediary devices (switches, APs) Static, for management
    Default gateway (router interface) Usually the first or last usable address, the same pattern in every subnet

    Reasons to subnet: location (a floor or building), group or function (users, engineering), and device type (servers, printers, IP phones). Smaller broadcast domains cut broadcast traffic, speed up the network and let you apply security per subnet.

    #Unicast, broadcast and multicast in IPv4

    Type Meaning Example
    Unicast One to one 192.168.1.20
    Directed broadcast All hosts on a specific network, can be sent from another network if routers allow it 192.168.1.255 for 192.168.1.0/24
    Limited broadcast All hosts on the local network only, never forwarded by routers 255.255.255.255
    Multicast One to a group of subscribed hosts 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255

    Routers do not forward broadcasts by default. Addresses 224.0.0.0 to 224.0.0.255 are link-local multicast for routing protocols (for example 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6 for OSPF).

    #Public, private and special addresses

    Range Use
    10.0.0.0/8 (10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255) Private (RFC 1918)
    172.16.0.0/12 (172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255) Private (RFC 1918)
    192.168.0.0/16 (192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255) Private (RFC 1918)
    127.0.0.0/8 Loopback. 127.0.0.1 is the usual one. Never leaves the host.
    169.254.0.0/16 Link-local (APIPA). A Windows host gives itself one when DHCP fails.
    0.0.0.0 This host or this network. 0.0.0.0/0 is the default route.
    255.255.255.255 Limited broadcast
    192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 Documentation (TEST-NET)
    Everything else in 1.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255 Public, globally routable

    Private addresses are not routed on the internet. A router doing NAT translates them to a public address.

    #Legacy classful addressing

    Class First octet Default mask Notes
    A 0 to 127 /8 (255.0.0.0) 0 and 127 are reserved
    B 128 to 191 /16 (255.255.0.0)
    C 192 to 223 /24 (255.255.255.0)
    D 224 to 239 none Multicast
    E 240 to 255 none Experimental

    Classful addressing wasted addresses and was replaced by classless addressing (CIDR) in 1993. The quiz still asks for class ranges.

    #Who hands out public addresses

    IANA allocates blocks to five Regional Internet Registries, which hand them to ISPs and large organizations.

    RIR Region
    ARIN North America
    LACNIC Latin America and parts of the Caribbean
    RIPE NCC Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia
    APNIC Asia Pacific
    AfriNIC Africa

    #Large broadcast domains

    A broadcast domain is everything that receives a Layer 2 broadcast. Switches forward broadcasts out every port, routers stop them. A large broadcast domain slows the network with broadcast traffic, slows each device (every host processes every broadcast), and widens the reach of attacks. Subnetting splits it into smaller domains joined by a router.

    #Subnetting practice problems with answers

    Work each one on paper first, then open it. Every answer was recomputed with a script.

    #Find the network, range and broadcast

    Q: Address 192.168.1.130/26. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.192. Block size 64 in octet 4: 130 falls in the block starting at 128. Network 192.168.1.128, first host 192.168.1.129, last host 192.168.1.190, broadcast 192.168.1.191, 62 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 10.45.200.77/20. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.240.0. Block size 16 in octet 3: 200 falls in the block starting at 192. Network 10.45.192.0, first host 10.45.192.1, last host 10.45.207.254, broadcast 10.45.207.255, 4,094 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 172.16.39.200/21. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.248.0. Block size 8 in octet 3: 39 falls in the block starting at 32. Network 172.16.32.0, first host 172.16.32.1, last host 172.16.39.254, broadcast 172.16.39.255, 2,046 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 192.168.50.94/27. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.224. Block size 32 in octet 4: 94 falls in the block starting at 64. Network 192.168.50.64, first host 192.168.50.65, last host 192.168.50.94, broadcast 192.168.50.95, 30 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 192.168.50.95/27. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.224. Block size 32 in octet 4: 95 falls in the block starting at 64. Network 192.168.50.64, first host 192.168.50.65, last host 192.168.50.94, broadcast 192.168.50.95, 30 usable hosts.

    This address is the broadcast address, so it cannot be assigned to a host.

    Q: Address 10.1.1.1/30. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.252. Block size 4 in octet 4: 1 falls in the block starting at 0. Network 10.1.1.0, first host 10.1.1.1, last host 10.1.1.2, broadcast 10.1.1.3, 2 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 172.31.255.5/29. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.248. Block size 8 in octet 4: 5 falls in the block starting at 0. Network 172.31.255.0, first host 172.31.255.1, last host 172.31.255.6, broadcast 172.31.255.7, 6 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 10.200.15.129/25. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.128. Block size 128 in octet 4: 129 falls in the block starting at 128. Network 10.200.15.128, first host 10.200.15.129, last host 10.200.15.254, broadcast 10.200.15.255, 126 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 192.168.7.250/28. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.240. Block size 16 in octet 4: 250 falls in the block starting at 240. Network 192.168.7.240, first host 192.168.7.241, last host 192.168.7.254, broadcast 192.168.7.255, 14 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 172.20.100.33/19. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.224.0. Block size 32 in octet 3: 100 falls in the block starting at 96. Network 172.20.96.0, first host 172.20.96.1, last host 172.20.127.254, broadcast 172.20.127.255, 8,190 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 10.0.0.200/23. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.254.0. Block size 2 in octet 3: 0 falls in the block starting at 0. Network 10.0.0.0, first host 10.0.0.1, last host 10.0.1.254, broadcast 10.0.1.255, 510 usable hosts.

    Q: Address 192.168.100.66/27. What are the network address, first host, last host, broadcast address and usable host count?

    Mask 255.255.255.224. Block size 32 in octet 4: 66 falls in the block starting at 64. Network 192.168.100.64, first host 192.168.100.65, last host 192.168.100.94, broadcast 192.168.100.95, 30 usable hosts.

    #Borrow bits for a number of subnets

    Q: Divide 192.168.10.0/24 into at least 6 equal subnets with as many hosts as possible. What prefix and mask do you use, and how many hosts fit in each subnet?

    Borrow 3 bits (2^3 = 8 subnets). New prefix /27, mask 255.255.255.224, 30 hosts per subnet. First subnets: 192.168.10.0/27, 192.168.10.32/27, 192.168.10.64/27. Last subnet: 192.168.10.224/27.

    Q: Divide 172.16.0.0/16 into at least 100 equal subnets with as many hosts as possible. What prefix and mask do you use, and how many hosts fit in each subnet?

    Borrow 7 bits (2^7 = 128 subnets). New prefix /23, mask 255.255.254.0, 510 hosts per subnet. First subnets: 172.16.0.0/23, 172.16.2.0/23, 172.16.4.0/23. Last subnet: 172.16.254.0/23.

    Q: Divide 10.0.0.0/8 into at least 1000 equal subnets with as many hosts as possible. What prefix and mask do you use, and how many hosts fit in each subnet?

    Borrow 10 bits (2^10 = 1024 subnets). New prefix /18, mask 255.255.192.0, 16,382 hosts per subnet. First subnets: 10.0.0.0/18, 10.0.64.0/18, 10.0.128.0/18. Last subnet: 10.255.192.0/18.

    Q: Divide 192.168.1.0/24 into at least 3 equal subnets with as many hosts as possible. What prefix and mask do you use, and how many hosts fit in each subnet?

    Borrow 2 bits (2^2 = 4 subnets). New prefix /26, mask 255.255.255.192, 62 hosts per subnet. First subnets: 192.168.1.0/26, 192.168.1.64/26, 192.168.1.128/26. Last subnet: 192.168.1.192/26.

    Q: Divide 192.168.200.0/24 into at least 16 equal subnets with as many hosts as possible. What prefix and mask do you use, and how many hosts fit in each subnet?

    Borrow 4 bits (2^4 = 16 subnets). New prefix /28, mask 255.255.255.240, 14 hosts per subnet. First subnets: 192.168.200.0/28, 192.168.200.16/28, 192.168.200.32/28. Last subnet: 192.168.200.240/28.

    Q: Divide 172.18.0.0/16 into at least 30 equal subnets with as many hosts as possible. What prefix and mask do you use, and how many hosts fit in each subnet?

    Borrow 5 bits (2^5 = 32 subnets). New prefix /21, mask 255.255.248.0, 2,046 hosts per subnet. First subnets: 172.18.0.0/21, 172.18.8.0/21, 172.18.16.0/21. Last subnet: 172.18.248.0/21.

    #Pick the prefix for a number of hosts

    Q: A subnet needs 25 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 25, so h = 5 host bits (30 usable). Prefix /27, mask 255.255.255.224.

    Q: A subnet needs 50 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 50, so h = 6 host bits (62 usable). Prefix /26, mask 255.255.255.192.

    Q: A subnet needs 100 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 100, so h = 7 host bits (126 usable). Prefix /25, mask 255.255.255.128.

    Q: A subnet needs 500 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 500, so h = 9 host bits (510 usable). Prefix /23, mask 255.255.254.0.

    Q: A subnet needs 14 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 14, so h = 4 host bits (14 usable). Prefix /28, mask 255.255.255.240.

    Q: A subnet needs 2 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 2, so h = 2 host bits (2 usable). Prefix /30, mask 255.255.255.252.

    Q: A subnet needs 1000 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 1000, so h = 10 host bits (1022 usable). Prefix /22, mask 255.255.252.0.

    Q: A subnet needs 254 hosts. What is the longest prefix (smallest subnet) that fits, and what is its mask?

    Need 2^h - 2 >= 254, so h = 8 host bits (254 usable). Prefix /24, mask 255.255.255.0.

    #Same subnet or valid host

    Q: Are 192.168.1.60/27 and 192.168.1.66/27 on the same subnet?

    No. 192.168.1.60 is in 192.168.1.32/27 and 192.168.1.66 is in 192.168.1.64/27.

    Q: Are 10.10.10.10/22 and 10.10.13.200/22 on the same subnet?

    No. 10.10.10.10 is in 10.10.8.0/22 and 10.10.13.200 is in 10.10.12.0/22.

    Q: Are 172.16.5.130/25 and 172.16.5.200/25 on the same subnet?

    Yes. 172.16.5.130 is in 172.16.5.128/25 and 172.16.5.200 is in 172.16.5.128/25.

    Q: Are 192.168.15.33/28 and 192.168.15.47/28 on the same subnet?

    Yes. 192.168.15.33 is in 192.168.15.32/28 and 192.168.15.47 is in 192.168.15.32/28. Also, 192.168.15.47 is the broadcast address of 192.168.15.32/28, so no host can use it.

    #VLSM design

    Q: Use VLSM to address 192.168.10.0/24 for: LAN A 60 hosts, LAN B 28 hosts, LAN C 12 hosts, WAN 1 2 hosts, WAN 2 2 hosts. Allocate the largest subnet first.
    Subnet Hosts needed Network First host Last host Broadcast
    LAN A 60 192.168.10.0/26 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.62 192.168.10.63
    LAN B 28 192.168.10.64/27 192.168.10.65 192.168.10.94 192.168.10.95
    LAN C 12 192.168.10.96/28 192.168.10.97 192.168.10.110 192.168.10.111
    WAN 1 2 192.168.10.112/30 192.168.10.113 192.168.10.114 192.168.10.115
    WAN 2 2 192.168.10.116/30 192.168.10.117 192.168.10.118 192.168.10.119

    Next free address after the plan: 192.168.10.120.

    Q: Use VLSM to address 172.16.4.0/23 for: Sales 200 hosts, Office 100 hosts, Lab 50 hosts, Printers 10 hosts, WAN link 2 hosts. Allocate the largest subnet first.
    Subnet Hosts needed Network First host Last host Broadcast
    Sales 200 172.16.4.0/24 172.16.4.1 172.16.4.254 172.16.4.255
    Office 100 172.16.5.0/25 172.16.5.1 172.16.5.126 172.16.5.127
    Lab 50 172.16.5.128/26 172.16.5.129 172.16.5.190 172.16.5.191
    Printers 10 172.16.5.192/28 172.16.5.193 172.16.5.206 172.16.5.207
    WAN link 2 172.16.5.208/30 172.16.5.209 172.16.5.210 172.16.5.211

    Next free address after the plan: 172.16.5.212.

    PreviousModule 10 basic router configuration and verificationNextModule 12 IPv6 addressing, compression, SLAAC, DHCPv6 and EUI-64
    NET

    Module 12 IPv6 addressing, compression, SLAAC, DHCPv6 and EUI-64

    jump:net-m12-ipv6

    Fast path: the three IPv6 question types

    1. Compress or expand: drop leading zeros in each hextet, then replace one run of all-zero hextets with :: (rules).
    2. Name the address type from the first hextet: 2000::/3 GUA, FE80::/10 link-local, FC00::/7 unique local, FF00::/8 multicast, ::1 loopback (type table).
    3. EUI-64: split the MAC in half, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit of the first byte (worked example).
    4. SLAAC or DHCPv6: read the RA flags A, O and M (RA methods).

    #IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence

    IPv4 public addresses ran out (IANA's free pool was empty in 2011), which drove IPv6. Both run side by side during the move.

    Technique How it works
    Dual stack A device runs IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time on the same interface
    Tunneling IPv6 packets travel inside IPv4 packets across an IPv4-only network
    Translation (NAT64) Allows IPv6 devices to talk to IPv4 devices by translating one packet format into the other

    Use tunneling and translation only where needed. Dual stack is the preferred approach.

    #IPv6 address format

    Fact Value
    Length 128 bits
    Written as 8 hextets of 16 bits, separated by colons
    Hex digits 32 (4 per hextet)
    Case Not case sensitive. Lowercase is recommended.
    Preferred format All 32 digits written out, for example 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
    Prefix length /0 to /128. A LAN is /64.

    #Compress an IPv6 address

    Rule What you may do Example
    1. Omit leading zeros Drop zeros at the start of any hextet. Trailing zeros stay. 0db8 becomes db8, 0010 becomes 10, 0000 becomes 0, 1000 stays 1000
    2. Double colon Replace one contiguous run of all-zero hextets with ::. Only once per address. 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1 becomes 2001:db8::1
    • Using :: twice is invalid, because the reader cannot tell how many zeros each one hides.
    • Best practice (RFC 5952): put :: on the longest run of zeros. On a tie, use the first run. Do not use :: for a single zero hextet. The course rule allows "one or more" hextets, so either answer can appear.
    • To expand, add leading zeros back to 4 digits per hextet, then fill :: with as many 0000 hextets as it takes to reach 8.

    Compression worked example:

    Full:             2001:0db8:00a0:0000:0000:0bcd:0000:0010
Rule 1:           2001:db8:a0:0:0:bcd:0:10
Rule 1 and 2:     2001:db8:a0::bcd:0:10

    The :: goes on the two zero hextets in a row. The single 0 later in the address stays as 0.

    #IPv6 address types

    IPv6 has three types: unicast, multicast and anycast (one address on several devices; traffic goes to the nearest). IPv6 has no broadcast.

    Starts with Type Notes
    2000::/3 (first hex digit 2 or 3) Global unicast address (GUA) Routable on the internet, like a public IPv4 address. 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation.
    FE80::/10 (FE80 to FEBF) Link-local address (LLA) Required on every IPv6 interface. Never routed off the link. Routers use it as the next hop and default gateway.
    FC00::/7 (FC00 to FDFF) Unique local address (ULA) Private addressing within a site. Not routed on the internet.
    FF00::/8 Multicast One to many
    ::1/128 Loopback Like 127.0.0.1
    ::/128 Unspecified Source address when a host has no address yet
    ::/0 Default route Not an address

    #Parts of a GUA

    Part Typical size Who sets it
    Global routing prefix /48 The ISP or RIR assigns it to the site
    Subnet ID 16 bits (bits 49-64) The site's administrator, one value per subnet
    Interface ID 64 bits The host (static, EUI-64 or random). Same job as the host portion in IPv4.

    A /64 interface ID is recommended because SLAAC needs it. The all-ones interface ID can be assigned in IPv6 because there is no broadcast address. The all-zeros interface ID is the Subnet-Router anycast address and should be given only to routers.

    #Static IPv6 configuration on a router

    Configure a GUA and a static link-local address on an interface:

    interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
no shutdown

    Let the router build the interface ID with EUI-64:

    ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::/64 eui-64

    Enable IPv6 routing so the router forwards IPv6, joins FF02::2 and sends RAs:

    ipv6 unicast-routing
    • Configuring any IPv6 address on an interface also gives it an LLA. ipv6 enable creates just the LLA.
    • A static LLA such as fe80::1 makes the default gateway easy to recognize. The same LLA can be reused on each router interface because it only has to be unique on its own link.
    • On a Windows host, set a static address in the adapter's Internet Protocol Version 6 (TCP/IPv6) properties.

    Verify:

    show ipv6 interface brief

    You should see:

    GigabitEthernet0/0/0   [up/up]
    FE80::1
    2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1
GigabitEthernet0/0/1   [administratively down/down]
    unassigned

    #Dynamic addressing with SLAAC and DHCPv6

    A host sends a Router Solicitation to FF02::2. The router answers with a Router Advertisement (RA) holding the prefix, prefix length and its own LLA as the default gateway. Flags in the RA tell the host how to finish.

    #RA flags and the three methods

    Method A flag O flag M flag Address from DNS and other info from
    1. SLAAC only (Cisco default) 1 0 0 Host builds it from the RA prefix The RA (DNS info if included)
    2. SLAAC with stateless DHCPv6 1 1 0 Host builds it from the RA prefix Stateless DHCPv6 server
    3. Stateful DHCPv6 0 0 1 Stateful DHCPv6 server, which tracks it Stateful DHCPv6 server
    • A = Address autoconfiguration (use SLAAC). O = Other configuration (ask DHCPv6 for other info). M = Managed address configuration (get the address from DHCPv6).
    • The default gateway always comes from the RA (the router's LLA). DHCPv6 does not hand out a default gateway.
    • "Stateless" means the DHCPv6 server does not keep track of addresses. "Stateful" means it does.

    Change the RA flags on a Cisco interface:

    Goal Interface command
    Method 2, set the O flag ipv6 nd other-config-flag
    Method 3, set the M flag ipv6 nd managed-config-flag
    Method 3, clear the A flag ipv6 nd prefix default no-autoconfig

    #Interface ID for SLAAC

    A SLAAC host makes its 64-bit interface ID one of two ways:

    • EUI-64, built from the 48-bit MAC address. Cisco routers use it for their automatic LLA.
    • Randomly generated. Windows does this by default, and also makes temporary addresses for privacy.

    After building the address, the host runs Duplicate Address Detection (an NS for its own address) before using it.

    #EUI-64 worked example

    MAC address 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E, prefix 2001:db8:acad:1::/64.

    1. Split the MAC into two 24-bit halves: 001A2B and 3C4D5E.
    2. Insert FFFE in the middle: 001A2B FFFE 3C4D5E.
    3. Flip the 7th bit (the U/L bit) of the first byte. 00 is 0000 0000, which becomes 0000 0010 = 02.
    4. The interface ID is 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E.
    5. Join it to the prefix: 2001:db8:acad:1:21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e. The LLA is fe80::21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e.
    First MAC byte Binary Flipped New byte
    00 0000 0000 0000 0010 02
    02 0000 0010 0000 0000 00
    C8 1100 1000 1100 1010 CA
    A4 1010 0100 1010 0110 A6

    Shortcut for the second hex digit of the first byte: 0 and 2 swap, 4 and 6 swap, 8 and A swap, C and E swap (and the odd ones: 1 and 3, 5 and 7, 9 and B, D and F).

    An interface ID with FF:FE in its middle (xxxx:xxFF:FExx:xxxx) was made with EUI-64.

    #IPv6 multicast addresses

    Address Group
    FF02::1 All-nodes. Every IPv6 device joins it. Works like a broadcast.
    FF02::2 All-routers. A router joins after ipv6 unicast-routing.
    FF02::5 and FF02::6 OSPFv3 routers and designated routers
    FF02::A EIGRP routers
    FF02::1:2 All DHCPv6 servers and relay agents
    FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx Solicited-node multicast. The last 24 bits match the last 24 bits of a unicast address. Used by Neighbor Discovery.

    The FF02 prefix means link-local scope (not forwarded by routers). FF05 is site scope and FF0E is global scope.

    Solicited-node worked example: unicast 2001:db8:acad:1:21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e ends in 3c:4d5e, so its solicited-node group is FF02::1:FF3C:4D5E.

    #Subnet an IPv6 network

    With a /48 global routing prefix and /64 subnets, the 16-bit subnet ID gives 2^16 = 65,536 subnets. Count up in hex in the fourth hextet. No binary borrowing is needed when you stay on a hextet boundary.

    Subnet Prefix
    0 2001:db8:acad::/64 (same as 2001:db8:acad:0::/64)
    1 2001:db8:acad:1::/64
    2 2001:db8:acad:2::/64
    10 (decimal) 2001:db8:acad:a::/64
    255 2001:db8:acad:ff::/64
    65,535 2001:db8:acad:ffff::/64

    Each /64 holds 2^64 interface IDs, about 18 quintillion.

    #IPv6 practice problems with answers

    #Compress

    Q: Compress 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

    2001:db8::1

    Q: Compress 2001:0db8:00a0:0000:0000:0bcd:0000:0010.

    2001:db8:a0::bcd:0:10. The :: replaces the run of two zero hextets. The lone zero later stays 0.

    Q: Compress fe80:0000:0000:0000:0212:00ff:fe34:5678.

    fe80::212:ff:fe34:5678

    Q: Compress 2001:0db8:0000:0001:0000:0000:0000:0000.

    2001:db8:0:1::. The longest zero run is at the end.

    Q: Compress ff02:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0002.

    ff02::2 (all-routers multicast).

    Q: Compress 2001:0db8:1000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000.

    2001:db8:1000::. The trailing zeros in 1000 stay.

    Q: Compress 2001:0db8:0000:0000:abcd:0000:0000:1234.

    2001:db8::abcd:0:0:1234. Two zero runs tie in length, so :: goes on the first one. 2001:db8:0:0:abcd::1234 is also a valid address, but RFC 5952 prefers the first run.

    #Expand

    Q: Expand 2001:db8::a:0:1 to the full preferred format.

    2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:000a:0000:0001. The :: stands for three zero hextets, because 5 hextets are written.

    Q: Expand fe80::1.

    fe80:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001

    Q: Expand 2001:db8:0:5::1:200.

    2001:0db8:0000:0005:0000:0000:0001:0200

    Q: Expand ff02::1:ff00:a.

    ff02:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001:ff00:000a

    #EUI-64

    Q: Build the EUI-64 GUA for MAC C8-0E-14-55-AA-01 with prefix 2001:db8:10:20::/64.

    Split C80E14 | 55AA01, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit of C8 (1100 1000 becomes 1100 1010 = CA). Interface ID CA0E:14FF:FE55:AA01. Address 2001:db8:10:20:ca0e:14ff:fe55:aa01.

    Q: Build the EUI-64 link-local address for MAC 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E.

    fe80::21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e

    Q: Build the EUI-64 GUA for MAC 02-00-5E-10-00-01 with prefix 2001:db8:1:1::/64.

    Flip 02 to 00. Interface ID 0000:5EFF:FE10:0001. Address 2001:db8:1:1:0:5eff:fe10:1.

    Q: Which MAC address produced the interface ID 0250:56ff:fec0:0008?

    Flip 02 back to 00 and remove FFFE: 00-50-56-C0-00-08.

    #Address types

    Q: Name the type of each address: fe80::a1, fd00:12:34::1, 2001:db8:5::9, ff02::1, ::1, ::

    Link-local unicast, unique local, global unicast (documentation range), all-nodes multicast, loopback, unspecified.

    Q: What is the solicited-node multicast address for 2001:db8:acad:1::10?

    FF02::1:FF00:10 (last 24 bits are 00:0010).

    Q: A company has 2001:db8:cafe::/48. What is the 12th /64 subnet if subnet 0 is 2001:db8:cafe::/64?

    The 12th subnet is subnet number 11, which is B in hex: 2001:db8:cafe:b::/64.

    PreviousModule 11 IPv4 addressing, subnetting and VLSMNextModule 13 ICMP, ping and traceroute
    NET

    Module 13 ICMP, ping and traceroute

    jump:net-m13-icmp

    Fast path: test connectivity in order

    1. Ping the loopback to test the host's own TCP/IP stack:

      ping 127.0.0.1

    2. Ping the default gateway to test the local network:

      ping <default-gateway>

    3. Ping a remote host to test the path through the router:

      ping <ip-address>

    4. If the remote ping fails, find the hop where it stops:

      tracert <ip-address>

    5. On Cisco IOS use ping and traceroute. Stop a running traceroute with Ctrl+Shift+6.

    #What ICMP does

    ICMP sends error and information messages about IP packet processing. It does not make IP reliable, and ICMP messages are often blocked by firewalls. ICMPv4 serves IPv4, ICMPv6 serves IPv6 and adds Neighbor Discovery.

    Messages common to ICMPv4 and ICMPv6:

    Message Meaning
    Host reachability (Echo Request and Echo Reply) Ping. Is the host up and reachable?
    Destination or service unreachable A router or host could not deliver the packet
    Time exceeded TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6) reached 0

    #ICMP type numbers

    Message ICMPv4 type ICMPv6 type
    Echo Reply 0 129
    Destination Unreachable 3 1
    Redirect 5 137
    Echo Request 8 128
    Time Exceeded 11 3
    Packet Too Big none (IPv4 uses "fragmentation needed", type 3 code 4) 2
    Router Solicitation / Advertisement 10 / 9 (ICMP router discovery, rarely used) 133 / 134
    Neighbor Solicitation / Advertisement none, IPv4 uses ARP 135 / 136

    #Destination unreachable codes

    Code ICMPv4 ICMPv6
    0 Net unreachable No route to destination
    1 Host unreachable Communication with the destination is administratively prohibited (for example a firewall)
    2 Protocol unreachable Beyond scope of the source address
    3 Port unreachable Address unreachable
    4 (Fragmentation needed) Port unreachable

    #ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages

    ICMPv6 adds four Neighbor Discovery messages plus Redirect. Full detail is in Module 9.

    Between Messages
    Router and device Router Solicitation (RS), Router Advertisement (RA)
    Device and device Neighbor Solicitation (NS), Neighbor Advertisement (NA)

    #Ping tests and what each one proves

    Ping target Success proves Failure points to
    127.0.0.1 or ::1 The TCP/IP stack on the host works. It does not test the NIC or cable. IP stack problem on the host
    Default gateway Host, NIC, cable and local LAN work, and the gateway router interface is up Wrong IP or mask, cable, switch port, gateway interface down
    Remote host The whole path works both ways Routing, remote host down, firewall, or the remote host's own gateway

    #Ping output to recognize

    Cisco IOS ping prints one character per echo request (5 by default, 100-byte packets, 2-second timeout):

    Symbol Meaning
    ! Echo Reply received
    . Timed out waiting for a reply
    U Destination Unreachable received
    Q Source quench (destination busy)
    M Could not fragment
    ? Unknown packet type
    & Packet lifetime exceeded

    Expected output on the first ping through a router:

    Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 192.168.20.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate is 80 percent (4/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/2 ms

    The first period is normal: the first echo timed out while the router resolved the next hop's MAC with ARP.

    Platform Default
    Windows 4 echo requests of 32 bytes. "Request timed out" or "Destination host unreachable" on failure.
    Linux Keeps sending until Ctrl+C (56 data bytes)
    Cisco IOS 5 echo requests of 100 bytes

    Type ping with no address in privileged EXEC to get the extended ping prompts (source interface, repeat count, size).

    #Traceroute

    Traceroute lists each router on the path and the round trip time (RTT) to each one.

    1. It sends packets with TTL 1. The first router drops them and returns ICMP Time Exceeded, which reveals that router.
    2. It repeats with TTL 2, 3 and so on until the destination answers.
    3. An asterisk (*) means no reply for that probe within the timeout. A row of asterisks shows where the path stops (or a router that does not send ICMP).
    Platform Command
    Windows tracert <ip-address> (uses ICMP echo)
    Linux, macOS traceroute <ip-address>
    Cisco IOS traceroute <ip-address>, stop it with Ctrl+Shift+6

    IPv6 traceroute works the same way with the Hop Limit field.

    Why ping alone is not proof of a broken host

    Windows Defender Firewall blocks inbound ICMP echo requests by default, and many routers rate-limit or drop ICMP. A failed ping with a working web page means ICMP is filtered, not that the host is down.

    PreviousModule 12 IPv6 addressing, compression, SLAAC, DHCPv6 and EUI-64NextModule 14 transport layer, TCP, UDP, ports and the three-way handshake
    NET

    Module 14 transport layer, TCP, UDP, ports and the three-way handshake

    jump:net-m14-transport

    Fast path: TCP or UDP and which port

    1. Port number question: look it up in the port table or Common ports.
    2. "Reliable", "acknowledgment", "sequence", "connection-oriented", "handshake", "flow control": TCP.
    3. "Low overhead", "fastest", "connectionless", "streaming voice or video", "DNS query", "DHCP", "TFTP": UDP.
    4. Handshake order: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Close: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK (details).
    5. Port range: 0-1023 well-known, 1024-49151 registered, 49152-65535 dynamic (private).

    #What the transport layer does

    Job How
    Track individual conversations Each application conversation is tracked separately
    Segment data and reassemble segments Breaks application data into sizes the lower layers can carry, puts them back together at the destination
    Add header information Port numbers, sequence numbers and more
    Identify the applications Port numbers say which application gets the data
    Conversation multiplexing Many conversations share the network by interleaving segments

    The transport layer has no idea about the destination host type, the media, or the path. It moves data between applications on the two hosts.

    #TCP and UDP compared

    TCP UDP
    Connection Connection-oriented: three-way handshake first Connectionless: just sends
    Reliability Acknowledgments, retransmits lost segments Best effort, no acknowledgments, lost data stays lost
    Order Sequence numbers put segments back in order Datagrams are processed in the order they arrive
    Flow control Yes, window size No
    State Stateful (tracks the session) Stateless
    Header 20 bytes minimum 8 bytes
    PDU name Segment Datagram
    Used by HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, SSH, Telnet DNS queries, DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, VoIP, IPTV, streaming video, online games

    The course lists TCP's features as: establishing a session, ensuring reliable delivery, providing same-order delivery, and supporting flow control.

    DNS uses UDP 53 for normal queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers and large replies.

    #TCP header fields

    Field Bits Purpose
    Source Port 16 Sending application's port
    Destination Port 16 Receiving application's port
    Sequence Number 32 Byte position of this segment's data, used for reassembly
    Acknowledgment Number 32 Next byte the receiver expects
    Header Length 4 Header size in 32-bit words (also called data offset)
    Reserved 6 Reserved for future use (course value)
    Control bits 6 Flags, see below
    Window Size 16 Bytes the receiver can accept right now
    Checksum 16 Error check of header and data
    Urgent 16 Points to urgent data when URG is set

    #TCP control bits (flags)

    Flag Meaning
    URG Urgent pointer field is significant
    ACK Acknowledgment field is significant. Set on every segment after the first SYN.
    PSH Push function, hand the data to the application right away
    RST Reset the connection after an error or timeout
    SYN Synchronize sequence numbers, used to open a connection
    FIN No more data from the sender, used to close a connection
    Six flags in the course, eight in RFC 9293

    The course shows 6 reserved bits and 6 control bits. Current TCP (RFC 9293) uses 4 reserved bits and 8 control bits, adding CWR and ECE for congestion notification. The experimental NS bit from RFC 3540 is now historic. Answer quiz questions with the course's six flags.

    #UDP header fields

    Field Bits
    Source Port 16
    Destination Port 16
    Length 16
    Checksum 16

    Four fields, 8 bytes total.

    #Port numbers

    Range Name Use
    0 to 1023 Well-known ports Common server services (HTTP 80, SSH 22)
    1024 to 49151 Registered ports Assigned by IANA to specific applications (for example RADIUS 1812)
    49152 to 65535 Private or dynamic ports (ephemeral) Chosen at random by the client OS as its source port

    A server listens on a fixed well-known or registered port. A client picks a random dynamic source port for each connection.

    #Port numbers to know

    The first 14 rows are the course table.

    Port Protocol Transport
    20 FTP data TCP
    21 FTP control TCP
    22 SSH TCP
    23 Telnet TCP
    25 SMTP TCP
    53 DNS UDP and TCP
    67 DHCPv4 server UDP
    68 DHCPv4 client UDP
    69 TFTP UDP
    80 HTTP TCP
    110 POP3 TCP
    143 IMAP TCP
    161 SNMP UDP
    443 HTTPS TCP
    123 NTP UDP
    445 SMB TCP
    546 and 547 DHCPv6 client and server UDP
    3389 RDP TCP

    More ports, including backdoor ports seen on images, are in Common ports.

    #Sockets and socket pairs

    • A socket is an IP address plus a port, written 192.168.1.7:80.
    • A socket pair (source socket plus destination socket) identifies one conversation. Example: client 192.168.1.5:49200 to server 192.168.1.7:80.
    • Two browser tabs to the same server use different client source ports, so each has its own socket pair.

    #netstat

    List active TCP connections with numeric addresses (no name lookups, which is faster):

    netstat -n

    You should see:

    Active Connections

  Proto  Local Address          Foreign Address        State
  TCP    192.168.10.20:49712    93.184.216.34:443      ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.10.20:49715    192.168.10.5:445       ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.10.20:49701    52.96.1.10:443         TIME_WAIT

    Add -a for listening ports and -o for the owning process ID (netstat -ano). Using netstat to hunt backdoors on an image is in Windows malware hunting.

    #TCP three-way handshake

    Step Sender Flags What it does
    1 Client SYN Asks for a session and sends its initial sequence number (ISN)
    2 Server SYN, ACK Acknowledges the client's ISN (ISN + 1) and sends its own ISN
    3 Client ACK Acknowledges the server's ISN. The session is open.

    The handshake checks the destination is present and accepting on that port, and tells it the client wants a session on that port.

    #Worked sequence and acknowledgment example

    Segment Seq Ack Notes
    Client SYN 100 none Client ISN = 100
    Server SYN-ACK 300 101 Server ISN = 300, expects client byte 101 next
    Client ACK 101 301 Handshake done
    Client sends 500 bytes 101 301 Bytes 101 to 600
    Server ACK 301 601 Next expected byte is 101 + 500 = 601

    The acknowledgment number is always the next byte expected, not the last byte received.

    #TCP session termination

    Step Sender Flag
    1 Client (no more data to send) FIN
    2 Server ACK
    3 Server (done sending too) FIN
    4 Client ACK

    Closing takes four segments because each direction is closed on its own. RST ends a connection at once without the exchange.

    #Reliability and retransmission

    • Sequence numbers let the receiver reorder segments and spot gaps.
    • The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects. If an acknowledgment does not arrive in time, the sender retransmits from that byte.
    • Selective Acknowledgment (SACK), negotiated in the handshake, allows the receiver to acknowledge segments that arrived out of order, so only the missing ones are resent.

    #Flow control and windowing

    Term Meaning
    Window size How many bytes the sender may send before it must wait for an acknowledgment. The receiver sets it in each segment. The starting value is agreed during the handshake.
    Sliding window As acknowledgments arrive, the window slides forward so the sender keeps sending without stopping after every segment
    Window size 0 Receiver is full, the sender pauses
    MSS (maximum segment size) Largest data payload in one segment. Typically 1,460 bytes on IPv4 Ethernet: 1,500 MTU - 20 IP header - 20 TCP header.
    Congestion avoidance When acknowledgments are late or missing, the sender reduces how much it sends before waiting for an acknowledgment

    Worked example: window size 10,000 bytes and MSS 1,000 bytes. The sender can send 10 full segments, then must wait for an acknowledgment. If the receiver lowers the window to 5,000, only 5 segments can be outstanding.

    The window size field is 16 bits, so the largest value without the window scale option is 65,535 bytes.

    Why UDP is fine for voice and video

    A late voice or video packet is useless, so retransmitting it would only add delay. Applications that need speed over completeness accept a small loss. The application itself can add any reliability it needs, as TFTP does with its own acknowledgments.

    PreviousModule 13 ICMP, ping and tracerouteNextModule 15 application, presentation and session layers
    NET

    Module 15 application, presentation and session layers

    jump:net-m15-application

    Fast path: match a protocol to its job

    1. Find the job word in the question: "send email", "retrieve email", "name to IP", "automatic addressing", "file transfer", "web page", "Windows file sharing".
    2. Look up the protocol and port in the protocol table.
    3. For email, sending is SMTP. Retrieving is POP3 (download, deleted from the server) or IMAP (copies stay on the server).
    4. For DNS record questions, use the record type table.

    #The upper three OSI layers

    OSI layer Job Examples
    7 Application Interface between the applications people use and the network HTTP, DNS, DHCP, SMTP, FTP
    6 Presentation Formats data for the destination, compresses it, encrypts it JPEG, GIF, PNG, MPEG, QuickTime, ASCII
    5 Session Creates and maintains dialogs between source and destination, restarts sessions that were interrupted or idle

    The TCP/IP model folds all three into its Application layer.

    #Client-server and peer-to-peer

    Model How it works
    Client-server A client requests, a dedicated server responds. Data flows up (upload) and down (download).
    Peer-to-peer network Two or more hosts share resources with no dedicated server. Each acts as client and server.
    Peer-to-peer application Each device runs the app as both client and server, sometimes with a central index. Examples: BitTorrent, Direct Connect, eDonkey, Freenet.

    The Gnutella protocol allows users to share whole files with other users. P2P networks are hard to secure and do not scale well because there is no central administration.

    #Application protocols by job

    Job Protocol Port and transport
    Web pages HTTP TCP 80
    Secure web pages HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) TCP 443
    Send email (client to server, server to server) SMTP TCP 25
    Retrieve email, download and delete from server POP3 TCP 110
    Retrieve email, keep copies on the server and sync folders IMAP TCP 143
    Resolve names to IP addresses DNS UDP 53 (TCP 53 for large replies and zone transfers)
    Automatic IPv4 addressing DHCPv4 UDP 67 server, 68 client
    Automatic IPv6 addressing and options DHCPv6 UDP 547 server, 546 client
    File transfer FTP TCP 21 control, TCP 20 data
    Simple file transfer with no login (used for IOS images and configs) TFTP UDP 69
    Windows file and printer sharing SMB TCP 445
    Remote CLI, encrypted SSH TCP 22
    Remote CLI, plaintext Telnet TCP 23

    #HTTP and HTTPS

    URL parts, using http://www.example.com/index.html:

    Part Value
    Protocol or scheme http
    Server name www.example.com (resolved to an IP by DNS)
    Requested file index.html
    HTTP method Use
    GET Client asks for data (a web page)
    POST Client sends data to the server (a filled-in form)
    PUT Client uploads a resource or file to the server

    HTTP sends everything in plaintext. HTTPS adds encryption and authentication with TLS (formerly SSL) and uses port 443.

    #Email protocols

    Protocol Direction Behavior
    SMTP Sending: client to server and server to server Pushes mail. If the destination server is down, the sending server queues and retries.
    POP3 Retrieving: server to client Downloads mail. By default deletes it from the server, so it lives on one device.
    IMAP Retrieving: server to client Downloads copies and keeps the originals on the server, so several devices stay in sync

    #DNS

    DNS turns names like www.example.com into IP addresses. The client sends a query to its configured DNS server on port 53. If that server does not have the answer cached, it asks other servers.

    Hierarchy, from the top:

    Level Examples
    Root servers The "." at the top
    Top-level domains .com (business), .org (nonprofit), .net, .edu, country codes such as .au and .jp
    Second-level domains example.com, cisco.com
    Hosts and subdomains www.example.com, mail.example.com

    #DNS record types

    Record Holds
    A IPv4 address of a host
    AAAA IPv6 address of a host
    NS Authoritative name server for the domain
    MX Mail exchange server for the domain
    CNAME Alias that points to another name
    PTR Reverse lookup, IP address to name
    SOA Start of authority, the zone's main settings

    The course lists A, NS, AAAA and MX. CNAME, PTR and SOA are common extras.

    #nslookup

    Look up a name and see which DNS server answered:

    nslookup www.example.com

    You should see:

    Server:  dns.example.net
Address:  192.168.10.2

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    www.example.com
Address:  93.184.216.34

    "Non-authoritative answer" means the server answered from its cache, not as the owner of the zone. On Windows, ipconfig /displaydns shows the local DNS cache and ipconfig /flushdns clears it.

    #DHCP

    DHCPv4 leases an IP address, mask, default gateway and DNS server to a client for a set time. The four-message exchange is DORA:

    Step Message Sender Sent as
    1 DHCPDISCOVER Client Broadcast (the client has no address yet)
    2 DHCPOFFER Server Usually unicast to the client's MAC
    3 DHCPREQUEST Client Broadcast, so every server learns which offer was accepted
    4 DHCPACK Server Unicast, confirms the lease
    • Before the lease ends, the client renews it by sending a DHCPREQUEST straight to the server.
    • A server that cannot honor the request sends DHCPNAK.
    • Static addresses suit servers and printers. DHCP suits end-user devices.
    • DHCPv6 uses SOLICIT, ADVERTISE, INFORMATION REQUEST and REPLY (plus REQUEST for stateful). How SLAAC and DHCPv6 work together is in Module 12.

    #FTP and TFTP

    • FTP opens two TCP connections: control (commands and replies) on port 21 and data on port 20.
    • FTP sends credentials in plaintext. SFTP (over SSH) and FTPS (over TLS) encrypt.
    • TFTP uses UDP 69, has no login and no directory listing, and is used to copy IOS images and configuration files.

    #SMB

    SMB is a client-server, request-response protocol for sharing files, printers and serial ports. It does three things:

    1. Starts, authenticates and ends sessions.
    2. Controls access to files and printers.
    3. Allows an application to send and receive messages to and from another device.

    SMB keeps a long-term connection to the server, where FTP opens a new data connection for each transfer. Linux and macOS share with Windows through Samba. Windows paths to a share look like \\<hostname>\<share-name>. Hardening SMB shares on images is in File shares and permissions.

    PreviousModule 14 transport layer, TCP, UDP, ports and the three-way handshakeNextModule 16 network security fundamentals and device hardening
    NET

    Module 16 network security fundamentals and device hardening

    jump:net-m16-security

    Fast path: secure a Cisco device with SSH

    1. In global configuration mode, set the name, domain and a local user:

      hostname <hostname>
ip domain-name <domain-name>
username <username> secret <team-password>

    2. Generate the RSA keys (the course example uses 1024 bits; 2048 is stronger):

      crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 1024
ip ssh version 2

    3. Allow only SSH on the vty lines and check the local user list:

      line vty 0 4
transport input ssh
login local
exec-timeout 5 30
exit

    4. Add password protections:

      service password-encryption
security passwords min-length 8
login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60

    5. Verify with show ip ssh and save with copy running-config startup-config.

    #Types of threats

    Threat Example
    Information theft Stealing a company's research data
    Data loss and manipulation Destroying or changing records
    Identity theft Using stolen personal data to get credit or documents
    Disruption of service Stopping legitimate users from reaching a service (DoS)

    #Types of vulnerabilities

    Vulnerability Examples
    Technological Weaknesses in the TCP/IP protocols (HTTP, FTP, ICMP are not secure), in operating systems, and in network equipment
    Configuration Unsecured user accounts, system accounts with easily guessed passwords, misconfigured internet services, unsecured default settings, misconfigured network equipment
    Security policy No written policy, politics, no continuity, logical access controls not applied, changes that do not follow policy, no disaster recovery plan

    #Physical security threats

    Category Examples
    Hardware Physical damage to servers, routers, switches, cabling, workstations
    Environmental Temperature extremes (too hot or too cold) or humidity extremes
    Electrical Voltage spikes, brownouts (low voltage), unconditioned power (noise), total power loss
    Maintenance Poor handling of components (ESD), no spare parts, poor cabling, poor labeling

    #Malware

    Type How it spreads
    Virus Attaches to a program or file and needs a person to run it
    Worm Runs by itself and copies itself across the network by exploiting vulnerabilities. Needs no human action.
    Trojan horse Looks like a legitimate or useful program, but does harm once run

    Patching all vulnerable systems is the main defense against worms.

    #Network attacks

    Category Attacks What the attacker does
    Reconnaissance Internet queries (whois, DNS lookups), ping sweeps, port scans Maps the network: which IPs are live, which ports and services are open
    Access Password attacks (brute force, dictionary), trust exploitation, port redirection, man-in-the-middle Gets in, takes over accounts or data
    Denial of service DoS, DDoS Overwhelms a device with traffic or sends malformed packets so legitimate users cannot connect
    Access attack Meaning
    Password attack Guessing or cracking passwords
    Trust exploitation Uses a compromised trusted host to reach other systems that trust it
    Port redirection Uses a compromised host as a relay to pass traffic through a firewall to another target
    Man-in-the-middle Sits between two parties to read or change their traffic (ARP spoofing is one way)

    A DDoS comes from many compromised hosts at once (zombies in a botnet), which makes it hard to block by source address.

    #Mitigation and defense in depth

    Defense in depth uses several layers so one failure does not open the network. The course's devices:

    Device Job
    VPN-capable router Encrypted remote access and site-to-site tunnels
    ASA firewall Stateful filtering between inside and outside
    IPS Detects and blocks attack traffic in real time
    ESA and WSA Email Security Appliance filters spam and malicious mail. Web Security Appliance filters web threats and URLs.
    AAA server Central authentication, authorization and accounting

    Backup considerations: frequency, storage (offsite and rotated), security (passwords on backups), and validation (test restores).

    Keep operating systems and software upgraded, updated and patched. Automate patching where possible.

    #AAA

    A Question it answers Credit card analogy from the course
    Authentication Who are you? (username and password, token) Who may use the card
    Authorization What are you allowed to do? How much may be spent
    Accounting What did you do and when? The statement of what was spent

    Central AAA servers use RADIUS or TACACS+.

    #Firewalls and endpoint security

    Firewall type Filters by
    Packet filtering IP addresses and port numbers (Layers 3 and 4)
    Application filtering Applications, by port number
    URL filtering URLs or keywords in web addresses
    Stateful packet inspection (SPI) Allows inbound packets only when they answer a request from inside

    Endpoint security protects the hosts themselves: antivirus and antimalware, host firewall, host-based intrusion prevention, and keeping software patched. The image-hardening sections (Windows firewall, Defender, Linux firewall) are the endpoint side of this module.

    #Strong password guidelines

    From the course:

    • Use at least 8 characters, preferably 10 or more.
    • Mix uppercase, lowercase, numbers, symbols and spaces.
    • Avoid repetition, common dictionary words, letter or number sequences, usernames, relatives' or pets' names, and personal details.
    • Misspell words on purpose.
    • Change passwords often.
    • Do not write passwords down where others can find them.

    Passphrases (a sentence of several words) are easier to remember and harder to crack than short complex passwords.

    #Device hardening commands

    Command Mode Effect
    enable secret <team-password> Global Hashed privileged EXEC password (use instead of enable password)
    service password-encryption Global Encrypts plaintext passwords in the config (weak type 7, stops shoulder surfing)
    security passwords min-length 8 Global Rejects new passwords shorter than 8 characters
    login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60 Global After 3 failed logins within 60 seconds, block logins for 120 seconds
    exec-timeout 5 30 Line (console, vty) Logs out an idle session after 5 minutes 30 seconds
    transport input ssh Line vty Allows SSH only, no Telnet
    login local Line Checks the local username database
    auto secure Privileged EXEC Cisco AutoSecure: a guided script that applies many hardening settings at once

    The full Packet Tracer hardening list is in Cisco device hardening checklist.

    #Enable SSH on a Cisco device

    The course's six steps, in order:

    1. Configure a unique hostname (not the default Router or Switch).
    2. Configure the IP domain name with ip domain-name.
    3. Generate RSA keys with crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus <bits>.
    4. Create a local user with username <username> secret <team-password>.
    5. Authenticate vty logins against the local database with login local.
    6. Allow SSH on the vty lines with transport input ssh.

    Key generation fails with a message about the hostname or domain name if step 1 or 2 is missing. SSH version 2 needs a key of at least 768 bits.

    Verify:

    show ip ssh

    You should see:

    SSH Enabled - version 2.0
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

    #Disable unused services

    List open ports on a router (newer IOS):

    show ip ports all

    Older IOS versions use show control-plane host open-ports. Turn off the HTTP management server if it is not needed:

    no ip http server

    Disabling CDP (no cdp run) stops the device from advertising its model and IOS version to neighbors. Only do it if no task needs CDP.

    Why type 7 encryption is weak

    service password-encryption uses a reversible Cisco type 7 scheme that free tools decode in seconds. It only hides passwords from someone glancing at the screen. enable secret and username ... secret store a one-way hash (type 5 MD5 on older IOS, type 8 or 9 on newer), which is why the course prefers them.

    NET

    Module 17 build and troubleshoot a small network

    jump:net-m17-small-network

    Fast path: troubleshoot a host that cannot connect

    1. On the host, check the address, mask, gateway and DNS server:

      ipconfig /all

    2. A 169.254.x.x address means DHCP failed: check the cable, the switch port and the DHCP server, then run ipconfig /renew.

    3. Ping the default gateway, then a remote IP (test order).
    4. Remote IP works but names do not: DNS problem. Test with nslookup <hostname>.
    5. On the router or switch, run show ip interface brief and look for anything not up/up.

    #Design a small network

    Factors for choosing devices:

    Factor Question to ask
    Cost Capacity and features against budget, including cabling and redundancy
    Speed and types of ports and interfaces Enough ports, fast enough, the right media
    Expandability Fixed configuration or modular, room to add ports or modules
    Operating system features and services Security, QoS, VoIP, NAT, DHCP support

    Other design points from the course:

    • Plan the IP addressing scheme: which devices get static addresses (servers, printers, network devices) and which use DHCP.
    • Add redundancy to remove single points of failure: duplicate devices, links and power.
    • Use QoS to prioritize traffic: voice and video first, then business data, then everything else.
    • Document the physical and logical topology as the network grows.

    #Applications and protocols in a small network

    Term Meaning
    Network-aware applications Programs that talk to the network directly (web browser, email client)
    Application layer services Programs that work with the network to prepare data (file transfer, print spooling)

    Common protocols in a small network: DNS, Telnet or SSH, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP, DHCP, HTTP and HTTPS, FTP.

    Voice and video need:

    Need Notes
    Infrastructure Must support real-time traffic, with QoS
    VoIP Voice over IP, using existing analog phones with a gateway
    IP telephony IP phones that do the call processing themselves, with a call controller
    Real-time applications Use RTP and RTCP to deliver audio and video with low delay

    #Scale a small network

    To grow, a network needs documentation (physical and logical topology), a device inventory, a budget, and traffic analysis.

    • Capture traffic with a protocol analyzer such as Wireshark at peak times and on different segments, because traffic varies by time and place.
    • Track employee network use: OS and versions, non-network applications, network applications, CPU and memory use, drive use.
    • A network baseline records normal performance (for example ping response times over time) so you can spot changes later.

    #Host commands to know

    Command Platform Shows or does
    ipconfig Windows IP address, mask, default gateway
    ipconfig /all Windows Also MAC address, DHCP server, lease times, DNS servers
    ipconfig /release and ipconfig /renew Windows Drop and request a DHCP lease
    ipconfig /displaydns Windows Cached DNS entries
    ip address Linux Interfaces with IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (ifconfig on older systems)
    ifconfig macOS Interfaces and addresses
    arp -a Windows, Linux, macOS ARP table

    #IOS show commands and what they reveal

    Command Use it to find
    show running-config Current configuration in RAM
    show interfaces Interface status, errors, counters
    show ip interface IPv4 settings per interface
    show ip interface brief One-line summary of every interface
    show arp or show ip arp ARP table
    show ip route Routing table
    show protocols Configured protocols and interface status
    show version IOS version, bootstrap version, uptime, last restart reason, image file, model and CPU, RAM, NVRAM and flash sizes, interfaces, configuration register
    show cdp neighbors Directly connected Cisco devices: device ID, local interface, holdtime, capability, platform, port ID
    show cdp neighbors detail Also the neighbor's IP address and IOS version

    Part of show version output:

    Cisco IOS XE Software, Version 16.09.04
ROM: IOS-XE ROMMON
R1 uptime is 2 hours, 15 minutes
System returned to ROM by reload
System image file is "bootflash:isr4300-universalk9.16.09.04.SPA.bin"
cisco ISR4321/K9 (1RU) processor with 1647778K/6147K bytes of memory.
Configuration register is 0x2102

    Configuration register 0x2102 is the normal boot setting. 0x2142 makes the router skip the startup configuration (password recovery).

    Part of show cdp neighbors output:

    Device ID        Local Intrfce     Holdtme    Capability  Platform    Port ID
S1               Gig 0/0/1         148            S I     2960        Fas 0/5
R2               Ser 0/1/0         163           R B      ISR4300     Ser 0/1/1

    #Troubleshooting process

    Step Action
    1 Identify the problem
    2 Establish a theory of probable causes
    3 Test the theory to determine the cause
    4 Establish a plan of action and implement the solution
    5 Verify the solution and implement preventive measures
    6 Document findings, actions and outcomes

    If the problem is beyond your authority or skill, escalate it to someone who can fix it, and document that too.

    #Troubleshooting approaches

    Approach How it works Use when
    Bottom-up Start at the physical layer and go up The problem looks physical (cables, links)
    Top-down Start at the application layer and go down The problem looks like one application
    Divide-and-conquer Start in the middle (often Layer 3 with ping), then go up or down depending on the result You do not know which layer failed, a good default
    Follow-the-path Trace the traffic path from source to destination Finding which device on the path fails
    Substitution Swap a suspected bad part for a known good one Hardware suspected
    Comparison Compare the broken setup with a working one A similar working device exists
    Educated guess Guess from experience Experienced staff, but least structured

    #debug and log messages

    • debug <feature> shows events live (for example debug ip icmp). It uses CPU, so turn it off when done with undebug all (same as no debug all).
    • Log and debug output shows on the console by default. On an SSH or Telnet session, run terminal monitor to see it, and terminal no monitor to stop.
    Level Name Level Name
    0 Emergency 4 Warning
    1 Alert 5 Notification
    2 Critical 6 Informational
    3 Error 7 Debugging

    A lower number means a more severe message. Setting a logging level shows that level and everything more severe.

    #Common problems and how to spot them

    Symptom Likely cause Check
    Slow link, late collisions on one side Duplex mismatch (one side full, the other half) show interfaces on both ends, set both to the same duplex
    CRC errors, input errors Bad cable, EMI, or duplex mismatch Replace the cable, check show interfaces counters
    Runts (under 64 bytes) or giants (over 1518 bytes) Collisions, bad NIC, or MTU mismatch show interfaces
    Host has 169.254.x.x DHCP server unreachable Cable, switch port, DHCP server, ipconfig /renew
    Host reaches the LAN but nothing remote Default gateway missing or wrong ipconfig, compare with the router's LAN interface IP
    Ping by IP works, by name fails DNS server wrong or down ipconfig /all, nslookup
    Interface administratively down shutdown applied no shutdown
    Two hosts with the same IP Static address conflict Windows shows an address conflict warning, check arp -a

    show interfaces counters to recognize:

    Counter Meaning
    Input errors Total of all input errors, including runts, giants, CRC and frame errors
    CRC Checksum failures, usually cable or electrical noise
    Runts Frames smaller than 64 bytes
    Giants Frames larger than the maximum
    Output errors Frames that could not be sent
    Collisions Normal in small numbers on half-duplex links
    Late collisions Collision after 512 bits were sent: duplex mismatch or a cable that is too long
    Why a duplex mismatch causes late collisions

    The full-duplex side sends whenever it wants. The half-duplex side thinks it owns the wire once it has sent the first 64 bytes, so traffic from the other side that arrives after that point is counted as a late collision. The link works, but slowly, which makes it easy to miss.
